This outcome in measured in two ways via a survey: as an unconditional decision and as a decision that can be contingent on the number of similar coworkers who also create an AI coworker. The conditional decisions will allow us to disentangle strategic complementarities. We may also be able to obtain a measure of intensity of interest based on whether employees who sign up go on to complete the intake form required to initiate the AI coworker creation process, as well as the time and effort they spend on that form.

secondary_outcome_explanation: Career concerns can lead workers to invest less in their AI Coworker and also lead employees to limit access to their AI Coworker when given the option. Our incentives tied to AI Coworker performance can counteract these career concerns and lead to greater knowledge sharing.
secondary_outcomes: At the end of the survey, we ask employees questions about the oversight and control they would want to have in place for their AI Coworker, including who would ideally have access. Along the process to creating an AI Coworker, employees invest time in training and supplying data the AI Coworker knowledge. Training and data supply will provide corroborating measures of our primary endpoints.

abstract: The Strengthening Preschoolers' Academic and Relational Skills (SPARK) study evaluates a comprehensive preschool intervention designed to improve both the academic and social-emotional skills of preschool children in Haiti. The intervention consolidates foundational literacy and numeracy (FLN) approaches with established social-emotional learning (SEL) programming through the Jaden Kajou Pre-K Level 3 curriculum. The trial will be conducted in approximately 50 Model School Network Catholic preschools in the Central Plateau department of Haiti. Schools will be randomly assigned in a 1:1 ratio to either the SPARK intervention or a business-as-usual comparison condition. Treatment schools will receive the Jaden Kajou curriculum package, teacher training, instructional materials, and ongoing coaching support; comparison schools will continue their usual preschool practices during the study period. Primary child outcomes are emergent literacy, emergent numeracy, and social-emotional development, measured using the International Development and Early Learning Assessment (IDELA) at baseline and endline. Secondary outcomes include teacher-reported instructional practices, occupational well-being, job satisfaction and stress, and assessor-reported children' s executive-functioning.
experimental_design: The study is a parallel cluster randomized controlled trial. 50 eligible Model School Network (MSN) schools in the Central Plateau department of Haiti will participate. Schools will be randomly assigned in a 1:1 ratio to either the SPARK intervention arm or the comparison arm. The unit of random assignment is the school. The primary unit of outcome measurement is the individual Pre-K Level 3 child. Baseline data will be collected before intervention delivery begins. Treatment schools will then implement the Jaden Kajou intervention, including classroom instruction, teacher training, materials, and coaching support. Comparison schools will continue business-as-usual preschool practices during the study period. Endline data will be collected from the same cohort of children and teachers assessed at baseline, to the extent possible.
intervention: Jaden Kajou is a school-based, comprehensive early childhood education intervention designed to improve foundational literacy and numeracy and social-emotional learning outcomes among Pre-K Level 3 children. The intervention consists of integrated classroom instructional activities, teacher training, instructional materials, and ongoing coaching support. The SPARK program uses the Jaden Kajou curriculum, a Pre-K Level 3 integrated curriculum in which Social-Emotional Learning (SEL) is woven throughout the full school day rather than taught as a standalone subject. SEL defines daily school and classroom routines, informs teacher-student and peer interactions, shapes classroom management, and is integrated into curriculum content and instruction, including literacy, math, reading, and science. The Jaden Kajou school day is organized into clear, predictable blocks, including welcoming and flag ceremony, Sek matine / Morning Meeting, Apesi jounen an / Morning Circle, daily read aloud, literacy, numeracy, Discover the World (science), closing circle, and dismissal routines. Read aloud activities use interactive storytelling to support letter knowledge, oral language, comprehension, SEL integration, and love of stories. Literacy activities use a multisensory, phonics-based and scaffolded station format, moving from exposure to kinesthetic engagement and fine-motor production. Numeracy activities move children beyond rote counting toward conceptual fluency across subitizing, counting, operations, measurement and data, and geometry. Discover the World uses the child's daily life as a setting for scientific observation and social responsibility. Treatment schools will receive core curriculum materials, including a Teacher Guide, Student Workbook, Facilitator Training Guide, classroom books and other instructional materials. Approximately 25 treatment-school teachers will participate in in-person training before implementation, including two five-day training sessions and a two-day booster session. Teacher training covers the Jaden Kajou curriculum and SEL integration approach, the new school day structure, routines and transitions, read aloud, literacy, numeracy, Discover the World, classroom management and positive discipline, use of teacher guides and student workbooks, and the coaching relationship. Five SPARK coaches will provide ongoing support to Pre-K Level 3 teachers across the 25 treatment schools. The coaching model includes weekly school visits, monthly cohort professional development meetings, and open communication through WhatsApp groups, phone calls, and unscheduled visits when urgent. School visits include classroom observation, structured feedback and debriefing, and data collection using KoboCollect-based tools. Coaching is intended to support continued improvement in teacher instruction and performance, strengthen school climate and non-violent conflict resolution, and generate field evidence for ongoing professional development and implementation improvement.

abstract: Many secondary students in developing countries cannot read fluently enough to learn from written text. This study evaluates whether an artificial intelligence reading tutor improves oral reading fluency and reading comprehension among struggling readers in public secondary schools in Barranquilla, Colombia. We randomly assigned 31 classes serving 845 students in 11 schools to a structured remedial reading program (Avanza+), or to the same program with its oral reading routines completed on Microsoft Reading Coach, which scores speed and accuracy through speech recognition and generates individualized practice on the words each student misses. Because both groups receive identical curriculum and instructional time, the design identifies the marginal contribution of automated, individualized feedback the alternative for education systems considering AI tutors as a complement to structured remediation.
experimental_design: The experimental sample includes 845 students in 31 instructional groups across 11 public schools in Barranquilla. The unit of randomization is the instructional group. Randomization was blocked by school: within each school, half of the groups were randomly assigned to treatment, and in schools with an odd number of groups a fair coin determined the extra assignment.
intervention: All students in the study receive Avanza+, a structured remediation program developed by the World Bank for secondary students who can decode but have not automatized reading. The program includes 48 one-hour sessions, delivered three times per week over approximately 16 weeks. Sessions are grouped into eight units and combine explicit instruction in phonological awareness, spelling, morphology, and vocabulary with repeated oral reading routines and formative assessments. Treatment classes implement the identical curriculum with one difference: the oral reading routines, consisting of three timed readings per unit and the end-of-unit fluency check, are completed on Microsoft Reading Coach using tablets/computers. In each exercise, the student reads aloud for one minute; the platform scores speed and accuracy through speech recognition, returns immediate feedback, and generates individualized practice on the words the student misread. Control classes complete the same routines on paper, working in pairs: one student reads aloud while the other times the reading and provides feedback, with occasional support from the teacher. The treatment effect therefore captures the marginal value of automated, individualized feedback relative to peer feedback, holding curriculum and instructional time constant.

abstract: Health workers face elevated rates of anxiety, burnout, and low emotional wellbeing, yet few seek support, and specialized mental health services in El Salvador are scarce. This study evaluates strategies to increase voluntary demand for a free emotional accompaniment service, which consists of up to four brief individual psychoeducation sessions on stress, anxiety, trauma, and grief, delivered by trained lay counselors through calls or messages. The study population is public hospital workers in El Salvador who have previously completed general trauma-informed care training between 2022 and 2025. Respondents (N = 1,057) will be individually randomized, with equal allocation across three arms. All arms offer the same underlying service and differ only in the outreach they receive: a control group receives general information about the service and may contact it on their own initiative, while the two treatment arms vary the informational content of the outreach and who initiates the first contact. The primary outcome is demand for the accompaniment service, measured from program administrative records as take-up of at least one session and the number of sessions used. Secondary outcomes are mental health and wellbeing indicators (GAD-7, WHO-5, PHQ-2, sleep-related impairment, and burnout, among others) measured in a follow-up survey six months after the intervention. All effects are estimated by intention to treat.
experimental_design: The study is an individual-level randomized controlled trial with three arms of equal size: a control group and two treatment groups that vary the outreach participants receive. Eligible participants completed the baseline survey, consented to the experimental phase, still work in a public hospital, and had not previously received follow-up activities delivered by the NGO. The 1,057 eligible participants were assigned to arms within eight blocks defined by sex crossed with age band (29 and under, 30 to 39, 40 to 49, 50 and over), with equal 1:1:1 allocation within blocks. Outcomes are measured in program administrative records and in an endline survey six months after the intervention.
intervention: The intervention consists of follow-up outreach to public hospital workers who have previously completed general trauma-informed care training. All study participants are offered the same underlying service: up to four individual wellbeing sessions of 10 to 15 minutes with a trained lay counselor, covering psychoeducation on stress, anxiety, trauma, and grief, together with practical emotion regulation exercises. Sessions are delivered by WhatsApp call or WhatsApp message, and each participant chooses the format at the start (calls or messages). Participation is voluntary at every step. The study arms differ only in the outreach participants receive, specifically in the informational content of the initial invitation message and in who initiates the first contact. The purpose is to identify which outreach strategies reduce the barriers to taking the first step toward using emotional support services.

Effects are estimated by intention to treat. As a complementary descriptive analysis, indicators will be compared by the delivery format each participant chose (calls versus WhatsApp messages). Because format is chosen rather than randomized, this comparison is exploratory and descriptive only.

abstract: This study tests whether offering and disclosing a loyalty bonus for immediate payment at the point of sale affects consumers' payment choices and purchasing behavior. It constitutes the second phase of a two-phase randomized field experiment; the first phase is registered under AEARCTR-0018591. In the treatment condition, sales staff inform each customer, before the payment decision is finalized, that paying the full purchase amount immediately — rather than using an installment or buy-now-pay-later (BNPL) plan — entitles the customer to a 15% loyalty bonus credited to a loyalty account. The listed price is identical across payment methods, so the incentive operates solely through the bonus. In the control condition, stores follow the standard price presentation and sales process, and no bonus is offered or disclosed. The primary outcome is the share of purchases paid in full immediately rather than through installment/BNPL plans. Secondary outcomes include total sales, average transaction value, conversion, product mix, and returns where available. Phase 2 will be conducted over four weeks, from July 27, 2026 to August 23, 2026, in the same three comparable retail stores as Phase 1. In each store, full business days are randomly assigned to the treatment or control condition, stratified by day of the week.
experimental_design: Overview This study is a randomized controlled field experiment evaluating whether a loyalty bonus for immediate payment, disclosed at the point of sale, affects customer payment choice and purchasing behavior in a retail setting. It is the second phase of the experiment registered under AEARCTR-0018591 and is conducted over four weeks in the same three retail stores. Control Condition In the control store and control time blocks, standard pricing communication remains in place, and no payment-method-contingent loyalty bonus is offered or disclosed. Baseline Period Data collected before the start of Phase 2, prior to July 20, 2026 - including data from Phase 1 (AEARCTR-0018591) - are used to assess baseline comparability across stores and to support the difference-in-differences analysis. Unit of Analysis The unit of analysis is the individual transaction. External Validity The study is conducted in a small number of comparable retail stores within one geographic area. Given the limited sample of stores and the specific retail context, external validity will be interpreted cautiously. The main objective of this phase is to obtain internally valid evidence on whether a loyalty bonus for immediate payment affects payment choice and purchasing behavior in the participating stores. The study will be conducted in the same three retail stores as Phase 1. The primary unit of observation is the individual transaction, and the realized number of transaction-level observations will be reported after data collection for the July 20 - August 20, 2026 study period.
experimental_design_details: Within-Store Day-Level Randomization All three stores follow the same within-store design. In each store, every business day of the four-week study period is randomly assigned to either the treatment condition, in which the loyalty bonus is offered and disclosed, or the control condition, in which standard operations continue unchanged. Assignment is made at the level of the full business day, so each store alternates between treatment and control days according to its randomized schedule and serves as its own control. Stratification and Balance The randomization is stratified by day of the week within each store: every weekday appears in the treatment condition in exactly two of the four study weeks and in the control condition in the other two. As a result, each store contributes 14 treatment days and 14 control days, and treatment and control conditions are equally represented across all days of the week, including weekends. The complete schedule consists of 84 store-days, split evenly between the two conditions. It was generated with a fixed random seed before the start of the intervention and remains unchanged throughout the study. Control Condition On control days, standard pricing communication remains in place, and no payment-method-contingent loyalty bonus is offered or disclosed. Baseline Period Data collected before July 27, 2026 — including data from Phase 1 (AEARCTR-0018591) — are used to assess baseline comparability across stores and to support supplementary analyses. Unit of Randomization Store-day (full business day within a store). Unit of Analysis The unit of analysis is the individual transaction, with standard errors clustered at the store-day level. External Validity The study is conducted in a small number of comparable retail stores within one geographic area. Given the limited sample of stores and the specific retail context, external validity will be interpreted cautiously. The main objective of this phase is to obtain internally valid evidence on whether a loyalty bonus for immediate payment affects payment choice and purchasing behavior in the participating stores. The study will be conducted in the same three retail stores as Phase 1. The primary unit of observation is the individual transaction, and the realized number of transaction-level observations will be reported after data collection for the four-week study period. Sample size: planned number of clusters 84 store-day clusters (3 stores × 28 business days), randomly assigned within stores with stratification by day of the week: 42 treatment days and 42 control days, 14 of each per store. Sample size: planned number of observations Approximately 1,200 completed transaction-level observations over the four-week study period, based on realized volumes in Phase 1; the final number will depend on realized sales. Sample size (or number of clusters) by treatment arms 42 treatment store-days and 42 control store-days across 3 retail stores; approximately 600 transactions per arm, subject to realized sales.
intervention: The intervention consists of a standardized verbal disclosure at the point of sale. On treatment days, sales staff are trained to inform each customer, before the payment method is finalized, that immediate full payment — by cash or by card without an installment plan — entitles the customer to a 15% loyalty bonus, whereas installment/BNPL payment does not. The listed price does not depend on the payment method; only the loyalty bonus is conditional on it. Staff are instructed to state the bonus terms neutrally and not to recommend either payment option.

primary_outcome_explanation: The primary outcome is the proportion of completed transactions in which the customer pays the full purchase amount immediately rather than choosing an installment/BNPL plan. Immediate payment covers cash, card, and any other non-installment payment method; installment/BNPL payment covers BNPL products and equivalent installment-based options offered at the point of sale. Construction The outcome is constructed from transaction-level sales data. The following variables are recorded for each completed transaction: Transaction ID: unique identifier of the purchase Payment method: immediate payment vs. installment/BNPL payment Store ID Date: linking each transaction to its assigned experimental condition Treatment/control status: assigned at the store-day level Loyalty bonus indicator: whether the bonus was applied, where available Product category and transaction value, where available At the transaction level, the outcome is defined as Immediate = 1 if the transaction is paid in full immediately, and Immediate = 0 if it is paid via an installment/BNPL plan. The immediate-payment share is the number of immediate-payment transactions divided by the total number of completed transactions, and can be computed by day, store, or experimental condition. Interpretation A statistically significant increase in the immediate-payment share on treatment days relative to control days would be interpreted as evidence that a loyalty bonus for immediate payment shifts consumers' payment choices away from installment/BNPL plans.

abstract: This study investigates how overconfidence and underconfidence about own ability shape inferences about the economic environment when outcomes depend on both ability and the environment. We focus on a setting where individuals can switch between environments. We test the hypothesis that overconfident individuals are more likely than underconfident individuals to select environments they perceive as more ability-contingent, and that this selection generates asymmetric belief correction (i.e., overconfident participants correct their biases more than underconfident participants do).
experimental_design: Participants complete a two-stage online experiment. In Stage 1, they take a 12-question logic quiz of randomly assigned difficulty and report an incentivized belief about how their performance on six shared questions compares to a reference pool of 100 earlier participants. In Stage 2, over two rounds, one of two managers generates 50 paid tokens per round. One manager pays a green token when the participant beats a randomly drawn member of the reference pool; the other pays green at a fixed rate that is disclosed to participants as a numerical probability. By design this rate equals the participant's own performance rate, so the two managers produce statistically identical token streams. After each round, participants report incentivized beliefs about their own performance and about which manager they face. A manager is randomly assigned before round 1. After round 1, all participants state whether they want to stay or switch; for half, randomly assigned, this choice is implemented (active-choice treatment), and for the other half the round-2 manager is randomly assigned (control). Further details are provided in the pre-analysis plan.

abstract: This study asks whether taking part in resolving other people's disputes changes how individuals behave in their own economic dealings. A classic idea, dating to Tocqueville's account of the American jury, holds that serving as a lay adjudicator acts as a "school of citizenship" that builds trust and respect for shared rules, while a competing view holds that an inside look at how rules and evidence are weighed instead teaches people how to work the system to their own advantage. The question has been hard to answer because real-world participation in judicial decision-making is rare and seldom random. We study it on the community adjudication feature of a large online secondhand marketplace, where ordinary users are invited to help decide disputes. In a randomized controlled trial, we invite a randomly selected group of users who have never served to participate, and compare their subsequent platform behavior with that of a control group.
experimental_design: We conduct an individually randomized controlled trial on the peer dispute resolution feature of a large online secondhand marketplace, where ordinary users can be invited to help decide disputes between buyers and sellers. From a pool of recently active eligible users who have never previously served as adjudicators, we randomly assign users to a treatment group and a control group at a 1:1 ratio. Treatment users receive an invitation, delivered through the platform's standard notification system, encouraging them to serve as an adjudicator. Control users receive no such invitation during the study period. Take up is voluntary, so the invitation functions as an encouragement rather than compelled participation. After the intervention, we track and compare the two groups' subsequent behavior on the platform, focusing on their conduct as buyers and sellers, their behavior in disputes, and their broader engagement with the platform community. The design allows us to estimate the causal effect of the invitation to serve, and, using the random invitation as an instrument for actual participation, the causal effect of adjudication itself on subsequent economic behavior.
experimental_design_details: The experiment is conducted in collaboration with Xianyu, China's largest online secondhand marketplace, on its peer adjudication feature, the "Small Court" (Xiaofating), where ordinary users review real transaction disputes and cast votes that contribute to a collective verdict. The study tests a long standing but empirically unresolved question in political economy: whether participation in adjudication cultivates civic capital, such as trust and respect for shared rules, or instead transmits strategic legal know how that participants later use for private gain. Sampling and randomization. The eligible pool consists of recently active users who have never previously served as adjudicators. Eligibility requires, among other criteria, at least one completed transaction in the past month and an enabled notification setting so that the invitation can be delivered. In addition, the platform excludes, before randomization, a set of users it designates as sensitive, according to internal criteria not disclosed to the research team, in order to manage complaint and regulatory risk. All eligibility restrictions, including this exclusion, are applied identically to the entire pool before random assignment, so that the treatment and control groups are drawn from the same restricted population and remain comparable. From this pool, we randomize at the individual level using a random number generated in SQL over the stored user records. The treatment group consists of approximately 900,000 users, and a control group of comparable size is drawn from the remaining eligible users at a 1:1 ratio, for a planned total on the order of 1.8 million users. Intervention. Treatment users receive a push invitation, through the platform's standard notification channel, encouraging them to serve in the Small Court. Control users receive no invitation during the study window. Compliance and estimands. Take up is voluntary and low. Among invited users, roughly 3 percent open the invitation and about one third of those accept, so the invitation induces about 1 percentage point of additional participation. In addition, about 1 percent of users in both arms participate spontaneously without any invitation (always takers). Expected participation is therefore about 2 percent in the treatment arm and about 1 percent in the control arm, giving a first stage of about 1 percentage point. We report the intention to treat effect of being invited to serve, and we use the random invitation as an instrument for actual participation to recover the local average treatment effect for compliers, that is, users induced to serve by the invitation, excluding always takers who would participate regardless of assignment. Outcomes. Following the intervention, we compare the treatment and control groups on four families of behavioral outcomes: trading conduct as a seller, including committed service terms such as return and shipping policies and the handling of buyers' refund requests; refund behavior as a buyer, including return and refund and refund only requests; formal dispute behavior, including whether the user brings a dispute into the peer adjudication process as a party; and pro social behavior, including whether the user donates a share of sales proceeds to charitable causes. We also examine secondary outcomes capturing the scale of trading activity, engagement intensity, and the realized resolution of disputes. Timing. We observe outcomes over a post treatment window and, where feasible, at multiple horizons, allowing us to trace the time path of any effects and to distinguish effects that appear immediately from those that emerge as users encounter later transactions and disputes. Comparing short and longer horizons also helps distinguish civic capital formation, which may build gradually and persist, from strategic learning, which may take effect quickly. External validity. Because the sample is restricted to recently active users with notifications enabled and excludes the platform's designated sensitive users, the estimated effects apply to this population and need not generalize to less active users, users who have disabled notifications, or the excluded group.
intervention: Among eligible users of an online secondhand marketplace who have never served as community adjudicators, we randomly select a treatment group to receive an invitation to participate in the platform's peer dispute-resolution feature. The invitation is delivered through the platform's normal notification system. Users in the treatment group are free to accept or decline; the remaining eligible users form the control group and receive no such invitation during the study period. The intervention therefore assigns the opportunity and encouragement to serve as an adjudicator.

abstract: This study evaluates the effectiveness of savings lotteries in increasing retirement savings among informal workers in Colombia. Participants were randomly assigned to receive lottery offers tied to savings deposits, including small cash prizes, large housing prizes, both types of prizes, or no lottery offers. Using administrative data from the public pension system, the study examines the effects of these lottery incentives on savings behavior, the timing of deposits, eligibility for complementary program benefits such as life and disability insurance, and the persistence of any behavioral changes after the intervention.
experimental_design: The study is a nationwide natural field experiment conducted among account holders in Colombia’s BEPS voluntary retirement-savings program. Individual accounts were randomly assigned to receive standard savings reminders or reminders advertising one of three lottery-incentive arrangements: cash prizes, housing prizes, or both cash and housing prizes. Lottery eligibility was tied to reaching specified savings thresholds over either two-week or six-month qualification periods. Administrative account records are used to measure deposits, total savings, the timing and frequency of transactions, and eligibility for associated social-insurance benefits.
experimental_design_details: The experimental sample consisted of 387,449 BEPS account holders registered by the end of 2018. Accounts were assigned in approximately equal proportions to Control, House, House-and-Cash, and Cash arms. Beginning on April 11, 2019, all four arms received text-message reminders on the same biweekly schedule. Control messages encouraged retirement saving without mentioning prizes. Treatment messages described the savings thresholds and prizes corresponding to the assigned lottery arm. The Cash intervention comprised 18 two-week qualification periods. Account holders received one ticket for every COP 55,000 deposited within a qualification period. Each drawing offered 200 prizes of COP 100,000. The House intervention comprised two six-month qualification periods. Account holders received one ticket for every COP 500,000 accumulated during the relevant period. Each drawing offered one housing voucher worth up to COP 102,000,000. The House-and-Cash arm combined both incentive structures. There was no cap on the number of tickets an account holder could earn. A randomly selected subset of the Cash and House-and-Cash arms received messages only during the first three months of the intervention, while the remaining accounts received messages through the end of 2019. The main analysis of the separate lottery treatments focuses on the full-dose groups where relevant.
intervention: The intervention used text messages to inform account holders in Colombia’s voluntary public retirement-savings program, Beneficios Económicos Periódicos (BEPS), about savings lotteries. Depending on treatment assignment, account holders were offered opportunities to win small cash prizes, a housing prize, or both, conditional on reaching specified savings thresholds. The control group received standard savings reminders without information about lottery prizes.

abstract: This study tests whether an affordable, scalable mental health program can reduce psychological barriers to work in a socially stratified labor market. I conduct a two-arm randomized controlled trial among working-age adults in India with moderate to severe depression. Participants in the treatment group receive a guided self-help program adapted from the World Health Organization's Step-by-Step protocol, delivered through a chatbot with weekly support calls from trained guides. The control group receives care-as-usual. Randomization is stratified by gender, baseline income, and baseline mental health. Outcomes are measured at 3-, 6-, and 12-month follow-ups and cover mental health, economic, and social outcomes, as well as the mechanisms linking mental health to economic participation. Treatment-effect heterogeneity by gender, baseline economic status, and social class is pre-specified.
experimental_design: Two-arm, individual-level randomized controlled trial. Eligible participants (working-age adults screening positive for moderate to severe depression) are randomly assigned to the guided self-help program or to a care-as-usual control. Randomization is stratified by gender, baseline income, and baseline mental health. Outcomes are measured through follow-up surveys at 3, 6, and 12 months.

abstract: We study how an intervention that teaches and encourages Instagram users to curate their own feed affects their content consumption, well-being, political attitudes, and gender norms. The study is a two-wave, individually randomized controlled trial with active Instagram users aged 18 to 35 from the United States (US). In the baseline wave, participants complete a survey and share data on their Instagram content; a randomly assigned treatment group is then shown how to use two built-in curation tools. Roughly six weeks later, an endline wave re-measures the same outcomes, measures further outcomes, and collects the same data on consumed content. We estimate intention-to-treat effects with baseline covariate adjustments and local average treatment effects using random assignment as an instrument for compliance.
experimental_design: Participants are US residents aged 18 to 35 who are active Instagram users, recruited via Prolific and Cloud Research in the US. Participants provide informed consent before any data are collected. We have access to basic demographics (e.g., age, gender, partisanship). After answering a short battery of baseline questions and sharing data on their Instagram use, participants are randomized into either the treatment or the control group using the platforms' built-in randomizers. The treatment group receives information on different tools to curate their feed, and is encouraged to use these tools. The control group receives no such information. Outcome measures and data on Instagram usage is collected in a second wave approximately six weeks after the baseline. Assignment is at the individual level, stratified (blocked) by the interaction of gender and partisanship, all measured at baseline prior to randomization.
experimental_design_details: Population and recruitment Participants are US residents aged 18 to 35 who are active Instagram users, recruited via Prolific and Cloud Research in the US. Eligibility requires using Instagram at least once a day (screening item). Participants provide informed consent before any data are collected. We have access to basic demographics (e.g., age, gender, partisanship). The study has two waves, approximately six weeks apart. - Wave 1 (baseline): Consent; screening; short baseline outcome batteries; Instagram export and upload; the randomized treatment. - Wave 2 (endline). The same outcome batteries as baseline (enabling baseline-adjusted estimation), endline-only outcome batteries, a second Instagram export and upload, and endline-only blocks measuring knowledge of curation tools, reported use of those tools, and perceived usefulness. Treatment The treatment follows an encouragement design. Treated participants are shown how Instagram's built-in tools let them shape their feed, and are encouraged to complete two concrete tasks during the baseline wave: (i) unfollowing accounts they are no longer interested in, and (ii) resetting their algorithm. The control group receives no such information and proceeds directly through the survey. Both arms answer the same outcome questions at both waves. The treatment delivers both tools together; we therefore estimate the effect of the combined intervention rather than separating the two tools. These two tools are paired because Meta presents them as strongly synergistic. Randomization Assignment is at the individual level, stratified (blocked) by the interaction of gender and partisanship, all measured at baseline prior to randomization. Within each stratum, participants are assigned to the treatment or control group with equal probability by the survey platforms' randomizer. Sample size Recruitment targets a range of 1,000 to 5,000 participants, with the final total determined by the budget.

abstract: Addiction remains a significant global public health challenge, highlighting an urgent need for more advanced behavioral and biological methodologies to accurately assess addiction severity and evaluate the effectiveness of rehabilitation interventions. Despite rigorous anti-drug regulations in China, which currently has more than one million officially registered people with substance use disorder (PwSUD), there remain substantial opportunities for improvement in treatment and preventive strategies. This methodological gap underscores the necessity of developing innovative behavioral strategies and predictive models that can enhance recovery and prevent relapse in substance abuse treatment. This research uniquely contributes by integrating behavioral economics techniques into addiction studies, applying experimental methods grounded in economic rationality by employing classical techniques, to measure the severity of GARP (Generalized Axiom of Revealed Preferenc) violations via metrics such as the Critical Cost Efficiency Index (CCEI). These methods provide precise quantitative measures of rationality and decision-making consistency, delivering insights for policymakers and treatment practitioners.
experimental_design: Subjects will be presented with a sequence of independent 25 decision problems under risk, 25 social choice decision problems, and 25 intertemporal decision problems on paper. Each decision problem will be presented as a choice from a 2 dimensional budget line. A choice of the allocation from the budget line represents an allocation of points between accounts A (x-axis) and B (y-axis). For each of the decision problems, subjects will choose their allocation with a cross on the budget line, as well as write the amount they want to allocate to the account A to ensure accuracy. Each graph clearly will be labeled and have gridlines. The maximum allocations to the A/B accounts are also shown for clarity. For risky choice, the payoffs of a particular choice are determined by the chosen allocation representing the tradeoff between the A and B accounts. Subjects receive the points allocated to one of the accounts, A or B, determined at random with equal chance (i.e. one arrow security for each account). For each of the A and B accounts, there is a natural price tradeoff between the two, which is determined by the slope i.e. the relative price. For social choice, the payoffs are similarly determined by a combination of A and B accounts. In each round, subjects allocate money to themselves (A) and their randomly matched and anonymous partner (B). Similarly, the slope refers to the tradeoff between money allocated to themselves and money allocated to their partner. The allocation that is implemented is determined by equal chance. For intertemporal choice, the payoffs are also determined by a combination of A and B accounts. In each round, subjects allocate money to today (A) and an amount of money one month later (B). Similarly, the slope refers to the tradeoff between money today and money one month later.

abstract: We study whether telling loan applicants what other borrowers ask for changes how much they themselves request. Does it matter whether the information is about male peers, female peers, or borrowers in general? And do men and women react differently? We work with a microfinance institution in Kenya, and the study is embedded in the institution's routine loan-application phone call. Applicants are randomly assigned to hear the average requested amount of a random sample of similar past borrowers (same area and age bracket): either male applicants, female applicants, or applicants in general. A control group receives no information.
experimental_design: We study whether telling loan applicants what other borrowers ask for changes how much they themselves request and whether the behavior varies by applicant gender. Applicants are randomized into four groups: information about male peers similar to the participant, about female peers similar to the participant, about peers similar to the participant (gender neutral), or no information. The information given to the participants in the treatment arms is an average from random draws from real past applications (a sample of 5 or 20 applications, randomized, and the participants are aware of how many peers they are getting the information from). This extra variation helps us examine mechanisms. The three treatment arms vary two things at once: the amount shown and who the information was about. Using this extra variation in the amount we can hold the information the clients were provided with fixed and test whether it is the amount or who the information is about that matters for behavior. We will also test what kind of rule borrowers follow: for example, do they only react when the number is above their own planned request? Differences between male and female applicants are of primary interest throughout. Details During the call, applicants first state how much they want to borrow. They are then asked what they think similar borrowers typically ask for. Applicants in the treatment groups then hear the average requested amount of a sample of comparable past applicants (male, female, or general, depending on the group); the control group hears nothing. Treated applicants are asked again about their beliefs about what other borrowers typically ask for. They are also asked some additional questions such as how common is taking a loan in their area and whether they know any other people who have borrowed from the same company. At the end, all applicants are asked whether they want to keep or change their requested amount, and it is made clear that keeping the original amount is fine. Approval and default rates are taken from the institution's records. Our main comparisons will be: 1) Does providing gendered information (about female or male peers) have differential effects compared to providing gender-neutral information. Do these effects vary by respondent gender? The no-information group will serve as a benchmark for secondary analyses. 2) Is it the amount shown or the group it describes? The three treatment arms vary both at once: the amount and who the information is about. Because the amounts are random draws from real past applications, we can hold the amount fixed and isolate the effect of who the information describes: other men, other women, or peers in general. 3) Test whether people mainly change the requested amount when the information provided exceeds their own planned amount and whether that trigger differs by treatment group.

abstract: How well do people anticipate the effects of social observation on their own behavior? We test this in an online real-effort experiment in which participants complete four within-subject 5-minute rounds whose output funds a charitable donation. The rounds vary along two dimensions: (i) whether the participant's effort is observed live by another person via video, and (ii) whether the participant receives a personal piece-rate bonus on top of the donation. Each participant is assigned to one of eight counterbalanced orders that nest the observability manipulation (Anonymous vs. Video) either in the first or second half of the experiment and the piece-rate manipulation (standard vs. higher rate) in the other half. Before any round begins, we elicit participants' predictions of their own effort under each of the four conditions.
experimental_design: The trial is an online within-subject behavioral experiment. Each participant completes a structured pre-survey, then four 5-minute real-effort rounds in one of eight counterbalanced orders, then a post-survey.
experimental_design_details: The four rounds vary in two binary dimensions: (i) observability, with two levels — Anonymous (effort is private) vs. Video (effort is observed live via webcam by a spectator); and (ii) monetary incentive, with three levels across rounds — no personal bonus, a standard piece-rate, and a higher piece-rate. Two of the four rounds have no personal bonus (one Anonymous, one Video); two have a personal bonus and are not observed (LowPaid, HighPaid). Effort in every round produces a donation to the American Red Cross at the same fixed donation rate. One of the four rounds is randomly selected at the end of the session, with equal probability, to determine the realized donation and, where applicable, the personal bonus. Experimental Design Details Pre-survey: For a sub-sample of individuals, we incentivize the prediction of own effort in each of the four conditions (the four predictions, one per condition, are incentivized via a randomly selected bonus, paid for one of the four predictions if the prediction is within a fixed tolerance (+/- 50 points) of the round selected for payment). Effort task: A real-effort A/B key-press task: the participant alternates pressing the "a" and "b" keys; each completed alternation registers as one task unit. Each round lasts up to 5 minutes; the participant may end a round early. Output is converted into a donation to the American Red Cross at $0.02 per 10 completed task units. The four conditions: Anonymous (A): Effort is private. Output produces a donation only. Video (V): Effort is live-streamed via webcam to a spectator, who watches for the duration of the round. Output produces a donation only — no personal bonus. LowPaid (L): Effort is private. Output produces a donation and an additional personal piece-rate (a per-task-unit personal bonus). HighPaid (H): Effort is private. Output produces a donation and an additional higher personal piece-rate. Order structure: Each participant is assigned to one of eight counterbalanced orders. We have two blocks: the anonymous + video block and a block with the two piece-rate incentives. We vary the block order and the condition orders within each block. Order is fixed at the session level: each session runs a single order. Across sessions, the eight orders are scheduled in equal proportion. Participants do not see the order assignment or learn that orders vary across sessions. Each individual will go through the conditions in the same order for the beliefs and the behavior part. Spectators (Video round): In the Video round, a spectator watches the participant via live webcam for the full 5 minutes. Payment: Participants receive a fixed Prolific show-up fee plus the realized payoff from the randomly selected round (donation always; personal bonus only if the selected round is LowPaid or HighPaid) plus the realized belief-bonus draw (if any).
intervention: Each participant completes four within-subject five-minute real-effort rounds. The rounds vary in (i) whether effort is observed live by another person via video and (ii) whether the participant receives a personal piece-rate bonus in addition to a fixed-rate donation to charity. Effort produces a donation to the American Red Cross at a rate of $0.02 per 10 completed task units; in the two "paid" rounds the participant additionally earns a personal bonus at a piece-rate that varies between the two paid rounds. Before any round begins, an incentivized belief elicitation asks each participant to predict their own effort in each of the four conditions.

abstract: Gender-marked language may influence attitudes, preferences, and behavior, with tangible economic consequences. In Italian, professional titles carry grammatical gender (e.g., avvocato/avvocata for lawyers), yet the feminine form remains rarely used, especially in stereotypically male professions. A pilot survey experiment conducted by the research team in 2022 found that, all else equal, female lawyers presented with the feminine title were less likely to be contacted — a penalty equivalent to roughly 10 years less experience (Burlacu et al., 2024). This study extends that design to a representative sample of the Italian adult population (N = 3,200) and to four professions that differ in gender stereotypicality, in the prevalence of women in the profession, and in the prevalence of feminine-title use (law, engineering, architecture, medicine). Through a survey experiment combining between-subject randomization of title gender-marking with within-subject variation in the mixed-title arm, we investigate: (i) the causal impact of the gender marking of professional titles on stated preferences; (ii) the mechanisms underlying the observed effects, drawing on perceived descriptive and injunctive norms about title use, first- and second-order beliefs, conformity thresholds, and individual attitudes toward gender roles and gender-inclusive language; and (iii) the prevalence of sensitive beliefs about feminine professional titles — their appropriateness, their potential to penalize women in certain professions, and their perceived ideological connotation — elicited through a list experiment.
experimental_design: The study is an online survey experiment on a representative sample of Italian adults (SWG CAWI panel; completion time approximately 15 minutes), comprising two blocks. In Block A, respondents complete 4 rounds of profile evaluation, one per profession (law, engineering, architecture, medicine); for each profession, one service-need scenario is drawn at random from three candidates. In each round they view 4 hypothetical professional profiles (2 male, 2 female) and rate each profile on the likelihood of contacting them on a 0–10 scale. Profiles display the professional title with first and last name, year of birth, year of professional-register enrollment, and two quality signals. The gender marking of professional titles is randomized between subjects: throughout the 4 rounds, some respondents see female profiles titled exclusively with the masculine form, others exclusively with the feminine form, and others encounter both forms (one female profile with each form in every round); male profiles are always presented with the masculine form. In Block B, respondents complete attitudinal and belief-elicitation sections: gender-typing of professions and sports (with randomized label formats), a list experiment on attitudes toward feminine professional titles, first- and second-order belief elicitation, direct attitude questions, a conformity-threshold scenario with randomized conditions, and validated attitudinal scales (POLID, Ulrich et al., 2021; Modern Sexism, Swim et al., 1995; ATGIL, Schwarz et al., 2026). Section order is fixed and designed to limit priming; item and response-option orders are randomized. All randomizations are assigned at the individual level, independently of one another.
experimental_design_details: Block A — Vignette rating experiment (within-survey RCT) Respondents complete 4 rounds, one for each profession. For each profession, one hypothetical service-need scenario is randomly drawn (uniformly) from three candidates: Law (Avvocato/Avvocata): an online fraud (criminal law), a condominium dispute over water damage (civil law), or an inheritance division (family law). Engineering (Ingegnere/Ingegnera): an energy-performance certification and efficiency consultation (energy), a suspected soil contamination on an owned plot (environmental), or suspicious cracks on a load-bearing wall (structural). Architecture (Architetto/Architetta): a full interior-design project for a new apartment (interior design), a building-compliance/amnesty and re-registration procedure ahead of a sale (building and planning), or the design of a new single-family house on a buildable plot (architectural design). Medicine (Dottore/Dottoressa): an orthopedic, dermatological, or gastroenterological consultation. In each round, respondents view 4 professional profiles (2 male, 2 female, in randomized on-screen order) and rate each profile on the likelihood of contacting them on an integer scale from 0 (“not at all”) to 10 (“for sure”). No forced choice between profiles is elicited: the rating is the only outcome collected in each round (the design was simplified relative to an earlier paired/forced-choice version). Each profile is described by the professional title followed by first and last name, the year of birth, the year of enrollment in the professional register, and two binary quality signals. First and last names are sampled with replacement from lists of common Italian first names and surnames. Each profile’s year of birth is drawn uniformly from 1966–1994, and the year of enrollment in the professional register equals the birth year plus a uniform draw between 25 and 29; the implied professional experience (computed with reference year 2026) therefore ranges from roughly 3 to 35 years. Each profile carries two quality signals. Signal 1 — membership in an associated firm (studio associato) for law, engineering, and architecture, or affiliation with the scenario-relevant scientific society for medicine (SIOT for orthopedics, SIDeMaST for dermatology, SIGE for gastroenterology) — is assigned Yes/No with probability 0.5, independently of all other attributes. Signal 2 is a senior credential — Cassazionista for law, structural-testing certification (abilitazione al collaudo statico) for engineering and architecture, and a university position for medicine — whose probability depends on experience: it is 0 for profiles with fewer than 12 years of experience, 0.30 for profiles with 12–24 years, and 0.65 for profiles with 25 or more years (probabilities calibrated on data from the lawyers’ professional register). The senior credential is therefore correlated with, but not collinear with, experience (except that it is deterministically absent below 12 years). Primary treatment — Gender marking of professional titles (between-subject) The primary treatment manipulates the gender marking of the professional titles displayed in the vignette profiles. Each respondent is randomly assigned to one treatment arm at the start of the survey, and the assignment remains constant across all 4 rounds. Male profiles always carry the masculine title; the treatment varies how female profiles are titled: T1 (probability 0.30): all female profiles are presented with the masculine form of the title (e.g., Avvocato). T2 (probability 0.30): all female profiles are presented with the feminine form (e.g., Avvocata). T3 (probability 0.40): mixed condition — in every round, exactly one of the two female profiles uses the feminine form and one the masculine form (the split is enforced within each round rather than drawn binomially). This condition allows a within-respondent, within-round comparison of feminine- and masculine-titled female profiles. The four professions and the corresponding masculine/feminine title forms are: law (Avvocato/Avvocata), engineering (Ingegnere/Ingegnera), architecture (Architetto/Architetta), and medicine (Dottore/Dottoressa). Block B — Attitudinal and belief-elicitation sections Before Block A, respondents report employment status and, depending on status, their current/last/intended profession and relevant region. After the vignette block, the following sections are administered in a fixed order designed to limit priming (belief elicitation about the vignette professions follows the list experiment but precedes the direct questions on feminine titles): Gender-typing. For each of 24 items (20 professions — 11 STEM, 9 non-STEM — and 4 sports), respondents indicate whether it suits a man, a woman, or both. - List experiment. Respondents see a list of labor-market statements and report only how many they agree with; treated arms include one additional sensitive statement (details below). - First-order beliefs. For each vignette profession, respondents estimate how many out of 100 practitioners in Italy are women, and how many out of 100 women practitioners use the feminine rather than the masculine title. - Direct questions. Binary (agree/disagree) versions of the sensitive statements, each shown to all respondents except those whose list contained it. - Second-order beliefs. Told that a representative sample of over 3,000 people in Italy is participating, respondents estimate how many out of 100 men, and out of 100 women, consider it more appropriate for a woman to use the feminine title — nationally and in the respondent's region (phrased according to employment status). - Conformity threshold. Respondents advise a fictional female character ("Anna"), newly graduated and entering a profession, whether to use the masculine form, the feminine form, or either, under five prevalence levels of title use among women in her profession. - Validated scales: political-cultural orientation (POLID; 8 items, conservatism/liberalism subscales; 4-point; Ulrich et al., 2021), Modern Sexism (8 items; 7-point; Swim et al., 1995), and attitudes toward gender-inclusive language (ATGIL; 7 items; 5-point; Schwarz et al., 2026), item order randomized within scale. Secondary randomized conditions In addition to the primary title treatment, the survey embeds several secondary randomized conditions, all assigned at the individual level, independently of the title treatment (T1–T3) and of each other. Label-format condition (gender-typing section). The labels of the 24 gender-typing items are randomized across three label conditions (1/3 each): masculine form only (e.g., Avvocato), double form (e.g., Avvocato/Avvocata), or field name (e.g., Avvocatura). Items whose Italian label has common gender nouns (e.g., farmacista, giornalista, ciclista, analista dati, assistente sociale) are identical in the first two conditions. This condition tests whether the gender marking of occupational labels itself affects the extent to which professions are gender-typed. List-experiment arms. Respondents are randomly assigned to one of four arms: a control arm receiving only the five baseline statements about the labor market, and three treated arms each receiving one additional sensitive statement. The sensitive statements are: List arm 2 (“appropriateness”): “It would be more appropriate for a woman to use the feminine form of her professional title (e.g., avvocata, ingegnera).” List arm 3 (“harm”): “In some professions, the use of the feminine form of the professional title (e.g., avvocata, ingegnera) risks penalizing the women who work in that profession, including those who do not use it.” List arm 4 (“signaling”): “A woman who uses the feminine form of her professional title (e.g., avvocata, ingegnera) conveys an image of herself closer to feminist positions.” Respondents report only how many statements they agree with (0–N), preserving individual anonymity on the sensitive item. Direct-question counterparts (binary agree/disagree, identical wording to the list items) are administered after the belief-elicitation section. Each direct item is shown to all respondents except those assigned to the list arm containing that same statement, so that no respondent directly evaluates a statement already seen in their own list: the direct “appropriateness” item is shown to list arms {1, 3, 4}; the direct “harm” item to arms {1, 2, 4}; the direct “signaling” item to arms {1, 2, 3}. Control-arm respondents therefore answer all three direct items and treated-arm respondents answer two; the order of the direct items is randomized at the respondent level. The second-order belief questions refer to the “appropriateness” statement only and are accordingly shown only to list arms {1, 3, 4}. Conformity-threshold scenario conditions. Two conditions are cross-randomized with probability 1/2 each: (i) the stated share of women in the fictional character’s profession (25% vs 50%); and (ii) the anchoring of the prevalence information, i.e., whether the five threshold rows describe the share of women in the profession using the feminine form or the share using the masculine form (complementary framings of the same objective distributions: fewer than 1 in 10, about 3 in 10, about 5 in 10, about 7 in 10, more than 9 in 10). For each row, respondents recommend the masculine form, the feminine form, or indicate that either is fine; the order of the response columns is randomized. Presentation-order randomizations. Presentation orders are randomized throughout to average out order effects: the order of the four professions in the vignette block, the on-screen order of the four profiles within each round, the scenario drawn for each profession (one of three, uniformly), the order of statements within the list experiment, the order of the direct questions on feminine titles, the order of items and response columns in the attitudinal sections, and the order of the belief-elicitation items.
intervention: The study examines how the gender marking of Italian professional titles (e.g., avvocato/avvocata for lawyer) affects people’s stated preferences when choosing a professional to contact, across four professions (law, engineering, architecture, medicine). Respondents are randomly assigned to conditions that vary whether the female professional profiles they evaluate are presented with the masculine or the feminine form of the title. The survey also investigates the social norms, beliefs, and attitudes associated with the use of feminine professional titles in Italian, embedding several secondary randomized components (a label-format experiment, a list experiment, and a conformity-threshold scenario).

primary_outcome_explanation: We expect negative effects of the feminine title, on average, in all professions except medicine, where the feminine title (Dottoressa) is prevalent and may be perceived as the social norm; medicine therefore serves as a “placebo” profession. Extending Burlacu et al. (2024), we estimate at the profile-rating level (16 observations per respondent, standard errors clustered at the respondent level): Rating = a0·Female + a1·T2 + a2·T3 + b1·Female×T2 + b2·Female×T3 + c1·Female×T3×FemTitle + d1·Age + d2·Experience + d3·QualitySignal1 + d4·QualitySignal2 + Scenario FE + Profile-order FE + Profession(round)-order FE + respondent characteristics + e where Rating is the 0–10 contact-likelihood rating assigned to each profile; Female indicates a female profile; T1 (omitted category) is the arm in which all female profiles carry the masculine title, T2 the arm in which all carry the feminine title, and T3 the mixed arm; FemTitle indicates that the displayed title is the feminine form (non-zero only for female profiles in T3, and 1 for female profiles in T2 — hence the triple interaction is identified only within T3). Age, experience, and the two quality signals are the randomized profile characteristics. a0 estimates the profile gender gap in ratings in T1; a1 and a2 estimate differences in male-profile ratings in T2 and T3 relative to T1; b1 replicates the feminine-title effect in Burlacu et al. (2024), comparing female profiles with the feminine title (T2) to female profiles with the masculine title (T1); b2 indicates whether the mere presence of feminine-titled profiles in the choice set affects female profiles carrying the masculine title (T3 masculine-titled women vs T1 women). The concern raised in the public discourse is that use of the feminine form affects all women in the profession, not only those who use it: if confirmed, b2 should be negative, with c1 negative as well only if there is an additional penalty on the specific profiles displaying the feminine title. The functional form yields two hypothesis tests: H0: c1 = b1. This compares the marginal feminine-title gradient in a mixed environment (T3, within-round contrast between the feminine- and masculine-titled female profile) with the gradient in a uniform environment (T2 vs T1): is the title gradient steeper when an individual evaluates profiles using both forms H0: b2 + c1 = b1. Are feminine-titled women in the mixed arm (T3) rated differently from feminine-titled women in the uniform feminine arm (T2) Following Burlacu et al. (2024), the main pre-specified dimension of heterogeneity is respondent gender. In addition, we will explore whether effects vary by the scenario drawn within each profession (randomized at the individual level): for each profession, one candidate scenario is relatively more stereotypically male, one more balanced, and one relatively more stereotypically female. Finally, we will investigate whether effects vary across the three target professions. Architecture and law have similar shares of women and similarly low use of the feminine title, but differ in STEM status; architecture and engineering are both STEM and have similarly low feminine-title use, but differ markedly in the share of women (high in architecture). For the placebo profession — medicine — the feminine title is expected to have a non-negative effect, given its prevalence. Since we do not have strong priors on heterogeneity separately for T2 and T3, when estimating heterogeneity we will pool profiles displaying the feminine title and estimate: Rating = a0·Female + a1·T2 + a2·T3 + b2·Female×T3 + d·Female×FemTitle + [same controls and fixed effects as the main specification] + e with each moderator interacted with the terms of interest.
primary_outcomes: Contact-likelihood rating: the stated likelihood of contacting each profile, on an integer 0–10 scale (0 = “not at all”, 10 = “for sure”). Each respondent provides 16 ratings (4 rounds × 4 profiles).
randomization_method: Randomization at the individual respondent level, implemented in software (oTree) at session start. All treatments and randomized orderings are drawn independently.
secondary_outcome_explanation: Additional heterogeneity analysis of the primary outcome will be performed along the following dimensions: - Socio-demographics: education level. - Language-specific norms and attitudes. After the list experiment, participants report agreement/disagreement with up to three direct statements (depending on their list arm) capturing norms on the appropriateness of feminine-title use, the perceived harm of the feminine title to women in the profession, and the perceived ideological signaling of the feminine title. We expect all three to moderate treatment effects in the same (negative) direction; to limit multiple-hypothesis-testing concerns they will be aggregated into an index, imputing the item missing by design (for treated-arm respondents) with the sample mean of respondents giving the same responses on the other two items. At the end of the survey, respondents also complete the ATGIL scale. We will combine the direct items and the ATGIL into one language-attitudes index using the inverse-covariance-weighting approach of Anderson (2008). - First-order beliefs: beliefs about the prevalence of women in each profession and about the prevalence of feminine-title use among women practitioners. - Gender attitudes. From the gender-typing section (24 professions and sports), we compute the share of items the respondent classifies as suited to both men and women, as a measure of (absence of) gender-typing. This measure will be combined with the Modern Sexism score into one gender-attitudes index (inverse-covariance weighting). - Misperception wedge (norm misperception). For respondents who answer the second-order belief questions at the national level (list arms 1, 3, and 4), an individual-level wedge is computed, following Bursztyn et al. (2020), as the respondent’s guess of the share of men (or, symmetrically, of women) who consider the feminine title more appropriate, minus the true share as measured in the study (from the list experiment and/or direct elicitation). The wedge is used as a moderator to examine whether the title-treatment effect varies with the extent and sign of a respondent’s misperception. - Conformity-threshold wedge. From the conformity scenario we compute each respondent’s switching point — the prevalence level at which the recommendation shifts from the masculine to the feminine form. Combining this with the respondent’s first-order beliefs about the share of women using the feminine title in each profession, we compute a conformity wedge, given by the difference between the believed prevalence and the respondent’s conformity threshold, and use it as a moderator. - Political orientation. We measure political-cultural orientation with the conservatism and liberalism subscales of the POLID instrument. Since we expect the two subscales to moderate treatment effects in opposite directions, we will reverse one and aggregate them into a single measure. In addition, the survey company provides a standard left–right self-placement measure. Carry-over checks. Since most moderators are measured after the vignette block, we will first test whether the vignette treatment (T1–T3) has any carry-over effect on each Block-B variable. If such effects are detected for a variable, we will not use it as a moderator and will report it descriptively only. While we expect no such effects, on some dimensions (e.g., first-order beliefs about title use, the direct statements, or ATGIL) they cannot be excluded a priori, e.g., seeing only feminine-titled profiles may inflate beliefs about title use or trigger emotional reactions in some respondents. Secondary experiments and additional exploratory analyses Each secondary randomized component is analyzed separately, as informative about potential mechanisms; we do not analyze the full cross-randomization. - Label-format experiment (gender-typing of professions and sports). Using the 24 gender-typing responses we test whether double-form labels (e.g., Avvocato/Avvocata) or field-name labels (e.g., Avvocatura) reduce gender-typing relative to masculine-only labels — overall, by category (STEM, non-STEM, sports, over the 4 vignette professions), and excluding professions with common gender nouns. - List-experiment prevalence estimates. Comparing mean counts between the control arm (five baseline statements) and each treated arm (five baseline statements plus one sensitive statement) yields an estimate of the population share agreeing with each sensitive statement (“appropriateness”, “harm”, “signaling”) while preserving individual anonymity. Because the method protects anonymity by design, these estimates are aggregate overall or at sub-group level (or, at finest, subgroup-level). - Social-desirability gap. Respondents who did not see a given sensitive statement in their own list answer the same statement directly (binary agree/disagree, identical wording, order of direct items randomized). The difference between the list-inferred prevalence and the directly stated prevalence estimates social-desirability bias for that attitude. Because list and direct responses on a given statement come from disjoint groups by construction, the gap is estimated at the aggregate level. Directly stated prevalences are computed pooling all eligible arms. As robustness checks, direct responses are tested for differences by list arm — assessing whether exposure to a different sensitive statement primes the direct response — and the gap is re-estimated using only control-arm respondents for the direct measure, controlling for the randomized position of the item within the direct-question block. - Conformity-threshold scenario. We will estimate the effect of the female-share condition (25% vs 50%) on the conformity threshold. References Anderson, M. L. (2008).
