abstract: This study evaluates the impact of Gemini Guided Learning, an AI-powered instructional experience within Gemini that provides personalised learning through guided questions, step-by-step scaffolding, and multimodal resources rather than supplying direct answers, on physic and chemistry lessons in grades 6,7 and 8 in India (ages 10–14). This evaluation is part of a multisite evaluation. The trial randomly assigns classrooms either to continue with regular teaching or to use Gemini in approximately a third of their science lessons over a 13 week period. The same teachers are responsible for both treatment and control classrooms; all will receive training on how to use the tool, though it will only be applied in treatment classes. Science performance of students will be assessed at the beginning and end of the intervention. The study will provide rigorous evidence on whether AI supported guided learning can strengthen science learning in junior secondary education.
experimental_design: This study employs a cluster randomised controlled trial with classrooms as the unit of randomisation. Randomisation is stratified by school, grade level (6, 7 and 8), using computer-generated random assignment with a pre-specified seed. This stratification approach ensures balanced allocation across key prognostic factors and prevents potential confounding between teacher effects and treatment effects. Classrooms are randomly assigned to either: (1) Treatment arm receiving access to an AI powered science tutoring platform in addition to standard instruction, or (2) Control arm receiving standard science instruction only.
experimental_design_details: Random assignment is stratified by classroom within each combination of school and grade. In most schools, classrooms are assigned in a 50/50 ratio between treatment and control. In three larger schools (Aliganj I, Gomti Nagar I and Kanpur Road) classrooms are assigned in a 40/60 ratio, with 40% treated and 60% control, because these schools did not have the device and computer lab capacity to support a larger number of treatment classrooms. This results in 112 treatment and 128 control classrooms overall. Classrooms that do not divide evenly within a stratum are reassigned at the overall sample level while preserving each stratum's target ratio. Randomisation includes only classrooms where almost all students are aged 10 years or older; so that Gemini is used under comparable conditions across the sample.
intervention: Gemini Guided Learning is an AI-powered instructional tool within Gemini, designed to support students’ science learning through guided questions, step-by-step scaffolding, adaptive feedback, and multimodal resources rather than providing direct answers. Infused with Google’s LearnLM research, Gemini encourages students to reflect on their own thinking, deepening metacognition while fostering curiosity and active engagement.The intervention will be implemented in grades 6, 7 and 8 (ages 10–14) over a 13-week period, during which students in treatment classrooms will use Gemini in one 35-minute chemistry module and one 35-minute physics module per week. This is equivalent to one third of the science lessons. Teachers will receive training on how to use the tool, although the tool will only be applied in treatment classrooms.

abstract: This study examines how providing information about hazardous facilities affects residents’ perceptions of environmental and health risks and their preferences for risk-management policies. We conduct a randomized survey experiment among residents of ten Czech municipalities hosting industrial facilities or landfills subject to heightened environmental or safety regulation. Respondents are randomly assigned either to receive factual, site-specific information about the facility located in their municipality or to a control group that receives no additional information before assessing the facility. The information describes the facility’s activities, relevant hazards and potential accident scenarios. The study evaluates whether information provision changes perceived environmental and health risks and support for regulatory and compensatory measures. It also examines whether responses to information differ according to residents’ prior knowledge, experience with the facility and perceived level of informedness. In addition, the study investigates how residents’ risk perceptions and policy preferences are associated with proximity to the facility, knowledge, perceived informedness, confidence in risk control, environmental attitudes and socio-demographic characteristics. The study contributes to understanding whether public information can influence risk perceptions and policy preferences in communities hosting potentially hazardous facilities, and under what circumstances information provision may be an effective risk-communication instrument.
experimental_design: The study uses a randomized survey experiment conducted among adult residents of ten Czech municipalities hosting industrial facilities or landfills subject to heightened environmental or safety regulation. Within each municipality, respondents were randomly assigned either to receive factual, site-specific information about the facility before answering the outcome questions or to a control condition that received no additional information. Outcomes were measured immediately after the intervention.
experimental_design_details: The experiment was embedded in a face-to-face computer-assisted survey conducted in ten Czech municipalities. Respondents were randomly assigned within municipality to either an information treatment or a control condition. Of the 514 respondents, 258 were assigned to the treatment group and 256 to the control group, with allocation balanced across the ten study sites. All pre-treatment characteristics, including environmental attitudes, self-reported proximity to the facility, frequency of contact with its surroundings, prior awareness of the facility’s activities, perceived informedness about risks, and perceived advantages and disadvantages of the facility, were measured before treatment assignment was revealed to the respondent. Respondents assigned to the treatment group then received a factual, site-specific information block describing the facility’s activities, relevant hazards, possible accident scenarios and potential consequences. Respondents in the control group proceeded directly to the outcome module without receiving this additional information. Outcome measures were administered immediately after the intervention.
intervention: The intervention consisted of providing respondents with factual, site-specific information about the hazardous facility located in their municipality. Respondents were randomly assigned either to receive this information immediately before the risk-assessment module or to a control condition that received no additional information.

abstract: Many financially distressed households who could benefit from Chapter 7 bankruptcy never file. Common misperceptions about bankruptcy – such as underestimating the likelihood of receiving a debt discharge, overestimating the likelihood of surrendering assets, or underestimating future access to credit – may discourage filing. This randomized experiment will test two questions: (i) does providing information about Chapter 7 filing outcomes bankruptcy increase engagement with the bankruptcy filing process, and (ii) which informational message is most effective at doing so? We test three hypotheses for why individuals do not file: (a) individuals underestimate the probability that bankruptcy will lead to a debt discharge, (b) individuals overestimate the probability that they will have to surrender property, and (c) individuals underestimate the credit-score benefits of filing. We partner with Upsolve, a nonprofit that helps individuals file for Chapter 7 bankruptcy. To test our hypotheses, visitors arriving at Upsolve’s website will be randomly assigned to one of four landing-page messages: (i) a control page with no information, (ii) the probability of receiving a debt discharge, (iii) the probability of receiving a debt discharge and not surrendering assets, or (iv) the average post-bankruptcy credit score improvement. We will assess how this exogenous shift in information about filing outcomes affects interest in filing, as measured through engagement with Upsolve’s website.

abstract: We conduct a correspondence study of unsolicited job applications for apprenticeship contracts (contrats d'alternance) in France, targeting a representative sample of employers located in and around several major French metropolitan areas. Eligible firms are drawn from an administrative database obtained through a data-sharing agreement with DARES (Direction de l'Animation de la Recherche, des Études et des Statistiques, French Ministry of Labour), and stratified on standard firm characteristics to ensure balance across treatment groups. The primary outcome is the callback rate, i.e., a positive response from an employer via email, phone call, or text message. Fictitious candidate profiles are constructed to vary along several dimensions relevant to hiring decisions, including candidate characteristics associated with disability status. Candidate identities are constructed using first and last names drawn from INSEE civil registry frequency data, to ensure realistic and representative fictitious applicants. Applications are sent to each sampled employer following a randomized assignment protocol designed to ensure comparability across treatment and control conditions, with safeguards in place to limit the risk of detection by recruiters.
experimental_design: We conduct the field experiment by sending resumes to apply to online job postings from different firms. We create resumes which are similar in all relevant dimensions (educational background, previous work experience, professional skills, etc.), except for the specific candidate characteristic under study.
intervention: Fictitious candidate profiles vary along dimensions relevant to hiring decisions in the context of apprenticeship recruitment, including characteristics associated with disability status. Each sampled employer receives two spontaneous applications from fictitious candidates, with random assignment of candidate characteristics designed to ensure comparability across conditions while limiting the risk of detection by recruiters.
mde_text: Power calculations rely on three empirical benchmarks drawn from prior correspondence studies. First, we use a baseline positive response rate of 13.26% for apprenticeship applications, based on Anne, Bagayoko, Chareyron & L'Horty (2024). Second, we use an alternative and more conservative baseline response rate of 4.5% for apprenticeship applications in a related occupational context, based on Anne, Challe, Chareyron, L'Horty & Noet (2025). Third, we use a hypothesized relative gap in success rates of 15.2% for candidates signaling a visual impairment, based on Challe, Chareyron, L'Horty, Du Parquet & Petit (2023), a correspondence study on housing access. Combined with the 13.26% baseline, the required combined sample size to detect this effect at 80% power (α = 0.05, two-sided) is 7,940 applications. Combined with the more conservative 4.5% baseline, the required combined sample size is 25,484 applications. Regardless of which baseline reference rate is used, the required combined sample size (7,940 to 25,484) remains well below our planned sample of 28,000 applications. We are therefore adequately powered to detect the expected effect under either scenario.

primary_outcome_explanation: The callback rate, defined as the share of applications receiving a positive response from the employer. A response is coded as positive if the employer invites the candidate to an interview, requests additional information or documents with a view to pursuing the application or otherwise indicates interest in continuing the recruitment process. Responses are collected via a dedicated email account associated with each fictitious candidate profile and coded by research staff.
primary_outcomes: The primary outcome is whether a job applicant receives a positive response (callback) from an employer via email, phone call, or text message. We examine variation in the callback rate according to the candidate characteristic under study, as well as according to application and firm characteristics, including sending order, candidate script set, region, qualification level, occupational field, legal form of the recruiting firm, firm size, location, industry sector, and firm size bracket.
randomization_method: Candidate profiles are assigned to employers using a computer-generated randomization procedure.
randomization_unit: The unit of randomization is the individual job application within each sampled firm.
secondary_outcome_explanation: 1.Response time is measured as the number of calendar days between application submission and the employer's response, among applications receiving a response. 2.Type of positive response is coded from employer replies as either an interview invitation (by type : email, phone call, or text message), or a request for additional information/documents, among applications coded as positive on the primary outcome. 3.Qualitative content of the response is coded from the text of employer replies, capturing elements such as number of words, questions asked, Phone number provide.
secondary_outcomes: In addition to the subgroup analyses of the callback rate, we will also examine response time, type of positive response, and qualitative content of the response.

abstract: We will conduct a large-scale online survey with a quota-representative sample of approximately 7,500 German adults. Using the case of rent control – a prominent and highly salient price-control policy on which economists and the public often appear to disagree – we study people’s understanding of the effects (mental models) of price control policies and the limits of expert persuasion. Our aims are to: a) elicit and characterize the mental models that individuals hold about the effects of stricter rent control, using both open-ended (unstructured) and structured elicitation, and relate these mental models to individuals’ economic literacy; b) test whether exposure to economists’ economic narratives against stricter rent control shifts individuals’ mental models and their support for the policy; and c) test whether the persuasiveness of these narratives depends on a signal that economists disagree about the policy, and whether responsiveness to the narratives and to the disagreement signal differs between individuals with high and low economic literacy. Using survey experiments together with a pre-treatment measure of economic literacy to distinguish subgroups of participants with high and low economic literacy, we address the following specific research questions: i) What mental models do individuals hold about the effects of stricter rent control, do these mental models depend on economic literacy, does support for stricter rent control itself depend on economic literacy, and which mental models are associated with support for stricter rent control? ii) Do economists’ economic narratives about stricter rent control causally affect individuals’ mental models and their support for the policy, and does this responsiveness depend on economic literacy? iii) Does the effect of economists’ narratives depend on whether there is a signal of disagreement among economists, and does the effect of the disagreement signal differ between individuals with high and low economic literacy?
experimental_design: We conduct the survey experiment with a quota-representative sample of approximately 7,500 German adults. The survey is programmed and hosted using the Tivian license of the ifo Institute; respondents are provided by the online panel provider Talk Online Panel, subject to representativeness quotas (gender, age, federal state, education, employment status, renter vs. non-renter, and municipality size). Participants answer questions autonomously on their own digital devices. Randomization is performed by the survey software. The panel provider also supplies survey weights; the main analyses are unweighted, and weighted estimates are reported in robustness checks. The survey proceeds in the following order: (1) landing page and a willingness-to-write screening item ; (2) quota demographics; (3) pre-treatment moderators, including housing situation and self-interest items, expectations about local rents and house prices, economic values, interest in and consumption of economic news, trust in and perceived competence of economists, self-assessed economic understanding, a 10-item economic-literacy test, and beliefs about own test performance; (4) an attention check; (5) information on rent increases since 2010 and an open-ended diagnosis of their perceived causes; (6) a description of the rent-control status quo and the proposed stricter policy; (7) an open-ended (unstructured) elicitation of the prior mental model and confidence in it; (8) randomization, in a single draw, into one of six conditions defined by the three narrative conditions and the two elicitation branches; (9) policy-support questions; (10) additional demographics and cognitive controls; and (11) an outro. The follow-up survey is fielded two to four weeks later and includes a reminder of (6) and repeats (7), (9), trust in economists, and additionally includes questions on perceived disagreement on rent control among economists, as well as two questions on whether people remember the treatment content from the main survey
experimental_design_details: Narrative texts (in German; the Control condition receives no narrative): Economists’ Economic Narrative: Die folgende Einschätzung zur Mietpreisregulierung basiert auf dem Jahresgutachten 2024/25 des Sachverständigenrats zur Begutachtung der gesamtwirtschaftlichen Entwicklung (die sogenannten „Wirtschaftsweisen“) – einem fünfköpfigen Gremium unabhängiger Wirtschaftswissenschaftler*innen, das die Bundesregierung berät. Die Mietpreisregulierung kann genutzt werden, um die Mieterinnen und Mieter temporär vor übermäßigen Preisanstiegen im Wohnungsmarkt zu schützen. Zudem kann eine gewisse Regulierung der Bestandsmieten sinnvoll sein, um die Verhandlungsposition von Mieterinnen und Mietern in bestehenden Mietverhältnissen zu stärken, da durch die hohen Kosten eines Umzugs eine Lock-in Situation entsteht. Eine zu restriktive Regulierung dürfte jedoch die privaten Investitionsanreize in Wohnraum verringern. Sie verhindert auch eine effiziente Nutzung von Wohnraum. Beide Effekte sind umso stärker, je weiter die regulierten Bestands- und Neumieten unter dem unregulierten Marktpreis liegen. Die Mietpreisregulierung ist zudem sozial wenig treffsicher. Die regulatorisch bedingte Verlangsamung des Anstiegs der Bestandsmieten entlastet insbesondere jene Mieterinnen und Mieter, die schon lange in ihrer Wohnung wohnen und in der Folge eine Miete deutlich unterhalb des Marktpreises zahlen. Entlastet werden daher vor allem immobile und ältere Menschen, während junge Menschen sowie Menschen, die z. B. aus beruflichen Gründen öfter umziehen, durch höhere Neumieten belastet werden. Economists’ Economic Narrative, Disagreement Frame: Die folgende Einschätzung zur Mietpreisregulierung basiert auf dem Jahresgutachten 2024/25 des Sachverständigenrats zur Begutachtung der gesamtwirtschaftlichen Entwicklung (die sogenannten „Wirtschaftsweisen“) – einem fünfköpfigen Gremium unabhängiger Wirtschaftswissenschaftler*innen, das die Bundesregierung berät. Vier der fünf Mitglieder vertreten die im Folgenden dargestellte Position. [Narrative text as above] Diese Einschätzung wird nicht von allen Mitgliedern des Sachverständigenrats in dieser Form geteilt. Ein Mitglied hat eine abweichende Position („Minderheitsvotum“) verfasst.
intervention: The survey experiment manipulates two dimensions, independently at the individual level. (1) Economic narrative. After respondents are informed about the status quo of rent regulation in Germany and the proposed stricter policy, and after an open-ended (unstructured) elicitation of their prior mental model, respondents are randomly assigned to one of three conditions: • Control: no narrative is presented. • Economists’ Economic Narrative: respondents read a short text summarizing the economic assessment of stricter rent regulation drawn from the 2024/25 annual report of the German Council of Economic Experts („Wirtschaftsweise“). • Economists’ Economic Narrative with Disagreement Signal: respondents read the same narrative, and, in addition, they receive information that the assessment is shared by four of the five Council members and that one member has issued a dissenting minority opinion. (2) Post-treatment elicitation. Orthogonally to the narrative treatment, respondents are randomly assigned to either a No-Elicitation branch (no structured elicitation of the post-treatment mental model) or a Structured-Elicitation branch (structured elicitation of the post-treatment mental model along a fixed set of eight outcome dimensions). This second randomization allows us to assess whether structured elicitation itself primes particular mechanisms and shapes policy-support responses. Both dimensions are assigned in a single draw, so that each respondent is allocated to one of six equally likely conditions (see Randomization Method).

primary_outcome_explanation: Support is measured on a Likert scale after the narrative treatment and again in the follow-up survey. Mental models are elicited in an open-ended (unstructured) format before the narrative treatment (all respondents) and again in the follow-up survey (all follow-up respondents), and, in the structured-elicitation branch only, in a structured format immediately after the narrative treatment; open-ended responses are coded into pre-specified indices (see the pre-analysis plan). primary_outcomes: (i) Individuals’ support for the proposed stricter rent-control policy; and (ii) individuals’ mental models about the effects of stricter rent control.
randomization_method: Randomization is carried out by the randomizer of the survey software (Tivian). Each respondent is assigned in a single draw to one of six equally likely conditions, defined by the cross of the three narrative conditions (Control; Economic Narrative; Economic Narrative with Disagreement Signal) and the two elicitation branches (No Elicitation; Structured Elicitation). This is equivalent to assigning the narrative condition and the elicitation branch independently at the individual level. Assignment probabilities do not depend on respondent characteristics.
secondary_outcome_explanation: Mental-model sub-measures are constructed from the open-ended and structured elicitations: mechanism uptake counts the narrative's causal channels that also appear in a respondent's response; residual and total breadth count, respectively, the causal channels invoked that are outside the narrative and in total; confidence is elicited after each mental-model measure; the low-effort indicator flags responses that are empty, off-topic, or disengaged; and the individual dimensions are the five signed and three unsigned items of the structured battery, analyzed separately as well as summarized in the primary directional-alignment index. Absolute support for all policies is measured on a Likert scale, and relative support for housing policies is measured with a ranking question. All policy support questions are measured after the narrative treatment and again in the follow-up survey. Trust in and perceived competence of economists and beliefs about disagreement among economists on rent control are measured on Likert scales in the follow-up survey (trust in economists is also measured pre-treatment). See the pre-analysis plan for full definitions.
secondary_outcomes: i) Individuals’ mental models about the effects of stricter rent control, including mechanism uptake, the residual and total breadth of the model, confidence in the elicited model, a low-effort-response indicator, and the individual dimensions of the structured elicitation battery; ii) support for other housing policies, relative support for rent control, and support for other price-control policies; and iii) trust in and perceived competence of economists and beliefs about disagreement among economists.
title: Economists’ Narratives, Economic Literacy, and Support for Rent Control

abstract: This study will investigate whether shared group identity, induced using the Minimal Group Paradigm, influences food standards monitoring decisions and whether a professional impartiality reminder reduces any ingroup bias. While inspectors are expected to be impartial, shared group identity may unconsciously influence their monitoring decisions. In a monitoring context, this may result in inspectors allocating fewer monitoring units to ingroup firms than to outgroup firms, increasing the risk that non-compliance remains undetected within the ingroup and undermining the integrity of food standards systems. This study will use an oTree-programmed online experiment conducted on Prolific Academic. Experimental sessions will be randomly assigned to either a control condition or a professional impartiality reminder condition. Each session will consist of 20 participants, where they will be randomly assigned to one of two arbitrary colour groups (Blue or Green) and to one of two roles (Food Standards Inspector or Food Producer). Their assigned colour groups and roles will remain fixed throughout the session. Across ten repeated rounds, inspectors will allocate five monitoring units between two ingroup and two outgroup producers, while producers will generate and report food quality grades and may choose to misreport. Participants will be randomly rematched in each round following a stranger matching design. The primary objective will be to test whether inspectors allocate fewer monitoring units to ingroup than to outgroup producers and whether the professional impartiality reminder reduces this ingroup bias. Some exploratory analysis will also be conducted to explore how inspectors update their monitoring decisions following the detection of ingroup and outgroup non-compliance and whether differential monitoring leads to higher rates of undetected non-compliance.
experimental_design: Participants will be recruited through Prolific Academic to take part in a multiplayer online experiment programmed in oTree. Eligible participants must be 18 years of age or older, fluent in English, have a Prolific approval rating of at least 95%, and have normal colour vision to distinguish the colours used in the experiment. All eligibility criteria will be screened using Prolific's prescreening filters before participants can access the study. Participants who meet the eligibility criteria and provide informed consent will complete a brief video-based attention check. Participants will be given a maximum of two attempts to answer the attention check correctly before proceeding to the experiment. Procedures: 1. 20 participants will join the online experiment session on Prolific Academic. Each session will be randomly assigned to either the control condition or the professional impartiality reminder condition. 2. Participants will provide their consent and complete a brief video-based attention check. 3. Upon completion, participants will remain on a waiting page until all participants have arrived and are ready to begin the experiment. If not all participants arrive within 10 minutes, the session will not proceed, and participants who did arrive will receive a fixed compensation payment for their time. 4. Participants will be randomly assigned to one of two arbitrary colour groups (Blue or Green). They will be informed of their assigned group, which will remain fixed throughout the session. 5. Participants will then be randomly assigned to undertake the role of either Food Standards Inspector or Food Producer. 6. Participants will receive role-specific instructions, earnings and complete a role-specific comprehension check before proceeding to their task. 7. The Inspector’s task is to allocate monitoring units across four Food Producers, two of which are their ingroup. 8. The Food Producers’ task is to report their food quality grade. Reporting higher than their actual food quality grade increases their earnings, but there are risks of being monitored for non-compliance. None, some or all Food Producers' reporting activities will be monitored in each round. 9. The experiment consists of 10 rounds. Each Inspector will be matched with four Food Producers comprising two ingroup and two outgroup producers. Participants will be randomly rematched using a stranger matching design in the subsequent rounds. Although repeated Inspector–Food Producer encounters may occur by chance, Food Producers will be assigned temporary identities in each round to prevent producer-specific reputation formation. 10. At the end of each round, participants will receive their round result. 11. After completing all ten rounds, one round will be randomly selected for earnings. Participants will received earnings from the selected round and the participation fee. 12. Participants will complete a post-experiment survey comprising demographic questions, risk attitude, group identity measures, and role-specific attitudinal measures.
intervention: Intervention 1: Control In the control condition, participants assigned to the Food Standards Inspector role will complete the monitoring experiment without receiving a professional impartiality reminder. They will receive the standard experimental instructions describing their assigned colour group, role and tasks. Intervention 2: Professional impartiality reminder In the professional impartiality reminder condition, participants assigned to the Food Standards Inspector role will complete the same monitoring experiment as the control group. In addition to the standard instructions, inspectors will receive a professional impartiality reminder based on the principle of impartiality in ISO/IEC 17020. The reminder will be presented before the first monitoring allocation decision and will be displayed once more as a pop-out at a randomly selected round between Rounds 4 and 10. Participants must acknowledge the pop-out reminder before proceeding with the monitoring allocation decision.

The primary analysis will compare monitoring units allocated to ingroup and outgroup producers and assess whether the professional impartiality reminder reduces any difference in monitoring allocation between the two groups. We expect inspectors to allocate fewer monitoring units to ingroup producers than to outgroup producers. We also expect the ingroup–outgroup difference in monitoring allocation to be smaller in the professional impartiality reminder condition than in the control condition.
primary_outcomes: Number of monitoring units allocated to each food producer in each round.
randomization_method: Randomization is programmed and implemented in oTree using its built-in random assignment functions.
randomization_unit: Session and Individual. Treatment assignment will occur at the session level, with each experimental session randomly assigned to either the control condition or the professional impartiality reminder condition. Consequently, all participants within the same session will receive the same experimental condition. Within each session, participants will be randomly assigned to one of two arbitrary colour groups (Blue or Green) and to one of two roles: Food Standards Inspector or Food Producer. secondary_outcome_explanation: 1.Undetected non-compliance will be measured as a binary outcome equal to 1 when a Food Producer misreports a food quality grade and not detected due to no monitoring allocated, and 0 otherwise. Exploratory analyses will examine whether the likelihood of undetected non-compliance differs between ingroup and outgroup producers. 2. Monitoring allocation updating will be measured as changes in the number of monitoring units allocated in subsequent rounds following the detection of non-compliance. Exploratory analyses will examine whether inspectors update their monitoring allocations differently after detecting ingroup versus outgroup non-compliance. In addition, the demographic information and post-experiment survey measures will also be collected, including risk attitude, role engagement, and group identity measures. For Food Standards Inspectors, this includes beliefs about ingroup and outgroup compliance rates, trust in ingroup producers, suspicion towards outgroup producers, and professionalism norms. For Food Producers, this includes beliefs about honest reporting as a social norm, perceived leniency from ingroup inspectors and scrutiny from outgroup inspectors, guilt associated with misreporting, and compliance pressure. These measures will be used descriptively and in exploratory analyses to examine potential mechanisms and sources of behavioural heterogeneity.

abstract: Village doctors in rural China are often few in number, aging, and have limited formal training, while chronic disease burdens are rising. This study evaluates whether giving village doctors access to an AI health assistant app ("Ant AFu," developed by Ant Group), along with structured training and support, changes how they deliver care. We conduct a village-level randomized controlled trial in a mountainous county in Guizhou Province, China, covering all 140 administrative villages. Villages are randomly assigned within townships to one of four groups: two groups where village doctors receive AI training and app access (in one of these, villagers are also encouraged to use the app), and two groups that continue current practice during the study period and receive delayed access afterward. We measure outcomes including how many patients doctors see, the quality of diagnosis and prescribing (assessed through case reviews, clinical scenarios, and unannounced standardized-patient visits), and patient recovery, using doctor surveys, monthly case records, and phone follow-ups with patients. We also study how doctors actually use the app, drawing on de-identified usage data, and whether any improvements persist after access to the tool is temporarily withdrawn for a subset of doctors.
experimental_design: This is a village-level cluster-randomized controlled trial conducted in a mountainous county in Guizhou Province, China, covering all 140 administrative villages in the county. After a baseline survey of village doctors and clinics, villages are randomly assigned within townships (stratified randomization) to one of four arms of 35 villages each: (1) Treatment 1, in which village doctors receive standardized training and supported access to an AI health assistant app; (2) Treatment 2, which adds village-level promotion of the app to residents; and (3)-(4) two control arms that continue existing practice during the study period, with the same training offered after the study ends. Randomization is stratified within townships to balance village population, doctor gender, and doctor education. The intervention period lasts approximately 6 months, with a baseline survey beforehand and an endline survey afterward (total study duration approximately 12-13 months). Outcomes are measured through doctor surveys, monthly case-record collection, sampled patient phone follow-up, household surveys, and standardized clinical assessment methods, with analysis conducted at the village level using intention-to-treat comparisons and village-clustered standard errors.
experimental_design_details: Sampling frame and selection: all 140 administrative villages in the county are included (no additional village-level sampling), each with a village clinic and 1-2 primary village doctors under the county's "county-recruited, township-managed, village-used" staffing model. Randomization procedure: randomization is conducted in office by computer after baseline data collection is complete, stratified by township, with re-randomization or balance checks used to confirm covariate balance (baseline standardized differences on village population, doctor gender, and doctor education fall within conventional thresholds, as confirmed in the approved ethics protocol). Contamination management: because townships contain multiple villages and information/behavior can diffuse across nearby villages, randomization avoids assigning immediately adjacent villages to different arms where feasible, and post-study analysis includes sensitivity checks for geographic spillovers and cross-village doctor interaction. Sub-study (durability test): approximately 1-3 months after the intervention period ends, AI app access is withdrawn from a randomly selected subset of Treatment-arm doctors. This subset, along with doctors retaining access and control-arm doctors, undergoes a second round of clinical vignettes and unannounced standardized-patient (SP) visits. This cross-randomized sub-design tests whether observed improvements reflect durable skill acquisition (learning-by-doing) versus dependence on continued tool availability (deskilling), which is the key input to assessing long-run scalability of the "AI + primary healthcare" policy. Process/mechanism data: de-identified backend usage logs (login frequency, session counts, feature-level usage, query-type classification) are obtained from Ant Group to support mechanism analysis distinguishing information, incentive, and capability constraints as explanations for baseline care-quality gaps, and to examine whether AI functions as a skill complement or substitute across doctor and village characteristics (e.g., doctor age, digital literacy, baseline caseload, acute vs. chronic case mix).
intervention: Village doctors in treatment villages receive standardized training on an AI health assistant app ("Ant AFu," developed by Ant Group) and supported access to the app for use in their daily clinical work. Training covers the app's core functions, guidance on when AI input is and is not appropriate, how to incorporate the tool into diagnosis, prescribing, chronic-disease follow-up, and home visits, and how to recognize high-risk cases requiring referral. Training is followed by hands-on practice with simulated and common real-world cases, and by several weeks of follow-up support (group chat/phone-based Q&A and periodic check-ins) after initial rollout, plus periodic refresher sessions and targeted outreach to low-usage doctors during the intervention period. There are two treatment arms: in one, only village doctors receive training and app access; in the other, villagers in the same villages are also encouraged and supported to use the app themselves. Villages in the two control arms continue current practice during the study period and are offered the same training after the endline survey (delayed treatment).

primary_outcome_explanation: Service coverage outcomes are drawn directly from monthly case-record/ledger data collected from each village clinic; no construction is needed beyond aggregation to the doctor-month or village-month level. The diagnostic/prescribing quality index is constructed for a small set of pre-specified tracer conditions (to be finalized from baseline ledger review; likely candidates include acute respiratory infection/fever, gastrointestinal symptoms, hypertension follow-up, diabetes follow-up, minor skin/wound infections, and chronic-disease medication management for the elderly). For each sampled case (from record audits, vignettes, and SP encounters), we score: completeness of history-taking, whether danger signs were asked about, whether necessary physical exams were performed, appropriateness of the prescription, absence of inappropriate antibiotic use, absence of inappropriate steroid/IV use, appropriateness of referral decisions, and clarity of medication instructions. These binary/ordinal sub-items are standardized and averaged (or aggregated via a weighted index, method to be pre-specified in the pre-analysis plan) into a single quality index per case, then averaged to the doctor level. The patient recovery outcome is constructed from a structured phone follow-up instrument covering symptom resolution, self-rated health, recurrence/repeat visits, hospitalization/ER use, complications, medication adherence, and satisfaction; these items will be combined into a summary recovery index (standardized and averaged, per the pre-analysis plan), with key individual items also reported separately.
primary_outcomes: (1) Service coverage: monthly number of unique patients seen per doctor, total monthly patient volume, monthly chronic-disease follow-up visits completed. (2) Quality of diagnosis and prescribing: a standardized diagnostic/prescribing quality score derived from (a) audited case records for tracer conditions, (b) doctor performance on standardized clinical vignettes, and (c) doctor behavior recorded during unannounced standardized patient (SP) visits. (3) Patient recovery: symptom improvement, self-reported recovery, repeat visits/ hospitalization, and adherence to prescribed treatment, measured via phone follow-up at fixed intervals after the index visit (e.g., day 7/14 for acute conditions, day 30/90 for chronic conditions).
randomization_method: Randomization was conducted in office using a computer-generated randomization procedure (stratified randomization within townships), implemented after completion of the baseline village/doctor survey. Balance across arms was verified using standardized difference tests on stratification and key baseline covariates.
randomization_unit: Administrative village (cluster). All doctors and patients within a given village clinic receive the same treatment assignment as their village. There is a single level of randomization (village-level, stratified within townships); the post-intervention access-withdrawal sub-study introduces a second, later-stage individual (doctor-level) randomization within the pool of previously treated doctors.
secondary_outcome_explanation: The home-visit-depth index is constructed from a checklist administered to sampled patients/households: whether a home visit occurred, whether vital signs were measured, whether medication adherence was checked, whether prior history was reviewed, whether danger signs were explained, whether follow-up was scheduled, whether records were kept, whether caregivers were contacted, visit duration, and visit frequency; sub-items are standardized and averaged into a single index. Cost and time-use outcomes are collected directly from patient/household follow-up surveys and require no construction beyond standard aggregation (e.g., total cost = consultation + drug + travel cost). The safety index aggregates the inappropriate-prescribing indicators listed above (antibiotic overuse, steroid/IV overuse, missed danger signs, delayed referral, adverse events) into a single standardized safety score, with each component also reported individually given their policy relevance. Usage/mechanism variables are drawn from de-identified backend log data provided by Ant Group (login frequency, session counts, function-level usage, query-type tags) and are used primarily for mechanism analysis (e.g., dose-response/TOT analysis, exploring what predicts effective use) rather than as headline treatment-effect outcomes.
secondary_outcomes: (1) Depth/quality of home visits and follow-up (a constructed home-visit-depth index). (2) Patient costs and time use: total visit cost, drug cost, referral/travel cost, time lost from work, and time from symptom onset to treatment. (3) Doctor knowledge, confidence, and behavior change: vignette test scores, case judgment accuracy, self-reported confidence, willingness to conduct follow-up visits or take on more complex cases. (4) Safety indicators: rate of clearly inappropriate prescriptions, antibiotic/steroid overuse rates, missed danger-sign rate, delayed-referral rate, and patient adverse events. (5) Mechanism/usage indicators: app activation, weekly/monthly active use, number of queries per session, functions used (symptom check, report interpretation, follow-up support, health education), and whether promotion to village doctors generates spillover use among villagers (in Treatment 2 villages).
title: AI-Assisted Village Doctors and Rural Primary Healthcare: A Randomized Controlled Trial in China

abstract: Many low-income workers remain in low-return local labor markets despite large spatial wage gaps, while others migrate for jobs that appear unattractive on purely pecuniary grounds. Standard accounts explain migration through wages, employment risk, liquidity constraints, and networks. We study whether occupational stigma also shapes the spatial allocation of labor. Manual work such as construction may carry a social penalty. The same work may be less socially costly when undertaken where the worker is not known or observed by their peers or reference groups. Migration may therefore be a way of escaping social stigma associated with certain jobs. We test this mechanism in a field experiment with male manual laborers in villages near Patna, Bihar where participants evaluate the same construction job—holding the task, hours, and duration fixed—at three locations that differ in social visibility. Because each worker evaluates all three locations, the design holds constant his underlying distaste for construction work and uses within-worker differences in job choices to measure the value of performing the work away from his local social audience. This allows us to estimate the effect of occupation stigma on migration choice of workers.
experimental_design: Households are sampled from villages in the Patna region of Bihar. A short screening module classifies each household by whether any member performs manual or daily-wage labour. Households containing such a worker receive the job-offer module described above; households without one receive a norms module only. Within the job-offer module, three attributes are randomised by computer prior to fieldwork: the sequence in which offers are presented, which single offer becomes binding, and whether the binding offer is implemented as a real referral. Assignments are preloaded into the electronic instrument and are not visible to the enumerator or the respondent before the relevant point in the interview. A secondary component is conducted with respondents aged 21 and above recruited in urban neighbourhoods, to examine whether the same mechanism operates for occupations outside manual labour. Respondents evaluate hypothetical offers for office work and for app-based gig work, and the location at which the gig work would be performed is varied so that exposure to people who know the respondent differs.
experimental_design_details: Take-up is modelled at the offer level: T_ij = α + βN·N_j + βP·P_j + γ·HS_i + δN·(N_j × HS_i) + δP·(P_j × HS_i) + λ·w_ij + φv + εij where T_ij is take-up of offer j by respondent i; N and P indicate the nearby-panchayat and Patna offers with the own-village offer omitted; HS_i indicates high-stigma status (primary: General/OBC versus SC/EBC); w is the offered wage; and φ_v are village fixed effects. Standard errors are clustered by respondent. δN and δP are the primary objects of interest and our hypothesis is that both are greater than zero. δN provides a lower bound on effects of occupational stigma. Pre-specified checks: Within stigmatized castes, the effect should be driven by those who report higher stigma.
intervention: Male manual workers in rural Bihar are presented with a series of real, incentivised job offers for construction work. The offers are described one at a time and the respondent accepts or declines each on its own terms. Offer attributes are varied experimentally across and within respondents. Choices are consequential: at the end of the module one offer is selected at random, and for a randomly chosen subset of respondents that offer is implemented as an actual referral to a contractor at the stated wage. A separate module elicits community norms regarding manual labour from households.

abstract: Anticipatory action (AA) aims to reduce the humanitarian impacts of forecast-based hazards by acting before disasters fully unfold. Effective AA relies on three key elements: pre-agreed forecast-based triggers, pre-agreed activities to be implemented, and pre-agreed financing that can be released when triggers are met. Current evidence suggests that AA has potential to mitigate the negative consequences of drought on individuals, households, and communities, but generating rigorous, causal evidence remains challenging due to short windows between trigger activation and activity implementation. To overcome this challenge and generate more evidence on AA for droughts, OCHA is collaborating with ISDC, WFP and FAO to jointly develop an impact evaluation in Chad. Following the activation of drought triggers in April and May 2026, ISDC is implementing a cluster-randomized controlled trial to estimate the impacts of coordinated AA implemented by FAO and WFP. The primary objective is to causally estimate whether and by how much coordinated AA in response to drought triggers helps households prepare for and better to withstand drought. Specifically, the evaluation examines: (1) the added value of combining unconditional cash transfers (WFP) with seeds (FAO), compared to cash transfers alone; (2) whether providing the same amount of cash as an early lump sum before the planting season leads to better outcomes compared to staggering transfers across the agricultural season; and (3) whether these impacts persist over time and strengthen household resilience to droughts. The evaluation will be implemented as a cluster randomized controlled trial (RCT) across three drought-prone provinces: Bahr El-Gazal, Batha, and Kanem. Villages are sequentially randomized twice. For the first evaluation question, 85 villages were randomized to receive either WFP cash transfers only (43 villages) or combined WFP cash transfers and FAO seed distributions (42 villages), with randomization stratified by department (WFP Cash versus WFP Cash + FAO Seeds). For the second evaluation question, 79 villages (after some villages were merged for implementation reasons) were further randomized to compare two cash transfer modalities: an Early Lump Sum, in which households receive two cash transfers before planting, and Staggered Cash, in which households receive one transfer before the planting season and a second transfer before the harvest (Early Lump Sum versus Staggered Cash). The total amount of cash transferred remains the same across both arms. This design enables the evaluation to separately identify the effects of combining agricultural and financial assistance and the timing of cash transfers across the agricultural season. By embedding a rigorous experimental design within an operational humanitarian response, this study will generate timely evidence on how the composition and timing of AA influence food security, agricultural production, coping strategies, mental health, and household resilience. The findings will inform the design of future drought AA programs and contribute to the growing global evidence base on effective humanitarian preparedness and early action.
experimental_design: The study is designed as a cluster randomized controlled trial with two sequential randomizations across three selected priority provinces: Bahr El-Gazal, Batha, and Kanem. In the first randomization, we test the impacts of Cash + Seeds versus Cash only. 85 villages were randomly assigned to receive: Cash + Seeds (treatment): 42 villages Cash only (comparison): 43 villages The randomization was stratified by Department to ensure balance across geographic locations and agro-climatic conditions. For the second randomization, 12 villages were merged into 6 villages for cash transfer implementation. 79 villages were randomly assigned to receive: Early Lump Sum Cash (2 payments in pre-planting season): 39 villages Staggered Cash (1 payment in pre-planting season + 1 payment in pre-harvest season): 40 villages The second randomization was stratified by the first randomization. The total amount of the cash transferred is the same across both study arms.
intervention: Cash transfers provided by WFP: Unconditional cash transfer worth 48,000 XOF (~USD 85) given to the head of household. Cash transfer framing includes using cash based on needs (food, drought management). Seeds distribution by FAO: Rainfed seeds distribution (vegetables, millet, maize, sorghum, cowpea) and small agricultural tools.

abstract: This study evaluates two school-based approaches to preventing violence against adolescents in Salvador, Brazil. In an RCT with 40 public schools, we compare a gender-norms and masculinities program ("MEN") against a cognitive behavioral therapy-based intervention ("CBT"), relative to a pure control group (N≈3,800 students). Both programs consist of eight weekly activities of about one class period (~50 minutes) delivered to 9th-grade students by trained facilitators over roughly eight weeks. We measure effects on (self-reported) violence, and second-order beliefs about others' behaviors and perceived approval two weeks after the program. To assess spillovers from the program, we also survey 8th-grade students in all 40 schools.
experimental_design: We randomize N=40 public schools in Salvador, stratified within each of 10 school regions (Gerências Regionais), into three arms: MEN (15 schools), CBT (15 schools), and comparison (10 schools). Randomization is stratified within each of the 10 school regions, following: - 8 regions of 4 schools each are randomly assigned to Type A (2 MEN + 1 CBT + 1 comparison) or Type B (1 MEN + 2 CBT + 1 comparison) - 1 region with 3 schools is split 1 MEN / 1 CBT / 1 comparison - 1 region with 5 schools is split 2 MEN / 2 CBT / 1 comparison. This yields 15 MEN + 15 CBT + 10 comparison. 9th graders participate in the activities, and 8th graders respond to the baseline and endline surveys. Note: one treated school has no 9th grade, so 8th graders will receive the activities instead. Within-school spillovers. 8th-grade students receive no activities but are surveyed in all 40 schools at baseline and follow-up. We estimate spillover from treated 9th graders to untreated 8th graders in the same school with a difference-in-differences design (comparing 8th-grade outcomes in treated vs. comparison schools, before vs. after). Network. We collect a rich set of student peer-network measures (friendship, and popularity nominations against a school roster). Heterogeneity cuts. - Student sex - Social-desirability score - Baseline self-reported violence index (incidence and victimization) - (Mis)perceptions of the norms (descriptive and injunctive)
intervention: Two programs, each eight weekly activities of about one class period (~50 minutes), delivered over roughly eight weeks to 9th-grade students by trained facilitators in treated schools: MEN (social norms constraining men and women). Activities on gender stereotypes and masculinities (e.g., "what men are taught to show," debunking gender myths, protecting rather than covering up). Targets the norms and beliefs that sustain violence against girls. CBT (emotional self-regulation and conflict resolution). Activities on identifying and naming emotions, anger management, relaxation/breathing, and structured problem-solving. Targets the self-regulation and conflict-resolution skills that reduce interpersonal aggression. Note: both MEN and CBT have one common activity at the end, which discusses violence against women. Comparison schools receive no activities during the study period and are offered the program in 2027.

abstract: Non-heterosexual identities and attitudes toward homosexuality are commonly measured using direct survey questions, which may be affected by social desirability bias. This study examines the extent of this bias in France using three double list experiments implemented within the nationally representative ELIPSS panel. The experiments measure (i) heterosexual identification, (ii) acceptance of having a gay son, and (iii) acceptance of having a lesbian daughter. Comparing prevalence estimates obtained through indirect and conventional direct questions will provide estimates of the magnitude of response bias. The study will then examine whether response bias varies across respondents’ characteristics, whether acceptance differs according to the gender of the hypothetical child, and whether respondents’ second-order beliefs accurately reflect observed levels of acceptance and are associated with response bias.
experimental_design: This study relies on list experiments, also known as the item count technique, to estimate the prevalence of sensitive characteristics while reducing social desirability bias. Respondents are randomly assigned to either a short-list condition, containing control items, or a long-list condition, which includes the same control items plus one additional sensitive/key item. Instead of asking respondents directly whether the sensitive statement applies to them, list experiments ask respondents to report the total number of statements in the list that are true for them, without indicating which specific statements they endorse. Under random assignment, the average count of true control items is expected to be identical across groups. The difference between the average number of statements reported in the long- and short-list conditions therefore identifies the prevalence of the sensitive characteristic, under the standard assumptions of the list experiment (treatment randomization, no design effect, and no liar). To increase statistical efficiency and strengthen the internal validity of the design, the study implements double list experiments (DLEs). For each key statement, respondents are presented with two different lists of control items (Lists A and B). Half of the respondents receive List A in its short version and List B in its long version, while the other half receive List A in its long version and List B in its short version. Prevalence is estimated separately from each list pair, and the two estimates are subsequently averaged. The study examines three key statements that are phrased so that the potentially stigmatized response corresponds to a negative answer: • KS1: I consider myself to be heterosexual. • KS2: If I had a lesbian daughter, I would accept her without any problem. • KS3: If I had a gay son, I would accept him without any problem. Applying the DLE to each key statement results in a total of six lists: Lists 1A and 1B measure heterosexual identification, Lists 2A and 2B measure acceptance of a lesbian daughter, and Lists 3A and 3B measure acceptance of a gay son.

abstract: This research project aims at investigating the effect of unconditional cooperation on monetary contributions to public good. According to existing evidence on cooperative types, especially based on influential works such as Fischbacher et al, 2001; Gachter, 2006 and Fischbacher and Gachter, 2006, individuals are mainly classified into two categories that is conditional cooperators and free riders. Conditional cooperators are individuals who contribute based on the observation of the others’ contributory levels or based on the belief that the others will contribute. Free riders are by definition individuals who never contribute and therefore reap the benefits of the others’ commitment and efforts. These represent the two most common cooperative types. Less observed cooperative types are the triangular cooperator, who are individuals who contribute only until certain levels and then gradually or suddenly withdraw from cooperation, and the unconditional cooperator (Thoni and Volk, 2018). Unconditional cooperators are individuals who provide constant positive levels of contributions in public goods, regardless of the level provided by other peers. These types have been observed and detected also in other studies (Hermann and Thoni, 2009; Thoni and Volk, 2018). The composition of social groups deeply affects cooperation levels. Based on existing literature on cooperation in public good games, within groups cooperation is expected to decline over time not just because of the presence of pure free riders but also because of conditional cooperators. In fact, according to Fischbacher and Gachter, conditional cooperators are imperfect in the sense that they do not tend to reciprocate in a proportional way. If they observe a certain level of monetary commitment from other peers, they give a little less. This eventually leads to general free riding for what regards public good outcomes. This study draws from existing evidence on cooperative types and focus on a rare type of cooperative agent, that is the unconditional cooperator, and its effect on groups’ trend in cooperation levels. We argue that unconditional cooperators may serve as social anchors for other peers, especially conditional cooperators, and their presence in groups may alter the tendency of cooperation to decline over time. To the best of our knowledge, no previous study has focused on the specific effect of positive unconditional giving on groups’ cooperative trajectories
experimental_design: The laboratory experiment consists of a two-stage design. In the first stage the participants are asked to fill in the Contribution Table from Fischbacher et al, 2001 where they are asked to indicate for each average contribution level of other group members how much they want to contribute to the public good. In this way we elicit individual preferences for cooperation. This subsequently allows us to analyze results from the second stage by cooperative type. In the second stage participants are randomly assigned to control and treatment sessions. In each session, participants are randomly matched in groups of 4 people, have the same endowment of z tokens and play a repeated public good game with a certain marginal per capita return MPCR (the return for 1 token contributed by a participant) for n rounds. Groups compositions are constant over rounds as well as the parameters z, n and MPCR (which need to be discussed of course). At the end of each round all members of a group are told the other members’ contributions. Treatment sessions differ from control sessions by the way groups are composed. While participants in the control sessions are assigned to groups randomly, participants in the treatment sessions are matched according to the cooperative preferences elicited in the first stage. Specifically, participants classified as conditional cooperators, unconditional cooperators, free riders, or other behavioral types are allocated to groups with predetermined compositions. Depending on the treatment, groups may consist of members with similar cooperative preferences (e.g., all conditional cooperators, all free riders, or all unconditional cooperators) or deliberately heterogeneous compositions combining different behavioral types. This design allows us to examine how the composition of cooperative preferences within a group influences contribution dynamics, the evolution of cooperation over repeated interactions, and overall public good provision relative to randomly formed groups.

abstract: Do individuals remediate negative externalities out of forward-looking concern for outcomes or backward-looking feelings of personal responsibility? I design a lab experiment that disentangles these mechanisms by holding present restoration consequences constant while exogenously varying the extent to which past harm was self-caused or externally generated. By systematically varying the unit price of restoration, I identify individual willingness to pay to restore self-caused versus other-caused harm. Finally, I estimate a structural random utility model via Maximum Likelihood to characterize preference heterogeneity across selfish, purely altruistic, purely clean-slate, and altruistic types who exhibit a responsibility premium for self-caused harm.
experimental_design: Participants make incentivized choices affecting their monetary earnings and a real-world charity selected at the beginning of the experiment. Negative externalities are operationalized as the cancellation of charitable donations. The experiment proceeds in three main parts: Stage 1 (Harm Generation): Participants complete a series of choices between increasing personal monetary earnings and preventing negative externalities (cancelled charitable donations). Stage 2 (Harm Restoration): Participants face choices where they can pay to remediate cancelled donations. The origin of the harm (self-caused in Stage 1 versus externally generated pre-existing harm) and the unit price of restoration are systematically varied to identify willingness to pay across harm types. Post-Experiment Survey: Participants complete a survey eliciting personal moral norms regarding harm restoration, self-reported decision reasoning, and baseline attitudes toward the selected charity.
experimental_design_details: Participants make decisions that have consequences for themselves and a charity they select at the beginning of the experiment. The negative externality corresponds to items (planting of trees, distribution of school lunches or provision of vaccines) which will not be provided by the charity. Stage 1 (Harm Generation): After general instructions, participants face 7 binary decision situations in which they choose between increasing their personal earnings by cancelling charity item donations or foregoing earnings to ensure the items are donated. Stage 2 (Harm Restoration): Participants receive Stage 2 instructions and face a randomized sequence of 58 decision situations. They can pay to restore item donations that were self-cancelled in Stage 1, externally cancelled (pre-existing harm), or both. Across these decisions, the unit price to restore harm is systematically varied to measure willingness to pay. Post-Experiment Survey: Participants complete a questionnaire eliciting personal norms regarding the appropriateness of restoring self-caused versus external harm, self-reported qualitative decision reasoning, and baseline preferences for the charity
intervention: A participant selects a charity at the beginning of the experiment from a given list and receives instructions for the decisions she will make in this experiment. Then he faces a sequence of decision situations with varying final consequences: 7 decision situations in the first stage and 58 decision situations in the second stage (random order). The first stage serves to generate the negative externality which can then be restored in the second stage. In addition, the participant observes existing harm whose origin she does not know ex-ante.

abstract: Many employees contribute too little to their employer-sponsored retirement plans to obtain the full employer match, even when doing so would generate a large and immediate financial return. A broader research project examines whether this behavior reflects informational frictions—such as uncertainty about how much to save or misunderstanding of the employer match—or frictions associated with engaging in and completing the contribution decision. In a field experiment with administrative contribution outcomes, personalized savings guidance and match clarification changed employees’ reported beliefs but did not measurably increase contributions, whereas a small, same-day engagement reward increased actual contributions. Because that field intervention combined a monetary reward with a same-day eligibility window, it does not separately reveal whether the response required such a short deadline. This individually randomized online experiment provides supplementary mechanism evidence by comparing a common recommendation to save more with a hypothetical $20 Amazon gift-card offer for increasing a 401(k) contribution by the end of today or within two weeks. Employed U.S. adults imagine that they earn $50,000, currently contribute 2 percent of salary, and can change their contribution in a few minutes. The experiment tests whether a reward with a longer eligibility window increases intended action during that window and whether shortening the window to the end of today accelerates intended action into the present.
experimental_design: This is an individually randomized, three-arm online vignette experiment. Every participant sees one condition and answers one required behavioral-intention question. The two reward conditions differ only in the eligibility window attached to an otherwise identical hypothetical $20 Amazon gift card.
experimental_design_details: Sample frame and Prolific eligibility • Recruited through Prolific. • Age 25 through 55, inclusive. • Current residence in the United States. • Currently employed full-time or part-time. • Fluent in English. • At least 20 completed Prolific submissions. • Prolific approval rate of at least 98 percent. • Prolific will be configured for one submission per participant. Preregistered exclusions and duplicate handling • Survey preview, researcher test, and other nonparticipant records. • Participants who do not consent or who withdraw their data when an applicable withdrawal mechanism is available. • Submissions specifically identified by Prolific as fraudulent, automated, or otherwise invalid under Prolific’s integrity procedures. • Qualtrics reCAPTCHA human score below 0.5 or missing. A score exactly equal to 0.5 will be retained. • Duplicate Qualtrics records from the same Prolific ID. If more than one completed record exists, the earliest completed record will be retained and later completed records will be removed. If only one record contains the required outcome, that completed record will be retained. • Records with no valid randomized condition or no recorded primary-outcome response because of a technical or incomplete submission.
intervention: Common scenario All participants are asked to imagine that they are employed by ABC Company, earn $50,000 per year, and currently contribute 2 percent of salary to the ABC Company 401(k). Contributions are described as automatically deducted from pre-tax pay over the year and invested in a diversified retirement fund. Participants are told that they can review and change their contribution at any time through the ABC benefits portal and that logging in and making a change takes only a few minutes. All participants then receive the same statement: “You receive an email from ABC Company recommending that you save more for retirement by increasing your contribution to the ABC 401(k).” Randomized conditions 1. Baseline: Participants receive only the common recommendation. The condition does not mention a reward or the absence of a reward. 2. Reward by end of today: Participants additionally read, “To encourage you to take action, ABC is offering you a $20 Amazon gift card if you log in to the benefits portal and increase your contribution by the end of today. The gift card will be emailed after you submit the increase.” 3. I would increase my contribution today. 2. I would increase my contribution in the near future—sometime between tomorrow and 14 days from now. 3. I would increase my contribution later—sometime between 15 days and six months from now. 4. I would not increase my contribution within the next six months.

abstract: This clustered randomised control trial tests the effectiveness of production system and value chain development for safe and agroecologically produced vegetables in the peri-urban zone of Hanoi, Vietnam. The intervention is planned to be rolled out between November 2026 and August 2027 and and will be carried out jointly by extension specialists from Vietnam National University of Agriculture (VNUA) and experts from selected retailers in close collaboration with 46 lead farmers from 23 villages, who will receive in-depth coaching. Contents will be shared by the lead farmers in each intervention village through a demo plot as well as videos and posters with practical advice on agroecological practices, cooperative organisation, and marketing opportunities. The impact will be evaluated jointly by researchers from VNUA and FiBL under the Vietnam-Swiss funded Agroeconfirm project. The primary outcomes for evaluation are the adoption of agroecological practices (e.g. legume and straw mulching, reduced tillage, biochar application) and farmers' attitudes towards cooperative membership and certification. Secondary outcomes include agroecology performance measured though FAO's Tool for Agroecology Performance Evaluation (TAPE), labour inputs, and marketing channels. The trial is powered to detect adoption effects of at least 10 percentage points for the selected practices, which have current adoption levels below 15%. Baseline data was collected in June 2026 and endline data will be collected in December 2027 from 46 villages (15-16 farmers per village). The study area includes Ha Noi, Hung Yen and Ninh Binh provinces. We sampled from a list of villages with at least 50 farm households that practice all-year vegetable production.
experimental_design: The experiment is carried out in the peri-urban zone of Hanoi, Vietnam covering three provinces. It is clustered at the village level, with 23 villages randomly assigned to the control group and 23 villages randomly assigned to the treatment group. The focus on villages with a sufficient amount of producers who engage in year-round vegetable production led to a concentration of eligible villages in some parts of the study area. Therefore, we implemented a 1000m distance rule in our randomisation. Balance checks confirmed appropriate balance among 27 selected variables at baseline.

The practices include legume and straw mulching, reduced tillage and biochar application. Potential buyers from shops for safe and organic vegetables will engage for information on value chain partnerships between retailers and farmers, including details on cooperative formation, post-harvest vegetable storage and transport, traceability requirements and market channels.

abstract: Public works programmes (PWPs) are one of the most popular forms of anti-poverty policy around the world. There is growing recognition of their short-run / contemporaneous benefits in rural settings, but evidence of longer-term / post-programme effects in urban settings is scarce. We study the City of Cape Town's Expanded Public Works Programme (EPWP), which randomly selects beneficiaries for short-term work opportunities. Surveying beneficiaries with programme experience up to over ten years ago, we assess whether the programme improves long-term outcomes, including employment, earnings, skills and mental health, and how these vary over job characteristics and over recipient characteristics, including gender.
experimental_design: We exploit the randomized allocation of public works jobs to unemployed jobseekers to study the causal effects of the program on employment and mental health outcomes. Since 2013, the City of Cape Town has allocated EPWP opportunities using a centralized algorithm that randomly selects workers from a database of unemployed jobseekers. Project managers at the City set up projects and hire workers from the database. For each work opportunity on a project, the manager can define basic eligibility criteria, such as address, minimum educational qualification, or disability status. Jobseekers are randomly selected from the (usually larger) pool of jobseekers satisfying these criteria, who are then returned on a randomly-ranked waitlist. Managers then call workers on the list to offer them work on the project along with relevant details (pay, duration, location, etc.) The randomized waitlist structure means that different individuals have different probabilities of being called with work offers, which offer causal analysis of the treatment effects of the program.
