relevant_papers: Abstract: We provide experimental evidence on when subject specialization improves learning in elementary schools. In a cluster-randomized experiment across 60 Japanese public elementary schools, experienced part-time specialists in mathematics or science were assigned while preserving the homeroom structure. Science specialists raise science achievement by 0.18 SD and mathematics by 0.13 SD; mathematics specialists yield no gains. This asymmetry reflects comparative advantage: student achievement is strongly linked to homeroom teachers\textquotesingle{} subject expertise, and specialists generate gains only where such expertise is scarce. In mathematics, specialists crowd out homeroom teachers who are themselves math-specialized; in science, where fewer than 8 percent of homeroom teachers report subject expertise, specialists fill a genuine skill gap. We find no increase in coordination costs and no deterioration in teacher-student relationships. The intervention delivers gains at roughly one-twelfth the cost of class size reduction. Specialization improves learning when its design aligns with teacher comparative advantage and subject-specific skill constraints. abstract: Health and education, in theory, could have large complementarities, with improvements in one yielding productivity gains in the other. Yet, experimental evidence on these complementarities remains limited. We conduct a factorial experiment, randomizing school meals access -- one of the most popular health interventions among governments -- alongside an effective educational approach, targeting instruction. We randomize 125 primary schools in Zambia, a context in which both of these interventions are scaling nationwide. Our factorial design enables us to identify a) the effect of school meals, b) encouragement to implement targeted instruction, and c) effects of school meals combined with targeted instruction. We identify effects and complementarities on several health and education outcomes: children's attendance and learning outcomes as well as their health and food security. Complementarities among these interventions could be consequential. If a child is receiving an education, but hungry, they might not be able to learn; vice-versa, if a child is well-fed, but the quality of education is low, the returns to school meals could be marginal. We analyze cost-effectiveness and welfare effects of each intervention alone, and when combined.
experimental_design: Our study sample includes 125 government primary schools in three districts within Luapula Province slated for the scale up of the HGSM program: Mwense, Chembe, and Samfya. Within each school, we randomly sample ten grade three children to participate in our baseline survey between November and December of 2025. Following our baseline survey, schools were randomly assigned to either be enrolled in the HGSM program immediately or to be enrolled in January 2027 (our control). This randomization was stratified by district and whether schools were located in an urban or rural area. Following the initial randomization, our study undertook a second randomization to assign schools to recieve the teacher incentive program described above. This second randomization is crossed with our initial randomization, and schools are chosen within strata based on their district, urban or rural location, and their HGSM group assignment. In total, this results in four, roughly equal-sized intervention arms: 1. Pure Control - Schools that will be enrolled in the HGSM program in January 2027 and will not receive the incentive intervention. 2. HGSM-Only - Schools enrolled in the HGSM program in early 2026 who will not receive the incentive intervention. 3. Incentive-only - Schools that will be enrolled in the HGSM program in January 2027 and will receive the incentive intervention. 4. HGSM + Incentives - Schools enrolled in the HGSM program in early 2026 who will receive the incentive intervention.
intervention: The Home Grown School Meals Program Our trial is embedded in the scale-up of Zambia's HGSM program in Zambia's Luapula Province. The program, already present in each of Zambia's ten provinces, provides participating schools with maize flour from the National Food Reserve Agency, together with funding to purchase perishable items such as beans on the spot market. The intent of the program is for schools to provide each child one mid-day meal each school day that consists of at least a staple grain and a legume. The program is being scaled nationally with support from the World Food Programme and the World Bank, which creates the opportunity to randomize the scale-up given logistical constraints that prevent immediate saturation. Within Mwense, Chembe, and Samfya districts, we study 63 schools that were early receivers of the program, compared to 62 schools that were randomly chosen to be enrolled in the program beginning in January of 2027. The Incentive Intervention Our incentive intervention is designed to provide teachers with a small amount of additional compensation for every TaRL session they hold. The intention is both to improve teachers' motivation and overcome any financial barriers associated with the additional scope of work that TaRL places on teachers. To do so, our intervention asks TaRL teachers to send in photographs of their learner-level register for each class that they send. In exchange, they receive 20 ZMW (approx. 1 USD) worth of mobile airtime, which serves as reimbursement for the airtime used to send the photographs, plus a small reimbursement. Teachers are eligible to receive up to three incentives per week, and payments are made bi-weekly. As such, the maximum payment a teacher can receive in a month is 260 ZMW (Approx. 13 USD). Teacher Interface. To track and administer the intervention, our study partners with the service provider engageSpark to create an automated chatbot for teachers to engage with and submit photos to. The application is administered through WhatsApp and is primarily teacher-prompted but sends reminders to teachers who have not submitted any photos within a week. One challenge of administering a WhatsApp chatbot in a setting such as Luapula is that many teachers will not have smartphones that engage with the chatbot. To address this challenge, given that we can verify that at least one teacher in every school has a smartphone, our intervention will assign teachers unique identifiers that the chatbot will prompt them for before they can submit their photos. Keeping such a backend roster will allow teachers to submit photos through a colleague's phone, but receive the airtime incentive to their own. Verification. The key challenge for an intervention that aims to incentivize teachers to hold class in a cost-effective manner is verifying that classes have indeed been held without visiting schools. Our intervention has landed on the learning-level register because it is a uniform document across government schools that tracks students' attendance on a daily basis. However, an intervention that provides incentives based on photographs of a form naturally creates perverse incentives for fraud through falsified records or photos that are unrelated to the level register entirely. Additionally, we expect to collect over 9,000 photos over the course of the intervention, and dedicating staff time to verify every register would reduce the cost-effectiveness of the intervention. As such, rather than verifying all photos, we will randomly select a 20 percent subset of photos to be manually verified by a staff member at our research partner, VVOB. This initial check will make sure that photos are 1) of the learning level register and 2) current and relevant to the class in question. In addition to these high-level checks, 25 percent of the subset (so 5 percent of the full sample) will be additionally verified via phone calls to the head teacher at the school. For any submission that is found to be fraudulent or otherwise unsatisfactory through this verification process, the teacher will be informed that their submission has not been accepted and will be given a chance to resubmit. Those who fail to resubmit a satisfactory level-register photo will not receive the incentive for that submission.

abstract: This paper evaluates whether targeted training enables workers to translate access to generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) into improved performance in a relational job. We conduct a cluster-randomized controlled trial involving more than 700 relationship managers across approximately 300 branches of a large global bank in Mexico and Spain. All participants retain access to GenAI tools, while managers in treated branches receive a short, intensive training program designed around their day-to-day workflows. This design isolates the effect of targeted training relative to GenAI access alone. Using individual-level data on GenAI usage, administrative processes, client interactions, commercial opportunities, customer satisfaction, and incentive-based performance measures, we examine whether training increases the adoption and sophistication of GenAI use and whether it improves productivity. We investigate two principal mechanisms: the automation or streamlining of administrative tasks, which may free time for client-facing activities, and the augmentation of client interactions through better preparation and more tailored proposals. We also study whether effects differ according to workers’ prior performance, age, experience, previous GenAI use, and risk-taking profiles. The study contributes to the emerging literature on workplace GenAI by examining its deployment in a real-world relational occupation combining analytical, administrative, and interpersonal tasks. It also provides evidence on whether brief training can convert widespread access to GenAI into measurable organizational value and whether it narrows or widens performance differences across workers.
experimental_design: The study is a cluster-randomized controlled trial conducted with relationship managers at a large global bank. Participating bank branches are assigned either to a treatment group that receives a short, intensive GenAI training program or to a control group that continues business as usual. Control group branches are expected to receive the training about six months later. Relationship managers in both groups retain access to the bank’s existing GenAI tools. Randomization is conducted at the branch level because relationship managers within the same branch work closely together and frequently exchange information. This design reduces potential contamination between treatment and control participants. Outcomes will be measured using internal administrative, CRM, GenAI usage, customer-experience, and performance data collected before and during an experimental period of approximately four months.
experimental_design_details: The study includes more than 700 relationship managers working across approximately 300 branches in Mexico and Spain. The intervention will be delivered in person, with training planned for August in Mexico and September in Spain. Branches assigned to treatment receive approximately three hours of targeted GenAI training, while branches assigned to control retain access to GenAI but receive no additional training during the experimental period. The training will be offered to the control group after the experimental period. The main analysis will compare outcomes for relationship managers in treatment and control branches according to their randomized assignment. Where available, pre-intervention measures of each outcome will be used to improve precision and account for baseline differences. Standard errors will account for clustering at the branch level. The study will examine effects on both intermediate and final outcomes. Intermediate outcomes include GenAI adoption, sophistication of use, administrative-process duration, time allocation, client interactions, and commercial-opportunity progression. Final outcomes include conversion rates, customer satisfaction, client-experience indicators, sales and value generation, customer acquisition, and risk-adjusted profitability. We will examine heterogeneity by baseline commercial performance, age, tenure, prior GenAI use, experience at the bank, gender, and baseline risk-taking profile. Because assignment occurs at the branch level, diffusion among workers within treated branches is considered part of the treatment environment rather than contamination. Potential spillovers from intensive users, colleagues, and branch managers will be examined descriptively.
intervention: The intervention consists of a short, intensive, in-person training program designed to improve relationship managers’ (RMs) ability to use generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) effectively in their daily work. The program lasts about three hours and focuses on practical applications of GenAI to the administrative, analytical, and client-facing tasks performed by relationship managers. The intervention will be implemented in two different countries (Spain and Mexico) in August, September and October in collaboration with a large Global Bank, BBVA. Relationship managers assigned to the control group retain access to the bank’s existing GenAI tools but do not receive the additional training during the experimental period. The intervention therefore evaluates the effect of targeted GenAI training relative to GenAI access alone. The training will be offered to the control group after the experimental period /about six months later).
mde_text: A provisional calculation based on 700 relationship managers distributed across 300 branches, equal assignment between treatment and control, a two-sided significance level of 5 percent, statistical power of 80 percent, and an intracluster correlation of 0.10 yields a minimum detectable effect of approximately 0.23 standard deviations, equivalent to approximately 23 percent of the outcome’s standard deviation. This estimate does not incorporate precision gains from controlling for baseline outcomes. The final minimum detectable effect will be recalculated using the definitive roster of participating branches and relationship managers, the actual distribution of managers across branches, and pre-intervention estimates of the intracluster correlation, outcome variance, and correlation between baseline and follow-up measures.

abstract: Does anticipation of discrimination, beliefs individuals have about the behavior of others toward them, affect trust and cooperation? We develop a novel design to isolate the role of anticipation of discrimination in cooperation dilemmas using a trust game. We capture the effect of anticipation as the double difference between the amount transferred by trustors to outgroup vs. ingroup trustees when the trustor's own identity is revealed vs. concealed. We conduct this study in UK and US in the context of affective polarization. In addition, we implement the trustee's decision using the strategy method. This allows us to study whether trustees hold taste for discrimination. We combine our game with survey measures of trust and affective polarization, and also collect data on beliefs. Finally, we also aim to implement an information treatment to test if anticipation disappears.
experimental_design: we conduct a trust game with a 2x2 design: identities revealed vs concealed and ingroup vs outgroup. These conditions are randomly assigned. We then give information on the average of conditional responses of trustees to trustors to see if anticipation still survives.

abstract: In this project, we plan to implement a large-scale randomized controlled trial (RCT) that provides newly elected mayors in Peru with training in managerial skills and democratic practices. The intervention, which will target mayors elected in October 2026, seeks to address shortcomings in local public service delivery and citizen dissatisfaction with democracy. Our experimental design will allow us to study three distinct questions: (1) whether strengthening public management skills enables mayors to improve the provision of public goods and services; (2) whether increasing mayors' knowledge of democratic institutions and practices, as well as their ability to negotiate with the political opposition, improves local governance and citizen satisfaction with democracy; and (3) whether managerial skills and democratic and institutional knowledge act as complements or substitutes in improving public service delivery and governance.
experimental_design: This study is a three-arm randomized controlled trial with treatment assignment at the mayor/municipality level. Newly elected mayors apply to participate through an online application, which also provides baseline and screening information. Applicants who satisfy the eligibility criteria are eligible for random assignment. Eligible mayors are assigned to one of two treatment groups or to a control group. Approximately 200 mayors will receive training, divided approximately equally between the Managerial Skills treatment (T1) and the Managerial Skills + Democratic Practices treatment (T2). Mayors assigned to the control group will receive no training during the study period.
experimental_design_details: We expect to receive applications from approximately 400 mayors, although the final size of the eligible applicant pool will depend on program demand and eligibility screening. We plan to train 200 mayors, with 100 assigned to T1 and 100 assigned to T2. Eligible mayors who are not randomly assigned to either of the two training arms, T1 or T2, will constitute the broader control group and will receive no training during the study period. From this broader control group, we will randomly select a subsample of approximately 100 municipalities for additional primary data collection. This control subsample will include, among other data-collection activities, the municipalities in which we will conduct the citizen survey that forms part of our evaluation strategy, as described in subsequent fields.
intervention: The intervention consists of a training program for newly elected municipal mayors in Peru, implemented in partnership with two local expert NGOs: one specializing in public management and the other in democratic practices. The program follows a hybrid format, combining three to four days of in-person training with additional online sessions between November 2026 and January 2027. All costs associated with participation are covered for mayors, including travel and accommodation for the in-person sessions and costs associated with participation in the online components. The intervention includes two treatment arms: T1 – Managerial Skills: Mayors receive training in public management, covering topics such as leadership, mayoral transitions, human resource management, civil service recruitment, and financial reporting and control. T2 – Managerial Skills + Democratic Practices: Mayors receive the same managerial training as those assigned to T1, along with additional training in democratic practices. Topics include decentralization, democratic principles, lawmaking, deliberation, and constructive dialogue with the political opposition and civil society. Mayors assigned to the control group receive no training during the study period. After the study concludes, control-group mayors will have access to recorded training modules, after any information identifying other participants has been anonymized.

abstract: This study tests whether human decision-makers in a simulated organ allocation setting deviate from rational behavior when given discretion to reorder a transplant waitlist ("out-of-sequence" offers). Participants act as an organ allocation agent choosing whether to list a donor organ and, if listed, whether to promote identified high-acceptance-probability candidates ahead of their default waitlist position. The design varies the amount of information about candidate types (none, partial, or full) across three simulated organ-quality markets (high, median, and low quality), each calibrated so a rational, profit-maximizing benchmark strategy is well defined. The study measures whether participants over-reorder the queue (promoting candidates beyond the point that improves placement) or over-list organs (listing when a rational benchmark would decline), relative to the model's optimal predictions.
experimental_design: We will use a mixed between/within design. Participants are randomly assigned to one of three simulated "market" conditions (manipulated between subjects) and complete a sequence of incentivized allocation decisions under four information conditions (manipulated within subjects) that vary how much candidate-level information is revealed before the decision. The within-subjects conditions are presented as contiguous blocks of five periods each (20 periods total), with block order counterbalanced across participants. In each period, participants make an entry decision (whether to process a simulated case) and, conditional on entry, a costly sequencing decision over candidates. Participant behavior is compared against an optimal benchmark and against pre-specified alternative decision rules, to test (a) whether participants take the costly action more than the benchmark prescribes, (b) whether they enter more than the benchmark prescribes, and (c) whether any such departures are stable across the session or attenuate with within-session experience (order and learning effects).
experimental_design_details: Participants are randomly assigned to 1 of 3 market arms (High: p_H=0.75/p_L=0.57; Median: p_H=0.60/p_L=0.35; Low: p_H=0.50/p_L=0.15). Within their assigned market, participants are assigned round-robin to one of four block-order sequences: Sequence 1: None-Quarter-Full-Half; Sequence 2: Quarter-Half-None-Full; Sequence 3: Half-Full-Quarter-None; Sequence 4: Full-None-Half-Quarter. Each block is 5 periods under a fixed information condition; candidates are drawn each period from 6 equally likely type orderings of 2 high-type/2 low-type candidates (N=4), with information revealing 0, 1, 2, or 4 types (logical deduction applied when both revealed types are low). Subjects complete a post-task incentivized risk elicitation and demographics questionnaire. In addition to the three main overshoot hypotheses (by market), we also have three order-effect hypotheses: (H-Order 1) over-re-ordering/over-listing declines from period 1 to period 5 within a block (within-block learning); (H-Order 2) overshoot in a given information condition is smaller when that condition's block falls later in the session, i.e., in a later ordinal position (position/experience effect); (H-Order 3) prior exposure to Full information reduces subsequent overshoot in later blocks, with the sharpest contrast between subjects who see Full first (Sequence 4) versus last (Sequence 2) (directional carryover/'Full-first teaches discipline'); (H-Order 4) carryover is asymmetric (information-rich blocks discipline later information-poor blocks more than the reverse), which would imply the pooled information gradient understates naive overshoot; first-block-only behavior is analyzed separately as the cleanest measure of unconditioned overshoot.
intervention: Participants make a series of incentivized decisions in the role of an organ allocation agent. In each round, they decide whether to list a simulated donor organ and, if listed, whether and how to reorder a 4-candidate waitlist before extending offers. The amount of information they have about which candidates are likely to accept the organ is varied (none, partial, or full), and the underlying organ quality is varied (high, median, or low).

We also are interested in how the order of the information condition leads to differential learning.

abstract: This study evaluates whether access to a natural-language large language model assistant improves consumer decision-making and scam avoidance in simulated online second-hand marketplaces. Adult participants recruited through Prolific will complete nine marketplace choice tasks. In each task, participants will evaluate five listings for a standardized used consumer electronic product and must select the listing they perceive to be the best available purchase. Participants will be randomly assigned at the individual level to one of two conditions: an AI-assistance treatment condition or a no-assistance control condition. Participants in the treatment condition will be permitted to consult an LLM-based assistant of their choosing while evaluating the listings. Participants in the control condition will evaluate listings generated through the same prespecified procedures without access to an assistant or other external resources. Listings will differ in prespecified characteristics associated with transaction risk, including seller reputation, urgency language, implausible discounts, off-platform communication or transaction requests, poor product photographs, and unsecured payment methods. The study is designed to determine whether AI assistance causes consumers to respond to these signals more similarly to a benchmark sample of hired scam experts. The observed primary outcome is whether each displayed listing is selected. A conditional logistic-regression model will estimate the effects of the prespecified listing flags for consumers assigned to AI assistance, consumers assigned to the no-AI control condition, and the expert benchmark sample while accounting for the one-of-five choice structure of each task. Average marginal effects on listing-selection probability will be the preferred common-scale representation. For each flag, the analysis will test whether the average marginal effect differs between AI-assisted consumers, control consumers, and experts. These comparisons will indicate whether AI assistance shifts consumer responses toward the pattern observed among experts. Conditional-logit coefficients will be retained as a secondary representation. Secondary outcomes include expert-consistent choice, decision confidence, decision time, assistant use, and prespecified treatment heterogeneity by marketplace experience, product familiarity, prior AI use, and other participant characteristics. The principal consumer sample will contain approximately 100 participants, randomized approximately equally between the two conditions. The study will be administered through Qualtrics, with consumers recruited through Prolific and experts recruited through Upwork. The expert sample is a nonrandomized benchmark group rather than a third treatment condition.
experimental_design: The principal experiment is an individually randomized, two-arm online experiment. Each consumer will complete nine marketplace choice tasks via Qualtrics on a fictional online retailer, ClaCo.com. Three tasks will involve a Nintendo 3DS, three will involve a Lenovo ThinkPad laptop, and three will involve a Dell P2417H monitor. Each task will display five listings, and participants must select exactly one listing. Listings will be drawn from product-specific pools of 128 prespecified listing variants. Each listing represents a particular combination of prespecified listing flags, such that listings may differ from one another in the number and types of flags they contain. Within each task, participants will compare the five displayed listings as a choice set and select the listing they judge to be the best option overall. The analysis will use the exact flag names and definitions contained in the final listing-level coding database. Current flag categories include seller reputation, urgency language, implausible discount cues, off-platform communication or transaction requests, poor product photographs, and unsecured payment methods. For each task, Qualtrics will display a randomized subset of five listings from the relevant 128-listing product pool. The selected listing will be identified through its fixed answer-choice recode value. The randomized viewing-order data will also be exported so that the identities and display positions of all five listings shown to each participant can be reconstructed. The same listing-generation procedure will be used in both consumer treatment arms. Experts will evaluate listings drawn from the same underlying product-specific pools but will complete more choice tasks than consumer participants in order to improve the precision of the expert benchmark estimates. Expert responses will be used to estimate benchmark relationships between listing flags and purchase decisions.
intervention: Consumer participants will be randomly assigned to one of two conditions. Participants assigned to the AI-assistance condition will be permitted to use a large language model (LLM) assistant of their choosing while completing the marketplace choice tasks and may interact with that assistant as they wish. Participants assigned to the control condition will complete the same marketplace choice tasks without the use of AI assistance or other external information sources. All other aspects of the choice environment and listing-generation procedure will be held constant across the two consumer conditions.

abstract: This study examines the long-run effects of two active labour market interventions implemented among young jobseekers in Addis Ababa in 2014-2015. One intervention subsidised transport for job search. The second provided skills screening, certificates reporting participants' performance on a set of tests, and guidance on using the certificates in job applications. The 2026 follow-up measures participants' current employment, earnings and job characteristics and reconstructs their employment, earnings, training and non-work histories since the original experiment. We will estimate long-run effects on current welfare, productivity and human capital, and cumulative career outcomes. We will also estimate spillover effects on individuals who were not offered an intervention but lived in clusters in which other sampled jobseekers were offered one.
experimental_design: The original experiment used two levels of randomization. Geographic clusters were assigned to transport-subsidy, skills-screening, or control arms. Within treatment clusters, eligible jobseekers were randomly selected to receive the assigned intervention. The 2026 long-run follow-up covers the transport group, the screening group, the pure control group, and untreated jobseekers living in transport or screening clusters. The latter groups allow us to estimate spillover effects. The study builds on AEARCTR-0000911.
experimental_design_details: The original sample contained 4,059 jobseekers in 234 geographic clusters. For the 2026 follow-up, the intended sample contains 3,052 people in 178 clusters: 774 assigned the transport subsidy (group 1), 768 assigned skills screening and certification (group 2), 823 in pure control clusters (group 5), 500 untreated people in transport clusters (group 6), and 187 untreated people in screening clusters (group 7). Groups 3 and 4, which were assigned to job fairs, are not included. Transport-cluster treatment saturation was randomized at 20, 40, 75, or 90 percent; screening-cluster saturation was 80 percent. Individual assignment was blocked by education and rerandomized to improve balance. This registration is being filed during the 2026 follow-up. Partial data collected before registration have been used to check questionnaire implementation, construct variables, assess missingness, and run exploratory treatment-effect estimates. The registered analysis will use the completed follow-up sample.
intervention: The study follows up on two active labour market interventions implemented among young jobseekers in Addis Ababa in 2014-2015. The first reimbursed transport costs for job search. The second provided skills tests, certificates reporting test performance, and guidance on using the certificates in job applications.

primary_outcome_explanation: EW1 is monthly wage earnings plus the monthly equivalent of bonuses, overtime pay and other employer payments received during the previous 12 months, plus monthly self-employment profits. Respondents without current work receive zero. EW2 equals one when the respondent currently holds a wage job with either a written fixed-duration agreement or a written agreement of undetermined duration, and zero otherwise. EW3 is an Optimus index with 11 fixed components: (1) permanent wage work; (2) a written agreement of undetermined duration; (3) expected tenure of at least five years or until retirement; (4) employer pension contributions; (5) employer health insurance; (6) severance protection; (7) workers' compensation or injury insurance; (8) paid sick leave; (9) paid annual leave; (10) paid maternity or paternity leave; and (11) reliable pay. These components equal zero for respondents without current wage work. PH1 is an Optimus index with 10 fixed components: (1) any formal training during the previous ten years; (2) number of training programmes; (3) total months in formal training; (4) any useful skill reported from formal training; (5) any useful skill reported from formal education; (6) any useful skill reported from work experience; and, for one past wage job selected at random by the survey software during the interview, (7) employer-provided training; (8) weeks of training; (9) a portable certificate; and (10) mentoring or informal training from senior colleagues. PH2 is one measure of the congruence between workers' skills and the jobs or occupations they enter. The exact measure will be specified after treatment-blind assessment of which occupational categories and worker characteristics can be measured reliably in the data collected before registration. PH3 is an Optimus index with 12 fixed components: (1) skill or training level required by the current wage job; (2) reading and writing at work; (3) arithmetic at work; (4) English use at work; (5) share of work time using a computer; (6) promotion by the current employer; (7) responsibility for at least one other worker; (8) share of current wage-job tasks spent on supervision or coordination; (9) mean within-spell change in real log wages across wage-job spells; and, for one past wage job selected at random by the survey software during the interview, (10) an automatic wage increase with experience; (11) a performance-related wage increase; and (12) applying for promotion. CW1 is the sum of monthly wage earnings and self-employment profits from the first-endline interview through the 2026 interview. CW2 is the number of observed months in wage work, self-employment or farming divided by the number of observed months. CW3 is an Optimus index with three fixed components: (1) the negative of the share of observed months in involuntary non-work; (2) the negative of the number of adverse wage-job or business exits; and (3) the share of observed months spent in wage work with a written agreement. All index components will be oriented so that higher values represent better outcomes. We will construct the Optimus indices following Anderson and Magruder (2022, Highly Powered Analysis Plans, NBER Working Paper 29843). Their procedure uses sample splitting to estimate weights that combine the fixed component outcomes and then applies those weights to held-out observations. Component definitions, sample means and estimated index weights will be documented. Conventional inverse-covariance and equal-weight indices will also be reported.
primary_outcomes: Endline welfare EW1. Current monthly labour earnings (one constructed outcome). EW2. Current formal wage work (one binary outcome). EW3. Current job quality (one index). Productivity and human capital PH1. Human-capital accumulation over the career (one index). PH2. Match Quality (one derived outcome). PH3. Skill use, advancement and responsibility (one index). Cumulative career welfare CW1. Cumulative labour earnings (one person-level aggregate). CW2. Share of the observed career spent in work (one person-level proportion). CW3. Career security and formality (one index).
randomization_method: Randomization was conducted by computer in the research office. Cluster assignment and individual assignment within treatment clusters were randomized. Individual assignment was blocked by education and rerandomized to improve balance.
randomization_unit: Geographic cluster and individual jobseeker. Clusters were assigned to the transport-subsidy, skills-screening, or control arms; individuals within treatment clusters were then randomly selected to receive the assigned intervention.
secondary_outcome_explanation: Event studies will use the finest credible interval supported by the recall data. We will estimate treatment-effect paths for: (1) any work, including wage work and self-employment, measured monthly where dates permit; (2) labour earnings, combining wage earnings and self-employment profits and normally measured annually; (3) wage work with a written agreement; (4) wage work with a written agreement of undetermined duration; (5) involuntary non-work, identified from non-work spells during which the respondent was actively searching; (6) dated education or training spells; and (7) promotion and responsibility where their timing can be measured. Current outcomes will use the 2026 follow-up. Cumulative outcomes will combine the life history with earlier survey waves. Where two sources cover the same period, the main measure will normally use the report collected closest to that period, while the overlapping report will be used to assess consistency. Alternative earnings definitions and the individual component outcomes will show which measured outcomes account for any effect on an aggregate outcome. These do not constitute additional primary outcomes. The open-ended analysis will use three pre-specified questions: whether respondents attribute where they are today mainly to their own decisions and effort, circumstances outside their control, or both; whether substantial periods without work felt like being stuck, waiting, or trying to move forward; and whether their work life so far has mostly moved them forward, held them back, or done both.
secondary_outcomes: Event studies Treatment-effect paths for work, labour earnings, formal wage work, open-ended wage work, involuntary non-work, training, promotion and responsibility. Open-ended questions Pre-specified questions about respondents' own decisions and external constraints, their experience of substantial periods without work, and whether their careers have moved them forward or held them back.

abstract: Across many conflict affected regions, many civilians live under contested sovereignty, where core state functions are performed by different non-state armed actors competing against each other. This raises important questions with consequences for stability and statehood. When civilians live under sustained rebel governance, does their sense of national identity and their trust in state institutions change, and if so, for whom, and through which channels? To answer these, the project fields an original survey of approximately 1,200 civilians in M23-controlled areas of eastern DRC. The survey measures three families of outcomes: attachment to Congolese national versus local and ethnic identity; trust in and the perceived legitimacy of state institutions; and attitudes toward the fiscal-social contract, including willingness to pay taxes and demand for public goods. Survey responses are paired with implicit and indirect measurement techniques to address the risk of biased answers under conflict conditions.
experimental_design: Respondents are randomized, within person, into the endorser attached to each policy statement they hear. Each respondent rates three statements, one each on dispute resolution, taxation and epidemic response, and the endorser is drawn separately for each.
experimental_design_details: The endorsement items sit in the fiscal-contract module, before anything is asked about control history or armed-group exposure. Three arms: the Congolese state, the authority now governing the village, and no endorser. Allocation is weighted toward the contrast between the governing authority and the no-endorser control. Person fixed effects difference out how agreeable a given respondent is, so the endorser contrast is identified within respondent. Blocking is on age bin and village, which are also our sampling strata. Standard errors cluster by village. We may vary the wording of statements across villages after piloting, and we may add statements per domain if survey time allows.

abstract: Digital credit through mobile money has expanded rapidly in Mozambique. Yet many users do not know the basic terms of the products available to them, including the service fee, the repayment deadline, the automatic deduction of wallet inflows while a debt is unpaid, and the consequences of non-payment. This study tests whether accurate information about Txuna, the digital credit product offered through M-Pesa, changes how market micro-entrepreneurs in Maputo understand and use digital credit. We interview approximately 1,400 micro-entrepreneurs aged 21 or older who hold an active M-Pesa account registered in their own name, in the 27 markets of the official municipal register of Maputo markets that meet our inclusion criteria. Within each market, respondents are approached using a random walk protocol with a fixed skip interval and pre-defined starting points. After consent and the collection of all pre-treatment modules, the survey software assigns each respondent, with probability one-half, to treatment or control. The treatment group watches a video stating the range of loan amounts, the service fee at each repayment term with worked examples, the fact that the fee is identical for every user and that the debt stops growing after the deadline, the automatic deduction of a share of every wallet inflow while a debt is unpaid, and the reporting of non-payment to the Credit Registry of the Bank of Mozambique. The treatment group is then offered an optional assisted eligibility check, which each participant completes on their own handset. Treated respondents also keep a wallet-sized card that restates the same terms in printed form, namely the minimum and maximum loan amounts, the fee at each of the three repayment terms with the worked example on a loan of 1,000 meticais, and the two steps needed to check one's own eligibility in the M-Pesa menu. The card stays with the participant, so the information remains available whenever they want to check it while considering a loan. The control group watches a placebo video on the everyday role of mobile money that carries no information on any service, cost, product, or credit, and receives neither the card nor the assisted check. We measure effects on beliefs about the terms of the product, on comprehension of the pricing rule at a loan amount never shown, on spontaneous knowledge, on stated intentions, on choices in hypothetical credit scenarios, and, for participants who consent to data linkage, on take-up, repayment, and mobile money use observed in administrative records 30, 90, and 180 days after the interview. The sign of the effect on borrowing is not predicted. Accurate terms can raise take-up when borrowers overestimate the cost or wrongly believe they are ineligible, and lower it when borrowers underestimate the cost or are unaware of the automatic deduction and the credit registry consequences. We therefore measure the direction of each participant's initial belief gap before the intervention, which is what separates these two cases.
experimental_design: One-visit survey experiment with micro-entrepreneurs trading in Maputo markets. We cover all markets that meet our inclusion criteria, select respondents within markets, and randomize treatment at the respondent level. We cover the 27 markets of the official municipal register of Maputo markets, Resolution number 94/AM/2008 of the Maputo Municipal Assembly approving the Markets and Fairs By-law, that meet our inclusion criteria. Markets serve as sampling units only. Both arms are present in every market, so markets are sampling clusters and not treatment units, and all specifications include market fixed effects. We allocate interviews across markets in proportion to market size rather than equally. Within each market, enumerators approach respondents by a fixed protocol with office-drawn starting points that leaves no selection to the enumerator, and they substitute neither refusals nor ineligible respondents. Eligibility requires being 21 years of age or older, owning or being self-employed in a business operating in the market, holding an active M-Pesa account registered in the respondent's own name with the handset present at the interview, and not working for M-Pesa. After consent, and after we collect all baseline covariates and prior beliefs, the survey software assigns treatment at the individual level with probability one-half. The respondent then watches the video assigned to their arm. We measure all survey outcomes in the same visit, with no follow-up survey. For participants who consent to data linkage, we add M-Pesa administrative records from 30, 90, and 180 days after the interview date.
experimental_design_details: Market frame. The register names 60 markets. We applied three inclusion rules before the draw. We excluded Katembe and Inhaca because water separates them from the mainland, making them logistically unreachable. We excluded entries without a verified market-level GPS coordinate, since the approach protocol needs a real entrance rather than a neighborhood or landmark proxy. We merged entries with identical coordinates as the same physical site. We did not merge markets that are merely close to one another, since any distance threshold would be arbitrary. The resulting set contains 27 markets, and the study covers all of them. Market coverage. We started with 14 markets and now cover all 27. The register names and classifies markets and is the only official source available to us. There is no census of traders, and no official estimate of the number of traders in each market, so the cost of covering a market was not known before fieldwork began. We therefore drew 14 of the 27 markets in Stata on 14 August 2026, stratified by municipal district. Fieldwork started on 17 August 2026 and gave us that cost. The budget covers the rest, so on 28 August 2026 we added the remaining 13 markets. Every market that meets the inclusion criteria is now included, so market design weights are equal to one. The 14 drawn in August were visited first, so the order of visits is not random and market fixed effects are included in the main specification. The target of 1,400 interviews is unchanged, so the power calculations are unaffected. Respondent approach. Enumerators follow a random walk with a fixed skip interval of three stalls, office-drawn starting positions, rotation of the entrance used across enumerator-days, the right-hand rule for traversal, and a birthday rule for choosing among eligible people at a single stall. The number of interviews per market is proportional to market size, measured as stalls per full traversal from the random walk tally. Interview flow. Screening and consent. Baseline covariates covering demographics, business characteristics, financial context, Txuna experience and reasons for non-use, credit demand, preferences, digital comfort, and account privacy. Practice with the trained 0-10 probability scale, with comprehension flags stored. Prior beliefs, with a ten-bean certainty measure attached to the open quantitative items where guessing is a concern. Treatment or placebo video. For the treatment group only, offer the assisted eligibility check immediately after the video. Posterior beliefs, using a panel with item wording and item order identical to the priors, followed by a transfer item at 2,000 MT at the seven-day term, a combination the video never shows. Spontaneous knowledge outcomes, coded against lists never read aloud. Stated intentions. Hypothetical choice scenarios. Closing script and the participation incentive for both arms. For the treatment group only, and last, the handover of the card. No corrective information at the interview, with the debrief deferred until the administrative outcome window closes. Instrument design. The choice scenarios use a hypothetical digital credit product explicitly framed as not being Txuna, so the instrument itself does not expose the control group to product information, and we randomize the reading order of the two options at the respondent level. We ask self-assessed knowledge after the open items in both the prior and the posterior battery. Heterogeneity. Dimensions specified in the pre-analysis plan: the direction and size of the baseline belief gap on each treated dimension, which separates participants for whom correct information lowers the perceived cost of borrowing from those for whom it raises it, prior Txuna experience and history of having been txunado, income predictability, digital comfort, account privacy, discomfort with borrowing from family, and anticipated liquidity needs.
intervention: Participants are interviewed once, in person, at their stall or place of business in a Maputo market. Every participant watches a video on the enumerator's tablet, at the same point in the interview, immediately after prior beliefs are collected. The treatment has three components, delivered at two points in the interview. The video and the eligibility check come together, immediately after prior beliefs are collected. The card comes at the very end, after the questionnaire is complete. Because the video and the check both precede outcome measurement, the survey outcomes reflect those two components jointly. The card is handed over after every survey outcome is recorded, so it can only affect the administrative outcomes measured 30, 90, and 180 days later. The treatment group watches a video on the terms of Txuna, the digital credit product offered through M-Pesa. It covers three things a borrower cannot readily infer from the handset menu: what the product costs, how much a given person can borrow, and what follows from late repayment. The price is given for each of the three repayment terms with worked examples, and it is the same for every user rather than something earned through a good repayment record. Borrowing capacity is explained as an individual limit within a stated range, set automatically and available to check free of charge. On late repayment, the video covers what happens to the balance once the term has passed, how money entering the wallet is used to repay, the potential legal consequences of non-repayment, and how reporting affects future access to formal credit. Each of these corresponds to a belief measured before the video. Treated participants are then offered an optional check of their own eligibility and borrowing limit, which each completes on their own handset. The check addresses a barrier the video cannot reach. A person may understand the terms perfectly and still not borrow because they do not know whether the product is open to them, or how to find out. Because the limit is set automatically from a person's transaction history, no general message can convey it. Only checking the participant's own account can reveal it. Treated participants also receive a wallet-sized card at the end of the interview, once the questionnaire is complete. It restates the same terms in print: the minimum and maximum loan amounts, the fee at each repayment term with a worked example, and the two steps needed to check eligibility. The card stays with the participant, so the information remains available whenever they want to check it while considering a loan. The control group watches a placebo video on the everyday role of mobile money in Mozambique. It names no product, gives no price, and never mentions credit or Txuna. It states in general terms that different operators and services carry different menus, costs, and conditions, which is the only reference to cost anywhere in it. The placebo holds constant the interruption of the working day, the presence of a video, the tablet, the enumerator's silence during playback, and the video's position in the interview, so the comparison turns on the message content rather than on having been given attention. The control group receives no check, no card, and no product information during the interview or afterward while borrowing behavior is measured. Once the administrative outcome window has closed, they receive the correct terms and the same card.

mde_text: With 1,400 individuals split equally, 80 percent power, and a 5 percent two-sided test, the minimum detectable effect for standardized survey outcomes is 0.15 standard deviations without covariates, and about 0.12 standard deviations for posterior beliefs controlling for the prior of the same item, assuming the prior explains 35 percent of posterior variance. For administrative take-up, assuming a 10 percent control group take-up rate over 90 days, the minimum detectable effect is 4.5 percentage points. At a 20 percent control rate, it is 6.0 percentage points. Because treatment is randomized within market, clustering at the market level does not inflate the standard error of the treatment coefficient once market fixed effects are included, so these calculations require no design effect correction for the treatment contrast. Covering 27 markets rather than 14 raises the number of clusters available for descriptive and weighted population statements. Because the study covers every market that meets the inclusion criteria, market design weights are equal to one, and these statements are reported with market-clustered standard errors. Market fixed effects are not credited in the calculations above. Detailed power calculations are reported in the pre-analysis plan. The administrative minimum detectable effects apply to the subsample consenting to data linkage. If consent falls materially below the full sample, the realized detectable effect rises in proportion, and we will report the achieved figure rather than the planned one.

primary_outcome_explanation: Belief questions take one of two forms, according to what they ask. For each quantitative term (e.g., service fees), we record an open numeric estimate, in meticais or in days as the item requires, with no response options read out. Monetary items are in meticais. For items where a respondent could plausibly guess, we also record certainty by asking them to place ten beans on a 0-10 scale so we can distinguish a confident wrong answer from an admitted guess. Items about the likelihood of alternative scenarios (e.g., consequences of not repaying on time) use a trained 0-10 scale, practiced with the respondent before the belief modules begin, and we store the comprehension flags. In both forms, we record "does not know" and "does not want to answer" as separate indicators, never as scale midpoints. Accuracy is how close the reported estimate lies to the true contract term. We compare accuracy in two ways. The first covers the items asked identically before and after the video, at the amounts the video uses, and assesses whether the respondent updated toward the signal. The second covers the item asked at 2,000 MT at the seven-day term, a combination the video never shows, and speaks to whether the respondent learned the pricing rule rather than a number. The pre-analysis plan sets out whether we report them item by item, as summary indices, or both, and the standardization and weighting behind any index, before we look at the outcome data. We report the bean measure alongside accuracy rather than folding it into a single number. Take-up is a binary indicator of at least one Txuna loan in the administrative records within the stated window. Both administrative primary outcomes depend on M-Pesa transferring records under the data processing agreement, which is being finalized at the time of filing. If the transfer does not take place, or takes place only in part, we will report the survey primary outcome and state plainly that we could not construct the administrative primary outcome. We will not substitute a self-reported measure of borrowing for the administrative one. We do not predict the direction of the effect on take-up. Correcting a belief that overstates the cost of borrowing or that wrongly rules out eligibility should raise take-up, and correcting a belief that understates the cost or omits the automatic deduction and the Credit Registry consequence should lower it. Both directions are informative, and we pre-specify the test of a difference in either direction rather than a one-sided prediction.
primary_outcomes: Beliefs about the terms of Txuna, measured in the same visit immediately after the intervention. Accuracy of posterior beliefs relative to the true contract terms, reported separately for the items asked identically before and after the intervention at the amounts used in the video, and for the transfer item asked at a loan amount never shown in the video. Txuna take-up. Any Txuna loan taken within 30 days and within 90 days of the interview, measured in M-Pesa administrative records for participants who consent to data linkage.
randomization_method: Market selection. Done by computer in the office, in Stata, before fieldwork began. The study covers all 27 markets that meet the inclusion criteria, built from the official municipal register of Maputo markets, as set out in Resolution number 94/AM/2008 of the Maputo Municipal Assembly approving the Markets and Fairs By-law. We drew 14 of them on 14 August 2026 and visited those first, stratified by municipal district, namely KaMpfumo, Nlhamankulu, KaMaxakeni, KaMavota, and KaMubukwana, with market category as an implicit stratum imposed by sorting each district's units by category before a systematic selection with a random start. We fixed the seeds before running it, with a master seed and one derived seed per district, so it is reproducible from the do-file. The remaining 13 markets were added on 28 August 2026. Respondent selection within market. No list of traders exists from which to draw a sample, so selection is systematic rather than a lottery. Enumerators follow a fixed traversal route from a pre-defined starting position, taking every third stall, which removes enumerator discretion, with a birthday rule to choose among eligible people at the same stall. Treatment assignment. Done by the survey software, SurveyCTO, on the enumerator's tablet during the interview. randomization_unit: Individual respondent, single-level randomization. abstract: This randomized online experiment, implemented in Qualtrics with participants recruited through Prolific, examines whether discriminatory purchasing patterns persist after seller identity ceases to predict product quality. Participants first learn a quality difference between two seller types and are subsequently assigned to information or procedural interventions under routine or deliberative decision environments. We test whether seller-based purchasing gaps persist after quality differences and measured beliefs have converged, and whether different interventions reduce this persistence.
experimental_design: The experiment has four phases. Phase 1 contains 50 decisions, Phase 2 contains 10 decisions, Phase 3 contains 15 decisions, and Phase 4 contains 10 decisions. Five arms belong to Group X and experience a Phase 1 quality difference between sellers. These arms are Routine Control, Routine Information, Routine Procedure, Deliberative Information, and Deliberative Procedure. The sixth arm is Group Y, in which both sellers have equal quality throughout the experiment, and serves as the pure control group for comparison. In Phases 2-4, both sellers follow the same quality schedule. In Phase 3, Group X participants receive their assigned intervention and decision environment. In Phase 4, all participants return to routine decisions without an intervention. The primary Phase 3 analysis compares each Group X intervention arm with Routine Control. The main interaction test compares the relative effectiveness of Information and Procedure across routine and deliberative environments. We also examine whether seller-based purchasing persists when Phase 2 beliefs about the two sellers are equal or nearly equal. The target sample is 1,500 participants, with 250 participants in each arm.
intervention: Participants are assigned to Group X or Group Y. In Phase 1, one seller is more likely to provide good products in Group X, conditional on the product rating. In Group Y, both sellers are equally likely to provide good products. In Phases 2-4, seller identity does not predict quality in either group. In Phase 3, Group X participants are assigned to one of five conditions: - Routine Control: no intervention and a decision timer. - Routine Information: participants are told that seller identity no longer predicts quality, with a decision timer. - Routine Procedure: participants confirm the product rating before deciding, with a decision timer. - Deliberative Information: participants receive the information intervention without a decision timer. - Deliberative Procedure: participants complete the rating-confirmation procedure without a decision timer. Group Y remains in the routine control condition. In Phase 4, all participants return to routine decisions without an intervention. Which seller is initially designated as the better seller is independently randomized.

abstract: This study examines how pharmacists recommend brand-name versus generic over-the-counter pain medications and whether the way a consumer asks for advice affects the recommendation they receive. Although generic medications contain the same active ingredients as their brand-name equivalents and are often less expensive, consumers may still rely on familiar brand names when choosing over-the-counter medications. Pharmacists are well positioned to help consumers make these choices, but relatively little is known about how they communicate this information during everyday interactions. The study will take place in community pharmacies in Ottawa, Canada. Researchers will visit pharmacies while posing as ordinary consumers seeking advice about an over-the-counter pain medication. Pharmacies will receive two different types of consumer inquiries on separate visits. One inquiry will be open-ended, allowing the pharmacist to make a recommendation without being presented with specific products. In the other, the consumer will explicitly present a choice between a brand-name and generic version of the same medication and ask the pharmacist which they recommend. The order of the two interactions will vary across pharmacies. We will compare pharmacists’ recommendations across the two types of interactions. We will also examine the explanations pharmacists provide, including whether they discuss differences or similarities in cost, effectiveness, active ingredients, or product equivalence. The study aims to improve our understanding of how expert advice and the way consumers frame questions can influence decisions between branded and generic medications.
experimental_design: This study uses a naturalistic field experiment in community pharmacies in Ottawa, Canada. Each pharmacy is observed under two different consumer inquiry conditions on separate visits. The order of the conditions varies across pharmacy locations. This paired design allows us to compare how the same pharmacy responds to different ways of framing a request for advice while reducing the influence of stable differences across pharmacy locations. The study focuses on whether consumer framing affects pharmacists’ recommendations between branded and generic over-the-counter pain medications and the information they provide alongside those recommendations.
experimental_design_details: The study uses a within-pharmacy paired audit design. Each pharmacy is visited twice and receives both experimental conditions: an Open-Ended inquiry and a Brand-versus-Generic inquiry. The order of the two conditions is randomly assigned across pharmacy locations, so that some pharmacies receive the Open-Ended condition first and others receive the Brand-versus-Generic condition first. The second visit uses the alternate condition. In the Open-Ended condition, the researcher poses as a consumer and asks what the pharmacist would recommend for a sister with a toothache, without initially presenting a specific medication. In the Brand-versus-Generic condition, the researcher presents branded and generic versions of ibuprofen and asks which product the pharmacist would recommend. A standardized follow-up question about the price difference may also be asked. Repeat visits are separated by approximately four to six weeks. Where feasible, a different researcher or research assistant conducts the second visit to reduce recognition and recall. Researchers follow standardized scripts and interaction protocols and do not disclose the research purpose during the interaction. The paired design allows within-pharmacy comparison of recommendation behavior across consumer framings. The study records the pharmacist’s recommendation as well as contextual characteristics including pharmacy type, owner status, queue length, number of staff, time of day, weather conditions, researcher identity, and other interaction-level information. The analysis will compare recommendation outcomes across conditions and may adjust for these observed contextual characteristics.
intervention: The study varies how a consumer requests advice from a pharmacist about an over-the-counter pain medication. Participating pharmacy locations are exposed to two standardized consumer inquiry conditions on separate visits. One condition allows the pharmacist to provide an unsolicited product recommendation, while the other makes the choice between alternative versions of the medication more explicit. The order of the two conditions is varied across pharmacy locations. This design allows us to examine whether the framing of a consumer’s request affects the advice provided by pharmacists.

abstract: This study examines how task difficulty and the correctness of AI recommendations affect decision-making performance. We plan to recruit approximately 600 participants aged 18–65, with approximately 300 participants in China and 300 in the United States, including university students and members of the general public recruited through online and in-person methods. In a 2 × 2 within-subject design, each participant completes eight reasoning and decision-making tasks accompanied by AI recommendations. Task difficulty and AI recommendation correctness are assigned at the task level according to pre-generated pseudorandom participant schedules, while the eighth task family is randomly selected at the participant level from three additional task families. The primary outcome is task-level decision accuracy, and decision confidence is the secondary outcome. The study tests whether greater cognitive demands change how individuals respond to correct and incorrect AI-provided information.
experimental_design: The study uses a 2 × 2 within-subject experimental design. The two experimentally varied factors are task difficulty (easy versus difficult) and AI recommendation correctness (correct versus incorrect). Participants complete multiple reasoning and decision-making tasks, allowing the study to compare decision accuracy across different combinations of cognitive demand and AI information quality.
experimental_design_details: The study uses a 2 × 2 within-subject experimental design with two task-level factors: task difficulty (easy versus difficult) and AI recommendation correctness (correct versus incorrect). Each participant completes eight core tasks drawn from ten task families. Seven task families are administered to every participant: representativeness and conjunction reasoning, rule reasoning, probability reasoning, argument reasoning, working-memory reasoning, fluid intelligence, and logical reasoning. One additional task family is randomly selected from three remaining families: exponential-growth reasoning, cognitive-reflection arithmetic, and Bayesian reasoning. Across the administered tasks, difficulty level and AI recommendation correctness vary according to pre-generated participant schedules. The mapping between task families and experimental conditions varies across schedules, so difficulty and recommendation correctness are not fixed characteristics of particular task families. The randomization procedure does not require each participant to complete exactly the same number of tasks in each of the four experimental cells. Each core task is followed by measures of decision confidence, perceived task difficulty, mental effort, and perceived helpfulness of the AI recommendation. The primary outcome is task-level decision accuracy.
intervention: Participants will complete a series of reasoning and decision-making tasks accompanied by AI recommendations. The study experimentally varies task difficulty and whether the AI recommendation is correct or incorrect. This allows us to examine how cognitive demands and the quality of AI-provided information affect decision accuracy and confidence.

abstract: The production and consumption of animal-based food have increasingly become a polarized and salient issue in political debates. The issue resembles the dynamics of a wedge issue – a topic strategically emphasized by parties, especially populist parties, to mobilize and polarize supporters. On 27 September 2026, Swiss citizens will vote on the «Initiative für eine sichere Ernährung (Ernährungsinitiative)» in a popular vote. The initiative calls for increased domestic food self-sufficiency and a shift from animal food toward more plant-based food production and consumption. This pre-registered study leverages this real-world vote to experimentally examine how the politicization around the issue of animal-based food consumption and production, specifically its salience and polarization, shapes citizens' attitudes, food policy preferences, and stated as well as reported voting behavior. Using a two-wave online survey experiment with approximately 2,200 eligible Swiss voters, we randomly assign participants in a first survey wave to one of four information conditions that vary in how salient and polarized the issue is presented. Attitudes, policy preferences, and voting intentions are measured following treatment exposure. A second survey wave, conducted shortly after the vote, reassesses these outcomes and captures participants' reported voting behavior. The study speaks to the broader literature on issue politicization and its consequences for democratic participation and policy preference formation.
experimental_design: This study employs a randomized controlled trial (RCT) using a two-wave online survey experiment fielded around a Swiss popular vote on the Ernährungsinitiative. In Wave 1, participants are randomly assigned to one of four conditions (placebo control, T1, T2, T3) that vary in the salience and polarization of information presented about the initiative (see Interventions). Following treatment exposure, participants report their attitudes, food policy preferences, and voting intentions. Wave 2, fielded shortly after the vote, reassesses these outcomes and collects participants' voluntarily reported voting behavior.
experimental_design_details: Participants are recruited through the commercial panel provider Bilendi, using quotas to approximate the demographic distribution of the Swiss population with respect to age × gender (crossed), education, and region. Bilendi handles recruitment, compensation, and recontact, but has no access to survey responses and no influence on the study design or research questions. Eligible participants must be at least 18 years old, be eligible to vote in federal popular votes, and be members of at least one of three major Swiss retail loyalty programs for a potential follow up study in the future. Random assignment to the four treatment conditions occurs after participants complete a baseline set of demographic, dietary, and political attitude items.
intervention: Participants are randomly assigned to one of four conditions. The placebo control condition presents neutral factual information on the instruments of direct democracy in Switzerland (popular initiatives and referendums), unrelated to the Ernährungsinitiative. The remaining three conditions present information about the Ernährungsinitiative that varies in the degree to which the topic is presented as salient and controversial: a condition presenting neutral factual information about the initiative (T1; salience treatment); a condition additionally presenting balanced pro and con arguments reflecting the existing controversy around the initiative, in neutral, factual language (T2; politicization treatment, neutral); and a condition presenting the same balanced arguments using authentic public campaign material, including campaign imagery (T3; politicization treatment, authentic). The four conditions are designed to vary the perceived politicization of the topic – i.e., its perceived salience and polarization: the placebo control involves no exposure to salient or polarizing information about the initiative; T1 introduces salience without indicating that the topic is controversial; T2 and T3 additionally present balanced pro/con arguments reflecting the existing controversy, with T3 using authentic campaign material and imagery, which may elicit a comparatively higher degree of perceived polarization than T2's neutral language.

abstract: Governments and international funders increasingly consider payments for ecosystem services (PES) as a mechanism for sustaining conservation gains, yet there is little experimental evidence on how the framing of a prospective PES scheme shapes what citizens expect and demand from their government. We embed a four-arm information-provision experiment in the endline household survey of a wetland-restoration and climate-adaptation program implemented by the Government of Uganda with support from the Green Climate Fund and the United Nations Development Programme, whose mid-term review recommended integrating PES into a successor phase. Approximately 1,600 respondents in sixteen wetland systems across eight districts of Eastern and Southwestern Uganda are randomly assigned to hear one of four short scripts about a prospective wetland-conservation program: a neutral description, an environmental framing emphasizing biodiversity and ecosystem services, a long-term economic framing emphasizing durable community gains, and a direct-payment framing describing a PES scheme funded by an international organization. We then measure comprehension, trust, perceived importance and benefits of conservation, willingness to vacate wetland areas and to join alternative-livelihood programs, perceived effectiveness of government policy, and the respondent's single most-preferred type of government action for wetland conservation. We plan to examine heterogeneity along dimensions such as household wetland dependence and respondent gender.
experimental_design: The experiment is embedded as a short module at the end of the endline household survey of a wetland-restoration and climate-adaptation program in Uganda, fielded in October 2024 under the Learning-Oriented Real-Time Impact Assessment (LORTA) programme. The survey covers a panel of approximately 1,600 households in sixteen wetland systems (six villages per system) across eight districts of Eastern and Southwestern Uganda, first interviewed at baseline in October 2022. After completing the main household questionnaire, each respondent is randomly assigned with equal probability to one of the four message arms, hears the corresponding script read verbatim by the enumerator, and answers the same battery of outcome questions. The three treatment scripts hold the underlying conservation program constant and vary only the framing of its benefits (environmental, long-term economic, or direct payment), so pairwise comparisons against the neutral arm identify the effect of each framing on perceptions and on preferred government action. We will estimate intention-to-treat effects by OLS, comparing each treatment arm to the neutral control, with heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors; a second specification adds pre-treatment household controls drawn from survey modules administered before the experimental script. We plan to adjust inference within the primary outcome family for multiple hypothesis testing and to examine heterogeneity along dimensions such as household wetland dependence and respondent gender.
intervention: At the end of the endline household questionnaire, after the modules on demographics, assets, income, expenditures, agriculture, wetland use, and food security, enumerators administer a roughly ten-minute survey-experiment module. Each respondent is randomly assigned to one of four groups and read the corresponding short script verbatim. The four arms are: 1. Neutral message (control): a generic description of the wetland-conservation program and its aim of protecting wetlands for future generations, with no specific framing of benefits. 2. Environmental framing: emphasizes the ecological benefits of wetlands, such as habitat for plants and animals, water purification, and flood control. 3. Long-term economic framing: emphasizes durable economic benefits to the community from conservation, such as improved soil fertility, higher crop yields, and opportunities for sustainable tourism. 4. Immediately after the script, respondents answer the same battery of outcome questions in all arms.
