primary_outcome_explanation: I analyse posterior beliefs in two ways. First, I regress beliefs on treatment indicators, controlling for signal precision. Differences between adjacent treatment coefficients measure each mechanism's contribution in percentage points of reported probability. Second, I estimate a Grether-style regression of the log-odds of reported beliefs on the log-likelihood ratio of the information interacted with treatment indicators. The interaction coefficients represent the weights placed on each information type in belief updating. Adjacent differences between these coefficients provide the corresponding decomposition. For both analyses, belief reports are winsorised at the 5th and 95th percentiles separately within each signal precision level. Both specifications control for individual, part-order, round-order, and signal-presentation-version fixed effects. Standard errors are clustered at the individual level.
primary_outcomes: Posterior beliefs: the reported probability (0–100%) assigned to the state favoured by the information received. The objects of interest are the three adjacent treatment comparisons, each measuring one mechanism's contribution to the overall difference in response to private and social information.
randomization_method: All randomisation done by a computer.
randomization_unit: The four information treatments vary within participant, and the order is randomised at the participant level.
secondary_outcome_explanation: For participants with a unique switching point, WTP for an information type is measured as the midpoint value between the highest amount at which they choose the information and the lowest amount at which they choose the money. WTP is coded as the boundary value for participants who always choose the information or always choose the money. Participants whose multiple-price-list choices exhibit wrong-direction switching (switch from money back to information as the monetary amount increases) will be excluded from the WTP analyses. If more than 20% of WTP observations are not well-defined, I will also use an alternative WTP measure: the number of rows in which the participant chooses the information. The main specification regresses WTP on information-type indicators, controlling for participant and price list order fixed effects. Standard errors are clustered at the participant level. Confidence is measured on a 0–100% scale and captures how certain participants are about their reported belief. The main specification regresses confidence on information-type indicators, controlling for signal precision, participant, part-order, and signal-presentation-version fixed effects. Standard errors are clustered at the participant level. Usefulness rankings are coded from first (most useful) to fourth (least useful). I examine how the distribution of these rankings differs across the four information types.
secondary_outcomes: The secondary outcomes are willingness-to-pay (WTP), confidence, and usefulness rankings for the four information types. Beyond belief updating, I examine additional aspects of participants' responses to private and social information: their valuation of each information type, their confidence in beliefs formed from it, and their subjective rankings of its usefulness. I also compare WTP, confidence, and usefulness rankings across the four information conditions to explore the potential mechanisms behind these differences. I also consider several exploratory analyses: 1. Individual-level associations across outcomes. I test whether participants' responses to different information types show consistent or different patterns across beliefs, WTP and confidence. 2. Heterogeneity by signal precision. I test whether each mechanism’s contribution varies across the five signal precision levels. 3. Heterogeneity in participant response types. I test whether participants can be grouped according to their response patterns across the four information conditions. For example, one mechanism may account for most of the overall difference for some participants, whereas others may respond similarly to all four information types. 4. Beliefs about others' rationality. I test how much this belief can account for the difference in behaviour between the A-bot and A-other conditions.
title: Decomposing Differences in Learning from Private and Social Information

abstract: Risks are often communicated in financial contexts using verbal categories (e.g. “very conservative” or “very risky”) for different ranges of risk. Previous studies have explored how decision makers interpret these labels, finding a large amount of heterogeneity in risk perceptions. In this project we study the reverse – how do decision makers themselves verbally communicate numerical risks. We draw data from an exploratory survey in which respondents are given 6 different numerical risks and are asked to describe them without using numbers or numerical terms. These 6 risks range from relatively small (2%) to quite large probabilities (95%). Respondents are presented these risks in either an ascending, descending or random order. We are primarily interested which terms and descriptions are commonly used for a given risk. We further link this to demographic factors, as well as financial participation and risk attitude.
experimental_design: Participants in the survey are presented with a fictional scenario in which they are asked to consider the risk of their retirement savings getting depleted prematurely. In 6 different questions based on this scenario, they are asked to describe specific percentage risks (e.g. 2%) in their own words. Participants face these 6 risk questions in 3 different treatment orders, which vary of the risks are presented randomly or in ascending or descending order. After the main task, participants answer a set of additional questions, as well as basic demographics (age, gender, education, and income). Participants are recruited from a representative US sample (in terms of age, gender, race and political orientation) and earn a flat payment for their participation.
experimental_design_details: Participants in the survey are presented with a fictional scenario in which they are asked to consider the risk of their retirement savings getting depleted prematurely. In 6 different questions based on this scenario, the specific percentage risk of premature depletion varies, ranging from 2% to 95%. In each of these questions the participants are asked to describe this risk in at least 5 words. Using numbers (“20”) or number words (“twenty”) is not allowed. Participants are informed about this and asked to modify their answer, if they use any numbers or number words. Participants face these 6 risk questions in 3 different treatment orders: In the “random” treatment, the questions are presented in random order on different screens. In the “ascending” and “descending” order, the risk questions are presented in ascending and descending order respectively on the same screen. Participants are randomly allocated to these treatments after correctly answering two control questions (failure to answer this control questions after a second try leads to exclusion from the survey). After the main task, participants answer a set of additional questions including questions on their financial market participation, confidence in their financial knowledge, risk tolerance (based on Dohmen et al. 2011), three questions on financial literacy, as well as basic demographics (age, gender, education, and income). Participants are recruited from a representative US sample (in terms of age, gender, race and political orientation) and earn a flat payment for their participation.

abstract: Background: Febrile illness is a leading cause of serious illness and death for millions of children across sub- Saharan Africa, despite the availability of diagnostics and appropriate medications. Unfortunately, many fevers are not treated appropriately due to financial barriers, incorrect or no diagnosis, and inappropriate use of medications. Inappropriate treatment has uncertain health and economic costs to individuals as well as at a population level. Objective: The primary objective of this trial is to determine the effectiveness and cost- effectiveness of pharmacy-based discounts for appropriately dosed azithromycin compared with incentives for facilitated referrals to a higher level health care facility in the management of malaria negative fevers in children under five years in Uganda
experimental_design: A sample of 200 eligible pharmacies in Uganda will be randomized into one of three study arms: (1) a control group, (2) a discounted azithromycin group, which offers subsidized prices for Azithromycin to eligible pediatric febrile cases who seek care in the pharmacy, (3) a facilitated referral group, which provides transport allowances facilitate referral visits for follow up care at nearby clinics to eligible pediatric febrile cases who seek care in the pharmacy
intervention: Control group: All study sites, including the control, have access to price subsidies for ORS, malaria RDTs, malaria ACTs, and over-the- counter painkillers. All study sites, including the control, will have access to referral information to nearby clinics. Azithromycin discount group: Pharmacies assigned to this arm, in addition to having access to the subsidies and information described in the control group, will also have access to subsidized azithromycin for malaria negative children under 5. Facilitated referral group: In addition to what is described for the control group, this arm will have access to subsidies for facilitated referrals to nearby clinics (incentives for patients and providers to complete referrals).

abstract: This project aims to shed light on the link between perceptions and expectations about macroeconomic aggregates such as inflation, unemployment rate, and stock market performance and household expectations about their subjective financial well-being. We provide randomized information on the past year’s macroeconomic aggregates to 75% of the sample. One-third of those receive information about the inflation rate over the past 12 months, one-third receive information about the change in the unemployment rate over the past 12 months, and one-third receive information about the past year’s stock market performance. We investigate the impact of the information treatments on households’ macroeconomic expectations as well as their micro-level expectations about their own job loss, household income growth, and household spending growth. We assess the perceived contribution of information about macroeconomic aggregates on households’ expected subjective financial well-being.
experimental_design: Our design is a randomized information intervention embedded within a survey. Eligibility to participate in the survey includes giving consent to be contacted after rotating out of the NY Fed’s Survey of Consumer Expectations panel. The randomization is done at the individual level. Respondents are divided into four groups: i) Control (25% of the couples) ii) Treatment (75% of the couples) The treatment group is divided into three groups: a) Treatment 1 (25% of all respondents, 30% of treated respondents) b) Treatment 2 (25% of all respondents, 30% of treated respondents) c) Treatment 3 (25% of all respondents, 30% of treated respondents) T1 provides information about the inflation rate over the past 12 months. T2 provides information about the change in the unemployment rate over the past 12 months. T3 provides information about the past year’s stock market performance.

abstract: We designed a randomized survey experiment in Bangladesh to investigate: (1) whether and how disability reporting differs between self-reports and proxy-reports, allowing us to estimate the extent of under- or over-reporting introduced by proxy respondents; (2) whether and how the gender of the proxy respondent systematically influences reported prevalence and severity of disability, and (3) whether and how survey protocol and proxy’s gender influence other forms of measurement error and cost-effectiveness of data collection.
experimental_design: We randomly assign each household to one of four treatment arms, which vary in the protocols used to collect data.
experimental_design_details: We randomly assign each household to one of four treatment arms, which will determine the protocol by which enumerators administer Block C. Block C is administered in all four treatment arms. Block D is administered only in treatment arms 1 and 4, using the same respondent structure as Block C in those arms. i. Treatment Arm 1 – General Proxy Protocol (DHS): In this treatment arm, enumerators and respondents follow the DHS protocol. The same respondent who completed blocks A and B (that is, a knowledgeable adult household member aged 15+) will answer block C (on functioning and affect) and block D (on psychological well-being). For blocks C and D, the respondent starts with their own self-reported answers about themselves and then answers both blocks on behalf of each of their adult household members (ages 15+). ii. Treatment Arm 2 – Male Proxy Protocol: An available and knowledgeable male household member aged 15+ responds to blocks C for themselves as well as for the other adult household members (ages 15+). In cases in which a 15+ male household respondent is not available during the first visit, enumerators are instructed to revisit the household at least two more times to locate a male household respondent to collect this data and record the time and date of the visits. iii. Treatment Arm 3 – Female Proxy Protocol: In this arm, an available and knowledgeable female household member aged 15+ responds to blocks C for themselves as well as for other household members. In cases in which a 15+ female household respondent is not available during the first visit, enumerators are instructed to revisit the household at least two more times to locate a female household respondent to collect this data and record the time and date of the visits. iv. Treatment Arm 4 – Self-reports Protocol (MICS): In this treatment arm, enumerators and respondents follow the MICS protocol. All household members aged 15+ are interviewed directly using the self-report versions of blocks C and D. In cases in which certain household members are not available, enumerators are instructed to revisit the household at least two more times to locate all 15+ adults who will respond to blocks C and D. Enumerators record visit number, date, and time for all or as many 15+ adults that can be completed during the multiple visits made to the households.

mde_text: We conduct ex ante power calculations for binary disability-reporting outcomes, accounting for the clustering of individual respondents within households. Assuming a baseline disability prevalence of 30 percent, a two-sided significance level of 5 percent, an average of three adult respondents per household, and household-level intra-cluster correlation coefficients ranging from approximately 0.03 to 0.11, we target approximately 250 households per treatment arm. This corresponds to approximately 750 individual respondents per arm. Under these assumptions, the proposed sample provides 80 percent power to detect at least a 7-percentage points reduction in disability prevalence.

abstract: We send a number of borderline cases to different AI systems and subsequently obtain varying feedback. This feedback is then randomly distributed to different experimenters, who will use the relevant AI recommendations to test the responses of real physicians.
experimental_design: This study uses a randomized field experiment design. Trained field staff will visit different hospitals in China and consult physicians using standardized thyroid-related case scenarios. Each hospital consultation constitutes one experimental observation. The study plans to complete approximately 200 experimental observations, of which approximately 100 have already been completed. During the consultation, field staff will present different types of AI-assisted recommendations, or no AI recommendation, according to random assignment. The study will compare physicians' diagnostic judgments, testing recommendations, and treatment recommendations across experimental conditions to assess whether AI-generated information affects clinical decision-making in borderline cases.
experimental_design_details: The experimental sample consists of thyroid-related consultations at different hospitals in China. The research team will use standardized case scripts to keep case information, wording, and consultation procedures as consistent as possible. Randomization will be conducted by the research team using a computer-generated random assignment before each field visit. Each visit will be assigned to one experimental condition, such as an AI recommendation favoring further treatment, an AI recommendation favoring observation or conservative management, or no AI recommendation. Field staff will provide the case information and AI recommendation according to the assigned script and will complete a standardized recording form immediately after the consultation. The main analysis will compare average differences in physicians' recommendations across experimental conditions, with possible controls for hospital level, city, physician department, visit timing, and field-staff fixed effects. Since approximately 100 experimental observations have already been completed, the remaining visits will continue to follow the same randomization and implementation protocol.
intervention: This study evaluates the effect of artificial intelligence-assisted diagnostic recommendations on physicians' clinical judgment. Trained field staff will visit different hospitals in China using standardized thyroid-related case scenarios. Depending on random assignment, field staff will present or refer to different types of AI-generated recommendations during the consultation and record physicians' diagnostic judgments, testing recommendations, and treatment recommendations for borderline thyroid cases. The study aims to examine whether AI-generated information affects physicians' clinical decision-making in borderline thyroid-related cases.
mde_text: Based on a planned sample size of approximately 200 hospital consultations or field visits, a 5 percent significance level, 80 percent statistical power, and approximately equal allocation across three experimental conditions, the study is powered to detect medium-sized treatment effects. For a binary primary outcome, such as whether the physician recommends further treatment, assuming a control-group mean of approximately 50 percent, the minimum detectable effect for a pairwise comparison is approximately 24-25 percentage points. For a standardized continuous outcome, the minimum detectable effect for a pairwise comparison is approximately 0.48-0.50 standard deviations. The actual minimum detectable effect will depend on the final allocation across conditions, the variance of the outcome variables, and whether standard errors are clustered at the hospital level.

abstract: Gender-based harassment in public spaces affects women directly through victimization and indirectly through fear. We survey women aged 19–40 recruited at randomly sampled public spaces (bus stops, metro stations, and markets) in New Delhi (N=2,249) and Bengaluru (N=2,290), measuring the prevalence of seven forms of harassment, the anxiety the risk of each form induces, and self-reported effects of harassment risk on work and mobility decisions. To quantify how questionnaire design affects measured prevalence, respondents were randomly assigned to either the main questionnaire (with 90% probability) which asks directly about specific experiences related to gender-based harassment or an alternative (with 10% probability) that used screener questions. The screener questionnaire asked two questions about women's experiences with either physical or non-physical sexual harassment before asking the same set of specific experiences as in the main questionnaire, conditional on a woman indicating she had been harassed.
experimental_design: In-person survey of women aged 19–40 recruited at sampled public venues (bus stops, metro stations, retail markets) in Delhi (Nov–Dec 2024) and Bengaluru (Mar–Apr 2025). Respondents were randomized in real time (via SurveyCTO) between two questionnaire versions: a behaviorally specific version with neutral framing (90%) and a screener-question version labeling behaviors as "sexual harassment" (10%). The screener-question version replicates the instrument previously fielded to the full sample in a companion (non-randomized) survey in Jaipur (May–Jun 2024, N=1,863), whose data provide a cross-city benchmark and are reported in the paper's appendix; the Jaipur survey is not part of the randomized trial registered here.

abstract: Small manufacturers in Punjab spend roughly 28% of operating costs on energy, and falling panel prices have cut solar payback to 1.5–2 years, yet few have adopted. Our completed randomized experiment among 657 firms (IGC PAK-22225; AEARCTR-0010691) shows the barrier is not information: short informational videos raised firms' knowledge of the correct savings range by 19–22 percentage points but left attitudes, perceived behavioral control, and adoption essentially unmoved. The evidence points instead to a financing constraint, as 95% of these firms have never held a bank loan, and toward a specific instrument: 64.7% would consider a rent-to-own arrangement versus 26% a bank loan, and rent-to-own willingness is the financing attitude most strongly tied to intended adoption. We aim to test whether asset-based, performance-contingent solar finance can close the gap for credit-excluded small firms. Because a solar system is discrete, resaleable, and directly metered, repayments can flex with realized generation at near-zero verification cost, making it an especially good fit for performance-contingent contracts. The current work comprises three linked components to support the development of a pre-registered design and power analysis for a full RCT: qualitative supply-side scoping of Pakistan's emerging asset-finance market, including value-chain anchor models; an incentivized discrete-choice experiment on 250 firms eliciting demand over contract terms and structures; and a small randomized real-offer pilot with a provider partner.
experimental_design: Treatment 1: fixed lease-to-own payments on solar panels Treatment 2: performance-based/contingent lease-to-own payments on solar panels
intervention: The current project It builds on an existing panel of 657 small manufacturers whose baseline beliefs, financing preferences, and firm attributes are already measured, and on a separately funded follow-up telephone survey that records actual adoption and the financing method used. In order to develop the full RCT, we are currently engaged in the following background research and piloting initiatives: (a) Supply-side market scoping. We will map the emerging market for asset-based solar finance through 20–30 structured interviews with installers/EPC firms, asset-finance and leasing companies, microfinance institutions, and DFI-backed investors, characterising the contract taxonomy (BOT, BOOT, PPA) and documenting the ~1 MW threshold below which fixed costs make these unviable, defining the sub-1 MW “missing middle” our MSMEs occupy (documented so far in a preliminary consultation with a local supplier; the interviews will establish them systematically). We will approach lease-to-own providers (Royal Solar Energy, Multan), providers that have declined the SME segment (e.g. Alpha Solar), and DFIs including BII and its investee platforms (e.g. Atlas Energy). Collecting contract templates and unit-economics, we will characterise pricing and the binding supply constraints (fixed costs, default/repossession risk, the documentation barrier), then assess the delivery-model design space that could serve the missing middle. (a-ii) Value-chain / anchor-financing scoping. A dedicated strand assesses whether solar finance can be delivered through supply-chain anchors (lead exporters, estate authorities, sector associations), which resolve both problems at once: aggregating many small suppliers into one program (spreading fixed origination cost) while deducting repayments at source from trade payments (the design proven by Cordaro et al., 2025) and pre-selecting creditworthy suppliers from the commercial relationship. In our existing panel, 24.8% of firms are value-chain-linked, concentrated in Sialkot (≈80%) and Gujranwala (36%). We will interview candidate anchors and their financiers on willingness to anchor, the legal feasibility of payment-linked repayment, exposure to buyer/brand decarbonisation mandates, and supplier single-buyer-dependence. (b) Demand-side contract-terms experiment. Among 250 firms (drawn primarily from the existing panel plus a targeted fresh sample including an oversample of women-owned firms) we will field an incentivised discrete-choice/conjoint experiment varying the salient features of an offer: up-front deposit, contract length, monthly instalment, early-buyout option, bundled maintenance/insurance, system size (partial vs. fuller coverage, directly targeting the “all-or-nothing” belief that was the strongest barrier in the completed study), and the contract’s performance-contingency: fixed lease-to-own vs. savings-linked vs. a hybrid that flexes with realised savings up to a capped total (Cordaro et al., 2025). For each offer, the firm makes a simple accept-or-reject choice; exactly one choice is made real using the Prince method (Johnson et al., 2021), more transparent for a low-numeracy population than BDM. (c) Small real-offer pilot and RCT design. With the partner provider, we will deliver 15–20 randomised real offers to firms from the demand-experiment sample to test operational feasibility and measure real take-up, verified against the provider’s origination/contracting records and, for installations, by site visit and metered generation. Contingency: if no provider commits by month 4, the module falls back to refundable-deposit bookings for independent site visits/quotes brokered by the team (still yielding a revealed take-up measure) and the pilot budget shifts to deepening the supply-side and anchor scoping. Candidate partners beyond Royal Solar Energy are identified in the month 1–4 interviews, which double as recruitment meetings. The deliverable is a pre-registered design and power analysis for a full randomised evaluation: the offer, unit of randomisation, outcomes, and the partnership and data architecture needed to implement it.

abstract: Workers in informal labor markets often rely on other workers for information about jobs, but passing along an opportunity can expose the source to blame if the job turns out badly, even though he controls neither the employer's behavior nor the recipient's decision. This study asks whether anticipated relational consequences reduce the transmission of job information. We conduct a field experiment with approximately 600 daily-wage workers at urban labor stands in Delhi, India. Workers learn about a real one-day paid task and decide whether to give the name of another worker who will be contacted about the same opportunity in a future round. We randomize whether the named worker will be told who supplied his name, holding fixed the job and the information conveyed. Each worker is told which condition he is in before he decides. Workers are told that providing a name does not affect their own chance of being selected for the task. We examine whether attribution suppresses workers' willingness to give a name and whether it affects the type of worker they nominate.
experimental_design: The main Source-Attribution Experiment uses individual-level random assignment. Approximately 600 workers from approximately 30 labor stands will be independently randomized with equal probability to the Anonymous or Attributed condition. In the Anonymous condition, if a nominated worker is contacted, the research team will not disclose that the respondent provided his name. In the Attributed condition, the research team will disclose that the respondent provided his name. Approximately half of nomination records will be randomly selected for nominated-worker follow-up within cells defined by labor stand and the nominating worker's treatment assignment. The study also contains separate randomized exercises. Respondents in the main worker survey are independently randomized between close- and less-close-relationship versions of the Relationship-Strength Vignette. Respondents completing the nominated-worker follow-up are independently randomized between the two versions of the Source Prior-Experience Vignette. A separate sample of approximately 200-250 workers is independently randomized to a normal or adverse job experience in the Costly-Punishment Experiment. Among workers who complete the paid task, the order of the anonymous pooled and individually named information-sharing formats is randomized.
intervention: The study consists of a real paid task, a randomized source-attribution intervention around the transmission of that opportunity to another worker, and several additional exercises designed to measure the relational consequences of sharing job information. 1. Paid task Workers receive a standardized description of a real one-day paid task located near the labor stand. They report their beliefs about the task and whether they are willing to undertake it. Conditional on accepting, each worker has an independent probability of being selected for the paid task. 2. Nomination decision Workers are told that additional workers may be needed for the same paid task under the same terms on subsequent days. They are told that, if a worker whose name they provide is selected for contact, the research team will approach that worker, provide information about the paid task, and ask whether he would like to undertake it. Workers are then asked whether they would like to provide the name of another worker whom they would send for the paid task. 3. Source-attribution treatment Immediately before the nomination decision, respondents are independently randomized with equal probability to one of two conditions: Anonymous: if the nominated worker is contacted, the research team will not tell him who provided his name. Attributed: if the nominated worker is contacted, the research team will tell him who provided his name. The paid task, the information conveyed to the nominated worker, the nominating worker's own probability of selection, and the nominating worker's formal responsibility for the nominated worker's performance are held fixed across conditions. 4. Follow-up with nominated workers A randomly selected subset of nominated workers is subsequently approached. Each receives the source-disclosure information corresponding to the nominating worker's assigned condition, receives information about the same paid task, and is asked whether he is willing and available to undertake it. 5. Additional randomized components The study includes additional exercises designed to measure the consequences of transmitting job information and workers' willingness to be identified as the source of such information. First, respondents complete a randomized vignette in which one worker tells another about a job that subsequently turns out badly. The vignette varies whether the two workers are close friends or workers who know each other from the labor stand but are not close. Second, nominated workers complete a randomized vignette that holds the adverse job outcome fixed but varies whether the information source had previously worked for the same employer without an adverse experience on the job. Third, a separate sample of workers participates in an incentivized costly-punishment exercise. Respondents may give up part of their own experimental endowment to reduce the payoff of a worker who passed along a job opportunity in good faith. The randomized condition varies whether the subsequent job experience is normal or adverse. Finally, workers who complete the paid task are asked whether information about their own experience may be shared with future workers under two formats: anonymously as part of a pooled summary or individually together with their name. Each participant makes a decision under both formats, with the order randomized.

abstract: Women in rural Tanzania devote substantial time to water-related work — collection, boiling, fuel gathering, and caring for household members with waterborne illness. Within a household-level randomised trial in six villages of Uyui District, Tabora Region, 900 households are assigned to one of three arms: free provision of a Solvatten solar water-treatment canister by World Vision Tanzania (360 households); an unconditional cash transfer calibrated either to the local cost of obtaining safe drinking water or to the local value of the Solvatten canister (180 households); or control (360 households). At the close of the endline interview, every sampled household in all three arms is offered entry into a lottery for a paid six-month community job for the wife. The offer is universal and not itself randomised. A household enters only if both spouses consent; consent is elicited privately and separately, and neither is told the other's answer. Because only a minority of dual-consenting households win, each spouse retains plausible deniability, making truthful reporting incentive-compatible. The primary outcomes are the two private willingness-to-accept decisions and the resulting four-cell agreement typology, measured on the 900 couples interviewed at endline.
experimental_design: A three-arm, household-level randomised controlled trial in six villages of Uyui District, Tabora Region — Kalangale, Kizengi, Lutona, Misole, Mwakadala and Nyankombe — with a universal elicitation module at endline. The six villages were selected because they contain unimproved dug wells without treatment and broken or missing pumps, so publicly provided safe water is limited and roughly comparable ex ante. The sampling frame was built from building footprints inside village boundaries; 150 main-sample households were drawn per village, giving 900. Enumerators screen each geo-located building for an eligible couple and interview two adults per household, yielding approximately 1,800 respondents per round. Kizengi is a pure-control village receiving no devices, which bounds spillovers. The endline round, roughly eleven weeks after distribution, closes with the job-offer module. Identifying variation for the primary outcomes is the parent trial's household-level arm assignment; the job offer is a constant. The lottery among consenting households makes the offer credible and creates deniability.
intervention: Arm 1 — Solvatten device, 360 households. A free Solvatten household solar water-treatment canister, distributed by World Vision Tanzania, with a short standardised demonstration of use, cleaning and storage at handover. No cash, no employment information, and no gender-related messaging accompanies delivery. Arm 2 — Cash, 180 households. An unconditional transfer in two equal cells of 90: one calibrated to the local cost of safe drinking water, the other to the value of the Solvatten canister. Arm 3 — Control, 360 households. Survey and economic games only. No device and no transfer. Universal end-of-endline module — the dyadic job-offer experiment. At the very end of the endline interview, every sampled household in all three arms receives an identical offer: entry into a lottery for a paid community job for the wife, such as street cleaning, at the going wage. Consent is elicited privately and separately from each spouse, and neither is told the other's answer. Only dual-consenting households enter the lottery, and the selection probability among them is deliberately low so that a household without a job cannot infer who refused. The job offer is not randomised and is not cross-randomised with device assignment. All identifying variation for the consent outcomes comes from the parent trial's three-arm household randomisation.

abstract: Access to safe water and inclusive and equitable education remain two fundamental development challenges. In its 2026 update on the Sustainable Development goals, the United Nations reports that 2.1 billion people still lack safely managed drinking water, and 273 million children and young people remain out of school. The latter problem is particularly stark in sub-Saharan Africa, which has the lowest school completion rates in the world. Our main question for this study is whether access to safe drinking water at home improves children’s schooling. Our study area lies in Uyui district in the region of Tabora in Tanzania, which is characterized by very poor access to clean water and the country’s lowest school enrollment and literacy rates. Within a household-level randomized trial in six villages of Uyui District, 900 households are assigned to one of three arms: free provision of a Solvatten solar water-treatment canister by World Vision Tanzania (360 households); an unconditional cash transfer calibrated to the local cost of obtaining safe drinking water or the local value of the Solvatten canister, including the value of collection time at prevailing local wages (180 households); or control (360 households). The cash arm holds the resource value of the technology roughly constant, so the device-versus-cash contrast isolates the time-savings channel from the pure income channel. A baseline survey will precede the intervention, followed by an endline study roughly 11 weeks after intervention. Only households with children aged 7-17 will be included in this study. The design means that we can capture within-household and age-specific short-run schooling effects of clean water provision at home. Our primary outcomes capture survey-based school attendance and absenteeism at primary and lower secondary levels, as well as equal schooling opportunity for children of genders in relevant households. These are supplemented by secondary outcomes measuring schooling attitudes and social norms elicited from both parents. We also examine the mechanisms through which safe water supply can affect schooling outcomes, namely health effects, time use of children, and education expenditure of households.
experimental_design: A three-arm, household-level randomised controlled trial in six villages of Uyui District, Tabora Region — Kalangale, Kizengi, Lutona, Misole, Mwakadala and Nyankombe — with a universal elicitation module at endline. The six villages were selected because they contain unimproved dug wells without treatment and broken or missing pumps, so publicly provided safe water is limited and roughly comparable ex ante. The sampling frame was built from building footprints inside village boundaries; 150 main-sample households were drawn per village, giving 900. Enumerators screen each geo-located building for an eligible couple and interview two adults per household, yielding approximately 1,800 respondents per round. Kizengi is a pure-control village receiving no devices, which bounds spillovers. The endline round will happen roughly eleven weeks after distribution. Note that our sample will constitute a subset of the sample of the parent RCT. The subset will include only those households with at least one child aged 7-17, i.e. eligible to attend primary (7-13 years) or lower secondary (13-17 years) school. According to the Sixth Census of Tanzania of 2022, the average household size in Uyui is 6.2, which translates to 3-4 children per household. With a conservative estimate of 2 school-age children, this yields expected 1800 (2*900) children in our sample.
experimental_design_details: Why a cash arm. A device relaxes two constraints at once — it saves time and it saves the money and fuel spent obtaining safe water. Device-versus-control cannot separate them. The cash arm delivers the resource relief without the time relief, so device-minus-cash is our preferred estimate of the time channel and cash-minus-control recovers the income channel. Device-minus-control remains the primary policy contrast. Both are reported for every primary outcome.
intervention: Arm 1 — Solvatten device (T), 360 households. A free Solvatten household solar water-treatment canister, distributed by World Vision Tanzania, with a short, standardized demonstration of use, cleaning and storage at handover. No cash, no employment information and no gender-related messaging accompanies delivery. Arm 2 — Cash (M), 180 households. an unconditional cash transfer calibrated to the local cost of obtaining safe drinking water or the local value of the Solvatten canister, including the value of collection time at prevailing local wages. Delivered with the same number of enumerator contacts as the device arm. This arm holds the resource relief constant, so device-minus-cash identifies the time-savings channel net of income. Arm 3 — Control (C), 360 households. Survey and economic games only. No device and no transfer.

mde_text: The trial will randomize 900 households, with 360 households allocated to the intervention arm and 540 to the pooled control + monetary treatment arms. We assume that we will have an average of two school-age children per household, yielding a total of 1,800 respondents. The primary outcome is the number of days of school missed during the preceding four weeks, assumed to have a standard deviation of 3.5 days (overall average 1-2 days/month in Tanzania). Randomization occurs at the household level, and the intra-household correlation coefficient (ICC) is assumed to be 0.30. With two respondents per household, the variance of the household mean is 3.5^2[0.30+(1−0.30)/2]=7.9625. Under a two-sided 5% significance level and 80% power, the proposed 900-household sample provides a minimum detectable treatment effect (MDE) of approximately 0.54 days of school missed. This corresponds to a standardized effect size of approximately 0.15 standard deviations. No allowance for attrition is included. ICC sensitivity: With ICC=0.5, we get MDE=0.58 (SD=0.17); with ICC=0.1, we get MDE=0.49 (SD=0.14).

abstract: This pre-analysis plan details a randomized controlled trial in rural Burundi designed to evaluate the adoption and impact of electric cooking (e-cooking) appliances among newly electrified households. Currently, over 90% of households in the study setting rely on biomass fuels like charcoal and firewood, which contributes to deforestation, increases local air pollution, and limits rural electricity demand. The study aims to identify which appliances and subsidy combinations maximize electricity demand, assess the environmental and economic benefits, and determine if carbon markets can cover appliance costs. The experimental design cross-randomizes the provision of e-cooking technologies—pressure cookers, induction stoves, hot plates, or a combination—and subsidy levels (free versus installment plans) across 66 newly electrified settlements, known as collines, encompassing a treated sample of 5,000 households. Using an ANCOVA empirical specification to estimate intent-to-treat effects, the analysis will evaluate primary outcomes including stove ownership, administrative electricity consumption, physical biomass consumption, and appliance-specific electricity usage. Additionally, the study will track secondary outcomes such as total energy expenditures, time spent cooking and collecting fuel, and overall household welfare, while testing for heterogeneous effects based on baseline household size, wealth, and cooking fuel.

abstract: This study is a laboratory replication and robustness check of a companion online experiment (Gain-Loss Framing and Feedback Visibility in Financial Decision-Making Under Uncertainty: A Randomized Experiment, registered separately on the AEA RCT Registry — see Secondary IDs) using the same 24-month simulated personal loan repayment task and the same 2×2 design crossing outcome framing (gain vs. loss) and score feedback visibility (displayed vs. hidden). Unlike the online study, where individual participants are independently randomized, this laboratory study randomizes at the session level: each of 8 laboratory sessions (≈24–28 participants per session) is randomly assigned to one of the four conditions, and all participants in a session complete the same scenario together. The study examines whether the framing and feedback-visibility effects observed online replicate in a supervised laboratory setting, and exploratorily examines the same psychometric trait moderators as the companion study. An earlier version of this study was pre-registered on OSF under the name of Neurocognitive Pathways to Risk: Affective Priming and Prediction Error in Dynamic Credit Simulation, here: https://osf.io/rd9ay/overview.
experimental_design: A 2×2 factorial design, randomized at the session level, assigns each of 8 laboratory sessions to one of four conditions crossing outcome framing (gain vs. loss) and score feedback visibility (displayed vs. hidden). All participants attending a given session complete a pre-task psychometric questionnaire, 24 simulated monthly decisions in a personal loan repayment scenario (identical scenario content to the companion online study — only framing and feedback visibility differ by condition), and a post-task questionnaire, under supervised laboratory conditions at VŠE Prague. This study is designed as a robustness check of the companion online (Prolific) experiment using the same design and materials in a supervised, in-person setting.
intervention: (1) a framing manipulation presenting the same monthly financial information using either gain-framed or loss-framed language, and (2) a feedback-visibility manipulation in which the running composite performance score is either displayed or hidden after each monthly decision. The sole procedural difference from the companion online study is the unit and method of randomization: here, treatment is assigned at the laboratory session level rather than to each individual participant.

abstract: This pre-analysis plan describes a research project with smallholder cattle farmers in the Eastern Cape region of South Africa. The broad goal of this study is to understand how the design of public good contracts shape individual contributions to the public good and resulting public good provision. The study design is a framed field experiment (a lab-in-the-field). Participants face five contracts varying multiple features of the payment scheme. Each contract is played both individually and in a group, so the design identifies how each contract feature performs by itself and how moving from an individual principal-agent relationship to a principal-collective agent setting affects performance. The study speaks to the design of payments for ecosystem services on communal land and to the classic input-versus-output contracting problem under partial observability.
experimental_design: The core of the data collection instrument is a multi-round public-goods game played on individual tablets. The framing of the games is around carbon storage: contributions to the global public good are framed as being contributions towards carbon storage in the community's rangelands. Participants play all public-goods games both in groups of about five players (a standard public-goods design) and individually (a group of one). Group membership is reshuffled across games and drawn from the entire session of participants, so that over the course of a session a participant interacts with essentially all session-mates. The games were designed as follows. In each round, participants receive an endowment of 100 tokens and decide whether to fund rotational grazing, a binary choice ($g = 20$ tokens or $g = 0$), and unobserved contributions, $e$, representing a continuous choice of an additional conservation margin that others cannot observe, from zero up to the total remaining budget. At the end of each round, the number of participants who contributed to rotational grazing are observable to all participants within the group, while individual decisions and unobserved contributions $e$ are not observable other than through their effect on the final aggregated payment outcome, which is contract-dependent and explained below. We designed five different payment rules for the public-goods game and refer to them as contracts. Each contract is played twice: first solo (a single-person group), which serves as the individual principal-agent benchmark, and then in a group. The combination (contract by individual-or-group mode) is referred to as a game. One game is randomly selected for payment, and the number of paid rounds per game is determined by a block-random-termination rule. The five contracts vary three design features: (a) whether the contract pays for observable (grazing) inputs or for measured output, (b) whether the output is exposed to a production shock, and (c) whether, in addition to the observed contributions, the output is affected by an additional unobservable margin, in which the individual chooses her contribution without revealing any signal to the group. The full carbon (public good) production function is set to $F(G,E) = (2G + 1.5E)\varepsilon$, where $G$ and $E$ are the sums grazing and unobserved (extra) contributions in the community that is playing together, respectively. The production shock $\varepsilon$ is drawn from a two-point (Bernoulli) distribution with equally likely outcomes 0.5 and 1.5. The shock is therefore mean-preserving, and it is applied to the public good production after all contributions have been summed but before payments are distributed. Therefore, the contracts that inherit risk pay participants on the final outcome after the risk shock. All five contracts pay participants for their grazing contribution. Furthermore, the expected private marginal return of this contribution is set equal across all contracts within the same game-mode (solo or collective), ensuring equivalence in grazing incentives. On the other hand, only some contracts pay for unobserved contributions. Contracts C3 and C5 offer a positive return for extra contributions, while the other contracts do not. The order in which the contracts appear is randomized across sessions. In every session, participants always begin with playing C1 then C2. From then on, the order of C3, C4, and C5 varies by community. For each contract, participants play the solo mode first, followed by the collective mode. All in all, experimental assignment happens in two ways. First is within individuals since we have every individual engage with different types of contracts in the lab. From this engagement, we extract within-individual changes in behavior caused by the contract features they are facing. The second experimental assignment is in the order that these contracts appear. This assignment is at the session level. The variation is in which contract features comes first, second, third, fourth and fifth. That is, the order in which different contract features appear to all participants in a specific session.

abstract: This study examines how young adults in urban Kenya respond to potentially misleading information on social media and whether short warning messages can help people assess such information. Approximately 5,000 people aged 18–40 in Nairobi and other urban areas of Kenya will participate in an online survey. Participants will be shown two examples of social media content concerning topics relevant to Kenya and international affairs. They will then see different types of messages designed to alert people to potentially misleading or manipulative information. These warnings vary in who provides the warning, how the source of the potentially misleading information is described, and how the warning is presented, for example as social media content or a radio advertisement. Some participants will not receive a warning, allowing us to compare responses across groups. The study will examine whether these different approaches affect people's willingness to share social media content, how credible they find the information, and their views on international actors. The broader aim is to better understand how people in Kenya respond to foreign influence and misleading information online, and which types of warnings may help people identify and resist such content.
experimental_design: The study uses a 2×2×2 factorial design, crossing three binary treatment dimensions, plus a control group, yielding nine experimental arms. The three treatment dimensions are: • Warning source: European Union (EU) vs. local independent fact-checking organization (hereafter 'Local NGO') • Actor attribution: the false message is attributed explicitly to Russia vs. attributed to a generic unspecified foreign power • Warning medium: the warning is delivered as a social media post or a radio add.
intervention: The study fields a cross-sectional survey with an embedded experiment among approximately 5,000 individuals aged 18–40 in Nairobi and other urban centres across Kenya. Respondents are asked to read two social media posts, one questioning the motive behind western companies selling gene-modified crops in Kenya, and the second mimicking the language used in posts trying to attract Kenyans to sign up for work in the Russian military. To encourage respondents to read the messages carefully they are asked to rate the posts based on spelling and grammar. Respondents are then randomized into a control group and eight treatment arms receiving variations of disinformation-debunking warnings. Warnings differ across three dimensions: the source of the disinformation warning (European Union vs. a local independent fact-checking organization), whether the spread of disinformation is attributed explicitly to Russia or to a generic foreign power, and the medium of the message (radio ad versus a social media post). The key outcome variable is social media sharing intention, but we also look at perceived message credibility, and opinions on global powers.

abstract: How does knowledge of past atrocities shape support for contemporary redress policies? More specifically, how do public memory projects shape political attitudes and support for transitional justice mechanisms? While lacking specific knowledge of past atrocities can be associated with denial of ongoing inequalities, recent research on the effects of memorializing past atrocities has shown that these efforts can increase support for democratic institutions and decrease support for previous repressive regimes. We build on this stream of research by exploring the effects of memorialization efforts across a long time horizon: the atrocities committed in the United States as part of the transatlantic slave trade and subsequent institutionalization of chattel slavery that have reverberated throughout American history and continue to shape contemporary politics. We conduct a field experiment using the 2.5-mile-long Slave Trail memorial in Richmond, VA, a former hub of the US slave trade, to evaluate the effects of remembering the legacies of past atrocities on public opinion and support for domestic transitional justice policies. As communities in the US begin to reckon with this history, it is important to understand how this reckoning might influence contemporary political attitudes and opinions about justice and reconciliation.
experimental_design: Between subjects design, field experiment and companion survey experiment.
experimental_design_details: We will recruit college students from the Richmond area, focusing in particular on Virginia Commonwealth University, Virginia Union University, and the University of Richmond to participate in the field experiment. We aim to recruit around 1000 participants using a baseline survey and expect to enroll between 180 and 200 participants in each of the control and treatment groups (400 participants total). The walking tour will take approximately 60-90 minutes and the tours will be led by both of the researchers with input from local tour guides. The tour of the train museum will be led by a museum employee. Immediately after the experiential or digital treatment, all subjects will complete a survey about their experience, including questions to measure our dependent variables. The field experimental participants will receive follow-up surveys approximately one week, one month, three months, and six months after the treatment to estimate the durability of attitudinal changes. We plan to compensate research participants for their time during the treatment and again after successful completion of each of the follow-up surveys to encourage participation. We will partner with the survey firm Verasight to recruit approximately 1000 adult residents of Virginia to participate in the companion survey experiment. They will take a survey that will take either 20 minutes (control) or 35 minutes (treatment) involving a virtual train tour (control) or virtual reality experience (control).

abstract: The research team will be partnering with the American Economic Association to launch a three-year randomized controlled trial of the effects of author-anonymized peer reviewing, commonly referred to as "double-blind." This evaluation will involve the AER, AER: Insights, and the four American Economic Journals. In the treatment group, information revealing author identities will be excluded from materials provided to reviewers, and reviewers will be asked to refrain from seeking them out through web searches or other means. The experiment will test the effects of removing author identities from the information routinely provided to reviewers, while recognizing that reviewers may become aware of author identities in other ways. Key outcomes that will be examined include (1) author and reviewer perceptions of fairness, (2) reviewer awareness of author identities in the treatment (author-anonymized) group, and (3) differential impacts of author-anonymized review on manuscript decisions by characteristics of the authors and their papers.
experimental_design: Authors will submit an anonymized manuscript and appendix files that allow the editorial staff to create anonymized manuscripts and manuscripts with author information. At the time of submission, authors will be asked their views and preferences on the review process. Reviewers will complete the review as instructed. At the time of submitting their reports, reviewers will be asked questions on their views of the review process. In addition, reviewers who received an author-anonymized manuscript will be asked whether or not they believed they knew the author(s) of the manuscript regardless. Editors receive referee reports and make editorial decisions. After receiving the initial decision, authors are sent a follow-up survey which will inform them of whether their manuscript had been anonymized (treatment status) and their views on the review process for that manuscript.
intervention: Manuscripts submitted during the study period will be randomly assigned with equal probability to author-anonymized or single-blind review. Single-blind review continues the status quo. In particular, referees receive the title page which contains identifying information (specifically, name and institution of submitting authors). Under author-anonymized review, referee reports are prepared without access to the authors' identifying information provided on the title page (specifically name and institution).

abstract: The University of Kansas, the state’s flagship institution, strives to retain and graduate all of its students. This goal is challenging, given its mission to accept and educate the vast majority of students who apply. This study evaluates the effectiveness of technology-driven outreach strategies in improving student success and retention at the University of Kansas. Despite widespread adoption of progress reporting tools like Navigate360 (Jayhawk GPS), faculty engagement and utilization remain low. Progress reporting is widely regarded as an effective retention strategy, yet causal evidence of its impact is limited. We propose a cluster-randomized evaluation across multiple sections of high-enrollment, high-DFW courses within KU’s required general education. Sections will be randomly assigned to one of three arms: (1) no progress reporting, (2) progress reporting only, and (3) progress reporting with navigator-led outreach. Outcomes will include course grades, DFW rates, term-to-term retention, and student survey responses, adjusted for demographic and course-level factors. This research aims to identify the most effective outreach approach, optimize resource allocation, and inform evidence-based retention practices. Results will contribute to the broader literature on randomized evaluations in higher education and guide institutional strategies for student success.
experimental_design: This study will include general education courses at KU with high levels of enrollment, high DFW rates (mostly from KU’s general education https://kucore.ku.edu/), and three or more sections. Within each course, each section (i.e., cluster) will be randomly assigned to one of the following treatment arms: - No Progress Reporting - Jayhawk GPS Progress Reporting - Jayhawk GPS Progress Reporting with navigator interventions Sections assigned to no progress reporting will not use Jayhawk GPS. Sections assigned to progress reporting only will input relevant information about student progress into the Jayhawk system. Sections assigned to progress reporting with navigator-led outreach will input relevant information about student progress into the Jayhawk system, and will have student outreach coordinators supporting efforts to communicate with students flagged in these systems as being at risk for not passing.
intervention: Navigate360 (called “Jayhawk GPS” at the University of Kansas) is a multifunctional tool available as an app and web platform that is used by universities across the country for student success and retention. Students can schedule appointments with various campus offices, receive important course alerts from faculty, request specific support from offices on campus, and view meeting notes from past appointments with advisors among other features. In addition to offering a range of student services, Jayhawk GPS includes several retention-focused functions for university staff including quick polls, progress reports, population health assessments, predictive analytics, and success markers. Progress reports are one of the primary functions that University of Kansas uses as a part of its proactive retention efforts. Progress reporting offers an opportunity to identify students showing signs of academic distress early, allowing staff to review options and connect students with appropriate campus resources before they have earned a low or failing final grade. How Progress Reporting Works Jayhawk GPS administrators send instructors a progress report campaign weblink at specific points throughout the semester (e.g., week two and week seven). Instructors or course TAs are asked to submit feedback on student performance in their courses. The system then generates student alerts, which are delivered either automatically through the platform or through directly by the outreach team. Student navigators begin outreach with a phone call to learn more about the challenges affecting the student’s academic performance and connecting them to the appropriate campus resources. During the call, student navigators may also escalate the case to the student’s academic advisor and assist with scheduling the appointment. If the student is not reached by phone call, student navigators will follow up with a text message.
mde_text: We used PowerUP! (Dong and Maynard 2013) for a power analysis. In Spring 2025, the mean outcome grade in the courses we sampled that would be appropriate for this intervention was a 2.80 (C+) with a standard deviation of 1.26 and a harmonic mean of 12.3 students per section. Using 163 student-level covariates (fixed effects for each value of class, grade, gender, first generation status, honors program enrollment, major, and instructor name), our adjusted R2 is 0.19. If we randomize 96 sections evenly across our 3 control/treatment arms, this yields a minimum detectable effect size of 0.156 standard deviations, which is 0.20 GPA points. This is comparable to the effect found by Carrell and Kurlaender (2023) which randomized sending supportive emails to struggling students in introductory economics, and so we believe our proposed pilot is reasonable.

abstract: Undeclared work remains widespread in many countries and has important consequences for workers, employers and society. Decisions about whether and how much employment to declare may depend on the perceived costs and benefits of declaration and the institutional circumstances in which these decisions are made. We study how people think about employment declaration decisions involving workers and employers in Italy and Spain. We first measure beliefs and views about the costs and benefits of declared and undeclared employment. We then use a randomized information experiment to test whether providing information about these costs and benefits affects beliefs and decisions.
experimental_design: The study is an individually randomized online survey experiment conducted in Italy and Spain. Respondents consider hypothetical employment situations involving decisions about declared and undeclared work. We first elicit baseline beliefs and views before randomly assigning respondents to different information conditions. Following the information intervention, we measure beliefs and decisions concerning employment declaration. Respondents subsequently consider changes in the broader institutional environment, after which we examine how their beliefs and decisions respond. The survey also measures broader views about undeclared work and related policies.
experimental_design_details: The study is an individually randomized online survey experiment conducted in Italy and Spain. Respondents are introduced to a hypothetical employment setting involving a worker and an employer deciding how many hours of a full-time job are officially declared. Before treatment, we elicit respondents’ views about the factors affecting the worker’s and employer’s decisions using open-ended questions, followed by prior beliefs about relevant financial consequences of declared employment. Respondents are then randomly assigned within country to one of three conditions: Control, Tax/Take-home information, or Tax/Take-home + Pension information. Following treatment, we elicit respondents’ assessments of declaration decisions for the worker and employer, considering monetary factors and then all factors. We subsequently elicit the relative bargaining power of the worker and employer and the expected declaration level in the final agreement. Respondents then report beliefs about the probability of detection of undeclared employment. All respondents subsequently receive the same change in the institutional environment related to the detection of undeclared work. We then re-elicit the worker and employer declaration decisions, bargaining power, and expected declaration level. Finally, the survey elicits posterior beliefs about financial consequences of declaration, broader views about undeclared work and related policies, and selected behavioural and engagement outcomes.

abstract: This study investigates how individuals perceive and respond to financial risk under uncertainty, using an incentivized 24-month simulated personal loan repayment task. Participants recruited via Prolific are randomly assigned to one of four conditions in a 2×2 between-subjects factorial design, crossing (a) outcome framing (the same financial information presented as gains vs. as losses) and (b) visibility of a running performance score (displayed vs. hidden) throughout the task. Each simulated month, participants decide how much to repay toward a fixed loan installment while managing income, expenses, and a sequence of life events common to all conditions. Behavioral outcomes — repayment amount, overdraft usage, and a composite monthly performance score — are recorded automatically each month. Participants complete a psychometric questionnaire before and after the task. The study examines whether framing and feedback visibility causally affect repayment behavior and risk-taking (overdraft use) over time, and exploratorily examines whether individual differences in psychological traits moderate these effects. An earlier version of this study was pre-registered on OSF under the name of Neurocognitive Pathways to Risk: Affective Priming and Prediction Error in Dynamic Credit Simulation, here: https://osf.io/rd9ay/overview. The companion study performed in laboratory is named "Gain-Loss Framing and Feedback Visibility in Financial Decision- Making Under Uncertainty: A Laboratory Experiment" also registered both AEA RCT Registry and OSF.
experimental_design: A 2×2 between-subjects factorial design randomly assigns participants to one of four conditions crossing outcome framing (gain vs. loss) and score feedback visibility (displayed vs. hidden). After a pre-task psychometric questionnaire, participants complete 24 simulated monthly decisions in a personal loan repayment scenario, facing an identical sequence of income, expenses, and narrative life events across all conditions—only the framing of the presented numbers and the visibility of the score differ by condition. A post-task questionnaire assesses perceived task stress, difficulty, and realism.
intervention: The intervention consists of two orthogonal treatment manipulations embedded in a 24- month simulated personal loan repayment task administered online via Prolific: (1) Framing manipulation: The financial information shown to participants each month (income, expenses, loan balance, interest, and running totals) is presented using either gain-framed language (emphasizing what participants retain, save, or gain) or lossframed language (emphasizing what participants owe, lose, or fall short of). The underlying numerical values are identical across both framing conditions — only the presentation differs. (2) Feedback visibility manipulation: After each monthly decision, participants either see (displayed condition) or do not see (hidden condition) their running composite performance score. Each participant is randomly assigned to exactly one combination of these two manipulations (four arms: gain/displayed, gain/hidden, loss/displayed, loss/hidden) and remains in that condition for the entire 24-month task.

abstract: Public health systems ration surgical capacity through waiting times, which can be extremely long for elective surgery in low- and middle-income countries. While waiting, patients make consequential decisions about their health, finances and work, often with limited information. In partnership with a public hospital in Chile, we combine administrative data, a survey and an RCT to study how rationing by waiting shapes patient behavior and which policies can improve its efficiency and equity.
experimental_design: The study uses two stages of random assignment. In the first stage, patients on the surgical waiting list who meet the eligibility criteria are randomly assigned to be contacted for recruitment or not contacted, stratified by surgical procedure. In the second stage, recruited participants who complete a baseline survey are randomly assigned in equal proportions to a treatment group, which receives an informational intervention, or to a control group. This assignment is stratified by surgical procedure and time on the waiting list.
experimental_design_details: First, from the eligible cohort (approximately 2,900 patients), we first define an initial sample of patients who have been waiting 250 days or less. Within this sample, we randomly assign 25% to a non-contact arm and the remaining 75% to a contact arm. Our recruitment target is 1,000 participants. If the contact arm is insufficient to reach this target, we expand it in successive rounds. In each round, we (i) raise the waiting-time threshold and add the newly eligible patients to the contact arm, and (ii) randomly reassign 20-40% of the initial non-contact arm to the contact arm; to reach the target size of the non-contact arm of 250 patients. All randomizations at this stage are stratified by surgical procedure. In the second stage, we randomize participants who were recruited and completed the baseline survey (target: 750 patients). Participants are assigned in a 1:1 ratio to a treatment group, which receives a personalized information message about expected waiting times, or to a control group, which receives no message. This randomization is stratified by surgical procedure and by time on the waitlist (above or below the within-procedure median).
intervention: We provide information to patients on the waitlist for elective surgery.

abstract: This study examines whether brief support after an early competitive setback affects students’ re-entry into competition and continued investment in leadership. Students who voluntarily run for their first-choice class-officer position but are not elected to that position will be randomized within classrooms to one of three standardized video messages: a neutral educational message, practical guidance on developing leadership skills through concrete actions, or support that separates a single setback from stable ability and self-worth. The two active treatments target distinct margins: the perceived effectiveness of leadership investment and the perceived personal cost of future failure. We will measure immediate beliefs and intentions, voluntary registration for a school speaking activity, and entry in the next scheduled class-officer election. Pre-specified secondary analyses will examine heterogeneity by gender and prior schooling at village teaching sites.
experimental_design: Before the class-officer election, all students in participating grades will complete a baseline survey. The baseline data will be used to characterize selection into candidacy and election success and to measure pre-treatment characteristics. Following the election, all students who voluntarily ran for their first-choice class-officer position but were not elected to that position will be eligible for the randomized experiment, subject to the approved consent and assent procedures. Students remain eligible if the teacher assigns them to a different role before the intervention. Such alternative appointments will be recorded before randomization. Unsuccessful candidates will be randomized within classrooms in approximately equal proportions to the neutral control, action-oriented treatment, or identity-protective treatment. Successful first-choice candidates will not be randomized. They will receive the neutral message and complete the same immediate questionnaire as a nonrandomized benchmark. The main causal analysis will estimate intention-to-treat effects among randomized unsuccessful candidates. Analyses of initial candidacy, election success, and comparisons with successful candidates will be reported separately as nonexperimental or benchmark analyses.
intervention: Eligible students will receive one of three brief, standardized video-based messages shortly after an unsuccessful class-officer election. The control group will receive neutral educational information unrelated to leadership, competition, or setbacks. The action-oriented treatment will provide practical guidance on translating leadership goals into relevant skills and concrete actions. The identity-protective treatment will emphasize that one election outcome does not define a student’s stable ability or personal worth and will provide a constructive way to interpret and recover from the setback. The three messages will use a similar format and duration. Successful first-choice candidates will receive the same neutral message and complete the same immediate survey. They will serve as a nonrandomized benchmark and will not constitute a fourth randomized treatment arm.

abstract: This study is a randomized field experiment with 179,706 credit card holders of a large retail issuer in Chile. During one billing cycle, cardholders received two email reminders before their payment due date. They were randomly assigned to one of four versions: a reminder with a warning about the consequences of paying only the minimum payment, a reminder with a warning about the consequences of not paying the full statement balance, a reminder with both warnings, or a reminder with no warning.
experimental_design: Cardholders were randomly assigned to one of four conditions. During one billing cycle, each cardholder received two email payment reminders, five days and two days before the due date. The emails reminded people about their repayment and due date, and varied in the warning they included: none (plain reminder or control), a warning about the consequences of paying only the minimum payment, a warning about the consequences of not paying the full statement balance, or both warnings. All cardholders received their regular credit card statement in a separate communication.
