abstract: The Power of Feedback is an international cluster-randomised controlled trial evaluating the effectiveness of AI-enabled formative feedback for primary school math students in four countries (Latvia, Germany, France and Slovak Republic). Teachers of Grades 4 and 5 are randomly assigned to use the OECD’s Platform for Innovative Learning Assessments (PILA) with their students, either with an integrated AI-enabled tutor or without the AI-enabled tutor. Both groups use the same mathematics modules, digital activities and teacher monitoring dashboard, so that the availability of AI-enabled feedback is main difference between the treatment and control. Over approximately 5-8 weeks, students use PILA during mathematics lessons twice a week for around 30 minutes under teacher supervision. The AI-enabled tutor provides formative feedback and support while students work on mathematics exercises, supporting reflection and different solution strategies rather than simply providing answers. The objective is to estimate whether access to AI-enabled formative feedback improves students’ math skills, measured using assessments administered after the intervention. The study also collects student and teacher questionnaire data and platform-use data to measure engagement, attitudes towards AI, and implementation quality.
experimental_design: The study uses a cluster-randomised controlled design, with the teacher as the unit of randomisation stratified by country. Participating Grade 4 and 5 teachers are randomly assigned 50:50 to the intervention (AI-enabled tutor) or control condition (no -enabled tutor) at account creation for the digital platform by country. Randomization method: Automated randomization up on sign-up of the teacher to the digital learning platform by country (50:50).
intervention: The intervention provides Grade 4 and 5 students with access to an AI-enabled tutor integrated into the OECD’s Platform for Innovative Learning Assessments (PILA) during math lessons. The AI-enabled tutor provides short, constructive, age-appropriate formative feedback while students work on math exercises, including prompts to reflect on their reasoning, identify mistakes and consider alternative solution strategies. Students in both the treatment and control group use the same PILA math modules teachers the same monitoring dashboard. PILA is used during regular math lessons approximately twice a week for 30 minutes over 5-8 weeks, under teacher supervision.

abstract: Greenhouse-gas (GHG) emissions are highly concentrated at the top of the economic distribution, yet the public systematically underestimates how concentrated they are. A less appreciated point is that "how concentrated" has no single answer: the emissions attributed to the richest 1% of Americans range from roughly 6% to roughly 39% of the national total depending on whether responsibility is assigned through consumption, income, or ownership of productive assets. We exploit this variation as an experimental design feature. In a pre-registered information-provision experiment on a US online sample (N ≈ 700 per arm), respondents are randomly assigned to receive one accurate, peer-reviewed statistic on the top-1% emission share under one of three accounting frames, or to a pure control. Policy preferences are then elicited through an eight-task conjoint experiment in which carbon-tax packages vary in household cost, revenue use, and whether an additional tax targets the richest households. This design allows us to test whether information dampens cost sensitivity, shifts demand toward high-emitter-targeted designs, and does so most strongly under the ownership frame. We also examine heterogeneity by prior beliefs, self-interest and partisanship, potential backlash on generic carbon-tax support, and an incentivised donation task.
experimental_design: This is a pre-registered information-provision experiment with an embedded conjoint policy-choice task, fielded on a sample of US adults recruited online. Respondents first report their prior belief about the share of total annual US greenhouse-gas emissions generated by the richest 1%, on a 0–100 slider, followed by a confidence item. They are then randomly assigned, with equal probability, to one of three arms: a pure control, which receives no statistic, and two treatment arms, each of which receives one accurate statistic on the top-1% emission share drawn from a published, peer-reviewed study, together with its source. The two treatments differ in the accounting frame used to attribute emissions to households: a consumption-based frame (Starr et al., Ecological Economics, 2023) and an ownership-based frame (Chancel & Rehm, Nature Climate Change, 2026). Treatment texts are harmonised across arms in length, structure and register: each names the source, states the attribution rule in one sentence, and gives a concrete household-level example. A third treatment arm, using an income-based accounting frame (Starr et al., PLOS Climate, 2023), is specified in the pre-analysis plan but is not fielded in this wave, as its implementation depends on funding beyond the committed base budget. It will be added in a subsequent wave if that funding is secured. All respondents then complete a conjoint policy-choice task. They see eight pairs of federal carbon-tax packages built from randomised attributes — annual household cost, use of revenue, and whether an additional tax applies to the richest households — and select their preferred package or the status quo of no carbon tax. Choice is the primary dependent variable. After the conjoint, all respondents report a posterior belief. To limit anchoring, the posterior is framed as the share attributable to the remaining 99% rather than to the top 1%. Secondary outcomes include a policy-builder task in which respondents assemble their own preferred carbon tax, two Likert items on general support for a federal carbon tax with and without an additional tax on the richest households, and an incentivised allocation of a $50 lottery prize between the respondent and two charities. Within the control arm, the timing of prior-belief elicitation is itself randomised: priors are elicited either before or after the conjoint task. This allows us to assess whether eliciting priors primes attention to inequality independently of any informational content.

Respondents see 8 pairs of climate-policy packages built from randomized attributes, choose the preferred package (forced choice). Choice is the primary dependent variable. Candidate attributes drawn from prior work on carbon-tax, climate-policy design and real policy proposal in the US or at global level (Beiser-McGrath & Bernauer, 2019; Dechezleprêtre et al., 2025; Ahrens et al., 2025; Chancel & Rehm, 2026). The first attribute, carbon price level, takes five candidate levels: $0/yr (status quo), $150/yr, $600/yr, $1,500/yr and $2,500/yr. The second, use of revenue, likewise takes five: none collected (status quo), climate investments (renewables, public transit, adaptation), equal yearly cash payments to all households, yearly cash payments to the lowest-income 10%, and yearly cash payments to the lowest-income 50%. The third, additional tax, takes the following levels: no additional tax; annual tax of $150 for every ton of CO₂ emitted by the luxury, high-emission goods an individual owns or uses (e.g., private jets, yachts); annual 10% income surtax on individuals with income above $1 million; annual 2% wealth tax on individuals with wealth above $50 millions; and annual tax of $150 for every ton of CO₂ emitted by the companies and assets an individual owns.
randomization_method: Randomization is performed by computer, using the built-in randomizer of the survey software (Qualtrics), at the point of survey administration. No researcher is involved in assignment.
randomization_unit: The unit of randomization is the individual respondent. There is no clustering: respondents are randomized independently of one another, and no group-level or session-level randomization is used. Two levels of randomization are present. Assignment to the information treatment (and, within the control arm, assignment to the timing of prior-belief elicitation) is at the individual respondent level. Randomization of conjoint attribute levels operates at the level of the individual policy profile, nested within choice task, within respondent: each respondent completes eight choice tasks, each containing two policies, and attribute levels are drawn independently for each profile.
secondary_outcomes: Secondary outcomes • Policy-builder Respondents design their own carbon tax by selecting one level per attribute; used for the convergent-validity check • General support — Likert (EXTRA POLICIES). Two 1–5 items: support for (a) a federal carbon tax, (b) a federal carbon tax with an extra tax on the richest households. • Donation split. Incentivized allocation of a $50 lottery prize among self, Feeding America, and The Nature Conservancy; a real-stakes behavioral proxy for redistribution/climate preferences
title: Carbon tax design, emissions-inequality information, and public support for progressive climate taxation: a survey experiment in the United States

abstract: This study proposes an experiment that examines how the magnitude of underlying likelihoods influences likelihood judgments and posterior beliefs. The experiment constructs information environments that hold the likelihood ratio—and therefore the Bayesian posterior—fixed while varying the absolute magnitude of the underlying likelihoods. By eliciting both likelihood judgments and posterior beliefs, the study investigates whether likelihood-reporting distortions depend on likelihood magnitude, whether these distortions propagate to posterior beliefs, and whether pure and mixed samples with identical likelihood ratios generate different likelihood judgments or posterior beliefs.
experimental_design: The study uses a belief-updating task based on a standard bookbag-and-poker-chip paradigm. Participants complete multiple independent rounds in which there are two bags containing different proportions of colored balls. In each round, one bag is selected at random, a small sample of balls is drawn with replacement, and participants report probabilities based on the observed sample. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two treatment conditions. In the Posterior (P) condition, participants report only the probability that each bag generated the observed sample. In the Likelihood/Posterior (L/P) condition, participants first report the probability of drawing the sample from each bag (likelihood judgments) and then report posterior beliefs. Across rounds, the experimental environments vary the sample size, bag compositions, and observed samples. The primary environments are constructed to hold the likelihood ratio—and therefore the Bayesian posterior—fixed while varying the absolute magnitude of the underlying likelihoods. Additional benchmark environments compare pure and mixed samples that imply the same likelihood ratio and Bayesian posterior. All questions are framed hypothetically, with probabilities fully determined by the stated bag compositions and samples. Additional details on the experimental procedures, analysis plan, and exclusion criteria are provided in the uploaded Pre-Analysis Plan.

abstract: We will conduct a survey experiment to measure how information about the Indian government’s air pollution policy (the National Clean Air Programme, NCAP), and about the policy’s success or failure, affects citizens’ satisfaction with the government. The experiment is designed to answer three research questions: (i) do citizens reward the government for promising to reduce air pollution, (ii) do citizens reward the government for success in reducing air pollution, and (iii) do citizens punish the government for failure to deliver, and if not, what informational conditions activate a failure penalty? Respondents are randomized across ten arms that combine five informational components: a description of the policy, its quantitative target, a factual framing of its results as either a success (emphasizing the pre-post improvement) or failure (emphasizing the null diff-in-diff estimate), a cue raising citizens’ awareness of the severity of local air pollution, and a cue attributing the policy’s failure to low government effort. The primary outcome is satisfaction with the government’s air pollution policy.
experimental_design: Ten arms: (1) control, no information; (2) policy description; (3) description + target (the full "promise"); (4) description + target + awareness cue; (5) description + target + low-effort cue; (6) description + target + success framing; (7) description + target + success framing + awareness cue; (8) description + target + failure framing; (9) description + target + failure framing + awareness cue; (10) description + target + failure framing + low-effort cue. The primary analysis is a regression of the outcome on arm indicators (control omitted) with city and enumerator fixed effects and heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors; every hypothesis is a pre-specified linear combination of the arm coefficients (promise premium, policy announcement, target above announcement, success framing, failure penalty, implementation incentive, low-effort cue, awareness x failure, effort x failure, awareness x success, awareness on the implementation incentive), plus one joint Wald test that all interaction contrasts are zero. Full details are in the attached pre-analysis plan.
intervention: Respondents are randomized into one of ten arms, each combining a subset of five informational components delivered by the enumerator during the phone interview: (1) a policy description: that NCAP was started by the central government in 2019 to reduce air pollution, that the respondent's city is covered, and what the program does; (2) the policy target: NCAP's goal of reducing air pollution by 40% from 2017 levels by 2026; (3) a policy result framing, either a success framing (pollution in NCAP cities has fallen by almost 20% since before the program) or a failure framing (NCAP cities have not seen any decline relative to cities not covered by NCAP), both factually accurate; (4) a pollution awareness cue: the current pollution level in the respondent's city as a multiple of the safe limit, and its health consequences; (5) a low-effort cue: a statement that the government has paid little attention to NCAP since its announcement. The control arm receives none of these components and is debriefed about NCAP at the end of the interview.

abstract: The aim of this project is to test whether the valuation of risky prospects depends partly on an individual's memory state: which past experiences are accessible at the moment of choice. Two online experiments hold the payoffs and probabilities of a common lottery fixed while varying access to prior experiences before eliciting incentivized certainty equivalents. A two-wave panel randomizes the order of a cue to the 2008 financial crisis against a matched neutral cue in two birth cohorts. An account-history experiment separates encoding from retrieval, randomizing whether a five-round gain–loss history determines the participant's own payoff or is instead observed in a study reference account, and which episode a later cue retrieves. Both experiments test whether cue effects are stronger when the cued content is part of the participant's own encoded experience — a potential short-run retrieval margin of experience effects.
experimental_design: • Crisis-cue panel: a two-wave within-person design with randomized passage order. Each main-panel respondent values the same lottery in both waves, roughly seven days apart, once after the 2008 financial-crisis passage and once after a length- and structure-matched neutral passage. A neutral–neutral calibration arm benchmarks week-to-week variation under matched content. The two birth cohorts contribute equally. • Account-history experiment: a single-session design separating encoding from retrieval. Participants earn a starting balance, are randomized to an own or reference account, and observe a locked five-round percentage-return history. Within each focal matched set the percentage-return history is held fixed while account arm and cued episode vary, so the cue contrast holds the realized history fixed by design. • The two experiments use independent samples. Participants may take part in only one experiment and can be randomized only once.
intervention: • Two-wave crisis-cue panel: Participants from two birth cohorts (1983–1990 and 2001–2008) complete two sessions approximately one week apart. Main-panel participants read a passage about the 2008 financial crisis in one session and a length- and structure-matched neutral passage in the other, with passage order randomized. A calibration arm reads two different neutral passages in randomized order, providing a benchmark for week-to-week variation in the certainty equivalent. • Account-history experiment: Participants earn a starting balance in a real-effort slider task and are randomized to monitor either a payoff-bearing own account or an otherwise matched study reference account. Every participant observes a five-round return history containing a focal −40% round, a focal +40% round, a zero-return round, and two filler rounds. A later randomized cue targets one episode by its serial position immediately before participants value the common risky lottery. A randomly assigned half of participants additionally rates the emotional intensity of each round. Among camera-qualified participants, facial-movement and webcam-gaze measures are recorded as secondary outcomes.

primary_outcome_explanation: The certainty equivalent is the sure amount of money that a participant values equally to the fixed lottery. Participants make ten binary choices between the lottery and a sure payment, adapting the staircase logic of Falk et al. (2023). Each offer depends on the participant's previous choices and is selected to be maximally informative about the participant's underlying point of indifference. Because individual choices may contain response error, the primary CE is not read off any single choice. Following the DOSE approach of Chapman, Snowberg, Wang, and Camerer (2024), a logistic response-error model treats each choice as a noisy signal of the participant's underlying valuation. The primary CE is the posterior mean of that valuation after all ten choices. One of the ten choices is randomly selected and paid as chosen. Three prespecified choice-based codings of the same ten choices are used as robustness outcomes: a model-free interval midpoint, a final-bracket coding, and a minimum-violation coding. Full definitions are provided in the pre-analysis plan. References: Chapman, J., E. Snowberg, S. W. Wang, and C. Camerer (2024). “Dynamically Optimized Sequential Experimentation (DOSE) for Estimating Economic Preference Parameters.” NBER Working Paper 33013. Falk, A., A. Becker, T. Dohmen, D. Huffman, and U. Sunde (2023). “The Preference Survey Module: A Validated Instrument for Measuring Risk, Time, and Social Preferences.” Management Science 69(4), 1935–1950. Primary hypotheses: • H1: In the account-history experiment, within the own-account arm, cueing the focal −40% episode lowers the CE relative to cueing the focal +40% episode. Thus, the prespecified loss-minus-gain CE contrast is negative. • H2: The focal loss-versus-gain cue contrast is attenuated in the reference-account arm relative to the own-account arm. The prespecified cue-by-account-arm interaction is positive, meaning that the loss-versus-gain contrast is less negative in the reference-account arm. • H3: In the two-wave panel, reading the 2008 financial-crisis passage lowers the CE within respondent relative to the matched neutral passage. The prespecified effect is negative. • H4: The crisis-cue effect is more negative for respondents born in 1983–1990 than for respondents born in 2001–2008. The prespecified cue-by-cohort interaction is negative.
primary_outcomes: The primary outcome in both experiments is the incentivized certainty equivalent (CE) of a fixed 50–50 lottery paying $5.00 or $0.00, elicited through ten adaptive binary choices between the lottery and sure amounts on a $0.00–$5.00 grid. The primary CE measure is the posterior mean of each participant’s underlying valuation, estimated from the ten choices. The posterior standard deviation is retained as a diagnostic of elicitation precision.
randomization_method: • Crisis-cue panel: Computerized individual-level randomization within birth cohort and recruitment batch. Participants are assigned to the main panel or calibration arm and then to passage sequence. The neutral passage used in each relevant design cell is randomized and balanced across cells. • Account-history experiment: Computerized individual-level randomization within three slider-performance strata (0–16, 17–33, and 34–50 correct). Focal assignments are organized in four-person matched sets containing one participant in each account-by-cue cell; all four members receive the same percentage-return history. Nonfocal assignments are organized in matched own/reference pairs. Intensity-rating status is randomized at the matched-set or pair level.
randomization_unit: The primary treatments in both experiments are assigned at the individual level. Passage sequence in the crisis-cue panel is randomized within cohort-by-recruitment-batch blocks. In the account-history experiment, focal assignments are organized in four-person matched sets and nonfocal assignments in two-person own/reference pairs. The secondary intensity-rating factor is assigned at the matched-set or pair level. • Planned clusters for the intensity-rating factor: 600 randomization sets, comprising 400 focal matched sets and 200 nonfocal pairs.
secondary_outcome_explanation: These outcomes characterize the behavioral and memory processes accompanying the primary valuation effects. H5 is a prespecified secondary hypothesis in the randomly assigned rated half of the own-account loss/zero/gain sample: the association between signed cue content and the certainty equivalent is predicted to be stronger for episodes rated as unusually intense relative to the participant's other episodes. Because encoding intensity is measured rather than randomized, H5 lies outside the H1–H4 confirmatory family. The remaining tested secondary outcomes are organized into prespecified families with Benjamini–Hochberg adjustment within family, never pooled across experiments: five families in the account-history experiment (three-level benchmark; memory and internalization; emotions and downside availability; background beliefs; open-text reasons) and three in the crisis-cue panel (recall source and quality; one combined family covering emotions, downside availability, vulnerability, recent context, and economic beliefs; open-text reasons). The facial-movement and gaze family is adjusted using a design-consistent permutation step-down procedure and is analyzed separately from the confirmatory behavioral outcomes. Manipulation checks and diagnostics, including the encoding manipulation check and perceived final account balance, are reported descriptively. Full definitions and estimation details are provided in the pre-analysis plan.
secondary_outcomes: In the account-history experiment, secondary outcomes cover the three-level loss/zero/gain cue benchmark; memory and internalization; negative affect and downside availability; background beliefs; open-text choice reasons; and camera-based facial-movement and gaze measures among camera-qualified participants. The camera-based measures include baseline-adjusted facial valence during encoding and the cue window, facial-pattern alignment between encoding and cue retrieval, first stable gaze orientation toward the lottery's $0 outcome, fixation-locked facial valence, and facial-pattern alignment between encoding and the fixation-locked response. In the crisis-cue panel, secondary outcomes cover recall source and quality; negative affect and downside availability; perceived financial vulnerability and recent financial context; economic beliefs; and open-text choice reasons.
title: Preferences as Memory States: Experience Effects at the Moment of Choice

abstract: About a quarter of Americans with disabilities are poor. One contributing factor is a lack of physical mobility, which may limit access to health care, social relationships, and economic participation. Although the Americans with Disabilities Act requires public transit agencies to provide riders unable to use fixed-route transit with paratransit alternatives, paratransit users are generally required to book trips a day in advance, constraining flexibility. In this study, we will conduct a randomized controlled trial of King County Metro’s new Access On-Demand program, which allows paratransit users to book same-day trips. This is the first study to evaluate the effects of an on-demand transportation option on paratransit customers’ mobility, transportation security, health, and wellbeing. The research design, which will leverage administrative data complemented by surveys, is the product of a long collaboration between the research team and King County Metro and is informed by an nonexperimental pilot.
experimental_design: Eligible riders who complete a baseline survey will be randomized into treatment and control groups. Participants in the treatment group will be offered on-demand paratransit services. All riders will retain access to traditional paratransit.

abstract: Adolescence and young adulthood are formative periods for sexual and reproductive health and emerging autonomy. During this period, young people navigate changing social roles and relationships, including expectations around gender and sexuality and ideas about what constitutes acceptable behavior. Social approval and perceived expectations may therefore shape not only how young women feel able to express their own views, but also whether they feel able to act on those views when engaging with sensitive topics such as contraception. Importantly, individuals respond to the social environment as they perceive it, which may differ from the underlying distribution of attitudes in that environment. Such discrepancies may lead individuals to make decisions partly on the basis of inaccurate perceptions of what others think or consider acceptable, even when these perceptions differ from their own preferences. In our study communities in Ghana and Burkina Faso, young people report high levels of acceptance of a young woman’s use of modern contraception if she wishes, but substantially underestimate the level of acceptance reported by other young people in the same cohort. We conduct an individually randomized survey experiment among adolescent girls and young women, embedded in an ongoing cohort study. Treated participants receive a short, site-specific video providing information about the measured share of young people in their community who support a young woman’s ability to use modern contraception if she wishes. We examine whether this information changes women’s social and health-seeking engagement with contraception and, among sexually active women for whom contraceptive behavior is immediately relevant, intentions to use contraception.
experimental_design: We conduct a survey experiment embedded in an existing cohort in two Health and Demographic Surveillance System (HDSS) sites: Nouna, Burkina Faso and Ningo-Prampram, Ghana. Female adolescents and young women that meet the eligibility criteria of being 13 years of age or older are randomly assigned in a 1:1 ratio to either a treatment or control group, with randomization conducted separately within each HDSS site. The experimental structure is as follows. First, prior to exposure to the treatment, we elicit participants’ prior second order beliefs about the attitudes of other young people in their cohort toward young women’s contraceptive use. Second, participants receive their randomly assigned treatment. Those assigned to the treatment group watch the information video, while those assigned to the control group proceed directly to the subsequent survey questions. Third, participants in both arms complete an identical outcome module, in which contraception-related measures are embedded within a broader set of questions on health-seeking and health-related discussions. Finally, both groups complete the post-outcome module.
intervention: The intervention is a survey-embedded information experiment. Eligible female adolescents and young women aged 13 or older are randomly assigned to either treatment or control group. Participants assigned to the treatment group watch a short video providing truthful information about attitudes toward young women’s contraceptive use among young people in their own community. Specifically, the video reports the measured proportion of young women and men in the study population who agree that a young woman should be able to use a modern contraceptive method if she wishes. This statistic is based on responses collected in an earlier wave of the same cohort and is presented to participants as a community-level statistic. The video visualizes the statistic to facilitate comprehension, and is shown to participants on a tablet during the survey interview. Because measured attitudes differ between the two study sites, site-specific versions of the video are produced for Nouna (Burkina Faso) and Ningo-Prampram (Ghana). Each version reports the corresponding statistic for that site and is translated into the relevant local language. Participants assigned to the control group do not receive the information video and proceed directly to the subsequent survey questions.

abstract: This study examines how theory-driven, targeted communication strategies influence public support for men’s health policies in Nigeria, with a specific focus on alcohol-related non-communicable diseases (NCDs). It responds to the disproportionate burden of alcohol-attributable harm among Nigerian men, the limited effectiveness of conventional health promotion approaches, and the need for behaviourally grounded, gender-responsive advocacy tools that can build legitimacy for population-level policy interventions. The research is grounded in behavioural economics, health psychology, and persuasion theory. It integrates Social Cognitive Theory (SCT), the Health Belief Model (HBM), and the Elaboration Likelihood Model (ELM) to develop a falsifiable and experimentally testable framework for targeted communication. SCT and HBM specify the belief, agency, and social modelling mechanisms through which communication may influence policy attitudes, while ELM provides the delivery rationale for using short narrative films under realistic attention constraints. Importantly, the study treats support for alcohol regulation as the primary outcome, conceptualized as an attitudinal and normative position toward collective policy instruments, rather than focusing narrowly on individual drinking behaviour. Behavioural intentions to reduce alcohol consumption are examined as secondary and exploratory outcomes. To situate the research empirically, the study begins with a secondary analysis of data from the Global Burden of Disease (GBD) study and the World Bank, documenting gender-disaggregated trends in Disability-Adjusted Life Years (DALYs), Years of Life Lost (YLLs), Years Lived with Disability (YLDs), Healthy Life Expectancy (HALE), and health expenditure in Nigeria between 2000 and 2019. This analysis is complemented by a structured review of the literature on alcohol consumption patterns, masculinity norms, Nigeria’s NCD policy response, and prior health communication and advocacy efforts targeting men. The core empirical component consists of an online randomized controlled experiment conducted with young adult Nigerian men recruited through digital platforms. Participants are randomly assigned to view short, AI-generated video interventions that convey identical factual information about alcohol-related harm but vary systematically in delivery format (narrative versus didactic) and messenger identity (authority-based versus relatable peer role model). The primary outcome is support for alcohol control policies, operationalized through a composite Policy Support Index. Secondary outcomes include intention to reduce alcohol consumption and theoretically specified mediators aligned with SCT and HBM, including perceived susceptibility, perceived severity, self-efficacy, perceived social norms, and identification with the messenger. By isolating messenger and narrative effects while holding content constant, the study provides causal evidence on how specific communication features shape policy-relevant attitudes in a norm-constrained context. Methodologically, it demonstrates the feasibility and internal validity of fully online experimental evaluation for health advocacy research in low-resource settings. Substantively, it contributes to the literature on men’s health, alcohol policy, and behavioural communication by shifting the focus from individual behaviour change to public support for regulatory interventions. The findings are expected to inform policymakers, civil society actors, and donors on the design of scalable, theory-driven communication strategies capable of strengthening public legitimacy for alcohol control policies in Nigeria and comparable contexts.
experimental_design: The study employs an individually randomized, four-arm online experiment. Participants are randomly assigned to exactly one of the following conditions: • T0 (Control): Placebo or neutral informational video with no alcohol-related content. • T1 (Didactic): Non-narrative informational video delivered via voiceover and infographics, with no identifiable messenger. • T2 (Narrative–Authority): Narrative video delivered by an authority-framed messenger. • T3 (Narrative–Peer): Narrative video delivered by a peer-framed messenger. Randomization is implemented at the individual level. Assignment probabilities are equal across arms. Treatment exposure occurs immediately after baseline survey sections. The four study arms will be: 1. T0: Climate-change control video - Placebo Participants assigned to the control condition will watch a placebo video concerning climate change and environmental issues. The video will be designed to provide an engaging piece of non-alcohol-related content while controlling for the general experience of watching a short informational video. It will not contain messages about alcohol consumption, alcohol-related harm, masculinity, or alcohol-control policies. Participants in this arm will complete the same main post-video questionnaire as participants in the alcohol-related arms. They will also be able to indicate whether they are interested in taking action on climate or environmental issues. This control-content question will help make the questionnaire relevant to their assigned video but will not constitute a primary study outcome. 2. T1: Didactic alcohol-information video Participants in this arm will watch a non-narrative, didactic video about alcohol consumption and alcohol-related harm. The information will be communicated directly using an explanatory voiceover and supporting visual material, such as images, text, statistics, or infographics. The video will present factual information about the individual and social consequences of harmful alcohol consumption and the possible role of alcohol-control policies. It will not rely primarily on a personal story or lived-experience narrative. This arm will provide the non-narrative alcohol-communication comparator for evaluating whether narrative communication is more effective than conventional factual communication. 3. T2: Narrative alcohol video with an authority-framed messenger Participants in this arm will watch an alcohol-related narrative presented through a personal or experience-based story told by a medical doctor. The narrative will communicate alcohol-related risks, consequences, and the relevance of action to reduce alcohol-related harm. The messenger will be framed as an authority or expert source. The authority framing is intended to encourage participants to interpret the message as advice or information coming from a knowledgeable and credible source. This condition will allow the study to examine the effect of narrative communication when the message is associated with an authority messenger. 4. T3: Narrative alcohol video with a peer-framed messenger Participants in this arm will watch an alcohol-related narrative corresponding to the narrative format used in the authority condition. However, the messenger will be framed as a peer or socially relatable person (young undergraduate man) rather than as an authority figure. The peer framing is intended to increase identification, social proximity, and the possibility that participants will see the experience presented in the video as relevant to themselves, their friends, or their families. Comparing this arm with the authority-narrative arm will test whether the social identity of the messenger changes the persuasiveness of the narrative.
intervention: This study will evaluate alternative video-based communication strategies designed to influence support for policies intended to reduce alcohol-related harm among young Nigerian men. The study will be conducted as a four-arm, individually randomized online experiment involving eligible men aged 18–35 years who currently reside in Nigeria. After providing informed consent, passing the eligibility screening, and completing the baseline questionnaire, each participant will be randomly assigned with equal probability to watch one of four pre-recorded videos. Participants will watch only the video corresponding to their assigned study arm. Assignment and video delivery will be automated through the online survey platform. The videos will be delivered under standardized online conditions. The final video files, scripts, durations, links, assignment mapping, and file checksums will be archived before analysis. Video-viewing time, arrival at the post-video questionnaire, and relevant implementation checks will also be recorded. However, participants will remain in their originally assigned groups for the primary intention-to-treat analysis regardless of their viewing time, attention-check performance, recall of the video, or assessment of the messenger.

abstract: This randomized online survey experiment, fielded on Verasight's national panel with 2,000 U.S. adults (1,000 gun owners and 1,000 non-owners), examines whether exposure to popular gun-related media shapes political attitudes. Within each gun-ownership group, participants are randomly assigned to watch a short, widely viewed social-media video showcasing an AR-15-style rifle at an outdoor shooting range or a comparable video about consumer electronics; a random half of those shown the gun video additionally read a brief summary of the Democratic and Republican parties' positions on gun policy before answering outcome questions. We test whether gun media exposure shifts partisan affect, gun-policy attitudes, gun purchase intentions, and gun-related political engagement; whether partisan cues amplify the translation of gun media into partisan affect; and whether effects differ by gun ownership, partisanship, and gender, including effects on the gender gap in partisan support.
experimental_design: This is a randomized online survey experiment fielded by Verasight to 2,000 U.S. adults from its national panel. The sample is stratified by personal gun ownership: 1,000 respondents who personally own a firearm and 1,000 who do not. Within each ownership group, every respondent is individually randomized to one of three arms. Control (40% of each ownership group; 800 respondents in total): the respondent watches an approximately two-minute popular social-media video about Apple consumer products. Treatment Condition1, gun video (30% of each ownership group; 600 respondents in total): the respondent watches an approximately two-minute popular social-media video showcasing an AR-15-pattern rifle being handled and fired at an outdoor shooting range. Treatment Condition 2, gun video plus partisan nudge (30% of each ownership group; 600 respondents in total): the respondent watches the same gun video as Arm 1 and then, immediately before the outcome questions, reads a brief, balanced written summary of the Democratic and Republican parties' positions on gun policy. The three conditions differ only in the assigned video and the presence of the nudge; everything else in the survey is identical. Survey flow: Consent -> Gun-ownership screener (assigns the respondent to the owner or non-owner group) -> Pre-treatment items: party identification, ideology, and two filler items -> Random assignment to Control, Treatment 1 or 2 within the ownership group -> Assigned video, played to completion -> Comprehension questions about the video -> Outcome questions: attitudes toward gun regulation, importance of gun policy in vote choice, perceived threat to gun rights, gun-related political action intentions, and, future gun purchase intention -> Partisan nudge (Treatment2 only) -> feeling thermometers for the Democratic and Republican parties -> Demographic questions -> Debriefing. Heterogeneity by gun ownership, partisanship, and gender, and the effect on the gender gap in partisan support, are pre-registered. A pre-analysis plan is registered before data collection begins.
experimental_design_details: Population and quotas. Verasight delivers 2,000 completed interviews with U.S. adults aged 18 and older from its national online panel. Two quota groups of 1,000 are defined by the screening items at the start of the survey. Gun owners are respondents who report that they, or they together with someone else in the household, personally own a handgun, rifle, shotgun, or other firearm. Non-owners are all other respondents, including those who live in a household where only another member owns a firearm; this household-only exposure is recorded. Verasight targets its standard demographic benchmarks within each quota group, and fielding continues until both quotas are filled. Arm 0, control video (40% of each ownership group; 400 gun owners and 400 non-owners; 800 respondents in total). The respondent watches a popular, approximately two-minute social-media video reviewing or showcasing Apple consumer products. It is consumer-product content with no political content, chosen to match the gun video in length, format, and popularity. Arm 1, gun video (30% of each ownership group; 300 gun owners and 300 non-owners; 600 respondents in total). The respondent watches a popular, approximately two-minute social-media video in which an AR-15-pattern rifle is presented and fired at an outdoor range, showing the rifle's features, handling, and shooting. The video depicts lawful recreational use only and contains no violence against people. Arm 2, gun video plus partisan nudge (30% of each ownership group; 300 gun owners and 300 non-owners; 600 respondents in total). The respondent watches the identical gun video and then, immediately before the outcome questions, reads two written paragraphs of roughly equal length summarizing the Democratic and Republican parties' positions on gun policy. The Democratic paragraph describes support for stronger regulation while preserving the right of law-abiding citizens to own firearms (universal background checks, closing loopholes in existing laws, red flag laws, restrictions on certain semiautomatic rifles and high-capacity magazines, federal investment in gun violence prevention). The Republican paragraph describes an emphasis on Second Amendment rights and opposition to new federal regulation (support for concealed carry, opposition to assault weapon bans and most purchase restrictions, reducing regulatory burdens on gun ownership, enforcing existing laws, addressing mental health, improving school security, prosecuting violent offenders). The summaries are worded neutrally, presented without evaluation, and shown with a minimum reading time. What is held constant. Both videos are embedded with skipping disabled and must play to completion before the respondent can advance; viewing time is recorded. Immediately after the video, respondents in every arm answer factual comprehension questions about the video they watched and receive a small bonus for correct answers. The arms therefore differ only in the content of the video (Arms 1 and 2 versus Arm 0) and in the presence of the partisan summary (Arm 2 versus Arm 1). Comparing Arm 1 with Arm 0 isolates the effect of gun media exposure relative to non-political consumer media; comparing Arm 2 with Arm 1 isolates the incremental effect of adding explicit partisan information to gun media exposure; comparing either treated arm with Arm 0 gives the total effect of that condition. Randomization. Assignment is stratified by personal gun ownership with a fixed 40/30/30 allocation within each stratum. It is performed by the survey software at the moment the respondent reaches the treatment module, after all pre-treatment questions have been answered, so that no pre-treatment measure can be affected by assignment. Respondents are not told which arm they are in or what the study's hypotheses are. Realized arm sizes and the assignment log are retained. Survey flow. The sequence is identical for all respondents apart from the assigned video and the nudge: Consent page, which notes that the survey includes short videos and questions about firearms and politics -> Screener: whether anyone in the household owns a firearm and, if so, who (the respondent, someone else, or both); this assigns the ownership group -> Pre-treatment political items: seven-point party identification (strong Democrat to strong Republican) and seven-point ideology (very liberal to very conservative); party identification with lean and demographics are also available from Verasight's panel profile, collected before the survey -> Pre-treatment filler and quality items: hours of sleep last night; open-text favorite ice-cream flavor, used to screen automated or inattentive responses before assignment -> Random assignment to Arm 0, 1, or 2 within the ownership group -> Assigned video, played to completion, viewing time recorded -> Outcome module in fixed order: (1) whether laws covering the sale of firearms should be made more strict, kept as they are, or made less strict (five categories) -> (2) favor or oppose six gun-policy proposals-> (3) how the respondent weighs gun policy when choosing a candidate (five categories, from not an important issue to deal-breaker) -> (4) how threatened the right to own guns is in the United States (four categories) -> (5) likelihood of contacting a public official about gun policy, of joining or contributing money to an organization that opposes stricter gun laws, and of joining or contributing money to an organization that supports stricter gun laws (seven categories each) -> (6) whether the respondent will buy a gun for themselves in the future (five categories, definitely will not to definitely will) -> Partisan nudge, Arm 2 only, with a minimum reading time -> (7) feeling thermometer for the Democratic Party (0-100) -> (8) feeling thermometer for the Republican Party (0-100) -> Post-treatment demographics: gender, age, education, Hispanic origin, race, family income, religion; census region and metropolitan status derived from ZIP code
intervention: Participants in an online survey experiment are randomly assigned to watch one of two short videos, each approximately two minutes long and drawn from popular social-media content. The treatment video showcases an AR-15-pattern rifle being handled and fired at an outdoor shooting range. The control video showcases Apple consumer products. Both videos are consumer-product content of similar length, format, and popularity, and neither contains explicit political messaging. A random half of the participants assigned to the treatment video additionally read a brief, balanced written summary of the Democratic and Republican parties' positions on gun policy immediately before the outcome questions. All participants then complete a survey measuring attitudes toward gun regulation, affective evaluations of the two major parties, intentions to purchase a firearm, and intentions to engage politically on gun policy.

mde_text: Assumptions: two-sided test at the 5% level, 80% power, individual-level randomization with no clustering, and outcomes standardized against the control group. Minimum detectable effects (MDEs) are stated in control-group standard deviations (SD), with and without covariate adjustment. The adjusted figures assume that the stratum indicator and pre-treatment covariates explain 50% of outcome variance (R-squared of 0.5), which is realistic for the partisan-affect outcomes given that party identification and ideology are covariates; the unadjusted figures are conservative. All figures were verified by Monte Carlo simulation of the primary specification with HC2 standard errors (2,000 replications per scenario; rejection rate at the computed MDE between 79% and 81%; size 5% under the null). Any gun video versus control (1,200 versus 800 respondents): 0.128 SD unadjusted, 0.090 SD adjusted. One treated arm versus control (600 versus 800): 0.151 SD unadjusted, 0.107 SD adjusted. Gun video plus nudge versus gun video alone (600 versus 600): 0.162 SD unadjusted, 0.114 SD adjusted. Any gun video versus control within one ownership stratum (600 versus 400): 0.181 SD unadjusted, 0.128 SD adjusted. Difference in treatment effects between gun owners and non-owners, or between men and women (two groups of about 1,000 each): 0.256 SD unadjusted, 0.181 SD adjusted. Difference between Republicans (about 950) and Democrats (about 850): 0.270 SD unadjusted, 0.191 SD adjusted. In native units, assuming control-group standard deviations typical of national surveys: for a single party feeling thermometer (SD about 33 points), the pooled MDE is 4.2 points unadjusted and 3.0 points adjusted; for net partisan affect, the Republican minus Democratic thermometer (SD about 58 points), 7.4 points unadjusted and 5.2 points adjusted, and 10.5 points (7.4 adjusted) within one ownership stratum; for the gun-policy attitudes index (SD of 1 by construction), 0.13 SD unadjusted and 0.09 SD adjusted; for the five-point purchase-intention item (SD about 1.2), 0.15 scale points unadjusted and 0.11 adjusted. For the binary purchase-intention indicator, assuming a control-group rate of 30%, the pooled MDE is 5.9 percentage points; within the non-owner stratum at an assumed control rate of 15%, 6.5 percentage points; within the owner stratum at 45%, 9.0 percentage points. For the Republican-preference indicator at a control rate near 45%, the pooled MDE is 6.4 percentage points and the MDE for the change in the gender gap is 12.7 percentage points.

primary_outcome_explanation: Orientation convention. Every gun-attitude measure is coded so that higher values are more pro-gun-rights (less regulation), and every partisan-affect measure so that higher values are more favorable to the Republican Party relative to the Democratic Party. Under this convention the hypothesized sign of every primary effect is positive. Net partisan affect is the Republican Party thermometer minus the Democratic Party thermometer, ranging from -100 to 100. The difference captures relative partisan affect, which is the construct linked to vote choice and political contributions in our observational work, and it is robust to respondent-specific use of the thermometer scale. The gun-policy attitudes index combines seven items. The first asks whether laws covering the sale of firearms should be made more strict, kept as they are now, or made less strict (five categories from much more strict to much less strict, coded 1 to 5 so that less strict is higher). The remaining six ask whether the respondent favors or opposes (five categories from strongly favor to strongly oppose): high capacity magazines ban; banning assault-style weapons; permit to purchase firearms; making private gun sales and sales at gun shows subject to background checks; allowing people to carry concealed guns in more places; and shortening waiting periods for people who want to buy guns legally. The four restriction items are coded so that opposition is high (1 strongly favor to 5 strongly oppose); the two expansion items (concealed carry, shorter waiting periods) are reverse-coded so that support is high. Following Kling, Liebman, and Katz (2007), each oriented item is standardized by subtracting the mean and dividing by the standard deviation of the pooled control group; the seven standardized items are averaged with equal weights; and the average is re-standardized against the control group so that the index has mean zero and standard deviation one among control respondents. The index is computed for respondents who answer at least five of the seven items and is missing otherwise. Gun purchase intention is the response to "Do you think you will buy a gun for yourself in the future, or not?", coded 1 definitely will not, 2 probably will not, 3 unsure, 4 probably will, 5 definitely will, and standardized against the control group. A binary indicator for "probably will" or "definitely will" is reported alongside. Treatment effects on all standardized outcomes are expressed in control-group standard deviation units and are also reported in native units (thermometer points, scale points, percentage points). The constructions above are the ones used for hypothesis tests and headline estimates. The following alternative constructions are pre-specified and will all be reported as robustness checks. For net partisan affect: each thermometer separately; the binary Republican-preference indicator (Republican rating exceeds Democratic rating); an indicator for a Republican rating of 50 or above; a rank-transformed version; and standardization within ownership stratum. For the gun-policy index: an inverse-covariance-weighted index (Anderson 2008); the first principal component with loadings estimated in the control group; the simple mean of items rescaled to 0-1; a count of pro-gun-rights responses; a six-item version excluding the strictness item; separate restriction and rights-expansion sub-indices; item-by-item estimates with Romano-Wolf adjustment; ordered logit per item; and standardization within ownership stratum. For purchase intention: binary indicators for a response of 4 or above, 3 or above, and equal to 5; an ordered logit; and estimates among non-owners only. If estimates differ materially across constructions, the pattern will be reported rather than a construction selected.
primary_outcomes: Research questions RQ1. Does exposure to popular gun-related media change attitudes toward gun regulation? RQ2. Does it change affective evaluations of the Democratic and Republican parties? RQ3. Does it change stated intentions to acquire a firearm and intentions to engage politically on gun policy? RQ4. Does information about the parties' gun-policy positions amplify the translation of gun media exposure into partisan affect, and does it sort gun-policy attitudes by party? RQ5. Do the effects differ by gun-ownership status, partisanship, and gender, and does exposure change the gender gap in partisan support? Three primary outcomes, each measured in the post-treatment survey module. (1) Net partisan affect: the difference between the respondent's 0-100 feeling-thermometer rating of the Republican Party and of the Democratic Party. (2) Gun-policy attitudes index: a summary index of seven survey items on gun regulation (the preferred strictness of laws covering the sale of firearms and six specific policy proposals), oriented so that higher values indicate more pro-gun-rights, less-regulation positions. (3) Gun purchase intention: the respondent's stated likelihood of buying a gun for themselves in the future, measured on a five-point scale.
randomization_method: Treatment is assigned at the individual level by the survey software Qualtrics at the moment the respondent reaches the treatment block, after all pre-treatment questions have been answered.
randomization_unit: Individual respondent. There is a single level of randomization, stratified by personal gun-ownership status (two strata); there is no group-level or cluster assignment.
secondary_outcome_explanation: The gender gap in partisan support is treated as an outcome defined at the group level. For a measure of partisan support S (net partisan affect, or the Republican-preference indicator), the gender gap in an arm is the mean of S among men minus the mean of S among women in that arm. The estimand is the gap among treated respondents minus the gap among control respondents, which equals the coefficient on the treatment-by-male interaction in a regression of S on the treatment indicator, a male indicator, their interaction, the ownership stratum indicator, and the pre-specified covariates. It is estimated for the pooled treatment indicator and separately for each treated arm, for both the continuous and the binary measure; the binary version expresses the change in the gap in percentage points. The gap in each arm and the treatment effect within each gender are reported alongside so that a change in the gap can be traced to its source. Respondents who select "Other" for gender are included in all pooled analyses but not in gender-specific estimates. Gender is taken from Verasight's panel profile, which predates the survey; the in-survey item is used only when the profile value is missing.
secondary_outcomes: Partisan affect: the Republican Party feeling thermometer; the Democratic Party feeling thermometer; a Republican-preference indicator equal to one when the Republican rating exceeds the Democratic rating; and the treatment effect on the gender gap in partisan support, defined as the male-female difference in net partisan affect and in the Republican-preference indicator. Gun policy: the gun-law strictness item; each of the six gun-policy proposal items; a restriction sub-index (four items) and a rights-expansion sub-index (two items); and perceived threat to the right to own guns in the United States (four-point scale from not at all threatened to very threatened). Political engagement: the importance of gun policy in vote choice (five-point scale from not an important issue to deal-breaker); likelihood of contacting a public official to express an opinion on gun policy; likelihood of joining or contributing money to an organization that opposes making gun laws more strict; likelihood of joining or contributing money to an organization that supports making gun laws more strict (each on a seven-point scale from very unlikely to very likely); and net pro-gun mobilization, the difference between the last two. Purchase: a binary indicator for stating that one probably or definitely will buy a gun. Composite: a gun-rights orientation index combining the seven gun-policy items, perceived threat to gun rights, and net pro-gun mobilization.

abstract: Using a laboratory experiment with student participants, we examine how non-promoted employees' response to the promotion of their peer. Specifically, we examine what non-promoted employees expect their promoted peer to set performance targets at for the non-promoted employees and how a peer's promotion affects non-promoted employees’ intention to leave the firm. We further examine whether these effects differ when non-promoted employees were could, versus could not, compete for the promotion their new manager received and whether the types of tasks previously performed with a promoted peer. Prior research suggests that non-promoted employees are more likely to leave the firm due to a perceived lack of upward mobility opportunities, but we examine other rationales for why employees may leave the firm following a peers’ promotion. Notably, our theory suggests that non-promoted employees anticipate the promoted peer to set more aggressive targets for them going forward. We expect this to be especially true for those non-promoted employees who competed for the promotion with the promoted peer, but lessened when the non-promoted employee had previously performed cooperative tasks with the promoted peer.
experimental_design: Experimental groups of 5 employees will complete the experiment. They will complete a general trivia task and then seven production periods. Before period five, it is announced that one employee from each group will be promoted to a role of manager, who will set performance targets for the group they oversee in periods six and seven. After period five, the promotion occurs and all non-promoted employees state what they expect the new manager to set their new targets at and whether they wish to work for another, lower-paying, firm in periods six and seven. We manipulate, between-subjects, whether a given employee is eligible for promotion (3 of 5 group members are always eligible). We manipulate, between-subjects, whether the promoted employee oversees the group they were previously in or another group within the same session. We manipulate, between-subjects, whether two of the first five periods involve a task where cooperation is necessary or whether all of the first five periods involve tasks that are independently completed. All manipulations occur at the session-level and apply to all participants in the session.
experimental_design_details: The experiment will take place across approximately 10-20 sessions, depending on the number of participants who attend each session. Participants will only attend a single session each. Each session will have a predetermined experimental “condition” that applies to all participants in that condition. There are four primary conditions (internal-individual, internal-cooperative, external-individual, external-cooperative). The details of each condition are discussed below. The first four sessions will include each condition once, but which session is which will be randomly drawn from a computer before the first session. After the first four sessions, a similar randomization mechanism will be used, but only for conditions that lack sufficient participants from prior sessions such that we end up with roughly equal number of participants in all four conditions. Upon arrival to the lab, participants who registered for an experimental session will read the consent form and give written informed consent. Each participant will head to a separate computer workstation to complete the experiment online. Each participant will receive a unique participant ID number. There is no link between this participant ID number and the participants’ names. Upon beginning the study, participants will read the instructions that apply to their condition. All participants will earn $7 for completing the experiment and earn additional money in “Lira,” which translates to USD at a rate of 400 Lira = $1. Each participant will first complete a 10-question, general knowledge, multiple-choice, trivia task for five minutes. Each correct response will generate 50 Lira of earnings for the participant. Next, participants will move into the primary portion of the experiment that is made up of 7 periods. At the start of this portion of the experiments, participants are placed into groups of 5 that make up their “division” within a hypothetical firm. In each of these 7 periods, participants will either perform 1) a “decoding” task where they translate numbers into letters using a decoding key, 2) a “letter search” task where they will be tasked with finding how many times a given search letter appears in a 10x10 grid of random letters or 3) a “word” task where they must create words from a set of seven given letters. Each period will consist of 4 minutes to do as many of the specific task for that period as possible. All participants will perform the decoding task in periods 1 and 3 and the letter search task in periods 2, 4, and 5. 80% of participants will perform the letter search task in periods 6 and 7 and the remaining 20% of participants will perform the word task in these two periods. Before period 5, it is announced that one employee from the division will be promoted to a role of manager that will set performance targets for the letter search tasks to be performed in periods 6 and 7. After period 5, the promotion occurs and all non-promoted employees state what they expect the new manager to set the targets at and whether they wish to work for another (lower paying) firm. If they select to work for the alternative firm, they will no longer be in their current division. Half of participants will be paid based solely on their individual performance in all periods (except the manager who is paid based on their employees’ performance in periods 6 and 7 in all conditions). The other half of participants will be paid based on their individual performance in all letter search tasks (except the manager who Is paid based on their employees’ performance in periods 6 and 7 in all conditions) and will be paid based on the highest group member’s performance during the decoding task (employees can choose to decode letters that increase a peer’s performance instead of their own in this task). Further, half of participants will be in a setting where the promotion makes an employee the manager of the division they have been in thus far. In the other half of participants, the promotion makes an employee the manager of a different division than the one they have been in thus far. Details of the pay and structure of each task are as follows. In the decoding task, participants receive a decoding key that assigns a random number to each letter of the alphabet to translate a given number into a letter. Each correct response generates a new decoding key and a new number to decode. Each incorrect response locks the screen, hides the key and number, and forces participants to wait 5 seconds before trying again. When pay is individual-based, participants earn 2 Lira per decoded letter by themselves during the four-minutes, plus a guaranteed 200 Lira. When pay is division-based, participants can choose to decode letters that increase either their own or a teammate’s output. Each participant earns 20% of the division earnings, which is calculated as 3 Lira per decoded letter attributed to the highest-performing employee, in addition to the guaranteed 200 Lira. In the letter search task, employees must correctly identify how many times a given search letter appears in a 10x10 grid of letters. Each correct response generates a new grid and search letter. Each incorrect response hides the grid and search letter, locks the computer, and makes the participant wait 5 seconds before trying again. Employees are presented with three different target levels of performance that generate different bonuses. Participants earn 200 Lira + (if they meet at least one of the targets) a bonus. The bonus is 200, 500, or 900 Lira for attaining the lowest, middle, highest target, respectively. These targets are set at 2, 5, and 8 in Period 2, 4, 7, and 10 in Periods 4 and 5, and set by the promoted manager in Periods 6 and 7. If an employee chooses to leave the division following Period 5, the target will be 5, 7, and 11 in Periods 6 and 7 but the guaranteed pay will be only 100 Lira. In the words task, only the promoted manager completes the task. They will receive 7 letters and be tasked with creating as many words as possible from these letters in one-minute. They will then receive a new set of letters and do the task again for a total of four minutes each period in Periods 6 and 7. Performance on this task does not affect participant pay. However, the promoted manager will receive 1,000 Lira plus 10 Lira for each letter search completed by their employees who chose to remain in the division following Period 5. The promoted manager must choose three target levels that determine the bonus levels of their employees before Period 6. Following the Period 7, all participants will complete a questionnaire about their approach to the experiment, their decision processes, and high-level demographic information. Then, all participants are paid their earnings privately in cash and leave the lab.

abstract: This study examines how information affects people’s preferences for recycled water in Sweden. Participants are randomly assigned to receive information about the quality and safety of recycled water, information about the societal goals of water reuse, both types of information, or no additional information. We then measure support for recycled-water policies, willingness to use recycled water, and willingness to pay for it under different household and service scenarios.
experimental_design: Adult respondents in Sweden participate in a randomized online survey experiment on preferences for recycled water. Participants are assigned to a Control group or to information treatments concerning the quality and safety of recycled water, the societal goals of recycled-water reuse, or both. We examine how these information treatments affect perceptions of recycled water, policy support, willingness to use recycled water, and willingness to pay for it. The survey also includes within-subject scenarios that vary access conditions, service provision, and environmental conditions in order to study how these factors influence preferences.
experimental_design_details: Adult respondents in Sweden first answer questions about sociodemographic characteristics and baseline attitudes. They are then randomly assigned to one of four groups: Control, Quality information, Goal information, or Combined Quality and Goal information. The Quality-information treatment provides information about the quality and safety aspects of recycled water, also using permitted uses as illustrations. This includes informing respondents that recycled water meeting the relevant EU quality class may be used for irrigating crops that are eaten raw. The Goal-information treatment provides information about the societal goals of recycled-water reuse, including replenishing natural water resources and reducing water-scarcity risk. The Combined group receives both information modules. All treatment information is presented in video form. After the information treatment, respondents answer questions about perceived quality and safety, perceived environmental and societal benefits, policy support, willingness to use recycled water, and willingness to pay for recycled water. We also ask about their willingness to pay for the use of recycled water by companies providing certain services, such as car washing, golf-course irrigation, and street cleaning. Respondents also evaluate scenarios that vary within respondents, including a water kiosk located 1 kilometer versus 10 kilometers from the respondent's home, collection from a water kiosk versus delivery by a water taxi, and normal conditions versus a warm and dry summer. We also ask respondents how total water use, regardless of whether tap water or recycled water is used, should change relative to today for municipal irrigation of public green spaces, street cleaning, private garden watering, and private car washing. For the experimental intervention, we test the following hypotheses: - H1: Quality information increases perceived quality and safety of recycled water and increases support for, willingness to use, and willingness to pay for recycled water. - H2: Goal information increases perceived environmental and societal benefits of recycled-water reuse and increases support for, willingness to use, and willingness to pay for recycled water. - H3: The Combined Quality and Goal treatment has the largest positive effect on support for, willingness to use, and willingness to pay for recycled water. Treatment effects on willingness to use and willingness to pay are examined across the water-kiosk and water-taxi scenarios and across different household and commercial applications. For the within-subject scenarios in the main survey, using data from the Control group, we test: - H4: Respondents are less willing to use and pay for recycled water when the water kiosk is located 10 kilometers rather than 1 kilometer from their home. - H5: Respondents are more willing to use and pay for recycled water when it is delivered to their home by a water taxi rather than when they have to collect it from a water kiosk. - H6: Respondents are more willing to use and pay for recycled water during a warm and dry summer.
intervention: One control group and three information-treatment groups.
