primary_outcome_explanation: We examine policy support, willingness to use recycled water, and willingness to pay as the main outcomes. To test H1--H3, we estimate the effects of Quality information and Goal information, as well as the interaction between the two information components. We also test whether the effect of Quality information differs from the effect of Goal information, without specifying a directional hypothesis for this comparison. To test H3 specifically, we compare the Combined Quality and Goal condition with the Control, Quality-information, and Goal-information conditions. The main analysis uses covariate-adjusted regressions controlling for the demographic characteristics collected in the survey. We also report unadjusted regressions. We use heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors and two-sided tests, and additionally report nonparametric tests. In the follow-up survey, conducted 5--7 days after the main survey, we test the persistence of treatment effects using one measure of support for municipal use of recycled water and one measure of willingness to use recycled water for private outdoor purposes. We compare the estimated follow-up treatment effects with the corresponding effects in the initial survey. As a descriptive benchmark, we assess whether the follow-up coefficients are of a magnitude broadly consistent with previous experimental studies, where follow-up effects are often around 40--70\% of the initial treatment effects. For the within-subject scenarios in the main survey, we compare willingness to use and willingness to pay for recycled water across the following scenarios, using data from the Control group: - a water kiosk located 1 kilometer versus 10 kilometers away; - collection from a water kiosk versus delivery by a water taxi; and - normal conditions versus a warm and dry summer. These comparisons are based on paired t-tests and corresponding standardized within-subject effect sizes.
primary_outcomes: Policy preferences: - Support for different household, municipal, and commercial applications of recycled water. - Support for introducing recycled water in the respondent's municipality - Support for municipal investment in recycled-water infrastructure. - Support for a petition promoting recycled water in Sweden. Behavioral preferences: - Intended use of recycled water for different household purposes. - Willingness to pay for recycled water for different household and commercial purposes. For household uses, respondents enter a willingness-to-pay amount between 0 and 170 SEK per cubic meter. A reference price of 85 SEK per cubic meter is shown for ordinary tap water. For commercial uses, respondents are shown a reference price for the same service using drinking water. For outcomes measured on a Likert scale, we additionally construct binary support indicators where applicable. We also construct standardized indices for policy preferences and behavioral preferences, as well as an overall index. Components are standardized to the Control group, averaged within each index, and the resulting index is restandardized to the Control group.
randomization_method: Randomization will be conducted using the survey software. We target approximately 30% of the final sample in Control and approximately 23.3% in each of the three treatment conditions. Pilot observations count toward these final target shares.
secondary_outcome_explanation: The perception measures are used to examine potential channels through which the information treatments affect preferences. Respondents' preferred prices for drinking water and recycled water are analyzed as additional secondary outcomes.
secondary_outcomes: Secondary outcomes include: - perceived quality and safety of recycled water; - perceived environmental and societal benefits of recycled-water reuse; - trust in recycled-water treatment; - perceptions of water scarcity; - normative views about whether water should generally be conserved; - respondents' preferred prices for drinking water and recycled water. The normative-view questions were added during the pilot. As secondary analyses, we estimate heterogeneous treatment effects by age, gender, education, household income, employment, municipality or region, household composition, housing characteristics, home ownership, garden ownership, number of cars, environmental attitudes, and previous experience with water scarcity, where available.
title: Preferences for Recycled Water

abstract: This study examines how restrictions on tenant screening affect landlord behavior and discrimination in rental housing. We conduct a correspondence experiment in Maryland around the October 1, 2026 implementation of two statewide renter-protection laws: HB 315, which restricts the use of income and credit information when screening applicants receiving income-based housing subsidies, and the Fair Chance Housing Act, which restricts criminal-history and substance-use screening. Rental inquiries independently vary applicants’ race, disclosed Housing Choice Voucher (HCV) status, and signals of applicant quality. We measure landlord responses, response timing, invitations to proceed, requests for additional information, and response content, as well as screening and subsidy-related language in rental advertisements. The study tests whether the policy changes alter landlords’ willingness to engage with subsidy recipients, affect racial disparities in landlord responses, increase reliance on race when other screening information is restricted, and change how landlords use race to infer unobserved subsidy receipt. We also examine heterogeneity across local legal regimes, neighborhood characteristics, property characteristics, and rents. The results will inform the design of fair-housing regulation and contribute to broader questions related to the economics of discrimination.
experimental_design: We conduct a pre/post randomized correspondence experiment using publicly available rental listings. In each stage of measurement (pre and post Oct 1) we will identify eligible listings using pre-specified criteria, and we will attempt to send two inquiries to each eligible listing. For the first inquiry, each eligible listing will be randomly assigned to one of 12 treatment cells defined by applicant race (Black- vs White-coded name), Housing Choice Voucher status (disclosed HCV receipt, disclosed non-receipt, or not disclosed), and applicant quality (high vs low). Race and quality are assigned with equal probability within each HCV condition; HCV=Yes and HCV=No each receive 32% of assignments and HCV=Not Disclosed receives 36%. Race, voucher status, and quality for the second inquiry will be assigned conditional on assignments made for the first inquiry. We use pre-specified rules, as defined in our Pre-Analysis Plan, to generate second inquiry assignments. We compare landlord responses and listing content before and after the October 1, 2026 policy changes. Treatment effects will be estimated using regression models that compare outcomes across randomized treatment groups and policy periods, including interaction terms corresponding to the study’s primary hypotheses. Specifications include pre-specified covariates and fixed effects for listing and inquiry characteristics, with standard errors clustered at the landlord level. We also estimate higher-order interactions to test whether post-policy changes differ by race, HCV status, and applicant quality. We describe these features in greater detail in our Pre-Analysis Plan.
intervention: Effective October 1, 2026, Maryland implemented two statewide changes to tenant-screening rules. HB 315 restricts landlords’ use of certain income and credit information when evaluating prospective tenants who receive income-based housing subsidies. The Fair Chance Housing Act (FCHA) restricts pre-offer inquiries and screening based on criminal history and substance use and imposes related restrictions on rental advertising. The study examines how landlord behavior changes following implementation of these screening restrictions. We describe these features in greater detail in our Pre-Analysis Plan.

abstract: We estimate the causal effect of attending an elite secondary school in a mid-sized city of a developing country on students' higher-education decisions and social capital. In 2020, the pandemic prevented the administration of the entrance exam to the Escuelas Medias de la Universidad Nacional del Sur (EMUNS), in Bahía Blanca, Argentina, and seats were instead allocated by lottery: 208 winners and 574 losers among 782 applicants, whom we survey in their final year of secondary school. Three confirmatory hypotheses structure the inference: the intention to pursue higher education, the perceived returns to higher education, and the economic connectedness of friendship networks. We estimate Intention-to-Treat (ITT) and Local Average Treatment Effects (LATE); heterogeneity by gender is pre-specified as exploratory.
experimental_design: We exploit a public lottery that randomly definede which EMUNS applicants were offered a seat on the school. This lottery took place on Friday, September 11, 2020, and was held using the City Lottery (Quiniela Nocturna) of Bahia Blanca. This draw is the source of exogenous variation in the study. From among the 782 applicants for admission to the EMUNS, 208 children aged 10 and 11 were randomly offered a seat. The unit of analysis is the group of individuals registered for the lottery. The treatment group consists of the 208 winners, and the control group comprises the 574 losers. The treatment consists of attending the pre-university school during secondary education (2021–2026). We regress each of the pre-registered outcomes on the binary treatment variable and covariates. Our covariates include gender, month of birth (binary, =1 if born before 30th June, =0 otherwise), SES of the attended elementary school (binary, =1 if located in a high SES neighborhood, =0 otherwise), address
intervention: Data collection consists of a 20–30 minute in-person survey administered in classrooms at the receiving schools (estimated at 40) and at the EMUNS, complemented by a form completed by the principal or the class supervisor (preceptor) of each class section.

abstract: In this project, we vary how we elicit job search behavior among the unemployed.
experimental_design: We will randomize how we ask about labor force participation.
experimental_design_details: The population of interest is all individuals who participated in the recent Labor Force Survey (LFS) AND who self-reported that they are unemployed (currently without job and actively looking for work) AND who are not identified between the timing of the LFS and the start of the experiment as starting a new job. From this population, we will select 2000 individuals for the experiment. We will select a stratified random sample where the strata are defined by interactions of: above median age (within the sample); gender; college graduate; region We will randomize individuals in the sample into three groups as described above: (1) Direct response; (2) Double list experiment with sensitive item in list A; (3) Double list experiment with sensitive item in list B. For groups (2) and (3), we will randomize the order of the statements in the list. Our main results will compare Direct response (1) to the inferred share of individuals actively looking for work in the double list experiment (2 and 3). We will test for heterogeneous effects by 4 strata variables: above median age, college grad, gender, and duration unemployed.

abstract: The green energy transformation requires a workforce that possesses a sufficient amount of green skills. Consequently, this requirement leads to increasing demand for workers in occupations that require green skills. To meet this rising demand, adolescents need to acquire those skills by learning occupations that contain green tasks. However, skills shortages in these occupations remain relatively high. Therefore, understanding how adolescents value the share of green tasks of their future jobs is crucial to secure the future green workforce. Using a discrete choice experiment with adolescent users of Switzerland’s largest private apprenticeship platform, we examine how the share of green tasks in an occupation shapes individual occupational preferences.
experimental_design: We conduct the experiment among German-speaking Swiss adolescents registered on the largest and most relevant private online job board for apprenticeship positions in Switzerland. The experiment will be carried out in collaboration with the respective job board.
experimental_design_details: We use a discrete-choice experiment (DCE) to investigate whether young individuals, all else equal, derive a positive utility from a green occupation (i.e., an occupation containing green tasks). Specifically, we conduct the field experiment among German-speaking Swiss adolescents in secondary education who are currently choosing an upper-secondary vocational education program in one of about 250 apprenticeship occupations and are registered on the largest and most relevant private online job board for apprenticeship positions in Switzerland. In the main part of the survey, we ask them to imagine that they are about to choose between two occupations. The choices the individuals get offered randomly vary in the following four attributes: 1) The share of green tasks (continuous, 3 levels): The share of tasks performed in an occupation that contribute to environmental protection or a sustainable economy. This is our main attribute of interest. 2) Gross monthly wage (continuous, 3 levels): Gross monthly wage upon 5 years after completion of the apprenticeship 3) Apprenticeship wage (continuous, 3 levels) 4) Travel distance to the apprenticeship position (continuous, 3 levels): Commuting distance to the apprenticeship position in minutes In the experiment, every student receives three choice sets for two hypothetical apprenticeship positions each. Our main interest lies in the willingness-to-pay (WTP) for a green occupation, and we measure it in three dimensions: (1) long-term WTP using the wage upon completion, (2) short term WTP using the apprenticeship wage, and (3) willingness-to-commute using the travel distance to the apprenticeship position. We analyze the choice data within the random utility framework of McFadden (1974). Specifically, an individual i derives utility from apprenticeship alternative j in choice situation s where the utility is a function of the occupation's attributes. We estimate mixed logit models that allow preferences for occupational attributes to vary across individuals, thereby capturing unobserved heterogeneity in green occupational preferences. The estimated coefficients are used to derive willingness-to-pay (WTP) measures for green occupational attributes. As a second primary outcome, we investigate how the respondents assess the presented occupations individually. Specifically, they rate each presented occupation individually on a Likert-Scale from 1-7. We test whether future-oriented individuals have a stronger preference for green occupations. We do this by including interacting the share of green tasks with i) the apprenticeship wage ii) the monthly gross wage upon completion of the apprenticeship and iii) the travel distance to the apprenticeship position. A dditionally, we analyze heterogenous preferences among different respondent subgroups using their responses from our survey. First, we are interested in respondents’ characteristics such as gender and educational path (VET vs. general education) as well as their general occupational interest (occupational field and industry of occupation(s) they are most interested in). Second, we analyze how their environmental attitudes and awareness, their self-efficacy regarding environmental issues as well as their support for green policies influences the preference for green occupations. Third, we test whether adolescents’ (dis-)preference for green tasks vary with their preferences for broader occupational interest, that is i) working with people, ii) working with hands, iii) working with new technology, iv) working outside, and v) make a contribution for the environment at work. Lastly, we are interested in how the local normative environment shapes preferences for green occupations. Therefore, we combine the survey responses with municipality-level voting data on environmental issues.

abstract: This field experiment studies whether managers can be trained to use charismatic communication to mobilize collective action and foster cooperative workplace behavior. The study involves 104 managers and their employees in a microfinance company in Kyrgyzstan. After baseline surveys and a baseline speech video, managers are randomized to one of two half-day leadership trainings. The treatment provides practical training in concrete, learnable charismatic leadership communication tactics. The active-comparison training covers closely related leadership concepts but does not train managers in the same concrete behavioral communication techniques. A distinctive feature of the study is a repeated panel of structured, task-specific managerial communication episodes. In addition to the baseline video, each manager prepares and records four post-training messages addressed to employees: an October message concerning a company team competition, a November message intended to foster a collaborative work environment, a January message concerning the office-specific performance target, and a February message concerning a second team competition. Within each wave, managers receive the same broad communication task, while choosing the content, framing, and delivery of their message. The videos are used to measure managers’ use of charismatic leadership tactics and overall video charisma. Their complete audiovisual and verbal content also permits analysis of communication channels, including goal clarity and actionability, collective framing and shared identity, leader commitment and confidence, appeals to coordination and coworker effort, and appeals to helping, advice, and information sharing. Each communication episode is linked to corresponding employee beliefs, survey outcomes, incentivized behavior, and administrative performance. Primary outcomes are organizational performance during two internal competitions and an office-goal period, and cooperative behavior in incentivized public-good and sabotage games. Mechanisms include employees’ knowledge of organizational goals, commitment, beliefs about coworkers, workplace helping and information sharing, collegiality. Additional secondary outcomes include leadership perceptions, trust, individual productivity, and retention. Outcomes are collected repeatedly from baseline through March 2027.
experimental_design: We compare two active, half-day leadership trainings delivered on September 11, 2026. Managers assigned to the charisma-training arm receive instruction and practice in concrete, learnable charismatic leadership communication tactics, drawing on Antonakis et al. (2011, 2012). Managers assigned to the active-comparison arm receive leadership training of similar duration and broad thematic content, but charisma is presented through outcome-based leadership theories rather than through the same concrete behavioral communication techniques. Following training, managers in both experimental arms complete four structured communication assignments embedded in actual organizational episodes. Managers prepare and record messages addressed to their employees concerning: 1. an October team competition; 2. the creation of a collaborative work environment in November; 3. attainment of an office-specific performance target in January; and 4. a second team competition in February. Within each wave, the broad topic and organizational context are common across managers, but managers choose how to formulate, structure, frame, and deliver their message. These repeated communication assignments allow us to observe whether the training changes managers’ actual communication behavior across different organizational tasks and over time. During the January competition period, managers assigned receive a booster reminding them of the trained tactics.
experimental_design_details: The charisma-training arm receives practical instruction in concrete verbal and nonverbal charismatic leadership tactics. The active-comparison arm receives a leadership course of the same approximate duration and concerning closely related leadership concepts, but it describes charisma primarily through desired leadership outcomes and does not provide training in the same concrete behavioral communication tactics. After training, managers in both arms complete the same sequence of structured communication assignments: Baseline • August 24, 2026: managers submit baseline speech videos. • September 3–4, 2026: employees complete baseline measures, including collective-goal mobilization, workplace-cooperation diary and collegiality, public-good and sabotage games, supporting-channel measures, administrative controls, and an IQ proxy. Randomization and training • After baseline measurement, 104 managers are randomized at the manager-office level to charisma training or active-comparison leadership training. • September 11, 2026: managers attend the assigned half-day training. October–November competition • Managers communicate about the internal office competition. • Organizational performance is obtained from company records. • Collective-goal mobilization and supporting-channel measures are collected. November–December cooperation episode • Managers record a video message intended to foster a collaborative workplace environment. • Employees complete the public-good and sabotage games. • Employees complete the Workplace Cooperation Diary and Collegiality measures and supporting-channel measures. January office-goal episode • Managers in both groups receive a booster reminding them of the tactics. • Managers record a video explaining the office target and the allocation or relevance of the target to employees. • Employees complete goal-knowledge, second-order-belief, commitment, effort, and alignment measures. • The percentage of the office target attained and office rank are obtained from company administrative data. February competition • Competition performance is obtained from administrative data. • Employees complete the public-good decision, collective-goal mobilization measures, and supporting-channel measures. March • Employees and managers complete the endline survey. Employees are not individually randomized. All employees associated with the same manager-office cluster inherit the manager’s randomized assignment. In the public-good game, employees are randomly grouped with four coworkers from the same office. In the sabotage game, employees are anonymously paired with a coworker. Monthly administrative productivity and retention data are collected throughout the study period. The repeated videos provide behavioral measures of how the training is translated into managerial communication. They are coded separately for: 1. use of the trained charismatic leadership tactics; 2. overall video charisma; 3. substantive message content and framing; and 4. other communication characteristics specified in the video-coding protocol. The theory of change is: charisma training → changes in observed managerial communication, including the use of charismatic tactics, overall charisma, and substantive message content → clearer and more actionable goals, stronger collective framing, stronger inferred leader commitment, stronger coordination beliefs, and more salient cooperation norms → improved employee goal knowledge and commitment, workplace cooperation, and collegiality → improved organizational performance and cooperative behavior. The videos therefore constitute both the principal first-stage measurement and an observed intermediate layer between randomized training and employee or office outcomes.
intervention: We compare two active, half-day leadership trainings delivered on September 11, 2026. Managers assigned to the charisma-training arm receive instruction and practice in concrete, learnable charismatic leadership communication tactics, drawing on Antonakis et al. (2011, 2012). Managers assigned to the active-comparison arm receive leadership training of similar duration and broad thematic content, but charisma is presented through outcome-based leadership theories rather than through the same concrete behavioral communication techniques. Both trainings are administered on the same day. After training, managers return to their offices and apply the material during ordinary communication about team goals, office performance, and workplace collaboration. During the January competition period, all managers receive a booster reminding them of the trained tactics.

abstract: This study evaluates whether personalized feedback and targeted information about transfer-related resources can support four-year college enrollment intentions and related preparation among Arizona Western College students. Students will be invited to complete a transfer survey about their academic background, transfer plans, perceived barriers, financial aid knowledge, and support needs. Based on the study design, students may receive personalized feedback and information about relevant resources, including free fall workshops and support sessions on topics such as FAFSA, scholarships, budgeting, building credit, and financial literacy. Students may also RSVP for events and complete brief post-event surveys. The study is intended to improve understanding of AWC students’ transfer-related needs and test whether providing personalized guidance and resource information increases engagement with transfer-support resources and four-year college enrollment preparation.
experimental_design: The study will invite Arizona Western College students to complete a transfer-focused survey. The survey collects information on students’ transfer intentions, academic preparation, financial considerations, information access, support needs, and perceived barriers. Students will be randomly assigned to receive different versions of follow-up information or feedback. The intervention provides personalized transfer-related feedback and/or information about relevant support resources, including fall sessions and workshops offered by AWC and its partners. The study will compare outcomes such as engagement with resources, RSVP/attendance behavior, post-event survey completion, and transfer-related preparation measures across study groups. This intervention extends a prior intervention with the same student population, but this time includes information events and post-event surveys.

abstract: This two-stage cluster-randomized trial evaluates RULER, a school-based social and emotional learning approach whose name refers to the skills of recognizing, understanding, labeling, expressing, and regulating emotions, and the incremental effect of a separate digital decision-making activity. Fourteen Italian school institutions participate. Twelve institutions were probabilistically assigned to one of two cross-grade configurations: RULER in grade 4 and comparison in grade 7, or the reverse. Two additional institutions had their assignments fixed ex ante for documented organizational reasons and are excluded from the primary Stage-1 causal analysis. The frozen roster contains 127 classes and 2,389 planned students; the primary Stage-1 causal cohort contains 110 classes and 2,070 planned students. At Stage 2, classes in the RULER-assigned grade that meet prespecified technological and operational eligibility criteria will be randomized approximately 1:1 to continue with RULER only or to receive RULER plus a separate class-based digital decision-making activity before the common post-test. The activity is distinct from RULER and will generate decision and process data from participating students. The primary outcome for the RULER-only strategy comparison is the Self-Awareness domain score from the age-appropriate Social and Emotional Learning Indicator System (SELIS) form, measured at the late-May 2027 student post-test. The primary Stage-2 outcome will be the SELIS domain matched ex ante to the digital activity’s focal competence, measured at the common post-test in both Stage-2 arms and specified before the Stage-2 randomization. Secondary outcomes include the remaining SELIS domains and a project overall SELIS index at post-test; the same SELIS outcomes at follow-up; harmonized school administrative indicators of attendance, assessments, and disciplinary actions; and delayed outcomes from Italy’s National Institute for the Evaluation of the Education and Training System (INVALSI) in Italian, mathematics, and English. Analyses will separately estimate the effect of the RULER-only strategy, the incremental effect of the digital activity, and the policy-relevant effect of assignment to the overall RULER-centered pathway. Implementation, teacher-practice, qualitative, platform-use, and resource-use data will support process analyses and a planned cost-effectiveness analysis.
experimental_design: The study uses a two-stage clustered randomized design. At Stage 1, each of the 12 probabilistically assigned institutions contributes a grade 4 cohort and a grade 7 cohort. These institutions were assigned to one of two configurations: RULER in grade 4 and comparison in grade 7, or comparison in grade 4 and RULER in grade 7. Two additional institutions had their assignments fixed ex ante because of documented feasibility constraints. These two institutions participate in data collection but are excluded from the primary Stage-1 causal analysis. Stage-1 randomization used a prespecified constrained assignment procedure. The institution and class rosters, assignment protocol, randomization code, and SHA-256 hashes were frozen and deposited with the co-investigators on July 5, 2026, before the official draw. Of 162 structurally admissible institutional allocations, 41 satisfied the prespecified balance criterion, and one allocation was selected uniformly from this acceptance set on July 8, 2026, using a reproducible seed derived mechanically from the frozen roster. At Stage 2, RULER classes meeting prespecified technological and operational eligibility criteria will be randomly assigned at approximately a 1:1 ratio to RULER only or RULER plus the digital decision-making activity. Eligibility will be defined using criteria that do not depend on study outcomes and will be assessed and frozen for both grade cohorts before the Stage-2 randomization. A versioned addendum filed before that randomization will report the eligible roster, blocking rules, exact conditional assignment probabilities, and the procedures required to combine the two assignment stages. The two institutions fixed at Stage 1 may contribute to the randomized Stage-2 comparison if their RULER classes meet the eligibility criteria. The primary Stage-1 estimand is the intention-to-treat effect of the embedded RULER-only strategy relative to the comparison condition in the frozen cohort of 12 randomized institutions. RULER-only observations arise both from RULER-assigned classes that are not eligible for the additional activity and from eligible RULER-assigned classes randomized not to receive it. This contrast will therefore be estimated using the exact joint assignment probabilities implied by the 41-allocation Stage-1 acceptance set and the Stage-2 blocked randomization; it will not be estimated as an unweighted comparison of the observed groups. The pooled Stage-1 estimand will assign equal weight to the student-average grade-specific effects for grades 4 and 7. Grade-specific effects will also be reported. The primary Stage-2 contrast will compare assignment to RULER plus the digital decision-making activity with assignment to RULER only among eligible RULER classes. Its primary outcome will be the SELIS domain corresponding to the activity’s prespecified focal competence, measured at the common student post-test in both Stage-2 arms. The focal competence, matched SELIS domain, and Stage-2 outcome-analysis procedures will be frozen in the versioned addendum before the Stage-2 randomization. Within-activity choices, response times, and operational logs will be observed only for students who participate in the activity within classes assigned to it. They will support prespecified within-arm analyses of their correspondence with the matched SELIS self-report measure and will not be treated as between-arm causal outcomes. A key policy-relevant secondary estimand will compare assignment to the overall RULER-centered pathway, comprising RULER only or RULER plus the activity as generated by the Stage-2 design, with the comparison condition. A secondary total-package comparison of RULER plus the activity with the comparison condition will be defined in the Stage-2 addendum. Analyses including all 14 institutions for the Stage-1 contrast will be reported as supportive and will not form part of the primary randomized causal analysis. The frozen July 2026 class roster defines the confirmatory Stage-1 cohort. Any subsequently activated sections invited to participate in measurement will constitute an extended measurement stratum and will be included only in secondary or sensitivity analyses. The initial student measurement is scheduled after initial teacher training but before the planned student-facing implementation of RULER. The post-test is planned for late May 2027, after implementation of the additional digital activity. The follow-up is planned during the 2027/28 school year. The comparison grade does not receive direct RULER implementation during the study year. Because RULER and comparison grades belong to the same institution, indirect between-grade exposure will be documented and considered when interpreting the estimates. All main estimates will follow assignment, irrespective of actual implementation or participation. Post-assignment measures of implementation intensity will not be used to redefine the primary treatment groups. Detailed estimation, inference, missing-data, multiplicity, and covariate-adjustment procedures will be specified in a versioned analysis plan before the research team accesses the corresponding post-treatment outcome data. Estimation and inference for each randomized contrast will respect its corresponding assignment mechanism, including the Stage-1 constrained randomization and, where relevant, the Stage-2 blocked randomization. Implementation resources will be measured prospectively to support a separately prespecified cost-effectiveness analysis linked to the trial’s effectiveness estimates. Within classes assigned to receive RULER, teacher-completed ratings of students’ observable social-emotional competence are planned as part of implementation monitoring and descriptive multi-method triangulation. These ratings are not included in the prespecified confirmatory impact-outcome family. The instrument and edition, administration schedule, rater assignment and continuity rules, and scoring procedures will be frozen and time-stamped before the first rating wave. The initial rating wave is expected in late October or early November 2026, after teachers have had sufficient opportunity to observe students in regular classroom settings.
intervention: RULER is a school-based social and emotional learning approach centered on emotional literacy. Teachers assigned to RULER receive three training modules totaling approximately 21 hours, continued implementation support during the school year, and access to structured classroom materials and tools. The approach includes the Charter, Mood Meter, Meta-Moment, Blueprint, and activities focused on recognizing, understanding, labeling, expressing, and regulating emotions. Teachers in the grade assigned to RULER are expected to integrate these tools and practices into ordinary classroom routines during the 2026/27 school year. The comparison grade is not assigned to receive the first-year RULER intervention and continues its usual educational activities. At the second stage, RULER classes meeting prespecified technological and operational eligibility criteria will be assigned either to continue with RULER only or to receive a separate classroom-based digital decision-making activity delivered in a single school session lasting no more than two hours. The activity is designed by the research team and informed by experimental and behavioral economics. Students will make individual decisions in structured digital tasks that may include interactions with classmates. The activity is an additional experimental component and is not part of RULER, its training program, or its standard classroom tools. Its final tasks, target social and emotional competence, incentive structure, within-activity behavioral measures, and scoring rules will be preregistered in a versioned addendum before the second-stage randomization.

primary_outcome_explanation: Self-Awareness was selected as the primary outcome for the Stage-1 RULER comparison because it is the student-level SELIS domain most closely aligned with RULER’s first-year emphasis on emotional awareness and emotional literacy. It captures students’ perceived ability to understand their own emotions, thoughts, and values and how they influence behavior across contexts. Grade 4 students will complete the SELIS form for grades 3–5, and grade 7 students will complete the form for grades 6–8. Responses will be coded from 0 to 3, with higher values indicating greater perceived ease in performing the described social and emotional skill. The primary domain score will be the mean of the age-appropriate Self-Awareness items when at least 80 percent of the domain items have valid responses. Scores will be standardized separately by grade using the pooled initial-measurement mean and standard deviation among respondents in the primary 12-institution randomized cohort, across Stage-1 assignment conditions. The same fixed grade-specific parameters will be applied to post-test and follow-up scores. The primary Self-Awareness measure will use all Self-Awareness items included in the relevant age-appropriate form. As a sensitivity analysis, the score will be reconstructed using only the Self-Awareness items included in the 41-item common core shared by the two grade-span forms. These procedures constitute the project scoring of the Italian SELIS adaptation and do not reproduce the official SELIS 1–999 Rasch scale. The primary endpoint is the student post-test planned for late May 2027. The initial student measurement is scheduled after the beginning of teacher training but before the planned introduction of RULER tools and activities in the classroom. Stage 2 will have a distinct, estimand-specific primary endpoint for the randomized incremental contrast. It will be one of the five predefined SELIS domain scores, selected ex ante to match the focal competence targeted by the digital activity. This domain is part of the common SELIS questionnaire administered to all study students and will be constructed using the same age-appropriate form, response coding, 80-percent item-completion rule, and fixed grade-specific standardization across study conditions. The focal competence and corresponding SELIS domain will be frozen in a versioned addendum before the Stage-2 randomization.

Stage-2 primary endpoint: One of the five predefined SELIS domain scores, selected ex ante to match the focal competence targeted by the digital activity. The focal competence and corresponding SELIS domain will be specified and frozen in a versioned addendum before the Stage-2 randomization.
randomization_method: Stage 1 used computerized constrained randomization. The institution and class rosters, assignment protocol, randomization code, and SHA-256 hashes were frozen and deposited with the co-investigators on July 5, 2026. The procedure generated 162 structurally admissible allocations, retained the 41-allocation acceptance set satisfying the prespecified balance criterion, and selected one allocation uniformly from that set on July 8, 2026, using a reproducible seed derived mechanically from the frozen roster. Stage 2 will use computerized class-level random assignment among eligible RULER classes, with an approximately 1:1 allocation within prespecified school or school-site blocks. Eligibility criteria, blocks, any allocation constraints, and exact conditional assignment probabilities will be frozen before the draw.
randomization_unit: Stage 1: school institution. Stage 2: class among RULER classes meeting prespecified technological and operational eligibility criteria.
secondary_outcome_explanation: Relationship Skills and Self-Management are designated as key secondary outcomes. Relationship Skills is prioritized because first-year RULER practice is expected to support students’ perceived ability to communicate, cooperate, seek help, and navigate interactions with teachers and peers. Self-Management is expected to be somewhat more distal, as changes in emotional regulation and stress management may require sustained practice and transfer across contexts. Social Awareness and Responsible Decision-Making are broader secondary outcomes that are theoretically related to RULER but are expected to change less proximally during the first year. Follow-up SELIS outcomes will assess the persistence and possible broadening of effects. Each secondary SELIS domain score will use the same response coding, 80-percent item-completion rule, and grade-specific initial-measurement standardization specified for the primary outcome. Follow-up scores will use the same construction and fixed standardization parameters. The project overall SELIS index will be the equally weighted mean of the five grade-standardized domain scores when all five domain scores are available. This composite will then be rescaled separately by grade using its pooled initial-measurement mean and standard deviation in the primary 12-institution randomized cohort; the same fixed parameters will be applied at post-test and follow-up. School administrative and INVALSI outcomes will be treated as distal exploratory outcome families. Their exact construction, aggregation level, harmonization, and multiplicity rules will be frozen before the research team accesses the corresponding post-treatment outcome data.

title: Promoting Social and Emotional Competencies in Italian Schools: A Two-Stage Randomized Evaluation of RULER and an Embedded Digital Decision-Making Activity

abstract: Progress in enabling machines to perform an expanding range of manual tasks depends on task-level data that encode how those tasks are carried out. Generating these data requires workers to record their actions as they perform their jobs. Workers thus supply a key input into the creation of labor-substituting capital, potentially facilitating their own displacement and shaping how the gains from automation are divided between labor and capital. We study how workers make this decision, and whether it is shaped by information asymmetry over the downstream use of their data and by weak worker bargaining power. In a survey experiment with factory workers in Delhi NCR, India, drawn from textiles, electronics, and other manufacturing, we elicit the minimum additional daily payment workers require to make first-person recordings of their work, cross-randomizing whether workers are informed that the resulting footage will be used to train a machine that could replace them. Each worker prices two counterparties in randomized order, their own employer and an outside research organisation, which identifies what the employment relationship does to the price of consent.
experimental_design: The workers in the experiment will receive hypothetical offers to wear a head-mounted camera which will record how they perform their usual work. The design will vary the downstream usage of the data, the length of recording at the individual level, and the nature of the party making the offer at within-worker level.
experimental_design_details: We individually randomize factory workers in Delhi NCR into five cells, stratified by industry within cell ( textiles, electronics, other manufacturing). The four main cells cross the information disclosure with the recording length. Each main-cell worker first answers an extensive-margin question and workers who would record for payment then state their price: an ascending price ladder. Because the counterparty order is randomized, the employer-versus-research comparison is balanced across elicitation formats. The fifth cell receives only the placebo overhead-camera offer.
intervention: The workers in the experiment will receive hypothetical offers to wear a head-mounted camera which will record how they perform their usual work.

abstract: This study examines how different types of class cadre positions affect student popularity among peers. Class cadre positions are a ubiquitous feature of school classrooms, yet their causal impact on peer relationships remains poorly understood, particularly across different role types. Using a randomized controlled trial, the study randomly assigns eligible students to serve as different types of class cadres or to a control group, and measures multiple dimensions of popularity along with underlying positive and negative mechanisms.
experimental_design: This study uses a paired randomized controlled trial design to estimate the causal effects of different class cadre positions on student popularity. Within each participating classroom, for each cadre type, two eligible students who are suitable for the position and comparable in baseline characteristics are identified and formed into a matched pair. One student from each pair is randomly assigned to the treatment group (serving in the cadre position) and the other to the control group. The analysis will compare outcome changes between treatment and control students using paired comparisons and regression methods.
intervention: Eligible students will be randomly assigned to serve as a specific type of class cadre—including class monitor, committee member, or course representative—or to a control group. Students in the treatment group will perform the regular duties associated with their assigned position, which may include classroom management, activity organization, or subject-related assistance depending on the role type. Control group students will not serve in any class cadre position during the study period. The intervention reflects standard cadre appointment practices in participating schools and does not involve additional training or modifications to normal duties.

abstract: This completed educational randomized controlled trial examined whether a fading process scaffold can improve how students evaluate generative-AI advice and whether the learned decision procedure transfers after support is withdrawn. The trial enrolled 480 second-year students in 24 intact classes across three higher vocational institutions in Chongqing, China. Randomization occurred at the class level within six school-by-teacher blocks. Within each four-class block, one class was assigned to each condition in a 2 x 2 factorial design crossing generative-AI access with TRACE process scaffolding: AI + TRACE, AI only, TRACE only, or neither. Each condition contained six classes and 120 randomized students. The intervention comprised four weekly 45-minute training sessions, followed by an assessment conducted while assigned support was still available. The two primary outcomes specified in the internal analysis plan were (H1) early unaided decision-process performance after both AI and TRACE were withdrawn and (H2) task-based appropriate reliance on identical version-locked AI advice after TRACE withdrawal. Secondary outcomes included support-present performance, delayed unaided transfer, judgment revision and final accuracy, selective access to standardized AI responses, and dynamic revision after new information. Class allocation was generated by computer using a Fisher-Yates permutation after class rosters were finalized. This registry entry is retrospective; the study was not prospectively registered.
experimental_design: Teacher-blocked 2 x 2 class-cluster randomized educational trial conducted in three higher vocational institutions in Chongqing, China. The factors were generative-AI access (yes/no) and TRACE process scaffolding (yes/no). The sample comprised 24 intact second-year classes and 480 students, with 20 registered students per class. Six teachers each contributed a four-class school-by-teacher block; within each block, one class was assigned to each of the four conditions. Every condition therefore included six randomized classes and 120 randomized students. Class rosters and individual consent were completed before allocation was released. All groups received the same curriculum, scenario structure, scheduled instructional time, and common teacher guidance; the intended contrasts were AI access and TRACE support. Students were required to attend the institutionally scheduled career-planning course, but consent for research use of their data was separate from course participation and had no effect on grades, credits, teacher evaluation, access to instructional resources, or other academic rights. The study is being registered retrospectively after completion.
intervention: The trial crossed two instructional factors: access to institutionally managed generative AI and access to TRACE, a structured decision-process scaffold. TRACE externalized five operations: Target the decision; Review evidence and uncertainty; Assess alternatives and consequences; Clarify criteria and trade-offs; and Execute, evaluate, and update. TRACE support was faded across sessions from full prompts to guided, reduced, minimal, and final-cue forms. Four conditions were implemented: (A) AI + TRACE, (B) AI only, (C) TRACE only, and (D) neither. All four groups followed the same career-decision curriculum, worked with parallel scenarios, received the same scheduled instructional time, and used the same core response structures. During S1-S4 and T1, both AI-access conditions used the same institutionally managed qwen3.5-plus service under a common system prompt and common access configuration. abstract: Advice is often received from a source whose reliability is not precisely known. This study asks whether reluctance to rely on such advice reflects ambiguity aversion, and whether it can be changed by altering how reliability is communicated while holding its expected value fixed. Participants estimate the caloric content of photographed meals, receive an estimate from an AI system, and revise. We randomize what participants are told about the system's accuracy: nothing (control), a point value ("accurate in 80 of 100 cases"), or an interval with the same expected value ("accurate in 65 to 95 of 100 cases; no more precise figure is available"). Expected accuracy is identical across the two disclosure arms, so expected-utility accounts predict no difference between them. Guided by an alpha-maxmin expected utility framework, we predict that interval disclosure lowers reliance for ambiguity-averse participants and raises it for ambiguity-loving participants, with the contrast reversing sign at ambiguity neutrality. We elicit ambiguity attitude and risk attitude with multiple incentivized instruments and correct for measurement error using ORIV. We additionally elicit participants' own beliefs about the system's accuracy as an interval, which allows us to estimate how much of the disclosed midpoint and the disclosed width they adopt, and to test whether that adoption depends on elicited ambiguity attitude.
experimental_design: The study is a laboratory experiment conducted on paper with groups of up to 20 participants. Each session lasts approximately 41 minutes. Participants are randomly assigned to one of three arms, and every participant completes three estimation tasks, so that treatment varies between participants while the tasks vary within them. The session proceeds in a fixed order. Participants first answer background questions and report general attitudes toward risk and uncertainty, their experience with artificial intelligence tools, and whether they experienced particular difficulties before the age of 18. They then complete an incentivized task measuring their attitude toward ambiguity, using two physical urns, one of known composition and one of unknown composition. An incentivized measure of risk attitude follows this. The intervention page comes next, followed immediately by questions checking attention and comprehension and by ratings of how clear the statement was and how certain participants feel about the system's accuracy. Participants then state what accuracy they expect from the system, and complete the three estimation tasks. Placing these parts together and instructing participants not to return to earlier pages ensures that beliefs are recorded after the statement is read and before any advice is seen. The final parts of the session measure ambiguity attitude and risk attitude a second time, using different question formats and unrelated sources, and collect measures of cognitive reflection and numeracy along with closing questions. Measuring each preference more than once is a deliberate feature of the design rather than a repetition, because preferences estimated from a small number of choices contain substantial measurement error, and correcting for that error requires more than one measure. Every decision in the session is incentivized. One decision is selected at random by dice at the end of the session and carried out with real money, in addition to a fixed participation fee. Because any decision may be the one that counts, participants have a reason to answer each question according to their true preferences.
experimental_design_details: The central comparison is between the point arm and the interval arm, and the quantity of interest is not the average difference between them but how that difference varies with the participant's own attitude toward ambiguity. We expect the interval statement to reduce reliance among ambiguity-averse participants and to increase it among ambiguity-loving participants. The difference between the two arms should therefore be positive at one end of the ambiguity attitude distribution, negative at the other, and zero at the point of ambiguity neutrality. We regard the location of that crossing as an important feature of the prediction, because theory specifies it in advance rather than allowing it to be estimated from the data. A confounding variable would have to change sign at the same point in order to produce the same pattern, which is a demanding requirement. The main estimating equation includes indicators for each disclosure arm, the participant's centred ambiguity attitude, and the interactions between them, with risk attitude and its interactions included alongside so that the two preferences compete directly. Our prediction is that ambiguity attitude carries the interaction and risk attitude does not. We attach importance to correcting for measurement error in the elicited preferences. Simulation shows that when ambiguity attitude and risk attitude are correlated and both are measured with the degree of error typical of short elicitation tasks, ordinary least squares attributes explanatory power to the more precisely measured of the two and fails to identify the correct one. For this reason each preference is elicited more than once, and the main specification stacks the measures and instruments each with the other, following the approach developed for exactly this problem in experimental economics. We report ordinary least squares results alongside, and treat the difference between the two sets of estimates as an estimate of how much attenuation the elicitation introduces. Because ambiguity attitude is measured rather than assigned, we do not claim that the interaction identifies a causal effect of ambiguity attitude. Assignment to arms is random and the arm effects are causally identified, but the interaction describes how a randomly assigned treatment operates differently across participants who differ in a measured characteristic. To assess whether that heterogeneity is specific to ambiguity attitude, we run the same interaction using risk attitude, cognitive reflection, numeracy, education, prior use of artificial intelligence tools, and age. We expect that only ambiguity attitude produces the change in sign. We report a pilot conducted before the main wave. The pilot tests whether the interval statement widens the beliefs participants state about the system's accuracy relative to the point statement. If it does not, participants are reading the range as equivalent to its midpoint, no ambiguity has been created, and the remaining hypotheses cannot be tested. We treat this as a condition for proceeding rather than as a robustness check.
intervention: Participants complete three estimation tasks in which they judge how many calories are contained in a photographed meal. In each task, they first record their own estimate, then see an estimate produced by an artificial intelligence system, and then record a final estimate. Payment depends on the accuracy of the final estimate, so participants have a financial reason to use the advice when they believe it is informative and to ignore it when they do not. The intervention is a single page shown before the estimation tasks. This page describes the system that produced the advice. Its content is identical across treatment arms except for one statement about how accurate the system has been in prior testing. Participants in the control arm read no statement about accuracy. Participants in the second arm read that the system was accurate in 80 of 100 test cases. Participants in the third arm read that testing produced varying results, with accuracy falling somewhere between 65 and 95 of 100 cases, and that no more precise figure could be determined. The second and third statements describe the same average level of accuracy. They differ only in whether that level is presented as a single number or as a range. This allows us to separate the effect of knowing how accurate a source is from the effect of knowing that accuracy precisely. Accuracy is defined for participants as an estimate falling within 15 per cent of the true value. Before the study begins, we verify the system's accuracy on 100 comparable meal photographs whose true calorie content has been measured, so that both statements shown to participants are factually correct. No misleading information is used at any point in the study. The advice shown for each of the three experimental photographs is generated once and held fixed for every participant. The advice itself is therefore identical across arms, and any difference in behaviour can be attributed to the accuracy statement rather than to the content of the advice.

mde_text: The outcome is weight on advice, which is a proportion. A value of zero means the participant ignored the advice and a value of one means the participant adopted it completely. Effects below are expressed in units of that proportion. Power was calculated by Monte Carlo simulation rather than by formula, because the primary test is an interaction between a randomly assigned treatment and a continuous measured characteristic, and because the outcome is averaged over three tasks per participant. The simulation assumes a standard deviation of 0.12 across participants and 0.22 across tasks within a participant in weight on advice, and a standard deviation of 0.22 in normalized ambiguity attitude. These values will be re-estimated from pilot data and the calculation repeated before the main wave begins. Primary test. The interaction between interval disclosure and ambiguity attitude, comparing 125 participants in the point arm with 125 in the interval arm. At 80 per cent power and a 5 per cent significance level, the smallest detectable slope is 0.30 units of weight on advice per unit of normalized ambiguity attitude. In practical terms, this means the design can detect a situation in which the interval statement raises reliance by about 0.15 for the most ambiguity-loving participants and lowers it by about 0.15 for the most ambiguity-averse. The effect implied by the theoretical framework under our calibration is 0.315, which the design detects with 85 per cent power. If measurement error in the elicited preference attenuates the slope to 0.24, power falls to 62 per cent. Secondary test. The difference in mean weight on advice between the point arm and the control arm, comparing 125 participants with 50. The smallest detectable difference is 0.08 units of weight on advice at 80 per cent power. This comparison is well powered at a small control group because it is a difference in means rather than an interaction, which is the reason for the unequal allocation. We state plainly that the design is powered to detect the predicted pattern but is not powered to rule it out. If the interaction is not statistically significant, that result will not distinguish between a genuine absence of effect and a sample too small to detect one of the size we expect. We note this in advance so that a null result is interpreted correctly rather than treated as evidence against the prediction.

primary_outcome_explanation: For each estimation task we record three numbers: the participant's initial estimate, the advice shown, and the participant's final estimate. Weight on advice is the share of the distance between the initial estimate and the advice that the participant travels when revising. A value of zero means the participant ignored the advice entirely, a value of one means the participant adopted it completely, and intermediate values mean the participant combined the two. The primary outcome is the average of this measure across the three tasks. This measure is standard in the literature on advice taking and allows our results to be compared with published benchmarks. It also has the useful property of being independent of the size of the numbers involved, so tasks with larger or smaller calorie values contribute on the same scale. The measure becomes unstable when the advice happens to fall very close to the participant's own estimate, because the denominator then approaches zero. For this reason our main specification does not compute the ratio directly. Instead we regress the final estimate on the initial estimate and on the advice, and take reliance to be the coefficient on the advice divided by the sum of the two coefficients. This produces the same quantity while remaining well behaved. We report two further versions to show that the finding does not depend on how the outcome is constructed. The first is the ratio measure itself, restricted to values between zero and one and excluding cases where the advice falls within 10 per cent of the initial estimate. The second is a simple indicator of whether the final estimate moved toward the advice at all. If the three versions agree, the result is not an artefact of the measure.
primary_outcomes: Weight on advice, measured as the extent to which participants move their estimate toward the advice they receive.
randomization_method: Randomization was carried out in advance of data collection by the principal investigator using statistical software. Assignment was blocked in groups of 30 and stratified by gender and by self reported frequency of artificial intelligence use, which keeps the arms balanced on these characteristics even if data collection is interrupted before the target sample is reached. Booklets were printed in three versions, numbered according to the allocation table, and sealed before sessions began. The three versions are identical in layout, length and appearance, and differ only in the wording of one statement on one page. Research assistants distribute booklets in numerical order and therefore do not know which arm any participant has been assigned to. No randomization takes place in the session itself.
randomization_unit: The individual participant. There is a single level of randomization. Treatment is assigned at the individual level and does not vary within a participant, while the three estimation tasks are completed by every participant regardless of arm.
secondary_outcome_explanation: Before the estimation tasks, participants state the smallest number, the largest number, and their best guess for how many correct answers the system would give in 100 comparable tasks. The distance between the smallest and largest figures measures how much ambiguity the participant perceives about the source. This elicitation is incentivized: a participant is paid if the system's verified accuracy falls inside the interval they state, minus an amount proportional to how wide that interval is. The penalty for width means participants gain nothing by stating a very wide interval simply to be safe. These beliefs allow us to estimate two quantities that describe how disclosed information is absorbed. The first is the weight participants place on the midpoint of the statement they read. The second is the weight they place on its width. The control arm identifies what participants believe when they are told nothing, and each disclosure arm then reveals how far beliefs move toward what was stated. Because the point arm and the interval arm each provide an estimate of the same width parameter, the two estimates can be compared, and disagreement between them would indicate that the framework does not describe belief formation well. We regard this as a strength of the design, since it allows the framework to be rejected rather than only confirmed. Three further measures serve as checks on the intervention rather than as outcomes of interest in themselves. We ask how clear the accuracy statement was, how certain the participant feels about the system's accuracy, and how much they trust the system. The design requires that the interval statement lowers certainty without lowering clarity. If both fall together, the range was confusing rather than ambiguous, and the results would need to be interpreted differently. We report these measures before the main results so that readers can judge whether the intervention worked as intended. After the estimation tasks we also ask how accurate participants believe such systems to be. Because this question comes after treatment, it is affected by the treatment and is used only descriptively. Its purpose is to confirm that participants regarded the system as capable of error. If participants believe the system is rarely wrong, a statement about its accuracy carries little information, and the intervention has nothing to work with.
secondary_outcomes: Perceived reliability of the source, measured by the width and midpoint of the belief interval participants report about the system's accuracy; the degree to which participants adopt the disclosed midpoint and width; confidence in one's own estimate; and perceived clarity, certainty, and trust regarding the accuracy statement.

abstract: The key idea of our research project is to test how social proof and coordination cost shape collective framing of technology adoption among smallholder farmers. In many agricultural technology adoption settings, an individual farmer's willingness to try a new product depends not only on her own information, but also on what she believes her peers are doing and on the extent to which successful adoption may depend on others' participation (Conley and Udry 2010). This distinguishes the mechanism we study from existing social-learning studies of technology diffusion, which are typically sequential, with early adopters acting first and neighbors subsequently learning by observing their outcomes (Foster and Rosenzweig 1995), rather than involving a simultaneous coordination problem that engineers simultaneous adoption of newer technology at scale. The study also moves beyond digital advisory platforms that operate primarily as information channels (Fábregas et al. 2019; Cole et al. 2025) by examining whether a platform can actively structure the social environment surrounding an adoption decision. We study this in the context of a sustainable crop-care campaign promoting agricultural products that are relatively unfamiliar to many smallholder farmers, where uncertainty about product efficacy may make peer behavior particularly relevant. We test these ideas using a four-condition cluster-randomized field experiment on an agricultural digital platform in India. Farmers receive either an Individual Offer, in which access to a 50% discount depends only on the farmer's own decision, or one of three Group Offer conditions, in which the discount is unlocked only if a required number of community members sign up for the offer. Within the Group Offer conditions, we vary the peer sign-up information farmers receive and the coordination cost associated with reaching the threshold for such sign-ups. We operationalize coordination cost as the number of additional farmer sign-ups required for the group to reach the threshold and unlock the discount. The primary comparison tests whether introducing a group-contingent offer increases sign-up relative to an otherwise individual offer. Additional comparisons examine whether favorable peer social proof under low coordination costs increases sign-up, and whether increasing coordination costs versus social proof reduces sign-up while holding the displayed number of prior farmer sign-ups fixed. We further examine whether initial offer sign-up translates into subsequent self -expressed interest in adoption as well as purchase conversion. The experiment therefore studies two stages of the adoption process: farmers' initial willingness to join the offer and their subsequent completion of a product purchase. The study has implications for how digital platforms in emerging markets can not only reduce informational barriers to agricultural technology adoption amongst resource-constrained smallholder farmers but also utilize social and coordination barriers surrounding the adoption decision to promote adoption of sustainable or unfamiliar products at scale.
experimental_design: This study is a four-condition cluster-randomized field experiment. Randomization occurs at the geographic sub-district-level (as officially categorized by the Government of India) digital-community level. All eligible farmers within a randomized community receive the same experimental condition. The four conditions are: • T1: Individual Offer • T2a: Group Offer – No Peer Sign-up Information • T2b: Group Offer [4 of 5 farmers have joined] • T2c: Group Offer [4 of 15 farmers have joined] The Group Offer conditions share the same basic collective contingency: access to the discount depends on the community reaching a required sign-up threshold. They differ in the peer sign-up information displayed and in the remaining coordination cost required to reach that threshold.
intervention: Farmers on the Krishify platform are exposed to a sustainable crop-care campaign offering a 50% discount on three agricultural products promoted under a common campaign theme. Depending on random assignment, the discount is presented either as: 1. an Individual Offer, in which the discount is available based solely on the individual farmer's decision to sign up; or 2. a Group Offer, in which the discount is unlocked only if a required number of farmers from the same digital community sign up for the offer. All farmers within the same randomized community (created at the geographic sub-district level) receive the same experimental condition. In the Group Offer conditions, once the required sign-up threshold is reached, all farmers in that community who signed up for the offer become eligible for the 50% discount. The discount is therefore not limited to the farmers whose sign-ups complete the threshold. If the required threshold is not reached, the group discount is not unlocked. The discount depth is fixed at 50% across all experimental conditions.

abstract: This study evaluates a school-based educational intervention designed to strengthen the prevention of and response to digital violence among children and adolescents in Bolivia. The study is conducted in participating schools in three municipalities and combines a cluster randomized controlled trial with a complementary qualitative component. For the experimental component, school classes are randomly assigned to receive the intervention either early or after a short waiting period. All eligible classes eventually receive the intervention. The primary comparison is conducted after the early-treatment classes have participated in the program but before the delayed-treatment classes receive it. Randomization occurs at the class level, while outcomes are measured at the individual student level. The intervention includes age-appropriate educational activities for children and adolescents aimed at improving understanding of digital violence, recognition of online risks, confidence in seeking help, intentions to respond safely, and awareness of shared responsibilities among students, families, schools, and other relevant actors. Student surveys are administered before the intervention, immediately after the experimental comparison period, and during subsequent follow-up. The primary analysis estimates intention-to-treat effects of early assignment to the intervention, accounting for the clustered randomization and baseline outcomes. The study also includes focus groups with parents, caregivers, and teachers, as well as semi-structured interviews with school leaders, institutional actors, and program implementers. This qualitative component is intended to help explain mechanisms of change, barriers to implementation, the usefulness of intervention materials, coordination between schools and families, and conditions for sustainability. Causal inference is restricted to the randomized student component.
experimental_design: The study uses a stratified cluster randomized controlled trial in participating schools in three municipalities in Bolivia. The unit of randomization is the school class/parallel, and the unit of observation is the individual student. Within predefined strata, comparable classes are assigned to either an early-intervention group or a delayed-intervention group. Baseline outcomes are measured before exposure to the intervention. The primary experimental follow-up is conducted after the early-intervention class has received the program and before the corresponding delayed-intervention class receives it. The delayed classes subsequently receive the same intervention, so all eligible classes eventually have access to the program. The primary analysis follows an intention-to-treat approach and estimates the effect of assignment to early intervention relative to temporary delayed intervention.
experimental_design_details: The experimental design is a stratified cluster randomized controlled trial with school classes/parallels as the units of assignment. The randomization frame contains 98 classes/parallels organized into 50 strata. Forty-eight strata contain two comparable A/B classes and are eligible for experimental randomization. Two strata contain only one class and are therefore classified as non-randomizable and excluded from the primary causal contrast. The resulting experimental sample contains 96 randomized classes: 48 assigned to early intervention and 48 assigned to delayed intervention. Randomization is conducted 1:1 within each eligible stratum. Strata are defined by municipality, school, age group/educational level, and grade. The allocation was generated reproducibly in Stata using a pre-specified Park–Miller “minimal standard” pseudo-random number generator with seed 20260729. One pseudo-random draw was generated for each stratum. If the draw was below 0.5, class A was assigned to early intervention and class B to delayed intervention; otherwise class B was assigned to early intervention and class A to delayed intervention. No re-randomization for operational convenience is permitted. Baseline measurement takes place before intervention exposure. The primary post-treatment measurement is administered after the early class receives the intervention but before the delayed class receives it. The delayed class then receives the intervention. Subsequent measurements assess persistence after broader intervention exposure. The primary analysis follows the intention-to-treat principle. The planned ANCOVA specification controls for the baseline value of the corresponding outcome and pre-specified baseline covariates and includes randomization-stratum fixed effects. Statistical inference accounts for clustering at the class/parallel level. Effective intervention exposure, attendance, implementation duration, and fidelity are recorded for complementary descriptive analyses but do not replace randomized assignment.

All eligible classes eventually receive the intervention.
