abstract: Chile has experienced a rapid expansion in the tertiary-educated workforce — from 21.9% of the labor force with completed higher education in 2010 to 41.6% in 2025 — without a commensurate expansion in demand for skilled labor. Roughly 250,000 people aged 25–35 are underemployed, close to 40% of all underemployment in the country, while about 60% of firms report persistent difficulty finding talent. Only 44% of affiliates aged 20–35 actively contribute to the pension system. This study evaluates Despega tu Pega (DtP), a national program combining (i) an individualized skills diagnostic delivered through the Relink platform using the MapHa skills taxonomy, across employability, digital and productivity dimensions; (ii) personalized training pathways ("skillpacks") designed to close the diagnosed gaps; and (iii) job linkage with participating firms, including the use of the Chilean training pre-contract (precontrato de capacitación) as a bridge into formal employment. Approximately 2,200 eligible individuals aged 25–35, with a completed higher-education qualification and currently underemployed or unemployed, are randomly assigned at the individual level, in waves, to a treatment group that receives DtP, a pure control group, or a waitlist group that may be offered the program if places become available. Assignment is stratified by sex, region, time since graduation, assigned training track and detailed labor market status, and is nested within two program modalities (precontrato and becas laborales). Enrollment is continuous: eligible individuals are randomized in sequential waves as they complete registration, consent and the baseline survey, and waves continue until the 2,200 target is reached. The first wave, executed on 26 August 2026, randomized 724 individuals — approximately one third of the target — of whom 161 were underemployed and 563 were unemployed or searching for work for the first time. At the time of registration the assignment had been generated and its balance verified, but the intervention had not begun: no participant had been contacted or informed of their assignment, and no outcome had been observed. Primary outcomes are formal employment, employment stability, monthly labor income and pension contributions, measured at 6, 12 and 24 months through participant surveys and, where access is obtained, administrative records from unemployment insurance, the pension supervisor and the tax authority. We estimate intention-to-treat effects and, instrumenting participation with random assignment, treatment-on-the-treated effects, together with a pre-specified set of conditional average treatment effects. The study provides causal evidence on a scalable, diagnostic-driven reskilling model and on the role of the private sector in reducing graduate underemployment.
experimental_design: Individual-level randomized controlled trial with three arms — Treatment, Control and Waitlist — implemented in sequential waves as participants complete registration, consent and the baseline survey. Eligible individuals are split into two mutually exclusive lists by baseline labor market status. Those who are underemployed are randomized within the becas laborales modality. Those who are unemployed (or searching for work for the first time) are randomized jointly across two modalities, precontrato and becas laborales. Within every list-by-modality cell the assignment shares are 30% Control, 50% Treatment and 20% Waitlist; within the unemployment list, 75% of participants are allocated to the precontrato modality and 25% to becas laborales. Assignment is stratified. Within each arm and training track, participants also receive a random priority number that determines the order in which they are contacted, so that operational contact sequencing is itself randomized and does not correlate with participant characteristics.
experimental_design_details: Eligibility. Age 25–35 at the reference date; a completed higher-education qualification (bachelor’s degree, university professional degree, or technical-professional qualification); at least six months since obtaining the qualification; residence in Chile (regions 1–16); and a baseline labor market status of underemployment, unemployment, or first-time job search. Eligibility is established from the baseline questionnaire completed at the time of informed consent, before randomization. Arms and shares. Underemployment list, becas laborales modality: Control 30%, Treatment 50%, Waitlist 20%. Unemployment list, precontrato modality: Control 22.5%, Treatment 37.5%, Waitlist 15%. Unemployment list, becas laborales modality: Control 7.5%, Treatment 12.5%, Waitlist 5%. Shares within the unemployment list sum to 100% across the two modalities. Stratification variables. (i) Female; (ii) resident in the Metropolitan Region of Santiago; (iii) years since graduation above or below the wave median; (iv) assigned training track; and (v) a status-specific variable — within the underemployment list, whether underemployment is due to insufficient hours; within the unemployment list, whether the individual is searching for work for the first time. Waves and stopping rule. Enrollment is continuous rather than a single draw. For each wave the eligibility database is frozen on a stated date, randomization is executed with a recorded seed, and deliverable contact lists are exported by modality and arm. Waves continue until 2,200 eligible individuals have been randomized; the wave at which that threshold is crossed is the final wave, and any surplus in that wave is randomized rather than discarded. The stopping rule is defined on the cumulative count of randomized individuals alone. It does not depend on any outcome, on any interim estimate, or on the balance results of earlier waves, and no interim analysis of outcomes will be conducted while enrollment is open. Enrollment to date. Wave 1 was executed on 26 August 2026, with the database frozen on 24 August 2026 and seed 202608251, randomizing 724 individuals — approximately one third of the target. The remaining waves are expected through 2027; their number and timing depend on the flow of eligible registrants and are not fixed ex ante. Waitlist arm. Waitlist participants are not offered the program at randomization. They are contacted only if capacity opens within their modality and track, in the pre-assigned random priority order, and after the Treatment group in that track has been exhausted. For the primary analysis the Waitlist arm is analyzed as a distinct arm rather than pooled with Control; a pre-specified secondary analysis pools Waitlist with Control conditional on the realized share of waitlist participants who were offered the program remaining below 10%.
intervention: Intervention(s) Participants assigned to treatment receive the full Despega tu Pega program over approximately six months, comprising three components: (1) Skills diagnostic. An individualized assessment delivered on the Relink platform using the MapHa skills taxonomy, measuring existing capabilities and gaps across three dimensions: employability, digital skills, and productivity. (2) Personalized training pathway. Assignment to a training track ("skillpack") built to close the gaps identified in the diagnostic. Courses run 50–80 hours, are delivered in three levels with roughly 30% asynchronous and 70% synchronous content, over about two months. Tracks cover employability (job search, job retention and progression), digital skills (digital management tools, applied artificial intelligence, content creation and editing, data handling and analysis, digital security), and productivity (self-management for sustainable work performance). (3) Job linkage. Articulation with participating firms, early linkage opportunities and, where applicable, use of the training pre-contract (precontrato de capacitación) as a bridge into hiring. Training is financed through two modalities: precontrato and becas laborales (training grants under the Franquicia Tributaria scheme).

mde_text: Power curves were constructed for sample sizes between 400 and 1,200 individuals at power levels of 0.70, 0.80 and 0.90, with α = 0.05 and two-sided tests. At 80% power the minimum detectable effects are: Formal employment: 6–8 percentage points. Employment stability at 6 months: 5–7 percentage points. Monthly labor income: 5–7% in relative terms. Pension contributions: 0.05–0.07 of the baseline mean. A complementary simulation exercise drew 100 bootstrap samples of sizes 300, 500, 800 and 1,000 from parameters observed in comparable training programs, and found power above 0.80 in all four primary outcomes for effect sizes in the range reported by recent skills-based employability interventions. These values are conservative: they do not model the residual variance reduction produced by stratification on sex, region, time since graduation, track and labor market status, so the realized MDE is expected to be somewhat smaller.

primary_outcome_explanation: Formal employment. Binary indicator equal to one if the individual holds a dependent job with a written contract and social security contributions in the reference month. Survey measure: situacion_laboral = 1 and contrato = 1. Administrative measure, where access is obtained: a positive taxable-earnings record in the unemployment insurance (Seguro de Cesantía) database in the reference month. Employment stability. Binary indicator for having contributed to the pension system in the reference month, and the count of months contributed over the follow-up window. Within each stratum, participants are assigned a uniform pseudo-random draw, sorted, and allocated to arms according to the modality-specific shares. The eligibility database is frozen before the draw, the do-files and seed are archived for each wave, and balance is verified after each wave using both classical F-tests and randomization inference with 2,000 within-stratum permutations.

Share of assigned participants who begin the diagnostic, who are assigned a track, and who complete their track. These serve as the first-stage measures for the treatment-on-the-treated estimates and are reported descriptively by arm and modality.

abstract: With this experiment, we aim to evaluate the effects of brief educational interventions on individuals’ ability to recognize financial self-interest and fraudulent intentions, when present, in investment tips on social media. We conduct a randomized controlled online experiment with individuals aged 18–45 residing in Germany. Participants are randomly assigned to one of three conditions: (i) a pure control group that receives no material, (ii) a treatment group that receives a text-based treatment describing key principles for navigating investment tips on social media, or (iii) a treatment group that receives the same information text supplemented with comic panels embedded throughout the text. Using simulated social media investment-tip videos, we examine the effects of the treatments on participants’ ability to recognize underlying financial self-interest and fraudulent intentions, both immediately and three months after the intervention. Furthermore, we investigate treatment effects on self-efficacy, knowledge, and (intended) behavior.
experimental_design: We conduct a randomized controlled online experiment with individuals aged 18–45 residing in Germany. We draw on a quota sample recruited through an online-access panel, with marginal quotas on gender, age group, region, and highest general educational qualification. After a baseline survey that elicits relevant sociodemographic variables for the quota sample as well as further variables, participants are randomly assigned at the individual level to one of three conditions: (i) a pure control group that receives no material, (ii) a treatment group that receives a text-based treatment describing key principles for navigating investment tips on social media, or (iii) a treatment group that receives the same information text supplemented with comic panels embedded throughout the text. We apply stratified randomization to the three experimental conditions by gender and age group.

abstract: In-person college advising programs generate large improvements in college persistence and success for low-income students but face numerous barriers to scale. Remote advising models offer a promising strategy to address informational and assistance barriers facing the substantial majority of low-income students who do not have access to community-based advising, yet the existing evidence base on the efficacy of remote advising is fairly limited. One notable exception is Matriculate, as part of the CollegePoint initiative, generated positive and statistically significant impacts on enrollment at high graduation rate colleges (4.5 percentage points) as part of a multi-cohort RCT (high school classes of 2018, 2019, and 2020). In this randomized control trial, we will investigate the impact of Matriculate advising as the organization scales its program. Specifically, they will roughly triple the number of students they serve for the high school classes of 2024, 2025, and 2026, relative to those served in the first RCT.
experimental_design: CollegePoint recruited students through the College Board and other partners. Among students who indicated interest in participating and who met 1) the academic (3.5 GPA or higher AND 90th percentile or higher of the SAT distribution OR who qualified for "test optional" eligibility based on taking multiple advanced placement courses in high school and 2) the income eligibility criteria (self-reported family income of $80,000 or lower for 2024 cohort; family income of $90,000 or lower for 2025 and 2026 cohorts), students from the high school classes of 2024, 2025, and 2026 were randomly assigned to receive Matriculate advising or to a control group that did not receive support from the program.
intervention: CollegePoint is a national remote college advising program that matches high-achieving, low- and moderate-income high school juniors and seniors with college advisors who provide one-on-one support with college exploration and preparation, college, financial aid, and scholarship applications, and college choice. College advisors begin working with students between the spring of their junior year of high school and the fall of their senior year of high school, and conclude advising during the summer after students graduate from high school.As part of the CollegePoint initiative, Matriculate provided advising services to high school seniors from the graduating high school cohorts of 2024, 2025, and 2026, through a near-pear advising model.

abstract: This project is a large-scale randomized controlled trial (RCT) to evaluate Personalized Learning Squared (PLUS), a hybrid human-AI tutoring program aimed at accelerating math learning among middle school students, particularly those from underserved communities. Tutoring boosts achievement, especially for students furthest behind, but it is costly and difficult to scale. Adaptive math software can deliver personalized practice at scale but often yields uneven engagement and results. PLUS integrates the strengths of both approaches by pairing remote human tutors with an AI-powered dashboard that synthesizes real-time and historical data from widely used platforms (e.g., iReady, IXL, MATHia, MobyMax). The dashboard helps tutors set, share, and track students' weekly math software practice, goals and target students most in need. The PLUS app housing the dashboard also provides AI-driven professional training to tutors to improve their tutoring practice. Finally, teachers are supported through regular e-mail reports on their students' engagement in PLUS tutoring and goal achievement (as set by PLUS tutors and their tutees in the PLUS app), which allows them to reward goal achievement. Eligible math or intervention course sections will be randomly assigned 1:1 within school × grade strata (or school x grade x teacher strata where teachers have more than one section of an eligible class within a grade) to this treatment or to business-as-usual (BaU) control, defined as either Tier I math instruction or a Tier II intervention class. The confirmatory research question asks whether PLUS improves student achievement on state math assessments compared with BaU instruction and support. Exploratory analyses will examine impacts on formative assessments, dosage, effort (e.g., time on task), and software engagement and progress. The study includes 20–25 schools across multiple states including California, Pennsylvania, Florida, and Oregon, involving approximately 210 classrooms and 4500 students. Findings will provide rigorous causal evidence on the scalability of hybrid human-AI tutoring and inform cost-effective strategies to reduce opportunity gaps in math learning.
experimental_design: The study is a two-arm, stratified classroom-randomized controlled trial. Eligible mathematics course sections in participating schools are assigned 1:1 to treatment (PLUS hybrid human–AI tutoring) or control (business-as-usual instruction — Tier I or the school's existing Tier II intervention — with access to math software at minimum). Random assignment is stratified primarily by school × grade. Where teachers teach two or more eligible sections within a grade, teacher ID is incorporated into the block, such that such teachers will have at least one class in each of the control and treatment. And, where schools identify section-level or track (e.g., advanced, co-taught, math intervention), strata are further defined within type. Strata containing a single eligible section are pooled at the district × grade level, and any section still unmatched is assigned by an independent 50/50 draw. The target sample is approximately 210 classrooms and 4,500 students across 20–25 schools in California, Pennsylvania, Florida, and Oregon. Districts and schools are recruited by PLUS. Eligible sections are identified by the school and shared — along with class rosters and baseline student data — with the research team. Randomization is planned to proceed in two to four waves, based on the timing of district roster submission and planned tutor start dates. Tutor capacity is tracked across waves as treated sections per tutoring time slot. Sections meeting in slots with no remaining capacity are removed from the eligible roster in the next wave. If a slot's remaining capacity is positive but insufficient for 1:1 assignment among its eligible sections, those sections are randomized in a separate cell with a fixed number of treatment assignments equal to the remaining capacity. No assignment is altered after randomization. The intent-to-treat sample is defined by section enrollment at the randomization cutoff; students are analyzed under their original assignment regardless of subsequent section changes.
intervention: Personalized Learning Squared (PLUS) is a hybrid human–AI tutoring program in middle school mathematics. Students in treatment classrooms receive remote tutoring from PLUS tutors during the school day, planned at typically two sessions per week of approximately 40 minutes each, with session length varying by school schedule, across the 2026–27 school year. Tutors work through the PLUS app, whose dashboard synthesizes real-time and historical learning data from the math software platforms in use at each school (e.g., iReady, IXL, MATHia, MobyMax). The dashboard helps tutors set, share, and track student weekly math software practice goals and target students most in need based on their recent effort and progress in each math software. The app also provides AI-driven professional training to tutors to improve their tutoring practice. Teachers are supported through weekly e-mail reports on their students' engagement in PLUS tutoring and goal achievement (as set by PLUS tutors and their tutees in the PLUS app), which allows them to reward goal achievement. The intervention aims to accelerate math learning among middle school students, particularly those from underserved communities. Control classrooms continue either business-as-usual Tier I instruction or their Tier II intervention. abstract: This project studies whether factual information about income inequality in Croatia affects public preferences for redistribution and preference for smaller income differences. We conduct a randomized online survey experiment with a planned final sample of 1000 valid completed respondents aged 18-65 in Croatia. Respondents are randomly assigned to receive factual information about the income distribution in Croatia or to a control condition. The main outcomes measure post-treatment inequality concern, support for government responsibility in reducing income differences, progressive income taxation, and social benefits for low-income people. The study estimates the average treatment effect of the information treatment, using assignment to treatment as the source of experimental variation, and examines heterogeneity by age, gender, income, education, and settlement size.
experimental_design: The study is a randomized online survey experiment conducted through the Ipsos Croatian opt-in online access panel. Respondents first answer pre-treatment socio-demographic and attitudinal questions. They are then randomly assigned to treatment or control. After the treatment/control screen, all respondents answer post-treatment outcome questions on inequality concern and redistributive preferences. The parameter of interest is the average treatment effect of exposure to the information treatment. If all respondents in the analysis sample receive the condition to which they are assigned, this equals the intention-to-treat effect of assignment to treatment. If there is any noncompliance or post-assignment exclusion, the assignment-based estimate will be interpreted as the intention-to-treat effect and exclusions will be documented.
experimental_design_details: The primary specification is an OLS regression of each outcome on treatment assignment and pre-treatment covariates, with heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors. The unadjusted specification with treatment assignment only will also be reported. Because the final sample is designed to be nationally representative of the Croatian resident population aged 18-65 with respect to gender, age, region, and settlement size, the estimates may also be interpreted as informative about the population average treatment effect for this target population. This population interpretation relies on the quota-sampling design and should be read in light of the non-probability nature of the Ipsos online panel.
intervention: Respondents assigned to the treatment group receive factual information about income inequality in Croatia based on official Eurostat/EU-SILC statistics. Respondents assigned to the control group receive a neutral message at the same point in the survey. The intervention is embedded in an online survey and is followed by outcome questions on inequality concern and redistributive preferences.

abstract: This study examines whether the free distribution of seeds generates sustained demand for sorghum and the extent to which sorghum serves as insurance against drought by investigating the consequences of its adoption on subsequent household behavior. To this end, we elicit farmers’ willingness to pay (WTP) for sorghum seeds through experimental auctions among farmers who received either red or white sorghum seeds in 2022 as part of a randomized controlled trial in rural Zambia. While both varieties are open-pollinated, yield losses from bird damage are minimal for red varieties because of their bitter tannins in the seed coat. Using the elicited WTP, we estimate the causal impact of exposure to and experience with free sorghum seeds on farmers’ subsequent demand for sorghum seeds. We also examine differences in WTP between red and white sorghum seeds, providing insights into farmers’ preferences and the potential development of a sorghum seed value chain. Finally, we exploit randomized purchase prices to examine the effect of sorghum adoption on subsequent household production and consumption behavior.
experimental_design: Our target is the 846 households that received either red or white sorghum seeds in September 2022 as part of a randomized controlled trial in five wards in Sinazongwe District, Southern Province, Zambia. During the survey period from September-October 2026, we will visit each target household twice. During the first visit, we will conduct three activities: 1) a short household survey, 2) practice rounds using a bar of regular soap to familiarize respondents with the BDM mechanism, and 3) the BDM auction for 3kg of sorghum seeds for production purposes. Specifically, we will measure WTP for ZSV36R (red variety) and ZSV17 (white variety) for each respondent, although only one variety will ultimately be auctioned. The market price of both ZSV36R and ZSV17 is 372 ZMW per 10 kg. For the BDM auction, the randomly drawn purchase price will be 0, 20, 40, 60, or 80 ZMW per 3kg, with each price having a 20% chance of being drawn. Approximately one week after the first visit, we will meet the target households again at a designated public location to finalize the BDM transactions, including the exchange of money and seeds for households whose bids result in a purchase. In July-August 2027, we will follow up with the surveyed households to ask about agricultural practices during the 2026/27 rainy season and other economic activities.
intervention: In the BDM auction to elicit willingness to pay for 3kg of sorghum seeds, we randomize purchase prices at 0, 20, 40, 60, or 80 ZMW across households. Given this randomization, we compare outcomes between households that adopt sorghum and those that do not, even when they have the same WTP.

abstract: This study examines how information about the territorial distribution of renewable-energy infrastructure affects beliefs, local acceptance, and policy preferences in Spain. We conduct an online information-provision experiment with approximately 2,000 Spanish nationals residing in Spain and aged 18–64, recruited through the Netquest online panel. The sampling design includes quotas by gender, age, and region and deliberately oversamples respondents living in municipalities with fewer than 5,000 inhabitants. Respondents are randomly assigned at the individual level, in approximately equal proportions within gender-by-age quota cells, to one of three experimental conditions. The control group receives no additional information. Treatment A provides information about the unequal territorial distribution of wind and solar installations and the concentration of their local impacts in rural and sparsely populated areas. Treatment B provides the same information and additionally describes municipal revenues, compensation, and benefit-sharing mechanisms associated with renewable-energy projects. The primary outcome is respondents’ willingness to accept a new wind or solar facility in their municipality or in a nearby municipality. Secondary outcomes measure posterior beliefs, territorial-justice perceptions, policy preferences, and support for alternative political platforms.
experimental_design: We conduct an online randomized information-provision experiment with approximately 2,000 respondents recruited from the Netquest online panel. Eligibility is restricted to Spanish nationals residing in Spain and aged 18–64. Sampling quotas are applied by gender, age, and region of residence. The design deliberately oversamples respondents living in municipalities with fewer than 5,000 inhabitants, targeting 750 such respondents (37.5% of the total sample). Respondents are randomly assigned at the individual level, in approximately equal proportions within gender-by-age quota cells, to one of three experimental conditions. Rural residence is not used as a blocking variable. The Control group receives no additional information relevant to the territorial distribution of renewable energy. Treatment A receives a short information video describing the unequal territorial distribution of wind and solar facilities in Spain, emphasizing their concentration in rural and sparsely populated municipalities and the geographically concentrated local impacts of renewable-energy infrastructure. Treatment B receives the same information and additionally receives information about municipal revenues, project-related payments, compensation, and benefit-sharing mechanisms that may return resources to host communities. All respondents complete the same pre-treatment questions before experimental assignment and the same post-treatment outcome modules after their assigned experimental condition. The main experimental comparisons are Treatment A versus Control, Treatment B versus Control, and Treatment B versus Treatment A.
intervention: The experiment includes two information treatments delivered through short videos of less than two minutes. Treatment A provides information about the unequal territorial distribution of wind and solar facilities in Spain. It explains that renewable-energy installations are disproportionately located in rural and sparsely populated municipalities, where suitable land and renewable resources are available, while much of the electricity generated is consumed elsewhere, particularly in urban areas. The treatment emphasizes that local impacts, including landscape change and land use, are geographically concentrated in host communities, whereas the broader benefits of renewable energy, such as electricity generation and lower emissions, are shared more widely. Treatment B provides the same information as Treatment A and additionally explains that hosting renewable-energy facilities can generate economic resources for local communities. In particular, it describes municipal revenues from taxes and other project-related payments, as well as compensation and benefit-sharing mechanisms through which part of the value generated by renewable-energy projects can be returned to host municipalities. The control group receives no additional information on the territorial distribution or local economic consequences of renewable-energy deployment.

abstract: Across the developing world, women face mobility barriers that constrain access to jobs, education, and social networks. Gender-targeted transport policies, such as Delhi's Pink Ticket Scheme, which grants women free bus travel, aim to ease these constraints but may generate unintended consequences at the point of delivery. We study whether free fares lead bus drivers to discriminate against female passengers, raising the effective cost of travel for the very group the policy targets. Descriptive data show that buses fail to stop for women roughly 50% more often than for men. Combining a mystery shopper field exercise with a lab-in-the-field experiment with bus drivers and conductors, we causally identify discriminatory non-stopping behavior and decompose its underlying mechanisms, distinguishing among gender norms, fairness concerns, economic incentives, and safety considerations. The findings will inform the design of inclusive public transport systems in low- and middle-income countries.
experimental_design: To identify gender-based discrimination in the usage of public buses, we conduct a randomized field experiment that generates exogenous variation in whether a male or female passenger is waiting at a bus stop in Delhi. We deploy male (control) and female (treatment) mystery shoppers, recruited to be comparable across all visible characteristics, to bus stops across a sample of routes in Delhi. Shoppers are recruited according to a set of predefined types, each a combination of age, marital status, religion, and SES, chosen to reflect real bus users. We hold these differences fixed across gender, so that any difference in outcomes between male and female shoppers can be attributed to gender. During the exercise, mystery shoppers wait for the bus and, for each passing bus of their assigned route, record variables indicating the bus's stopping behavior. We use these variables to investigate gender-based differences in stopping behavior and ability to board. We complement the mystery shopper exercise with a lab-in-the-field experiment designed to identify the potential reasons behind the discriminatory behavior we document in the field. Bus drivers play an incentive-compatible game in which they take on the role of a driver completing his shift. To isolate the motives that drive discriminatory behavior, we vary the environment in which they make their stopping decisions.

abstract: Households in rural Kenya often choose among several water sources that differ in price, reliability, convenience, and perceived safety. This study examines how households’ use of communal water taps responds to temporary changes in water prices and to information about water availability and safety. Temporary price conditions are assigned at the tap-cluster level and rotated over several weeks. Households are separately randomized to receive information about the availability and safety of water from the taps. Administrative transaction data will be used to measure changes in water purchases before, during, and after the intervention. Complementary household surveys collect information about alternative water sources, willingness to pay, perceptions of water quality and reliability, and household water-storage practices and capacity.
experimental_design: The study uses a two-level randomized experimental design. Approximately 80 communal taps are grouped into 39 clusters constructed before randomization using overlap in their baseline customer populations. Households are associated with a tap cluster before the intervention on the basis of their registered or usual tap. The customer analysis sample includes registered customers who make no purchases at baseline, allowing the study to measure whether the intervention activates previously inactive households. For the first intervention week, the 39 tap clusters are stratified by baseline water consumption and assigned in equal numbers to three price conditions: 13 clusters at KES 5 (control), 13 clusters at KES 3, and 13 clusters at KES 0.50 per 20-liter unit. When the price at a cluster changes, registered customers associated with that cluster receive an SMS communicating the applicable price. During weeks two and three, clusters follow randomized price sequences that rotate them among the three price conditions. Eligible households are separately assigned in equal proportions to receive information about tap-water availability and safety or to receive no information. Household assignment is stratified by tap cluster. The analysis examines administrative outcomes during the first intervention week and across the complete three-week price rotation, as well as survey outcomes measured immediately after the first week. Heterogeneity analyses examine whether treatment effects vary with baseline water-storage capacity, elicited willingness to pay, administrative water purchases, survey-reported use of other water sources, and distance to study taps.
intervention: The study includes two interventions. Communal water-tap clusters receive temporary prices of KES 5, KES 3, or KES 0.50 per 20-liter unit. KES 5 is the prevailing comparison price. Price conditions rotate across clusters over three weeks. Second, eligible households are individually assigned either to receive information about the availability and safety of water from the communal taps or to a no-information comparison group. The information intervention is assigned independently of the cluster-level price intervention.

abstract: We study how information about fertility and about the time it takes to form a family affects Koreans' expectations and plans regarding marriage and childbearing. In a nationally representative online survey of adults aged 19–59, we elicit expectations about the timing of marriage and births, recalled expectations from early adulthood, beliefs about age-specific fecundity, and partner-search behavior. Respondents under 50 are randomly assigned to one of three arms: a control group receiving unrelated health information; an information arm receiving statistics on age-specific conception and miscarriage probabilities; and a planning arm that, based on the respondent's own fertility goals, computes and displays the ages by which they would need to meet a partner, marry, and begin trying to conceive, given the durations realized by recent cohorts. We measure effects on beliefs, expectations, stated timing plans, and intentions, immediately after the treatment and again in a follow-up survey.
experimental_design: Individual-level randomized information experiment embedded in an online survey of a nationally representative quota sample of Korean adults aged 19–59. Eligible respondents are assigned with equal probability to a control arm or one of two treatment arms. We compare post-treatment beliefs, expectations, plans, and intentions, using pre-treatment measures of the same objects as covariates, and re-contact respondents in a follow-up survey approximately 3-6 months later.
intervention: Respondents under age 50 are randomly assigned to one of three arms embedded in an online survey. A control arm receives unrelated information on adult health. A second arm receives information on how conception, IVF success, and miscarriage probabilities vary with age. A third arm goes through a personalized planning exercise that, based on the respondent's own fertility goals and on durations realized by recent cohorts, shows the ages by which they would need to meet a partner, marry, and begin trying to conceive. All arms then answer the same post-treatment questions.

abstract: In this experiment, participants scroll through randomized feeds of TikTok videos for 20 minutes, and we measure their engagement with videos of different types.
experimental_design: ### Video sampling procedure The videos sampled from this experiment come from four sources: (A) Videos randomly sampled from the universe of videos posted on TikTok in the US, using TikTok's Research API. (B) Videos scraped from the recent posts of news organizations, drawing from the list of the top 100 news organizations appearing in the sample of TikTok feeds we collected as part of a previous experiment. (C) Videos created by participants in our previous "creator" experiment. (D) Videos scraped from the recent posts of accounts appearing repeatedly in each of the TikTok feeds we collected as part of a previous experiment. Below, we describe each of these sampling procedures. We then describe how these sources are combined to create participants' experimental feeds. ### A These are videos scraped from TikTok's Research API across four repeated uses of our daily API quota. We randomly sample from the pool of videos posted 48-96 hours ago in the US. (Videos typically take 48 hours after being posted to appear in the API, so we aren't able to scrape more recently). Half of our API requests sample from the pool of videos with at least 10 views, and half sample from the pool of videos with at least 10k views. We then scrape the metadata and content of these posts. We exclude posts flagged as ads, posts for which scraping or classification fails due to inaccessible metadata, and posts that our classification flags as being in a language other than English. We also exclude posts whose classification does not fall into one of our four primary content quadrants (lifestyle, produced entertainment, cheap talk, and politics.) ### B These are videos scraped from the top 100 English-language news organizations appearing in the TikTok feeds we previously collected as part of an experiment. For each organization we scrape their six most recent posts in the previous 7 days. We then scrape and classify them, including according to whether they are a piece of explicitly political news or not. ### C These are videos we paid participants in our creator experiment $10 to post on their accounts. Each participant was randomly assigned one of our four content quadrants and offered $10 to create a post of this type on their account; these are the posts from people who accepted the offer and sent us the link to the video. As above, we exclude non-English posts and posts not falling into one of our four quadrants. ### D These are videos scraped from accounts appearing frequently in the feeds of the participants in a previous experiment who provided us with their TikTok viewership histories. For each of these participants, we randomly sample twenty creators who appeared in their feed at least 3 times, replacing creators whose recent profile we fail to scrape. For each of these creators, we scrape their most recent post. These videos are primarily for insertion into the feeds of these previous participants when they now participate in our viewership experiment. ### Constructing participants' feeds Videos from the aforementioned four sources compose the pool we draw on for the experiment. We then sample posts into participants' feeds stratified in the following way (participants do not have fixed-length feeds, they scroll until 20 minutes have elapsed): 1. For each participant, we independently draw a lifestyle fraction and politics fraction from {0, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3}, with probabilities {0.2, 0.2, 0.4, 0.2}. "Lifestyle" and "politics" means videos from our lifestyle or politics classification quadrants, respectively. Of the remaining videos, 5ppt are non-political news videos posted by news organizations, 1ppt are drawn from the full pool of Source D videos, and the rest are equally split between our cheap-talk and produced-entertainment quadrants. Those are the probabilities for participants who are not part of our previous TikTok-history collection. For participants who are, instead of the 1% drawn from the full pool of Source D videos, they get the 20 videos scraped from creators who previously appeared in their personal feed randomly interleaved into the first 100 posts they see. 2. Within the politics category, 70% of videos are drawn from Source A, 20% from Source B, and 10% from Source C. Nonpolitical news videos are drawn from Source B. Within the other categories, 90% are drawn from Source A and 10% from Source C.

The aggregate composition of the feed is randomized as described in the attached details pdf, the specific videos of each type are randomly drawn from a larger pool, and the order of the videos is random.

abstract: This classroom-randomized crossover trial, involving approximately 31 classrooms and 670 students, evaluates two approaches to supporting student persistence and mathematics learning in i-Ready Mathematics. The first is Personalized Learning Squared (PLUS), a remote tutoring program in which tutors support students during i-Ready practice and conduct weekly goal support. The second is teacher-led Goal Orchestration (GO), delivered through the GO Platform, which provides teachers with weekly i-Ready data, personalized goal recommendations, progress information, reward eligibility reports, and tools for individual and small-group support. Business-as-usual (BaU) classrooms continue their usual i-Ready routines without PLUS tutoring or the GO Platform. During Fall 2026, each participating classroom is assigned to two different conditions across two study periods. The six possible sequences are PLUS-BaU, PLUS-GO, BaU-PLUS, BaU-GO, GO-PLUS, and GO-BaU. Randomization occurs at the classroom level within school-by-grade strata. The primary learning outcome is change in i-Ready Diagnostic scale score from the baseline Diagnostic administered before Period 1 to the endline Diagnostic administered after Period 2. Weekly i-Ready Personalized Instruction practice time and lessons passed are additional primary outcomes used to estimate within-period effects of PLUS, GO, and BaU. For the weekly outcomes, the study will estimate pairwise effects of PLUS, GO, and BaU within each study period. Analyses of Diagnostic growth will account for the randomized two-period treatment sequences, with treatment-level contrasts specified prospectively in the pre-analysis plan. Eligible students are in grades 5-8 and enrolled in participating classrooms at schools that use i-Ready Mathematics as part of regular mathematics instruction. Students are eligible for inclusion unless a parent or legal guardian opts them out of study participation.
experimental_design: The study is a three-condition, classroom-randomized crossover trial conducted during Fall 2026. Eligible classrooms are assigned to one of six two-period sequences: PLUS-BaU, PLUS-GO, BaU-PLUS, BaU-GO, GO-PLUS, or GO-BaU. Each classroom therefore receives two different conditions and does not receive the same condition in both periods. Period 1 runs from September 14 through October 16, 2026. Period 2 runs from October 19 through December 4, 2026. Randomization is stratified by school and grade. Within each school-by-grade stratum, the numbers of classrooms assigned to PLUS, BaU, and GO in each period are made as even as mathematically possible. Across the full sample, the six crossover sequences are also kept as evenly represented as the total number of classrooms permits. The current planning rosters imply approximately 31 classroom sections across three participating schools: about 9 classrooms at School 1 (TN) and 10 at School 2 (TN), and 12 at School 3 (PA). Current planning rosters contain 669 participating students, including 414 students in TN and 255 students in PA. The final classroom and student counts will be based on finalized rosters. A brief scheduled pause in PLUS tutoring occurs around the crossover due to the university academic calendar, but the study does not include a formal washout period.
intervention: The study includes three conditions. In the PLUS condition, students receive remote tutoring during scheduled i-Ready practice, planned at approximately two 45-minute sessions per week. PLUS tutors support students' i-Ready work and conduct weekly goal setting and progress review using student learning data. Teachers receive weekly goal-achievement reports by email and can distribute rewards to students who meet their goals. In the Goal Orchestration (GO) condition, students do not receive PLUS tutoring. Teachers use the GO Platform to review updated i-Ready data, set or revise weekly student goals, review goal recommendations and progress, recognize goal achievement, and identify students or groups who may benefit from additional support. Teachers can configure goal metrics, thresholds, reward requirements, and the rule used to establish students' starting goals. Teachers can also help students review their current goals and progress through a dedicated view. In the business-as-usual (BaU) condition, classrooms continue their usual i-Ready instructional and practice routines without PLUS tutoring or access to the GO Platform. Each classroom receives two different conditions across two consecutive Fall 2026 study periods.

abstract: This study evaluates how SMS communications affect residential property-tax payment behavior. Individual taxpayers with outstanding property-tax liabilities were randomly assigned to a no-message control group or to one of twelve SMS treatment arms. The twelve treatment arms crossed four informational interventions with three behavioral interventions. Administrative payment records were used to measure whether and when taxpayers paid their full annual liability during the study period. A follow-up survey will be conducted after the experiment to explore potential mechanisms.
experimental_design: The study sample consists of taxpayers with outstanding annual residential property-tax liabilities. The experimental design consists of twelve treatment arms corresponding to all combinations of four informational interventions and three behavioral interventions. A pure control group receives no experimental message. Taxpayers are therefore randomly assigned to thirteen groups, with randomization stratified by gender, age, and tax liability. Each treated taxpayer receives two separate SMS messages in close succession: one containing the assigned informational intervention and the other containing the assigned behavioral intervention. Among taxpayers who remain unpaid, a randomly selected subset may receive follow-up messages consistent with their original treatment assignments. In addition, the study includes a complementary follow-up survey to explore potential mechanisms.
intervention: The experiment targeted individual taxpayers who had not yet paid their annual property tax. Each treated taxpayer received two separate SMS messages sent in close succession: one containing the assigned informational intervention and the other containing the assigned behavioral intervention. All informational messages provide tax-related information. The richer informational interventions additionally provided personalized information, made the consequences of late payment salient, or combined the two. The three behavioral interventions contained the same call to act promptly but differed in whether they provided a behavioral explanation for delay. The pure control group received no message.

abstract: When actions generate externalities, market prices alone fail to reflect their full social costs or benefits, leading to inefficient outcomes. The classical remedy is a Pigouvian tax, which restores the first-best on its own. Yet such price instruments rarely operate alone: informal social norms governed by punishment are also widespread and discipline the same behaviors. If a tax suffices in theory, why do people punish those engaging in externality-inducing actions? We answer this question using an incentivized experiment uncovering the psychology of punishment. Our experiment tests whether individuals’ willingness to punish others engaging in externality-inducing actions depends on two theoretically important inputs: the extent to which externalities are internalized by policy and the expected behavioral response to punishment.
experimental_design: We study how people view the role of social norms alongside taxes and fines in addressing externalities. We test the hypothesis that people use social punishment to correct externalities left uninternalized by policy. Under this rationale, willingness to punish should depend on both the external costs left unpriced by the policy and the expected behavioral response to punishment.
experimental_design_details: Participants in the role of spectators decide whether to punish other individuals who engage in various externality-inducing actions. In each scenario, the spectator is presented with a different action and matched with a different individual drawn from the U.S. population. A spectator is presented with five actions, randomly selected from a set of actions, presented in randomized order. These matched participants are recruited in a companion survey, in which they report which everyday actions they take. Decisions: In each scenario, the participant and recipient each have a $10 bonus. The spectator chooses whether to decrease the recipient’s bonus by $5, leave it unchanged, or increase it by $5. Spectators who choose to change the bonus state the maximum amount of their own bonus they would give up to implement that change. This decision is incentivized using a Becker–DeGroot–Marschak procedure. Treatments: Each scenario describes the action the matched participant takes, a policy that applies to that action, and what the matched participant says about their own behavior. Spectators are randomly assigned to one of six treatments, held fixed across all five of their scenarios. The four main treatments form a 2 × 2 between-subjects design. The first treatment dimension varies the degree of internalization. Under Treatment Low Internalization, the policy prices only a small part of the external cost; under Treatment Full Internalization, the policy prices the entire external cost. In both cases, the matched participant states that they would engage in the action under the hypothetical policy described. The second treatment dimension varies the matched participant’s stated behavioral response to punishment. Under Treatment No Response, the matched participant states that having their bonus reduced would not change how often they take the action in the future; under Strong Response, they state that it would make them substantially less likely to engage in the action again. If punishment is motivated by correcting externalities, we would expect less punishment under Treatment Full Internalization than Treatment Low Internalization, because the policy already makes the actor bear the full external cost of the action. If punishment is motivated by the expected behavioral response of punishment, we would expect more punishment under Treatment Strong Response than Treatment No Response. Crossing the two treatment dimensions gives the four main treatments, all of which use hypothetical policies. To validate these hypothetical decisions, we include additional treatments in which the same hypothetical policies are described truthfully as real policies. In these treatments, the matched participant states that they do engage in the action under the real policy, rather than that they would. Furthermore, the policy presented to participants is described as pricing only a small part of the external cost, consistent with the limited extent to which the real policies selected for the experiment price the relevant external costs. We randomly vary the matched participant’s stated behavioral response between No Response and Strong Response. Finally, within each of the eight treatments, we include two sub-treatments that randomly vary whether the externalities of the actions are presented. Additional measures: For the first two scenarios, after making their punishment decision, spectators answer additional questions. These include (i) a spoken explanation of their punishment decision, (ii) an optional text message to the matched participant, (iii) second-order beliefs about the appropriateness of the action, and (v) their assessment of how the action affects the well-being of affected parties. These measures are used for exploratory analyses. Spectators also report beliefs about the share of the external cost that actors are responsible for paying under the policy described and about how likely the matched participant is to engage in the action in the future, elicited separately for the case in which the bonus is decreased and the case in which it is left unchanged; these measures are used as manipulation checks. At the end of the survey, we elicit spectators’ demographic characteristics and political affiliation, as well as their trust in government and views about the scope of government. Sample size and Recruitment: We aim to recruit 3000 spectators from the U.S. general population using the platform Prolific. We exclude responses of spectators who do not provide consent, do not have a working microphone, fail an attention check, do not complete the survey, or attempt to take the survey more than once. Spectators are randomly assigned to one of the six treatments. To incentivize spectators’ decisions, they are matched to participants recruited in a companion survey conducted on Prolific. Analysis: Treatment effects. To study the role of external costs left uninternalized by policy, our primary test compares spectators’ punishment decisions in Treatments Full Internalization vs. Low Internalization; we conduct this comparison separately in the subset of spectators in Treatment No Response and Treatment Strong Response. Similarly, to study the role of the expected behavioral response to punishment, we compare spectators’ punishment decisions in Treatments Strong Response vs. No Response, separately in the subset of spectators in the Low Internalization and Full Internalization treatments. These comparisons use the four hypothetical-policy treatments, pooling all five decisions of each spectator. Real versus hypothetical policies: To assess whether punishment differs between real and hypothetical policy settings, we compare spectators’ punishment decisions in the two treatments with hypothetical policies with the corresponding treatments with real policies. We conduct this comparison separately among spectators in the No Response treatment and those in the Strong Response treatment. If we do not find meaningful differences in the share punishing between the hypothetical and real treatments, we will pool these treatments for our main analysis.

abstract: We will conduct a two-arm, individual-level trial among customer-service representatives who handle asynchronous consumer complaints and dispute-resolution cases at a large global e-commerce company. Eligible representatives will be randomly assigned in equal proportions to a treatment group that receives access to a human-supervised AI agent or to a control group that continues using the existing customer-service workflow. The trial will take place within the company’s ordinary operations. We will use administrative records from the experimental period to compare the two groups’ work efficiency and service performance. The primary analysis will estimate the intention-to-treat effect of being assigned access to the AI agent.
experimental_design: We will conduct a two-arm cluster-randomized controlled trial across customer-service sites of a large global e-commerce company. Participating sites will be randomly assigned in approximately equal proportions to either a treatment group or a control group. All eligible customer-service representatives at treatment sites will receive access to a human-supervised AI agent, while representatives at control sites will continue using the existing customer-service workflow. We will use administrative records from the experimental period to compare work efficiency and service performance between treatment and control sites. The primary analysis will estimate the intention-to-treat effect of assigning a customer-service site to receive access to the AI agent.
intervention: We will conduct a worker-level randomized controlled trial in the customer-service division of a large global e-commerce company. Eligible customer-service representatives who handle asynchronous consumer complaints and dispute cases will be randomly assigned in equal proportions to a treatment or control group. Treatment representatives will receive access to a large-language-model-based agent embedded in their existing work interface. The agent uses available case information to recommend and, where authorized, carry out resolution steps under the department’s standard operating procedures. Representatives can monitor the agent, review its proposed actions, interrupt the automated process, and take over the case at any time. Control representatives will continue using the existing workflow without access to the agent.

abstract: There is almost no causal evidence on whether shelters reduce intimate partner violence. This 16-month pilot randomized controlled trial tests the feasibility, safety and acceptability of integrated shelter-based support for women experiencing severe intimate partner violence in rural Mara Region, Tanzania, in preparation for a full-scale trial. Forty women are randomized 1:1:1:1 to four arms: delayed-shelter control; shelter for up to six months; shelter plus an economic empowerment program; and shelter plus a non-violent conflict management program for husbands. Women are interviewed at baseline and at 2, 7 and 12 months. The pilot is not powered to detect treatment effects. It is judged against pre-specified feasibility thresholds and estimates outcome variance for the full trial.
experimental_design: A 16-month individually randomized pilot feasibility trial: four arms, 1:1:1:1, 40 women in one rural district of Mara Region, 10 per arm. Eligible women are 18 or older, married, cohabiting or recently separated, not pregnant, have experienced intimate partner violence in the past year and need shelter for safety, and can be interviewed privately. Danger level is not a ground for exclusion. The baseline survey comes before randomization. Women are interviewed privately by trained female enumerators, never at home. Husbands in Arm 4 are interviewed separately.
intervention: All arms receive safety planning and referrals. Arm 1 (control) Arm 2: shelter for up to six months. Arm 3: shelter plus an economic empowerment program (vocational and business skills, coaching). Arm 4: shelter plus a non-violent conflict management program for the husband, using cognitive behavioral methods, offered only with the woman's permission and after a safety review.

abstract: This study aims to measure the true consumer surplus of Douyin (Chinese version of TikTok) and to quantify the welfare loss induced by attention capture—a behavioral state in which users immersed in algorithmically curated feeds systematically undervalue the opportunity cost of their time. We design a randomized experiment with a fully crossed 4×2 factorial design over a two-week intervention period. Participants are randomly assigned to one of eight groups, crossing four price tiers for Douyin usage (¥0, ¥0.01, ¥0.02, and ¥0.03 per minute) with two reminder conditions (no reminder vs. daily reminders prompting users to recall unfinished tasks). We exploit the price variation to estimate Douyin’s demand curve and measure consumer surplus in both the local equilibrium (attention-captured state) and the global equilibrium (rational state). We also assess the treatment effects on Douyin usage duration, willingness to accept (WTA) and willingness to pay (WTP) for Douyin, time allocated to alternative activities, subjective well-being, addiction tendency, post-intervention persistence. Outcomes are measured through online surveys.

Participants are randomly assigned to one of eight groups, crossing four price tiers for Douyin usage with two reminder conditions. abstract: As demographic change increases the importance of older workers in the labor market, understanding the conditions that facilitate longer working lives becomes increasingly important. This project uses an online vignette experiment to examine how employee characteristics, wages, and non-wage job characteristics affect the age up to which German employers are willing to retain older employees.
experimental_design: We implement a factorial survey experiment with managers and HR decision-makers in German firms. We use this to study employers’ decisions regarding the continued employment of workers approaching retirement age. In the experiment, respondents evaluate four hypothetical scenarios describing a 59-year-old employee from the most common occupational group at their firm and the conditions under which this employee would prefer to continue working. For each scenario, employers indicate the age up to which they would continue employing the person under the stated conditions, assuming they could make their preferred choice. Each scenario is characterized by seven attributes. Two describe the employee; five attributes describe the conditions under which the employee would prefer to continue working: • Replaceability of experience: Not easily replaceable; Easily replaceable • Work performance: Average; Above average • Gross monthly wage: Anchored to the firm's reported wage level ~U(0.8,1.3) • Work-time flexibility: Yes; No • Training opportunity: Yes; No • Time and performance pressure: Low; High • Working hours: 75% (with corresponding wage adjustment); 100% Each respondent evaluates four scenarios, using a single profile design. One scenario is constructed using the respondent's previous answers about conditions in the firm's most common occupational group (wage, working-time flexibility, training opportunities, time and performance pressure, working hours). If respondents do not answer the voluntary pre-vignette questions, we randomly select the corresponding attribute levels. The two employee attributes are set to “average” and “easily replaceable”. For the other three scenarios, all seven attributes are varied randomly. The gross monthly wage remains anchored to the wage level and is varied randomly around this value as in the scenario described above. In each scenario, respondents use a slider from 59 to 72 years to indicate the age up to which they would continue employing the person under the described conditions. To study mechanisms, respondents revisit the fourth scenario after completing the main task. Respondents are asked to explain in an open-text response the reasons for their decisions, including any advantages and disadvantages of continuing to employ the person that they considered. We will use the open-ended responses to detect spillovers – that is whether an attribute evokes considerations not explicitly included, e.g., flexible working hours being interpreted as a signal for low intrinsic motivation. The experiment is embedded in a questionnaire structured in several blocks, including preliminary questions that are feed into the factorial survey experiment as well as postexperimental questions that are used for heterogeneity analyses.

primary_outcomes: The primary outcome is the age up to which the employer would retain the employee under the wage and non-wage job characteristics described in a vignette. The possible values range from 59 to 72 years. Each respondent evaluates four vignettes. We will examine whether and how the experimentally varied employee and job attributes affect the employer’s willingness to retain that employee. For each attribute, we will estimate the average marginal component effect (AMCE) on the retention age. To express the estimated effects of the non-wage attributes in monetary terms, we will additionally calculate wage-equivalent valuations by dividing each attribute coefficient by the coefficient on wages. These ratios indicate the wage change that would have an equivalent effect on the retention age. We will conduct several analyses of treatment-effect heterogeneity by testing interactions of the attributes with each other and interacting attributes with information on the firm, inquired after the vignette study.
randomization_method: One of the four vignettes is constructed using respondents’ answers to preliminary questions about the work conditions in their firm's most common occupational group, including gross monthly wage, training opportunities, working-time flexibility, time/performance pressure and working hours. The employee characteristics are predefined. Because the preliminary questions are voluntary, missing attribute levels are also assigned randomly. In the other three vignettes, all employee and job attributes are randomized using the survey software Tivian. The gross monthly wage is drawn randomly around the firmspecific wage level reported before the vignette experiment. If no wage is reported, the German average full-time wage is used as the reference value. Employee characteristics are presented in a short text, whereas job characteristics are displayed in a table. The order of these two blocks is fixed, with employee characteristics presented first. Within each block, however, the order of the attributes varies across three randomly assigned respondent groups, allowing us to assess and mitigate potential attribute-order effects. In each scenario, respondents use a slider from 59 to 72 years to indicate the age up to which they would continue employing the person under the described conditions.
randomization_unit: Randomization is at the individual choice scenario level (attribute values) and at the respondent level (order in which attributes are presented). The randomized attribute levels in three vignettes are assigned at the respondent-by vignette level. The employee characteristics in one vignette and any attribute levels replacing missing preliminary responses are assigned at the respondent level. The presentation sequence is also randomized at the respondent level.
secondary_outcomes: We will construct two secondary outcomes. First, we will translate the reported retention age into full-time-equivalent years of continued employment after age 59. This outcome captures the total volume of labor that the employer would retain rather than only the duration of continued employment. Second, we will construct a binary indicator equal to one if the employer would retain the employee at least until the applicable statutory retirement age and zero otherwise. Furthermore, after the fourth vignette, respondents will be asked to explain their retention decision of the fourth vignette in an open text question. We will code these responses using a hybrid procedure combining human coding and automated text classification. A response may be assigned to multiple themes. Our primary text outcomes will be binary indicators of whether a theme is mentioned. We will regress these indicators on the randomized attributes of the fourth vignette. These analyses will show whether particular vignette attributes affect the considerations that respondents report as salient.

abstract: A well-established literature documents that women are, on average, less likely than men to enter competitive environments. This gender gap may be exacerbated by beliefs about biased evaluation of competitive performance. Most existing experimental studies documenting gender differences in competition entry assume that performance is evaluated objectively based on a measurable ranking. However, in many real labour-market settings, evaluation is, to some extent, subjective and carried out by human assessors who may hold stereotypes or exhibit biases. Such subjectivity can generate anticipated discrimination, which may further distort competition-entry decisions. Building on a previous study of ours in which we measure how workers adjust their willingness to apply to competitive jobs by job domain and mandatory gender revelation, this experiment measures the actual evaluation decisions of human assessors in a male-stereotyped mathematics task. These assessors, in the role of managers, assess groups of four workers and choose the worker they predict will perform for the best in a future task. To make their decision, managers are given worker-specific signals of this future performance and an avatar of each worker which is either neutral or displays their gender. In the role of recruiters, assessors are tasked with selecting a worker who they believe a manager will select. In this sense, the recruiter acts as a third party decision maker that must accommodate to their belief of another's preferences.
experimental_design: The experiment involves selection of workers from a menu according to who is most likely to perform in the future.
experimental_design_details: In a previous experiment, we hired participants to act as workers. These workers completed a maths-memory task over 3 rounds. In each round, the difficulty of the task varied together with the incentive scheme. Round 1 served as a practise round in which participants played 1 minute in easy mode and 1 minute in hard mode, earning a piece rate amount per point scored. In round 2, workers were randomly assigned to have either a mostly easy round or a mostly hard round and completed their assigned tasks for 2 minutes. This round was paid as a competition: the top scorer in a randomly formed group of 4 earned a high piece rate per point scored while the others in the group scored nothing. In round 3, all workers completed the task on hard mode for 2 minutes. The remuneration scheme was a choice: workers could choose the round 1 piece rate payment or receive a high piece rate per point scored if and only if they would be selected by a recruiter. Two other participants, a manager}and a recruiter chose one worker per group observing their round 2 score and a gender revealing avatar. The manager was incentivised to select the worker that they believed would score the highest in the group in round 3. The recruiter was incentivised to select the worker that they believed the manager would select. All participants knew that the manager was a male. In the current experiment, participants act as hiring managers and recruiters. Each participant evaluates 10 randomly matched worker groups of four in the role of manager, with the required worker data being taken from a previous experiment of ours. In each worker group, the participant observes the round 2 performance scores of the four workers. The manager chooses one worker in each group and receives a bonus of £1 if no worker in that group achieves a higher round 3 score than their chosen one. On top of these 10 manager decisions, the participant acts as a recruiter. They evaluate the same 10 groups of four displayed in a random ordering with the four workers arranged differently. The recruiter chooses one worker in each group and receives a bonus of £1 if a randomly selected male/female manager making the same decision chose the same worker as them. The participant plays in these two roles in random order; about half of the participants will first act as managers and then as recruiters, while the other half does the opposite order. This allows us to do both a within- and a between-participant analysis of manager and recruiter stereotypes in hiring decisions. Aside from varying the roles in which they are acting, participants are randomised to a treatment determining the gender - male or female - of the manager for whom their decision is incentivised as a recruiter.

abstract: Small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) often lack the time, financial resources, and expertise needed to identify suitable public funding opportunities and prepare competitive grant applications. These constraints may prevent promising firms from applying for funding or reduce their chances of success. This study examines how targeted outreach and application support can help firms overcome these barriers and improve their public funding outcomes. We first test whether different outreach messages increase firms’ interest in applying to a grant-support programme. Second, we test whether machine-learning methods can help identify and target firms with greater potential to succeed in competitive public grant programmes. Finally, we test whether providing firms with an AI-based grant-support tool, either on its own or combined with human expert support, improves their ability to identify relevant funding opportunities, develop and submit competitive applications, and ultimately secure public funding.
experimental_design: The study uses a three-stage experimental design as follows: Stage 1: Behavioural Messaging Experiment Firms are randomly assigned to receive one of three types of outreach: (i) a process-focused message, (ii) an outcome-focused message, or (iii) general information about the programme without either framing. Outreach is conducted first by email and later through social media, with firms remaining in the same treatment group across both channels. We test whether the different messages affect firms’ likelihood of expressing interest in the grant-support programme. Stage 2: Algorithmic Targeting Experiment The second stage tests whether algorithmic targeting can identify firms that benefit more from additional outreach. Firms are first randomly divided into two groups. In one group, a machine-learning model ranks firms based on their predicted potential to succeed in a competitive research and innovation funding programme, and the 500 highest-ranked firms are selected to receive additional outreach by phone. In the other group, 500 firms are selected at random to receive the same outreach. Comparing outcomes across these groups allows us to test whether ML-based targeting improves engagement and subsequent funding-related outcomes relative to random targeting. Stage 3: Application Support Experiment Firms that register interest and meet the programme’s eligibility requirements enter the third stage. These firms are randomly assigned to one of three groups: (i) access to an AI-based grant-support tool, (ii) access to the same AI tool combined with support from a technology scout, or (iii) a business-as-usual control group with access to existing support and publicly available resources. This stage tests whether AI-based support increases firms’ likelihood of applying and improves application quality, and whether adding human expert support provides additional benefits.
intervention: The study includes three interventions described as below: Intervention 1: Outreach and Communication Firms receive communications, through email and social media, informing them about a grant-support programme and encouraging them to register their interest. The study tests different approaches to communicating information about the programme. Interested firms are directed to a common expression-of-interest page. Intervention 2: Machine Learning Based Targeted Outreach The study tests a machine learning based approach to identifying firms for additional outreach about the grant-support programme. Selected firms receive additional encouragement, using phone calls, to consider the programme and register their interest. Intervention 3: AI+Human Based Application Support Firms interested in pursuing research and innovation funding receive additional AI plus human support to help them identify relevant funding opportunities and navigate the application process. The study compares different forms of AI plus human application support.

abstract: This study examines how individuals interpret financial performance information and make entrepreneurial and business decisions. Participants evaluate business scenarios presenting different financial-performance conditions and provide judgments concerning business performance, financial indicators, and potential business actions. The study collects measures of participants’ use and understanding of accounting and financial information, familiarity with and use of financial ratios, accounting and finance education or training, entrepreneurship experience and background, and experience using artificial intelligence and other technology-assisted resources for business analysis. The study also includes measures of regulatory focus and fit to examine individual differences in decision orientation and how those differences may relate to the interpretation of financial information and business decisions. Additional background and demographic information is collected to support analyses of heterogeneity across participants and settings. Participants were recruited online through Prolific from multiple countries. The resulting data are intended to support research on entrepreneurial decision making, accounting-information use, financial-performance evaluation, regulatory focus and fit, technology-assisted analysis, and individual differences in business judgment. Analyses may include descriptive statistics, comparisons across experimental conditions, and multivariate analyses examining relationships among financial-performance signals, participant characteristics and experience, information use, psychological orientation, financial judgments, and business decisions. Specific research questions, hypotheses, variable definitions, sample restrictions, and statistical specifications are developed and reported separately for individual studies and papers using the data.
