experimental_design: The broader study supports two types of analysis. The randomized component examines how assigned industry, focal financial indicator, financial-performance condition, and presentation order relate to financial judgments and intended business actions. Separate nonrandomized analyses examine relationships among prior artificial-intelligence experience, actual financial-ratio use, beliefs about whether artificial intelligence complements or substitutes for ratio analysis, accounting and finance training, regulatory focus or fit, entrepreneurial experience, and demographic characteristics. Only the assigned vignette conditions are interpreted as randomized treatments.Participants were recruited from multiple countries. Country of residence was not part of the treatment-assignment mechanism. Paper-specific analyses may examine whether experimental responses or measured relationships differ across countries. The study also measures entrepreneurial and venture characteristics that may be used to define subgroups or entrepreneur profiles in later analyses. Such country-based and attribute-based analyses are observational heterogeneity analyses unless they examine interactions with the randomly assigned vignette conditions.
experimental_design_details: The artificial-intelligence paper uses dependent variables that are distinct from the post-vignette action outcomes. Its behavioral accounting-information outcomes are reported use of gross margin, operating margin, return on assets, use of any of these ratios, and the number of these ratios used. Its attitudinal outcomes are the seven-point artificial-intelligence/ratio-use measure and the nominal categories representing analytical complementarity, substitution, verification complementarity, no change, and uncertainty. Business-specific artificial-intelligence experience is the focal measured explanatory variable in these analyses. Formal accounting or finance training is examined as a potential moderator, with country, age, and gender serving as controls. A subsequent paper may examine whether promotion focus, prevention focus, or a derived regulatory-fit measure moderates artificial-intelligence-related information use or responses to the financial-performance vignettes. Such analyses involve measured characteristics and will be distinguished from the randomized vignette comparisons. Statistical analyses of the vignette outcomes will account for the repeated financial-performance observations nested within individual participants. Depending on the paper-specific research question, country may be represented through categorical indicators, country-specific estimates, multilevel specifications, or other methods appropriate to the number and distribution of participants across countries. Measured entrepreneurial attributes may be examined individually as moderators or may be used to construct theoretically specified subgroups or data-derived profiles. Possible attributes include venture-starting experience, number of ventures, current venture operating status, business duration, revenue pattern, closure experience, entrepreneurship education, accounting or finance training, financial-ratio familiarity and use, regulatory orientation, artificial-intelligence experience, and demographic characteristics. Neither country groupings nor entrepreneur-attribute groupings were used to assign participants to vignette conditions. Accordingly, direct relationships involving these measured characteristics will be interpreted as observational associations. Interactions between measured characteristics and randomized vignette conditions may be used to examine heterogeneity in the randomized treatment effects.
intervention: Participants completed an online randomized vignette experiment concerning entrepreneurial financial-performance interpretation and intended business decisions. Each participant was assigned to a hypothetical service, retail, or manufacturing business and to one focal financial indicator: gross margin, operating margin, or return on assets. Within the assigned business and financial-indicator context, each participant reviewed three financial-performance conditions—healthy, mixed or ambiguous, and distressed—in randomized order. The scenarios varied whether the focal financial indicator was around or above the benchmark for similar firms or below that benchmark and whether performance had improved or declined relative to the prior year. After each vignette, participants reported how they interpreted the financial signal and what business action they would be most likely to take. The survey also collected nonrandomized measures concerning promotion and prevention focus, entrepreneurial experience and venture history, entrepreneurship training, accounting and finance training, financial-ratio familiarity and use, artificial-intelligence-assisted business analysis, performance-decision self-efficacy, and demographic characteristics. These participant characteristics were measured variables and were not randomized interventions.

mde_text: An a priori power analysis informed the planned sample of approximately 800 participants, with recruitment distributed across nine countries. Calculations assume a two-sided significance level of 0.05 and 90% statistical power. Treatment assignment occurs at the individual-participant level; therefore, no cluster-randomization design effect is applied. Repeated responses to the three financial-performance conditions are nested within participants. For pooled within-participant comparisons using approximately 800 participants, the design provides 90% power to detect a standardized mean difference of approximately 0.115 standard deviations, or 11.5% of one standard deviation. For pooled comparisons across three approximately equal groups of about 267 participants each, the minimum detectable omnibus effect is approximately Cohen's f = 0.126. A pairwise comparison between two groups of approximately 267 participants each provides 90% power to detect approximately Cohen's d = 0.281, or 28.1% of one standard deviation. For a binary outcome with a baseline probability near 50%, this corresponds to an approximate detectable difference of 13.8 percentage points between two groups. For the four-category intended-business-action outcome—continue the current strategy, undertake strategic restructuring, seek or add funding, or exit the venture—a three-group comparison provides approximately 90% power to detect an association of Cramér's V = 0.104. Country may be analyzed in theoretically defined groups, including two-, three-, or four-group classifications. For a roughly balanced two-group classification, the minimum detectable pairwise effect is approximately 0.23 standard deviations. For three approximately equal country groups of about 267 participants each, the minimum detectable pairwise effect is approximately 0.28 standard deviations. For four approximately equal groups of about 200 participants each, the minimum detectable pairwise effect is approximately 0.33 standard deviations. Where multiple pairwise country-group comparisons are treated as co-primary, multiplicity-adjusted inference will be used. These calculations support the principal pooled experimental analyses and broad country-group comparisons. Analyses involving artificial-intelligence experience, regulatory focus or fit, accounting or finance training, entrepreneurial characteristics, or outcomes restricted to participants with venture experience may have smaller effective samples. Paper-specific analyses of these relationships will therefore report sensitivity or minimum-detectable -effect calculations based on the final eligible sample, outcome distribution, and statistical model.

primary_outcome_explanation: The randomized vignette outcomes and the artificial-intelligence/accounting-information outcomes are analytically distinct. For the randomized vignette component, each participant evaluates one healthy, one mixed or ambiguous, and one distressed financial-performance condition. Each participant therefore provides repeated observations for intended action, action likelihood, concern, and perceived ambiguity. Intended action is treated as a nominal four-category outcome. The four action-likelihood ratings are analyzed separately. Concern and ambiguity are treated as ordered seven-point outcomes after the exported Qualtrics values are recoded to preserve the response order displayed to participants. For the artificial-intelligence and accounting-information component, actual ratio use is measured only for participants who report having started or co-founded at least one business. Respondents without prior venture experience were not asked the actual ratio-use question and will not be coded as nonusers. Separate indicators will identify reported use of gross margin, operating margin, and return on assets. An any-ratio-use measure will equal one when the respondent reports using at least one of these three ratios and zero when an eligible respondent reports using none of the three. A ratio-count measure will range from zero to three. Prior use of artificial intelligence to understand or evaluate business performance is a focal explanatory variable rather than the primary dependent variable in the initial artificial-intelligence paper. Business-specific artificial-intelligence experience may include use for a currently owned or managed business, a previously owned or managed business, or another actual business. Experience limited to coursework, training, consulting, or work-related analysis may be retained as a separate category in paper-specific analyses. The seven-point artificial-intelligence/ratio item measures the extent to which access to artificial intelligence is associated with an increased stated likelihood of using financial ratios. The categorical artificial-intelligence/ratio item is treated as nominal because increased reliance, no change, reduced reliance, verification, and uncertainty are conceptually different configurations rather than points on a single ordered continuum. For paper-specific analyses, the categories may also be grouped as follows: analytical complementarity, consisting of artificial intelligence explaining, calculating, comparing, or interpreting ratios; substitution, consisting of reduced ratio reliance because of broader artificial-intelligence advice or trust in an overall artificial-intelligence explanation; verification complementarity, consisting of using ratios to check artificial-intelligence recommendations; no change; and uncertainty. Formal accounting or finance education and training may be examined as a moderator of the relationships between business-specific artificial-intelligence experience and both actual ratio use and artificial-intelligence/ratio orientation. Country, age, and gender may be included as control variables. Promotion focus, prevention focus, and paper-specific regulatory-fit measures may be examined as additional moderators in separately specified analyses. The artificial-intelligence analyses are observational because prior artificial-intelligence experience, accounting training, regulatory focus, and ratio use were measured rather than randomly assigned. Results involving these variables will therefore be described as associations rather than randomized treatment effects. Return on equity was not measured. The ratio outcomes in this study are gross margin, operating margin, and return on assets.
primary_outcomes: The study has two primary outcome families corresponding to two analytically distinct components of the broader research project. A. Randomized financial-performance vignette outcomes 1. Intended business action following each vignette: continue the current strategy, undertake strategic restructuring, seek or add funding, or exit the venture. 2. Reported likelihood of taking each of the four business actions, with each action rated separately on a seven-point scale. 3. Perceived concern regarding the financial-performance pattern, measured on a seven-category ordered scale. 4. Perceived clarity versus ambiguity of the financial signal, measured on a seven-point ordered scale. B. Artificial-intelligence and standardized accounting-information outcomes 5. Reported use of gross margin, operating margin, and return on assets among respondents with prior business-starting or co-founding experience. Outcomes include use of each individual ratio, use of at least one of the three ratios, and the total number of the three ratios used. 6. Agreement that access to artificial-intelligence tools makes the respondent more likely to use financial ratios to understand business performance, measured on a seven-point agreement scale. 7. The respondent’s stated orientation toward how artificial intelligence affects the use of financial ratios. The response categories distinguish: artificial intelligence helping explain ratios; artificial intelligence helping calculate, compare, or interpret ratios; no change in ratio use; reduced ratio reliance because artificial intelligence provides broader business advice; reduced ratio reliance because the respondent may trust an artificial-intelligence-generated overall explanation; use of ratios to check or verify artificial-intelligence recommendations; and uncertainty regarding the effect.
randomization_method: Computer-generated randomization was implemented through Qualtrics Survey Flow. An outer Qualtrics Block Randomizer set to “Evenly Present Elements” assigned each participant to one of three hypothetical industry contexts: service, retail, or manufacturing. Within the assigned industry context, a nested Qualtrics Block Randomizer, also set to “Evenly Present Elements,” assigned each participant to one of 18 focal-ratio-by-presentation-order combinations. These combinations were formed by crossing three focal financial indicators—gross margin, operating margin, and return on assets—with six possible presentation orders of the healthy, ambiguous, and distressed financial-performance conditions. The procedure generated 54 possible industry-by-ratio-by-order assignment sequences and was designed to maintain approximately balanced assignment across the sequences. Assignment was performed entirely by the Qualtrics computer system. No participant was manually assigned by the investigator. Country of residence, entrepreneurial background, venture experience, regulatory orientation, accounting or finance training, artificial-intelligence experience, and other participant attributes were not used as treatment-assignment units. These measured characteristics may be used in paper-specific subgroup, moderation, or heterogeneity analyses.
randomization_unit: The unit of randomization was the individual survey participant. Each participant was individually assigned to an industry context, a focal financial ratio, and one of six presentation orders for the financial-performance conditions. Financial-performance signal was a repeated within-participant factor because every participant evaluated one healthy, one ambiguous, and one distressed vignette. The three financial-performance signals were therefore not assigned to separate groups of participants. Country of residence and measured entrepreneurial attributes were not randomization units. Later papers may group participants by country or by measured characteristics for subgroup, moderation, profile, or heterogeneity analyses, but those groupings do not represent randomized treatment assignment.

secondary_outcome_explanation: Financing preference is observed only when a participant selects seek or add funding as the primary intended action for a vignette. Benchmark classification and focal-ratio identification may be used as interpretation measures, comprehension measures, or secondary outcomes in research examining the processing of accounting information. Performance-decision self-efficacy is measured using five seven-point confidence items addressing the respondent’s ability to assess financial ratios, judge whether business performance is improving or declining, select an appropriate business response, identify a useful strategic change, and explain or justify a business decision. A paper using this construct will report the final scoring rule, missing-item rule, and reliability assessment. Promotion focus and prevention focus will be scored as separate motivational-orientation constructs using the applicable item assignments and reverse-scoring rules. A regulatory-fit analysis may construct fit as the theoretically specified congruence between a participant’s regulatory orientation and an action, decision orientation, financial condition, or artificial-intelligence-related information-use configuration. The exact construction and corresponding hypotheses will be stated in the separate analysis plan and paper using that measure. Regulatory focus and regulatory fit are measured or constructed participant characteristics; they are not randomized interventions. They may be examined as moderators of responses to randomized financial-performance conditions, as moderators of relationships involving artificial-intelligence experience and accounting-information use, or both. Entrepreneurial experience, training, ratio familiarity, prior ratio use, artificial-intelligence experience, and demographic measures may serve as explanatory variables, moderators, controls, or outcomes depending on the research question addressed by an individual paper. Analyses using these measured characteristics will not be represented as randomized treatment effects. This umbrella registration documents the full scope of the data collected. Individual papers will identify their own focal dependent variables, hypotheses, sample restrictions, variable constructions, and statistical specifications.

abstract: We estimate the optimal mix of subsidies to achieve universal electrification. In Rwanda, expensive grid connections provide reliable and scalable electricity access, while cheaper off-grid solar home systems offer basic lighting and mobile phone charging. We cross-randomize subsidies for grid and off-grid electrification across 180 villages to estimate supply and demand for grid and off-grid electrification, and their impacts on households’ subjective welfare. We apply these results to identify subsides that minimize costs, both explicit (subsidy payouts) and implicit (below marginal cost pricing), while “justly” electrifying a target number of households: they increase subjective welfare at least as much as grid electrifying the same number of households. More broadly, our approach reconciles economic surplus- and equity-based viewpoints on achieving development objectives including universal electrification.
experimental_design: Villages were randomized into four experimental arms, with one quarter of villages assigned to each arm. Our initial sample of villages were all 193 villages in four Districts in which new electrification was planned under the EAQIP project. (No Readyboards/No SHS) The first arm is a control arm, in which electrification proceeds as under the status quo. (Readyboards/No SHS) In the second arm, all vulnerable households who were not already electrified (whether through a grid connection or SHS) were offered a free readyboard (if they had not already interally wired at the time of the offer) and installation, which substitutes for the need to do costly internal wiring. (No Readyboards/SHS) In the third arm, all households in the village are offered SHS at a 90% subsidy. SHS subsidy implementation begins after readyboard implementation is completed. (Readyboards/SHS) In the fourth arm, both readyboard program and SHS subsidies are implemented. Randomization was stratified by lot (the unit at which new electrification was planned, with five lots total) and village size (above and below median within lot, yielding ten randomization strata). 48/48/48/49 villages were assigned to the four arms. 12 villages in one District were dropped from electrification under EAQIP, leaving 181 villages. 1 village was fully resettled before the listing, reducing our final sample to 180 villages. These villages had been assigned 46/45/45/44 to the four arms.

abstract: This thesis examines whether an extraordinary municipal debt communication increases tax compliance and whether adding information about the use of public resources produces an additional effect. We implement a randomized controlled field experiment involving more than 16.000 municipal accounts. Accounts are assigned with equal probability, within 48 strata, to four arms: no debt statement; a standard debt statement without an additional municipal message; a statement containing a public-safety message; or a statement containing a public-space message. Stratification is based on valid-email availability, property locality, and four categories of overdue installments. Accounts in the three active treatment arms with a valid email address receive the same statement through both physical and digital channels. The primary outcome is full repayment of the outstanding debt through payment option 1, using either the QR code or barcode, within a 30-day follow-up period. The main secondary outcomes are enrollment in a payment plan through option 2, payment of current bill 20265A/B, and payment of the full debt in 1 installment without using the QR code number 1. The primary analysis follows an intention-to-treat approach and uses account-level regressions with randomization-stratum fixed effects and heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors. The design identifies the effect of receiving a debt statement, the incremental effect of adding a public-service message, and the difference between the two messages. At the time of writing, outcome data are not yet available.
experimental_design: This is a four-arm, account-level randomized controlled trial using administrative data. Eligible accounts are assigned with equal probability to a no-statement control group or to one of three debt-statement groups. Randomization is stratified by valid-email availability, property locality, and four approximately equal-sized categories of the number of overdue installments. The primary analysis will compare outcomes across assigned groups using an intention-to-treat framework.
experimental_design_details: The final experimental sample contains 16,125 municipal accounts: 4,031 assigned to C0, 4,031 to B, 4,032 to S, and 4,031 to O. Assignment was performed by computer within 48 strata defined by valid-email status, property locality, and quartiles of the number of overdue installments. Within every stratum, the target probability was 25 percent for each arm; realized arm sizes differ by at most one account within each stratum. The complete operational file also contains almost 3,000 nonexperimental accounts excluded from causal analysis because of repeated valid email addresses, repeated normalized document identifiers, or total debt strictly above the 95th percentile after the duplicate-based exclusions. These observations were not randomized. The primary estimands are intention-to-treat effects of assignment to B, S, and O relative to C0. Additional pre-specified comparisons can distinguish the effect of receiving the standard statement from the incremental effect of adding either message. Treatment heterogeneity by pre-treatment variables such as email availability, location of the property, previous tax-compliance, debt amount and enrollment in digital billing|.
intervention: The study evaluates whether sending a municipal debt statement, and whether adding different messages to that statement, affects debt repayment. Eligible municipal accounts are randomly assigned with equal probability to one of four groups: no debt statement; a debt statement without an additional municipal message; the same debt statement with a public-safety message; or the same debt statement with a public-space message. When an account assigned to receive a statement has a valid email address on file, the same statement is also sent by email. Email availability is a pre-treatment account characteristic and is not randomized.

abstract: This study examines how students choose academic teammates when they have limited information about potential partners. It takes place in undergraduate economics courses where students must be assigned to teams for a graded, semester-long project. Rankings collected in the study are used to help form those real teams. The study has two parts. In the first session, students complete incentivized tasks and a short survey. The tasks measure traits such as dominance, assertiveness, diligence, self-reliance, confidence, and cognitive ability. The survey records background information, including gender, race, and whether the student is a domestic or international student. In the second session, students rank anonymized classmate profiles. Each profile shows a small set of characteristics, such as gender, research-topic overlap, trait scores, cognitive ability, or domestic versus international student status. Across rounds, the information on the cards changes in a controlled way, so the study can measure whether students prefer one gender over the other when other information is the same, and whether those preferences change when more information about ability or traits is provided. A later follow-up survey collects peer evaluations after the group project. The main goal is to measure gender preferences in academic partnership: whether students favor a teammate’s gender even when other information is the same, and whether that preference changes when competence is shown more clearly. Secondary goals are to measure how students value agentic traits such as assertiveness, diligence, self-reliance, confidence, and dominance when choosing teammates, and whether information on those traits changes gender preferences
experimental_design: This is a lab-in-field experiment in undergraduate economics courses. Enrolled students are the participants. The study has two sessions, held on different days, plus a later peer-evaluation survey after the group project. In session 1, all students complete the same incentivized trait and cognitive-ability tasks and a background survey. Some tasks are completed in pairs, so session 1 is run with an even number of students present. In session 2, all students rank anonymized classmate profiles. The main variation is within student: each person sees several rounds in which the information on the cards changes. Some rounds differ only by gender. Other rounds add information on agentic traits, dominance, cognitive ability, or research-topic overlap. Round order and the left-to-right order of cards are randomized. Students may give the same rank to more than one profile. Most students are in the standard version, which includes research-topic overlap on some cards. One course section does not complete the topic survey and does not see that information. After the ranking rounds, students answer questions about beliefs, how much they would pay for different team gender compositions, and which profile elements matter to them. Rankings are used to help form real course project teams of four or five. The later survey asks students to rate their teammates after the project.
experimental_design_details: This is a two-session, lab-in-field experiment in undergraduate economics courses at Purdue, with a later end-of-semester peer-evaluation survey. Participants are enrolled students. Session 1 measures traits and background characteristics. Session 2 elicits teammate rankings that feed a team-assignment algorithm for a graded project. The unit of analysis for ranking outcomes is the evaluator-by-comparison: pairwise implications of ranks on a given screen, with ties coded at 0.5. Between-section factor. Most sections are the standard cohort and complete a research-topic survey between sessions. Interest-match scores from that survey appear on some session 2 cards. One section of about 75 students is the no-research-interest cohort: no topic survey, no interest-match lines on cards, and a shorter Block A that includes two-profile gender baselines. Within-student factor. Every student sees both ranking blocks. Block A comes first (no dominance). Block B follows, after students are told that the trait average now includes dominance. Round order within each block is randomized. Card positions on each screen are randomized. This within-student structure is used because class size is small and between-student assignment to dominance would cut power on that contrast. Session 1. Incentivized tasks measure dominance, assertiveness, diligence, self-reliance, confidence, and cognitive ability (eight-item pattern test). A survey records gender, race (checkboxes, select all that apply), domestic or international student status, and other background items. Session 1 requires an even number of students because some tasks are paired. Session 2 ranking rules. Students rank profiles from 1 (most preferred) to 4 (least preferred). Ties are allowed. Skipped ranks are not. Most screens show four profiles: two men and two women, crossed with a high and a low information type. Age band and major are constant within a round. When a cognitive score is shown, all cards on that screen show the same score: either 7 out of 8 (precise high) or 4 or more out of 8 (noisy). Comparing same-type gender choice across no cognitive information, noisy information, and precise information is the taste-versus-statistical test. Block A, standard cohort (11 rounds). Six interest-match rounds (two with no cognitive score, two precise, two noisy), two average-of-four-traits rounds (assertiveness, diligence, self-reliance, confidence), two smaller domestic versus international rounds that also vary interest match and do not show gender, and one attention check. Block A, no-interest cohort (7 rounds). Three two-profile gender baselines (gender only; gender plus precise cognitive score; gender plus noisy cognitive score), one two-profile domestic versus international baseline with no gender on the cards, two four-profile average-of-four-traits rounds, and one attention check. Block B, all cohorts (7 rounds). Two rounds show the average of five traits (the four above plus dominance). Four rounds show dominance only, at two high/low thresholds, each with the precise or noisy cognitive score. One round is an attention check. Main comparisons. Same-type man versus woman cards identify gender preference and same-gender homophily by evaluator gender. Holding gender fixed, high versus low trait cards identify preference for agentic traits and for dominance. Packet contrasts identify whether gender choice changes when four-trait, five-trait, or dominance-only information is added. Domestic versus international rounds are a small additional comparison teammate preferences. After ranking. All students complete the same mechanism module: first-order beliefs about otherwise identical Man and Woman profiles; second-order beliefs about what own-gender and opposite-gender classmates believe; six first-order trait screens (Man and Woman × high four-trait, high five-trait, and high dominance); willingness to pay up to 100 dollars for all own-gender, majority own-gender, or majority other-gender teams, with one student from the semester potentially selected; then optional harassment items and open text. Students then rank six profile elements for themselves and for what they think the class prefers. Team assignment. After session 2, a sequential algorithm uses the rankings to form teams of three to five. Follow-up. The fielded Qualtrics peer-evaluation survey collects teammate ratings after the project. Attention and exclusions. Each ranking block includes an instructed-rank attention check. The mechanism module includes an instructed-response item. Analyses will be reported with and without students who fail these checks.
intervention: Students take part in a two-session, lab-in-field experiment in an undergraduate economics course. In session 1, they complete incentivized tasks that measure agentic traits (assertiveness, diligence, self-reliance, confidence, and dominance) and cognitive ability, plus a short background survey. In session 2, they rank anonymized classmate profiles. The intervention is the information shown on those profiles. Across rounds, cards vary by gender and by information on agentic traits, dominance, cognitive ability, and research-topic overlap. Some rounds hold other characteristics fixed so that profiles differ only by gender. Other rounds vary trait or ability information, including a clearer versus noisier cognitive-ability signal. A smaller set of rounds varies domestic versus international student status without showing gender. Rankings from these rounds are used to help assign real course project teams.

The outcome is the pairwise ranking measure coded 1 / 0 / 0.5 (man strictly preferred / woman strictly preferred / tie). This outcome has an approximate standard deviation of 0.40. Discrimination against a 50% benchmark: whether P(rank man above otherwise identical woman) differs from 0.5. Overall MDE ≈ 0.06 (6 percentage points, about 0.15 SD). Within each evaluator-gender group, MDE ≈ 0.08 to 0.10 (8 to 10 percentage points, about 0.20 to 0.25 SD). Evaluator-gender gap in that same probability (same-gender homophily): MDE ≈ 0.10 (10 percentage points, about 0.25 SD). Change in that probability across information packets (agentic traits, dominance, or cognitive-signal precision): planned MDE ≈ 0.08 (8 percentage points, about 0.20 SD).

primary_outcome_explanation: All primary outcomes are built from session 2 ranking ranks. Students rank profiles from 1 (most preferred) to 4 (least preferred). Ties are allowed. The analysis does not use the full four-way ranking as the outcome. It uses pairwise comparisons implied by those ranks. For any two profiles on the same screen, the constructed outcome is 1 if the focal profile receives a strictly better (numerically lower) rank, 0 if the other profile receives a strictly better rank, and 0.5 if the two profiles tie. Analysis is at the evaluator-by-comparison level. Under no gender preference, the pairwise gender-choice mean should be 0.5 (ties pull toward 0.5; strict choices should split evenly). Discrimination is defined as a statistically significant departure from 0.5. This is estimated overall and separately by evaluator gender. Outcome 1 uses same-type comparisons only: the man and woman cards show the same other information (same interest match, same trait standing, and the same cognitive descriptor when one is shown). The focal profile is the man. We do this analysis split by evaluator gender as well. The object of interest is same-gender preference: whether women are more likely than men to rank the woman above the otherwise identical man, and whether men are more likely than women to rank the man above the otherwise identical woman. Outcome 2 uses the same constructed gender-choice variable as outcome 1, compared across rounds with no cognitive score, a noisy score (4 or more out of 8), and a precise high score (7 out of 8). When a cognitive score is shown, all cards in that round carry the same score. Outcome 3 holds gender fixed and compares the higher-trait profile with the lower-trait profile. The focal profile is the higher-trait card. This is constructed separately for the average of four traits (assertiveness, diligence, self-reliance, and confidence), the average of five traits (those four plus dominance), and dominance only. Outcome 4 uses the same constructed gender-choice variable as outcome 1, compared across rounds with no trait scores, rounds that show the four-trait average, rounds that show the five-trait average, and rounds that show dominance only.
primary_outcomes: 1.Test of gender discrimination against a 50% benchmark: whether the probability of ranking the man above the otherwise identical woman differs from 0.5, overall and separately for men and women evaluators. 2.Pairwise gender choice by precision of the cognitive-ability signal 3.Pairwise preference for higher versus lower agentic-trait profiles, holding gender fixed 4.Pairwise gender choice when agentic-trait or dominance information is shown
randomization_method: Randomization is done by computer in the oTree session, using Python’s random number generator at the participant level. For each student, round order within each ranking block and the left-to-right order of cards on each screen are randomly shuffled. Team-assignment processing order is also shuffled by computer after session 2.
randomization_unit: Individual student. Within a section, every student sees the same ranking blocks for that section. What is randomized at the student level is round order within each block and the left-to-right order of cards on each screen. After session 2, the order in which students are processed for team assignment is also randomized at the individual level.
secondary_outcome_explanation: Outcome 1 is constructed from session 2 ranks in the same way as the primary pairwise outcomes: 1 if the focal profile receives a strictly better rank, 0 if the other profile does, and 0.5 if they tie. Gender is held fixed. The comparison is higher versus lower research-topic interest match. The focal profile is the higher-match card. This is collected only in sections that complete the research-topic survey. Outcomes 2 through 5 come from the session 2 mechanism module, administered after all ranking rounds. Outcome 2 is the student’s own belief about a classmate whose profile differs only by gender. For the Man card and the Woman card, students rate expected contribution relative to a fair share, competence, ease of communication and coordination, comfort working closely, and likelihood of creating costly conflict. The constructed objects are Man–Woman gaps on each item, and whether those gaps line up with same-gender ranking choices. Outcome 3 asks what the student thinks other students believe, not what the student personally believes. One block asks what the average student of the respondent’s own gender believes about the Man and Woman cards. A second block asks what the average student of the other gender believes about those cards. The same contribution, competence, communication and coordination, comfort, and conflict items are used. The constructed objects are own-gender versus other-gender belief gaps, and whether anticipated others’ beliefs line up with ranking choices. Second-order answers are incentivized by closeness to the leave-one-out mean of first-order answers in the named gender group. Outcome 4 uses six first-order trait screens: Man and Woman, each shown as high on the four-trait average, high on the five-trait average (including dominance), or high on dominance only. Items are contribution, competence, communication and coordination, and conflict. Comfort is not asked on trait screens. The constructed objects are belief gaps between high-trait or high-dominance profiles and the gender-only profiles, and whether those inferences differ by profile gender and by evaluator gender. Outcome 5 is the maximum the student is willing to pay, from 0 to 100 dollars, for three team compositions: all teammates of their own gender, majority own gender, and majority other gender. One student from the semester may be selected for payment and implementation. Outcome 6 is collected after the mechanism module. Students rank six profile elements from most to least important for their own teammate choice: gender, cognitive ability, research-topic interest match, average of four traits, average of five traits, and dominance only. Ties are allowed. Outcome 7 uses the same six elements. Students rank them by what they believe the average student in the class prefers. Outcome 8 comes from the fielded end-of-semester Qualtrics peer-evaluation survey. Each student rates each teammate on contribution relative to a fair share, competence, and related project-performance items. Outcome 9 compares a domestic-student profile with an international-student profile. These cards do not show gender. This is a small part of the design. The focal profile is specified in analysis (for example, the domestic-student card, or the card that matches the evaluator’s own status). The mechanism module also includes two unpaid harassment-exposure items and an optional open-text question about why the student ranked otherwise identical Man and Woman profiles as they did. Those items are exploratory moderators and descriptive text. They are not confirmatory secondary endpoints.

title: Gender Discrimination in Teammate Choice

abstract: This project evaluates the impact of different instructor feedback methods on student learning and engagement. We conducted a randomized controlled trial in an undergraduate mathematics course, assigning students to different feedback conditions for periodic assessments. The study tracks the effects of these feedback methods on student learning outcomes and proactivity over both the short and long term.
experimental_design: This study is a three-arm randomized controlled trial conducted among undergraduate students in an introductory mathematics course. Students are assigned at the individual level (1:1:1 ratio) to receive different forms of qualitative written feedback on their regular quizzes: (1) an evaluative control group, (2) an instructional feedforward group, or (3) an integrated feedback group combining wise feedback with instructional guidance. The experiment tracks weekly assessment scores, voluntary problem attempts, and survey-based measures of student study habits across the semester.
experimental_design_details: 1. Research Context and Sample The study was conducted within the framework of an introductory mathematics course for undergraduates at a university in Hanoi, Vietnam, spanning a 10-week semester. The study sample consisted of approximately 120 students enrolled in two course sections. All participants completed identical weekly learning materials, lecture content, and in-class assessments. 2. Stratified Randomization To prevent baseline imbalances in small-to-medium-sized samples, participants were assigned using stratified block randomization. Within each class, students were stratified into blocks based on prior academic performance (from an entrance test or admission records) and geographic background (urban vs. rural). Within each stratum, students were randomly allocated at a 1:1:1 ratio to one of three experimental groups: - Score-only control group (C): Received standard grading consisting of a final score and conventional objective error markers (ticks or crosses) without qualitative comments. - Feedforward (T_1): Received a score accompanied by forward-looking guidance that identified technical errors and provided specific steps for future exercises, excluding elements related to emotion or motivation. -Integrated feedback ($T_2$): Received a score accompanied by comprehensive comments combining high academic standards, clear affirmation of individual competence, and specific, immediately applicable guidance for subsequent tasks. 3. Evaluation Schedule and Timeline: The 10-week trial followed a longitudinal panel design comprising three phases: - Baseline Phase (Week 1 / Test 1): Established initial academic proficiency and verified the balance of variables across groups; all students received standard scores without specific feedback. - Active Intervention Phase (Weeks 2–7 / Tests 2–7): Specific intervention feedback (C, T1, T2) was consistently applied when returning weekly tests. - Withdrawal/Maintenance Phase (Weeks 8–10 / Tests 8–10): All qualitative feedback was discontinued without prior notice; students in all three groups received only standard scores to assess the rate of decline and the retention of established study habits. 4. Safeguards and Trial Integrity: Two-stage blind grading: To eliminate grader expectancy bias, test scoring followed a strict double-blind procedure. Instructors graded anonymized papers and entered scores into a secure database before accessing group assignment records to append group-specific feedback. Contamination Control: Qualitative feedback was provided discreetly—written on the back of the test paper—to minimize information leakage among students in the same room. 5. Outcome Measures: - Academic performance:Continuous numerical scores (0–10 scale) derived from weekly tests. Voluntary effort: A weekly binary indicator tracking whether students voluntarily completed an optional, ungraded challenge problem attached to each test. Academic autonomy (self-assessed): A composite psychological index constructed from brief surveys administered at the beginning (Week 1) and end (Week 10) of the course, designed to capture self-regulated learning strategies and proactive error-monitoring behaviors

mde_text: Power calculations assume a standard significance level of (alpha = 0.05) and 80% statistical power (beta = 0.20), evaluating pairwise comparisons between any treatment arm (n = 40) and the control arm (n = 40). 1. Primary Continuous Outcome: Academic Quiz Score, Cross-sectional baseline benchmark: In a simple two-arm comparison without covariates (n_1 = n_2 = 40), the minimum detectable effect size (MDES) is approximately 0.63 standard deviations (SD).Panel estimation with baseline controls & fixed effects: Accounting for the longitudinal repeated-measures design (10 weekly quizzes; 6 active intervention rounds and 3 washout rounds) and controlling for baseline score (Quiz 1), the effective residual variance is substantially reduced. Assuming a moderate-to-high quiz score autocorrelation (rho is in [0.50, 0.70]), the MDES shrinks to approximately 0.28 to 0.36 SD for average treatment effects across the intervention period. 2. abstract: Since January 2025, the United States has repeatedly demanded that Denmark cede Greenland, alongside tariffs on European goods, statements questioning NATO Article 5 commitments, and withdrawal from multilateral agreements. This pre-registration covers an online survey experiment fielded to 400 Danish adults. Respondents are randomly assigned to read either a factual compilation of recent news on the Greenland crisis and US unilateralism, or a length-matched placebo text on international sport. Both arms then complete an identical outcome battery: an incentivised divestment decision with real monetary consequences, stated boycott and petition behaviour, two injunctive norm items, incentivised second-order beliefs about the same five behaviours, and an emotion and concern module. The study estimates the intention-to-treat effect of salience on economic retaliation, and measures the gap between first-order behaviour and second-order beliefs about peers.
experimental_design: A two-arm, individually randomised online survey experiment fielded to a quota-sampled panel of 400 Danish adults aged 18 and over. Respondents are randomised at survey entry to a salience condition or a length-matched placebo condition, then complete an identical post-treatment battery: an incentivised divestment decision, stated boycott and petition behaviour, two injunctive norm items, incentivised second-order beliefs about the same five behaviours, an emotion battery, and a concern and expectations module. Two tasks carry real monetary consequences. Median completion time is approximately 15 minutes. The design supports two objects of interest: the intention-to-treat effect of salience on economic retaliation, and the within-sample gap between first-order behaviour and second-order beliefs about peers.
intervention: Respondents are randomly assigned, with equal probability, to one of two conditions presented immediately after consent and before any outcome is measured. Salience arm (n = 200): respondents read a short factual compilation of recent news items covering the US demand that Denmark cede Greenland and the refusal to rule out economic or military pressure, unauthorised US military flights over Greenlandic airspace, US tariffs on European goods, US withdrawal from the WHO and the Paris Climate Agreement, and US statements questioning NATO Article 5 commitments. The text is presented explicitly as a curated compilation of news items and not as a statement by the survey provider. Control arm (n = 200): respondents read a length-matched placebo text in the same format covering recent international sport.

abstract: We run a randomized control trial as part of a survey of mortgage customers of a large German bank we collaborate with. When German mortgagors refinance at the end of their rate-fixation period into a lower rate, most do not let the monthly payment fall. Instead, they keep the payment close to or above its previous level, which shortens the term and accelerates repayment. Our objective is to understand whether this behavior reflects a preference for faster repayment or a mistake, namely a failure to recognize that additional amortization is illiquid saving that earns the (low) mortgage rate. Survey participants work through a hypothetical refinancing scenario in which the rate falls from 3% to 1% and the bank’s standard offer lowers the monthly payment by €100. Before making their choice, we randomly assign participants to one of two arms. The control group receives neutral definitions of loan terms. The treatment group receives information that additional repayment earns a fixed return equal to the loan rate, that money used for repayment forgoes any higher return available elsewhere, and that it is tied up in housing wealth. Participants then choose whether to accept the bank’s offer, change the monthly payment, and/or make a one-time repayment, and explain the reasons behind their choices. In a second, smaller experiment, participants choose between using a freed-up €100 per month for faster repayment or for a randomly assigned savings product: a liquid deposit at the loan rate, a liquid deposit at the loan rate plus one percentage point, or an equity fund savings plan. We investigate treatment effects on hypothetical refinancing choices, on the reasoning behind them, and on hypothetical consumption and savings adjustments.
experimental_design: The partnering bank invites by e-mail all customers with an outstanding mortgage who can be contacted electronically and have consented to such contact (around 70,000 customers are eligible; the bank sends invitations 2026-09-03 and sends a reminder on 2026-09-15). Participation is voluntary and compensated with a voucher. Participants first answer questions about their property and mortgage. Participants who refinanced before mid-2022, that is, in the low-rate period, report the terms of and reasoning behind that refinancing and do not take part in the information experiment. All other participants work through a hypothetical refinancing scenario: the rate-fixation period of a €110,000 mortgage ends, the rate falls from 3% to 1%, and the bank’s standard offer lowers the monthly payment by €100 while leaving the balance and the date of full repayment unchanged. Before making their choice, we randomly assign participants to one of two arms with equal probability. The control group receives neutral definitions of loan terms: the monthly payment comprises an interest and a repayment component, the interest rate in the scenario is 1% per year, and the remaining term is the time until the loan is fully repaid. The treatment group instead receives information that additional repayment (a higher monthly payment or a one-time repayment) earns a fixed return equal to the loan rate of 1% per year, that money used for repayment forgoes any potentially higher return available elsewhere, and that it is tied up in housing wealth rather than available for expenses or emergencies. Both groups answer a comprehension question on their respective text and receive the correct answer as feedback. Participants then choose whether to accept the bank’s offer, change the monthly payment (from €100 below to €200 above the offer), and/or make a one-time repayment out of their savings (up to €30,000), with the implied payment and repayment date displayed live. They subsequently state the reasons for their choices in an open-ended question, indicate whether the level of the new rate, access to the money, and alternative uses of the money spoke for or against additional payments, rank the most important reasons, and report how they would adjust consumption, savings, investment, and hours worked. If faster repayment reflects a mistake, the treatment should reduce additional payments, shift stated reasoning toward opportunity costs and liquidity, and shift intended uses of the freed-up money toward savings and investment. If faster repayment reflects a preference, choices should not respond to the information. In a second, smaller experiment shown to all participants, respondents choose between using a freed-up €100 per month from a refinancing at a lower rate for faster repayment or for a savings product. We randomly assign each respondent to one of three products with equal probability: a liquid deposit at the loan rate (1%), a liquid deposit at the loan rate plus one percentage point (2%), or a diversified equity fund savings plan with a higher but uncertain expected return. The 2% deposit strictly dominates faster repayment. The share preferring repayment across the three arms measures how sensitive the repayment preference is to the return and liquidity of the alternative. The survey closes with a mirror scenario in which the rate rises, questions on financial traits and interest-rate perceptions, a hypothetical income-windfall allocation, and background questions on income and the balance sheet. Bank data allow us to relate stated choices and reasoning to actual refinancing behavior and to study heterogeneity in treatment effects.

abstract: This study extends the previously registered randomized controlled trial “Excuse My Behavior: Social Norms and Moral Costs” (AEA RCT ID: AEARCTR-0015264), which examines how replacement and waste excuses affect environmentally relevant consumption choices. Participants make incentivized decisions between cheaper, more carbon-intensive options and more expensive, less carbon-intensive alternatives in the domains of clothing, food, and transportation. The extension addresses two questions. First, it examines what happens when the excuse statements focus on the more sustainable rather than the less sustainable option. Second, it varies whether social norms and moral costs are elicited before or after the consumption choices. This allows us to study whether the previously observed effects on reported norms and moral costs may partly reflect adjustments made after a decision. The study examines effects on consumption choices, descriptive and injunctive social norms, moral costs, and perceived replacement and waste likelihood.
experimental_design: Participants are randomly assigned to one of eight experimental conditions. All participants receive objective information relevant to three incentivized consumption decisions. In the Info condition, participants receive only this information. The Replacement Excuse (RE) and Waste Excuse (WE) conditions additionally present statements focusing on the less sustainable option: either someone else may choose the option or it may otherwise remain unused or be wasted. The reversed conditions (RRE and RWE) apply the corresponding reasoning to the more sustainable option. Finally, three additional conditions repeat the Info, RE, and WE treatments but elicit social norms and moral costs before rather than after the consumption decisions.
intervention: In a survey experiment, participants face three hypothetical but incentivized consumption decisions. We provide them with different replacement and waste statements that focus either on the less sustainable or the more sustainable consumption option.

abstract: This study examines whether recent exposure to different types of probabilistic information affects subsequent belief updating. Participants complete a standard bookbag-and-poker-chip task in which they infer which of two bags generated an observed sample of colored balls. Before the main test trials, participants are randomly assigned to different adaptation conditions that vary the distribution of sample proportions they observe. The study tests whether this prior exposure changes how responsive participants are to new evidence and whether it shifts beliefs at the Bayesian decision boundary.
experimental_design: The study uses a belief-updating task based on a standard bookbag-and-poker-chip paradigm. Participants complete multiple independent rounds in which there are two bags containing different proportions of colored balls. In each round, one bag is selected according to stated prior probabilities, a sample of balls is drawn with replacement, and participants indicate which bag they believe is more likely to have generated the sample. Participants are randomly assigned to one of several adaptation conditions that differ in the distribution of sample proportions observed during an initial adaptation phase. Participants are also assigned to one of two prior-probability environments: one with equal prior probabilities over the two bags and one with unequal prior probabilities. Following the adaptation phase, all participants complete a common set of test trials within their assigned prior environment. The primary analysis examines whether exposure to different distributions of sample proportions affects how responsive participants are to new evidence during the test phase. Additional analyses examine whether adaptation shifts choices at the Bayesian decision boundary. All questions are framed hypothetically, with probabilities fully determined by the stated bag compositions, prior probabilities, and observed samples. Additional details on the experimental procedures, analysis plan, and exclusion criteria are provided in the uploaded Pre-Analysis Plan.
intervention: Participants are randomly assigned to one of several adaptation conditions that differ in the distribution of sample proportions they observe during an initial adaptation phase. They are then randomly assigned to one of two prior-probability environments (symmetric or asymmetric) before completing a common set of test trials. The intervention therefore varies participants' recent exposure to probabilistic information while holding the test task constant across conditions.

abstract: This project builds on previous studies conducted in 2021 on Code in Place, an online programming course where we found that automated feedback to instructors can improve their instruction and student satisfaction. The current study was conducted in the spring of 2024 on Code in Place, and its goal is to understand whether providing feedback to students as well, in addition to providing feedback to instructors, influences the quality of their discourse and student outcomes. Feedback to teachers is known to be an effective way to improve their instruction, but few empirical studies have examined the effect of joint feedback to both teachers and students. To answer this question, the study leverages a randomized controlled trial design and computational natural language processing techniques.
experimental_design: We randomized participants at the student level, implemented as a cluster randomization over pre-course section rosters. Concretely, the list of 606 pre-course section rosters was shuffled and split into three equal parts, and every student on a given roster was assigned to that roster's condition. Treatment then travelled with the student for the rest of the course: a student's condition never changed, including in the weeks when they attended a section other than their own. Two consequences follow for the analysis. First, the unit of randomization is the pre-course section roster, so confirmatory standard errors are clustered at that level rather than at the level of the section a student happened to attend. Second, because rosters were revised between randomization and the first section, and because students moved between sections during the course, sections are not pure with respect to condition (see Prior knowledge below). Before the course began: We randomized students once they were accepted to the course, before the first section. Third of the students (n=2188 name=StudentFeedback group) were assigned to receive automated feedback in addition to their instructors receiving feedback. Another third of the students (n=2187, name=StudentSLFeedback group) both received feedback, similar to the StudentFeedback group, and also had the option to share feedback back to their instructor. Control group students did not receive feedback. Control-group students were not given personalized feedback. They saw a static acknowledgement message (“thank you for showing up”) in the same place in the roadmap where treated students saw their personalized feedback, so the contrast between arms is the content of the feedback rather than the presence of a roadmap item. Once the course began: On the Monday following each section, students were able to access the automated feedback within their roadmap (checklist before their next section). The feedback for the StudentFeedback group looked had the following components: ● Introduction to the feedback ● Number of student questions asked ● List of student questions asked with timestamps ● Reminder about the importance of asking questions ● Link to class and section forum to ask further questions ● Student talktime percentage + percentile ● Opportunity to write a reflection
intervention: The goal of our intervention was to answer the following research questions: RQ1: Does joint feedback to both students and instructors improve student outcomes (attendance, engagement in section, assignment completion) above and beyond feedback provided to instructors alone? RQ1.1.: Does giving students the option to also give feedback back to the instructor further improve these metrics? RQ2: Does joint feedback to both students and instructors improve instructor outcomes (talk time, talk move rate, NPS, instructor engagement with the course) above and beyond feedback provided to instructors alone? RQ2.1.: Does giving students the option to also give feedback back to the instructor further improve these metrics? RQ3: How do treatment effects vary by instructor and student characteristics (demographics=location,age,gender, baseline engagement before feedback, etc.)? The experimental design is described below.

abstract: This follow-up study to AEA #0012065 examines how people think about targeting the provision of in-kind goods and whether they think those goods should be considered rights. In AEA #0012065, one task asked participants to allocate goods across recipients of different incomes. We expand the set of goods considered and have participants complete two tasks: a targeting-allocation task and a task assessing whether the good should be considered a right. A key purpose of this study is to explore whether patterns in #0012065 generalize to a broader set of goods.
experimental_design: Our experiment proceeds in several parts. First, we randomize participants to complete one of the two modules.They then complete either the targeting module (where one of 13 goods is selected as the focus) or the rights module (where six of 13 goods are selected for our primary question, and one of those six is selected for additional questions). Finally, we ask demographic and political questions. We recruit participants on Prolific.
intervention: There are two main modules, and each participant is randomly assigned to complete only one of the two modules. Unlike AEA #0012065, all tasks in this follow-up are hypothetical. In the targeting module, participants choose between concentrating benefits on fewer, poorer applicants and providing smaller benefits to a broader group. Participants are asked to choose between giving an in-kind good plus $100 in cash to a subset of the poorest of 10 applicants or giving the in-kind good alone to all 10 applicants. Using an adaptive multiple-price list that varies the number of applicants receiving the targeted benefit, we identify each participant’s indifference point between targeted and universal provision. We randomize the good across participants from a set of 13 goods (lawyer for an eviction proceeding, bus passes, health care vouchers, YMCA membership, community college tuition, food, child care, rental assistance, contraception, job training, pre-K tuition, internet access, and cash as a benchmark). In the second module (rights), participants are randomly assigned to consider six of the 13 goods and indicate whether it should be considered a right. The module then includes several qualitative questions about one of the six goods (randomly selected) intended to understand the reasons for their response.

abstract: Despite severe and widely recognized air pollution in large developing cities, citizen demand for government action remains limited. This project studies why private concern and protective behavior often fail to translate into political pressure for pollution-reducing policy. We focus on potential constraints faced by citizens: misperceptions about pollution severity and health damages, pessimism about the effectiveness of feasible policies, skepticism about political responsiveness to citizen action, and coordination failures in collective action.
experimental_design: We field an in-person survey experiment with Delhi residents recruited face to face in selected neighborhoods, administered by trained enumerators in English and Hindi. The survey elicits demographics, beliefs about air pollution and pollution policy, and prior civic engagement, and includes randomized informational and cost interventions described above.
intervention: We will provide information treatments relevant to the value of civic action, a treatment designed to shift beliefs others' civic action participation, and a treatment that changes the cost of participating in civic action.

abstract: Job search frictions — including limited access to information, weak networks, and skills mismatches — are significant barriers to employment for technical diploma graduates in low- and middle-income countries, with women facing additional constraints around mobility, household responsibilities, and discriminatory norms. In Bangladesh, employment outcomes for technical diploma graduates remain weak despite substantial government investment in technical and vocational education and training, and use of digital job search platforms is limited. This study aims to identify scalable approaches to improving the school-to-work transition for technical diploma graduates in Bangladesh, with a particular focus on gender. The intervention introduces and trains final-year technical diploma students to use an online job matching platform, with continued support through AI-enabled job search tools. Using a randomized controlled trial design, we will estimate impacts on job search behavior and labor market outcomes, and examine differential effects by gender.
experimental_design: This study uses a cluster-randomized controlled trial. 137 technical diploma institutes in Bangladesh are randomly assigned to Base Treatment or Control, with roughly two-thirds of institutes assigned to treatment and one-third to control. Randomization is conducted at the institute level. Control: Half day in-person CV-making and job search strategy workshop. Base Treatment: Half day in-person CV-making and job search strategy workshop, identical to Control, plus an additional session teaching students how to use an online job matching platform. Students receive continued support through the platform's AI-enabled tools. Outcomes are measured at the individual student level. A baseline survey is administered to all participants at the start of the workshop. The baseline survey collects data on basic demographics, job search and employment, labor market expectations and job preferences, agency, gender attitudes, and digital access and skills.
intervention: Job search training sessions were conducted at each participating institute between May and July 2026. Students in their 7th (penultimate) semester at each institute were invited to attend, and completed a self-administered baseline survey at the start of their session. Students at institutes assigned to Control received a half-day workshop covering CV-making and job search strategies. Students at institutes assigned to Base Treatment received the identical CV-making and job search strategy workshop, plus an additional session in which they were introduced to an online job matching platform and guided through creating an account. Following the training, Base Treatment students continued to receive support through the platform's AI-enabled tools.

abstract: Can responsible AI use make generative AI a complement to students’ skills rather than a substitute for skill-building effort? We study this question through a Responsible AI Use curriculum for Grade 6 and Grade 7 students. Forty schools are randomized to the curriculum or control. The curriculum teaches prompting, follow-up questioning, verification, critical judgment, and avoidance of answer copying. We distinguish AI-assisted performance from learning using standardized AI-use tasks and independently completed examination scores. We also test heterogeneity by baseline skills.
experimental_design: We randomize schools into treatment and control conditions using a stratified matched-pair design. Within each school level and urban/rural stratum, schools are ranked by the mean baseline Chinese and mathematics scores of students in the two preselected classes and paired adjacently. Within each pair, one school is randomly assigned to treatment and the other to control, yielding 20 schools per arm. In treatment schools, the Responsible AI Use curriculum is delivered during regular ICT classes to the two selected classes. Control schools continue their regular ICT curriculum and receive no guided AI instruction. Students and instructors cannot be blinded to assignment, but routine examination grading will be blinded where feasible.
intervention: The intervention is delivered by trained instructors and teaches students to use AI productively for learning rather than as an abstract technical subject. It focuses on problem decomposition, structured prompting, follow-up questioning, verification, creativity, critical judgment, and responsible use. Students use the Qwen web interface with pre-provisioned accounts. Each standardized 40-minute session combines a brief introduction, instructor demonstration, and guided practice. The seven sessions cover an introduction to AI and responsible use, mathematics applications emphasizing structured problem solving and verification, Chinese applications emphasizing interpretation and textual evidence, and English conversation practice, with critical thinking and responsible AI use integrated throughout the curriculum.

abstract: Despite growing recognition that socio-emotional skills are critical for human capital development, evidence on whether public school systems can deliver such skills at scale in low-resource settings remains scarce. We evaluate an arts-integrated social-emotional learning (SEL) program embedded in compulsory art classes in government schools in Punjab, India. The intervention by Punjab’s State Council of Education Research and Training (SCERT) provides 3 days of teacher training and an SEL-integrated art curriculum aligned with India’s National Education Policy. We implement a school-level cluster randomized controlled trial across 200 government schools and approximately 5400 Grade 6 students. The study tests whether holistic skills can be cultivated through existing instructional time and government school teachers.
experimental_design: We use a school-level cluster randomized controlled trial. 200 schools were randomized to treatment and control in equal proportion, stratified by district. Schools are randomly assigned to treatment or control before the baseline survey. Our primary analyses follow an intention-to-treat specification based on randomized assignment: we compare outcomes for students in treatment and control schools at endline, with district fixed effects and school-level baseline controls, and an ANCOVA specification that additionally controls for the baseline value of the outcome measured at the student level. Standard errors are clustered at the school level, the unit of randomization.
intervention: The intervention is an arts-integrated social-emotional learning (SEL) curriculum delivered through compulsory art classes in Punjab government schools. It is developed and implemented by Slam Out Loud (SOL), a non-profit with over ten years of experience working on arts-based education in Indian government schools, in partnership with Punjab's State Council of Education Research and Training (SCERT). The intervention bundles two components. First, a new SEL-integrated art textbook, aligned with India's National Education Policy (2020), is provided to every Grade 6 student in treatment schools. The textbook comprises five chapters delivered through approximately twenty lessons of forty-five minutes each. Second, teachers responsible for delivering the Grade 6 art curriculum in treatment schools participate in training organized by SCERT and SOL for three days, delivered directly by SOL trainers, covering all five chapters of the textbook, arts-based SEL facilitation skills, and classroom implementation. The intervention does not add instructional time, and only changes how the existing art period is used. Control schools continue with business as usual: the standard government art curriculum and textbook, with no additional teacher training, materials, or support from SOL.

primary_outcome_explanation: We measure emotional awareness, a student's ability to identify and verbally share their own emotions, using a shortened Emotional Awareness Questionnaire that covers the differentiating-emotions and verbal-sharing subscales (Rieffe et al., 2008). We capture emotion regulation with the Emotion Regulation Questionnaire for Children and Adolescents (Gullone and Taffe, 2012). Subjective wellbeing, the child's recent emotional state and positive outlook over the prior two weeks, is measured with the Stirling Children's Well-being Scale (Liddle and Carter, 2015), dropping its built-in social-desirability items, which we capture separately. We measure curiosity using items adapted from Alan and Mumcu (2024), and creativity through an alternative-uses task in which students are given an everyday object and have two minutes to list as many uses for it as they can (Guilford, 1967). We measure prosocial behaviour through a stated willingness to help others and a hypothetical sharing decision in which the student allocates a gift of ten chocolates between themselves and a peer who received none (Falk et al., 2018; Kosse et al., 2020). We additionally measure students' social behaviour as rated by their teacher, using an adapted short form of the Social Behavior Questionnaire (SBQ; Tremblay et al., 1991; Collet et al., 2023), covering the prosocial behaviour, disruptive behaviour, and hyperactivity-inattention subscales; the teacher responsible for the Grade 6 art period rates a random subset of students per class, drawn from the baseline enrolment roster, and this measure is collected at endline only. Each scale is scored following its source instrument, with the indicated items reverse coded so that higher values denote more of the outcome being measured, and then standardized so that treatment effects are expressed in control-group standard deviations.
primary_outcomes: Students' socio-emotional skills, measured through a battery of validated, age-appropriate scales collected at both baseline and endline: emotional awareness, emotion regulation, subjective wellbeing, curiosity, creativity (divergent thinking), and prosocial behaviour. Additionally, we will measure teacher-reported student behavior in the classroom using a modified version of the Social Behavior Questionnaire (SBQ).
randomization_method: Randomization done via STATA by the research team, using school-level administrative data, stratified by district.
randomization_unit: The school is the unit of randomization because the intervention is delivered at the school level, through the teacher conducting Grade 6 art classes. There is a single level of randomization.
secondary_outcome_explanation: The teacher who delivers the Grade 6 art period is surveyed in all 200 study schools at both baseline and endline. We examine teachers' teaching and learning beliefs, covering growth mindset and openness to new pedagogy; their self-reported teaching practices along a student-centred versus traditional dimension; their own emotion regulation, using the adult Emotion Regulation Questionnaire (Gross and John, 2003); their art self-efficacy and enjoyment of teaching the art period; and their perceived student engagement. These outcomes let us test whether the training shifts how teachers think about learning and how they teach, a plausible channel for effects on students. The teacher who handles the art period usually teaches a regular subject too, often to the same Grade 6 students; using a baseline item that records whether the art teacher also teaches their main subject to the same class, we test for spillovers to students' grades in that subject.
secondary_outcomes: Learning and school outcomes: academic performance, measured using students' final-year Grade 6 examination scores obtained from administrative records; attendance, measured from Grade 6 attendance records; and classroom behaviour, captured through structured classroom observation. Teacher outcomes: teachers' teaching and learning beliefs, self-reported teaching practices, their own emotion regulation, art self-efficacy, and perceived student engagement.
