abstract: Low-fee private schools (LFPS) in Kenya are expanding rapidly, serving a growing proportion of primary school students, particularly in urban and peri-urban areas. Despite this growth, student learning outcomes in many LFPS remain stagnant, with schools struggling to translate enrollment gains into meaningful improvements in foundational literacy and numeracy skills. The Incentives for Learning (IfL) program addresses this gap by embedding financial incentives into school loan structures. Schools that take out IfL loans can earn financial rewards for demonstrated improvements in student learning outcomes. We are conducting an RCT to assess the impact of the IfL program on student learning and related outcomes. 510 eligible low-fee private primary schools in Kenya were randomly assigned to receive offers of IfL loans (treatment) or standard loans (control) from their financial institutions. To determine the impact of the IfL program on learning outcomes, we are assessing over 5,000 students from treatment and control schools on foundational literacy and numeracy skills. As of this submission, endline data collection is ongoing and will finish in October 2026
experimental_design: Eligible schools were identified by FIs. (see the attached pre-analysis plans for details on eligibility). Selected schools were randomly assigned to receive an offer of an IfL loan or to the control group, which received the traditional loan offerings from their FI. Randomization proceeded in three batches between September to December 2025. The reason for three rounds of randomization was because, following the first round of randomization (Batch 1, N = 360), FIs identified some schools in the randomization sample that were not eligible for IfL loans, due to payment history, school closures, and other reasons. Thus, the FIs provided lists of additional eligible schools in November (Batch 2, N = 114) and December (Batch 3, N = 76), which were then randomized into treatment and control groups. In Batch 1, schools were assigned to one of 12 strata, defined by which FI’s portfolio they fell in, whether the school had baseline assessment scores from participating in the benchmarking exercise, whether the school’s baseline reading performance was above or below the median school’s performance, and whether the school’s average per-term fee was above or below the median school. In Batches 2 and 3, due to the smaller number of schools and the absence of baseline data, strata were only defined by FI portfolio. Within each stratum, 50% of schools were randomly assigned to the treatment group and the remainder to the control group. This process resulted in a study frame of 510 schools (255 treatment, 255 control). However, we faced two challenges with including all 510 schools in our endline sample. First, take-up was lower than expected. In our sample size calculations, we assumed that take-up would be at least 70%. However, by July 2026, only 48% of treatment schools had taken on an IfL loan. With 48% take-up, minimum detectable effects are roughly twice as large as when take-up is 100%. Since we believe that even modest impacts from IfL loans on learning outcomes are important to identify, this reduction in precision was unacceptable. Second, our budget assumed that we would conduct assessments in 300 schools. Given these challenges, we sought to remove schools from our sampling frame such that the resulting treatment sample would have higher take-up, without undermining the integrity of random assignment. We describe this process in detail in the attached pre-analysis plan. This process resulted in 267 schools remaining for our endline assessment. These 267 schools are well-balanced across treatment/control overall and within each FI subsample: PC treatment: N = 62, PC control: N = 62; JF treatment: N = 72; JF control: N = 71. Critically, the 134 treatment schools in our endline sample have higher take-up rates (70%), as of July 2026, than the original 255 schools assigned to treatment (48%). We will attempt to conduct assessments in all of these schools; however, based on our experiences during the benchmarking exercise and midline, we expect that a few schools may refuse to participate.
intervention: Low-fee private schools (LFPS) in Kenya are expanding rapidly, serving a growing proportion of primary school students, particularly in urban and peri-urban areas. Despite this growth, student learning outcomes in many LFPS remain stagnant, with schools struggling to translate enrollment gains into meaningful improvements in foundational literacy and numeracy skills. The Incentives for Learning (IfL) program addresses this gap by embedding financial incentives into school loan structures, making student performance a business priority for school proprietors. The program operates through two financial institutions (FIs), Jackfruit Finance and Premier Credit, that offer incentivized loans to eligible treatment schools in their portfolios. Schools that take out IfL loans can earn financial rewards for demonstrated improvements in student learning outcomes. The reward amount is based on the amount of the school’s loan and interest rate and is administered by applying the reward against the outstanding balance on their loan. By linking financial returns to educational performance through a tiered reward system, the program aims to sustainably raise education quality while supporting the financial viability of FIs and participating schools. More details are provided in the attached pre-analysis plan

abstract: Do women dampen career ambition to improve marriage prospects (``acting wife'') or to conform to gender norms about appropriate female behavior (``acting female'')? The mechanisms imply different behavior but are observationally equivalent when every male observer is a potential partner. We break this equivalence using Indonesia's near-absolute religious endogamy, randomizing third and final-year students into four-person discussion groups and comparing women's career signaling under same-religion male peers (marriageable), different-religion male peers (non-marriageable), and female-only peers, against privately elicited baseline ambition. Acting wife predicts dampening only under same-religion men; acting female, under men of either religion; social conformity, under any audience including women. We pre-register two primary contrasts against the female-only benchmark; secondary tests of social conformity and of privately measured beliefs about the marriage-market penalty; and falsification tests. This proof-of-concept speaks to female labor supply in a Muslim-majority, middle-income setting where marriage sharply reduces women's employment.
experimental_design: The study is a lab-in-the-field experiment with 440 third and final-year undergraduates at the Faculty of Economics and Business of a large public university in Indonesia, drawn equally from four demographic groups: Muslim men, Muslim women, Christian men and Christian women. Participants first complete a private online baseline survey. They are then invited to a career discussion workshop held over five rounds on separate days within a single week, each round comprising 88 participants in 22 four-person groups. There are six group types: all-female, all-male, same-religion mixed-gender, and different-religion mixed-gender, with the number of men in mixed groups varying from one to three. The same 22 configurations are implemented in every round. For women, the all-female groups are the reference condition; the contrast between same-religion and different-religion male peers isolates marriage-market signaling from a general male-audience effect, exploiting Indonesia's near-absolute religious endogamy. Men serve as a placebo group. The study is funded for five workshop rounds. Should additional funding be confirmed before data collection begins, the same 22 group configurations would be implemented in seven or eight rounds, scaling all cell sizes proportionally. The design, hypotheses and analysis plan are unchanged in that case, and the registration would be updated before data collection.
experimental_design_details: Within each of the four demographic groups, baseline respondents receive a computer-generated random invitation rank and are contacted in that order. A computer-generated schedule assigns confirmed respondents to workshop rounds using only their reported availability and the demographic quotas required by the 22 configurations, so scheduling determines when a participant attends but not which condition she is assigned to. After each round's roster is confirmed, a single program randomly permutes the 22 participants in each demographic group and matches them to the 22 slots requiring that profile. The allocation is fixed before participants arrive. A waitlist of 20 additional respondents per demographic group covers cancellations, with the next available waitlisted respondent of the same demographic group taking any vacated slot.
intervention: Participants attend a one-hour career discussion workshop in four-person groups. The intervention is the randomly assigned composition of the group: whether a woman's three peers are all female, include male peers of her own religion, or include male peers of a different religion. All other elements of the workshop — the ice-breaking activity, the career questionnaire, the facilitated career discussion, and the post-discussion survey — are identical across groups. Participants are informed that group composition is randomized but are not told that it varies by gender and religion.

abstract: AI tools are increasingly available to support student learning, but they carry a built-in pitfall: students are tempted to use them for quick, direct answers rather than genuine problem-solving. AI tutors can be designed to resist this shortcut-taking behavior, but doing so often comes at the cost of low student engagement when their use is voluntary. This study examines that tradeoff in the context of a custom AI tutor deployed in an introductory college physics course over a full semester. Students are randomly assigned to one of three AI tutors that vary in the way a direct answer can be provided. Five class sections are assigned to one control condition and four incentive conditions. Along one dimension, we compare student engagement and learning outcomes across sections that differ in how AI tutor use is incentivized. Along the second dimension, we examine whether delaying the availability of direct answers affects student performance, engagement with the AI tutor, and the tendency to seek shortcuts versus reason through problems incrementally. Student performance will be measured through proctored course exams without AI assistance, and homework performance will be recorded throughout the semester. Students will complete two detailed surveys after each midterm, reporting their experience with the AI tool. The results of the study aim to improve AI tutor designs and incentive conditions that can limit shortcut-seeking behavior while sustaining the engagement needed for productive learning in higher education.
experimental_design: The study uses a two-dimensional, semester-long design within a single introductory physics course, split into several sections (about 100 each). First, at the start of the semester, each of the 11 seating tables (in a section) used during in-class problem solving is assigned to one of three chatbot conversation styles, held fixed for that table all semester (students in that table remain fixed throughout the semester). Second, independent of table assignment, the incentive attached to chatbot use varies by class section across the semester: one baseline section with no chatbot (students instead use an in-person help center), and four subsequent sections following a 2x2 design crossing voluntary vs. incentivized in-class use with voluntary vs. incentivized at-home use. Learning outcomes are assessed using exams completed without AI assistance. Engagement outcomes are assessed using survey response and objective measure of classroom and office hour participation.
experimental_design_details: Conversation-style assignment: tables 1-3 = Socratic, tables 4-7 = Delayed-Didactic-Option (Offer Didactic Option after 5 rounds of Socratic), tables 8-11 = Didactic-Option (offered at conversation start and any time during the entire conversation). Incentive-condition assignment across the five sections: Section 1 = baseline/no chatbot; Section 2 = voluntary in-class + voluntary at-home; Section 3 = voluntary in-class + incentivized at-home; Section 4 = incentivized in-class + voluntary at-home; Section 5 = incentivized in-class + incentivized at-home. In-class incentives are equally awarded to all active users at a table. At-home incentives is awarded based on individual usage data. Incentive bonuses are tallied weekly and added to the gradebook. The specific mapping of conversation style to table, and the fact that styles vary at all, is not disclosed to students.
intervention: The intervention is a custom AI chatbot tutor made available to students in an introductory college physics course for use during in-class problem-solving sessions and for independent study at home throughout the semester. Students interact with one of three versions of the tutor, which differ in how readily they provide a direct answer to a question, ranging from a purely Socratic style that never reveals the solution to a style that offers a direct answer on request. Separately, the course varies whether using the tutor in class and/or at home is voluntary or tied to a small extra-credit incentive across the entire semester. One class section serves as a no-chatbot baseline.

Shortcut-seeking behavior will be constructed from the proportion of conversations (or conversation rounds) in which a student under the DO or DDO condition chooses the direct-answer option, and how quickly they do so. Learning outcomes will be constructed from standardized exam and homework scores, and, where relevant, from the graded reflection on the designated chatbot-use problem in each problem set. Text entries extracted from the chatbot will be used in text analysis.
primary_outcomes: (1) student performance on course exams (individual portions of two midterms, completed without AI assistance in-class) and graded homework/in-class problem-set items (completed with AI assistance at home); (2) chatbot engagement, measured by usage frequency, number of conversation turns, and word counts, both in class and at home; (3) Text content extracted from chatbot conversation (4) shortcut-seeking behavior, measured by the frequency and timing with which students opt into or request a direct (Didactic) answer rather than continuing Socratic dialogue (only in DO and DDO treatments); (5) other type of engagement activity (class attendance, Office Hour attendance through Physics Help Center, number of direct email inquiry with TAs or instructors) (6) self-reported experience and perceived learning, students' self-reported attitudes toward AI use from the two post-midterm surveys (both Likert scale and open ended text entry); graded reflections submitted for the designated chatbot-use homework problem (7) demographics, from the two post-midterm surveys
randomization_method: Students will be randomly assigned to conversation-style condition via a computer-generated random draw process conducted by the research team before the semester begins. Sections 1-5 are ordered based on the timing of the section on the day of the class.
randomization_unit: Two units of assignment: (1) seating table (11 tables per section) for the conversation-style dimension; (2) class section for the incentive dimension, applied to the whole section.

abstract: Older investors who are unaware of their cognitive decline can suffer substantial financial wealth losses. A simple model predicts that awareness should lead investors to reduce their risky-asset share and delegate financial control. In an experimental survey of affluent older US investors, we study whether information designed to raise awareness changes their stated financial decisions. We separately provide general information on the financial costs of memory decline and personalized feedback on respondents’ memory performance. We then study how these interventions affect stated preferences for portfolio risk and the delegation of financial decision-making, distinguishing between investors who are initially aware and unaware of their memory decline.
experimental_design: This is an individually randomized online survey experiment conducted among members of the American Association of Individual Investors (AAII). The survey was administered through Qualtrics from September 4 to October 15, 2025. Invitations were emailed to AAII members by the association, with reminders sent during the field period. Respondents first answered demographic and financial questions and self-rated their current memory. They then completed an eight-word memory task. After the memory task, respondents were assigned to an information experiment consisting of four arms: (1) no information, (2) personalized feedback on the respondent’s memory-task score, (3) educational information about the financial consequences of memory decline, and (4) both personalized feedback and educational information. Following treatment assignment, respondents answered a vignette question and a personal question about potential financial responses to cognitive decline. The vignette independently randomized the sex and age of the hypothetical individual (male/female × age 70/85). The order of the vignette and personal modules and the ordering of the response alternatives were also randomized.
intervention: After completing an eight-word memory recognition task, respondents were randomly assigned to one of four information arms. Score treatment: respondents were informed of their performance using the message, “In the previous test, you correctly recalled X out of 8 words!” Education treatment: respondents received information explaining that managing money requires concentration and memory, that serious memory decline is common among older adults, that investors who are unaware of cognitive decline may experience substantial portfolio losses, and that memory decline may also increase exposure to fraud and scams. Joint treatment: respondents received both personalized score feedback and the educational information. Control: respondents received neither piece of information.

abstract: Based on a discrete choice experiment conducted online among 800 respondents aged 40 and over, residing in France, this study aims to understand their preferences for different types of home care contracting arrangements, in the context of caring for a hypothetical elderly relative experiencing loss of autonomy. Two modes of home care provision are compared: direct employment (a direct contractual arrangement with the care worker) and the agency-based model (an indirect contractual arrangement via a service-providing organization). This comparison is based on five attributes: guarantee of service continuity, staff turnover, administrative burden, deviation from the agreed scope of intervention, and the hourly out-of-pocket cost, each with two or three levels. Each respondent is randomly assigned one of four situations: he or she is an informal caregiver - who helps with choosing between these two types of care - a dependent older relative who has severe motor limitations, moderate motor limitations, severe cognitive limitations, or moderate cognitive limitations. This design allows us to examine the heterogeneity of preferences according to the type of limitation (physical or cognitive) and its severity, as well as the possible existence of hypothetical bias, by comparing the preferences of hypothetical caregivers with those of actual caregivers of an elderly parent or spouse experiencing loss of autonomy.
experimental_design: Each respondent, aged 40 or over and recruited via the online platform Panel Labs, is randomly assigned 10 choice cards (the last of which must be the same as one of the first three, to check that the choices are consistent). These choice cards were generated using a D-efficient experimental design in SAS software, reducing the 1152 possible combinations to 36 (4 blocks of 9 choice cards). These cards present the two main types of home care services in France, namely direct employment and the agency-based model, with attribute levels randomized across cards. The order in which the two services are presented is also randomized. These attributes are the following: guaranteed continuity of care, staff turnover, deviation from the scope of te intervention, administrative burden, out-of-pocket (per hour). Each attribute may have between two and three levels. For each choice card, respondents are asked to indicate which home care service they would prefer for the hypothetical older dependent relative. At the end of each card, they are also asked to rate their certainty regarding their choice on a dedicated scale.
intervention: This discrete choice experiment aimed at eliciting the preferences of (hypothetical) informal caregivers regarding the contractual arrangements for home care service for an older dependent relative.

abstract: This study examines whether competing media narratives about South Korea's December 3, 2024 martial law declaration causally affect economic behavior, expectations, political attitudes, and institutional trust. Approximately 5,000 adult respondents will be recruited from a nationwide online panel designed to approximate the South Korean adult population. After completing pretreatment measures, respondents will be randomly assigned at the individual level, in approximately equal proportions, to one of three groups: a no-information control group; a crisis/accountability treatment presenting the declaration as an unconstitutional attack on democratic institutions; or a legitimizing/order-restoration treatment presenting it as an exceptional response to severe political obstruction. All respondents will then complete the same outcome modules. Primary outcomes include durable-goods purchase intentions, savings and financial-portfolio intentions, intentions to move assets abroad or prepare for overseas migration, risk and intertemporal preferences, labor-income and job-loss expectations, expectations regarding consumer prices, unemployment, and real GDP, policy preferences, institutional trust, government evaluations, and attitudes toward the martial law declaration. Secondary outcomes include subjective well-being and stress, interpersonal trust, ideal time allocation, expectations regarding South Korea's future child-rearing environment, fertility intentions, preferred information sources, presidential-election voting intention, and attitudes toward a potential special pardon of former President Yoon Suk Yeol. Attitudes toward the martial law declaration will be measured on the same 0-to-10 scale before treatment and near the end of the survey, after the main substantive outcome modules. The analysis will follow an intention-to-treat approach and compare each treatment with the control group as well as the two treatments directly.
experimental_design: This study is a single-wave online survey experiment with pretreatment and post-treatment measures. Approximately 5,000 adult respondents will be recruited from a nationwide online panel in South Korea. Before treatment, respondents will report demographic and socioeconomic characteristics, political attitudes and behavior, media use, economic circumstances, actual time use during the previous 24 hours, and their evaluation of the December 3, 2024 martial law declaration. Respondents will then be randomly assigned at the individual level to one of three groups: a no-information control group, a crisis/accountability framing group, or a legitimizing/order-restoration framing group. Following treatment assignment, all respondents will complete the same modules measuring economic behavior and intentions, economic preferences and expectations, policy preferences, subjective well-being, institutional trust, political attitudes, and ideal time allocation. The evaluation of the martial law declaration will be measured again near the end of the survey, after the main substantive outcome modules.
experimental_design_details: The study will recruit approximately 5,000 adult respondents through the Embrain online panel. The sample will be recruited to approximate the national adult population of South Korea using population-based sampling quotas. No demographic or regional subgroup will be intentionally oversampled. After providing consent, respondents will complete pretreatment questions covering demographic and socioeconomic characteristics, employment and income, household finances, political orientation and behavior, voting in the 2025 presidential election, usual sources of political and socioeconomic information, media trust, economic circumstances, and actual time use during the previous 24 hours. Immediately before treatment assignment, respondents will evaluate the December 3, 2024 martial law declaration on a 0-to-10 scale. The survey software will then randomly assign respondents at the individual level, in approximately equal proportions, to the no-information control group, the crisis/accountability framing group, or the legitimizing/order-restoration framing group. The control group will receive no passage. Each treatment group will view its assigned passage on a separate survey page before proceeding to the common outcome modules. All three groups will subsequently answer the same outcome questions. The survey will not include a factual manipulation check or an immediate post-treatment agreement question. After completing the main substantive outcome modules, respondents will answer the same 0-to-10 martial-law evaluation question used before treatment. They will then report preferred sources for obtaining additional information, current presidential-election voting intention, and attitudes toward a potential special pardon of former President Yoon Suk Yeol. Questions designed to assess possible experimenter-demand effects will appear at the end of the survey. The main treatment contrasts will compare each treatment group with the no-information control group and will directly compare the two treatment groups. All main estimates will follow an intention-to-treat approach based on randomized assignment.
intervention: This study examines how competing media narratives about South Korea’s December 3, 2024 martial law declaration affect political attitudes, economic expectations, and economic behavior. Adult respondents in South Korea are randomly assigned to one of three groups: a no-information control group or one of two treatment groups that read a short passage based on Korean news reports and opinion columns. One passage presents the declaration as an unconstitutional attack on democratic institutions, while the other presents it as an exceptional response to severe political obstruction intended to restore government functioning.

primary_outcome_explanation: Economic behavior and intention outcomes will be analyzed using their original response scales. These outcomes include the likelihood of purchasing durable goods over the next 12 months; the expected direction of change in savings or financial assets; desired percentage shares allocated to deposits, stocks, funds or ETFs, bonds, cryptocurrency, and other financial assets; the likelihood of shifting assets abroad; and the likelihood of seeking information or preparing for overseas migration. Risk preferences will be measured using general self-assessments and incentiveless lottery-choice items. Intertemporal preferences will be measured using self-assessed patience, willingness to give up a present benefit for a future benefit, and choices between smaller immediate and larger delayed payments. Components within each preference domain will be oriented in the same direction and combined into an equally weighted standardized index. Component-level estimates will also be reported. Personal economic expectations will include expected labor-income growth over the next 12 months and the respondent's subjective probability of losing their job, measured from 0 to 100 percent. Macroeconomic expectations will measure expected changes over the next 12 months in South Korea's consumer prices, unemployment rate, and real GDP. Each expectation will be elicited using a slider ranging from -20 to 20, where negative values indicate an expected decrease, zero indicates no expected change, and positive values indicate an expected increase. The policy-support index will combine four five-point items measuring support for income redistribution, stronger social safety nets, countercyclical fiscal spending, and active government intervention during economic crises. Items will be coded so that higher values indicate greater support. Institutional trust will be measured separately for each listed institution. An equally weighted standardized index of trust in governmental institutions will combine trust in the government, National Assembly, courts, Constitutional Court, National Election Commission, and police. Evaluations of the former and current governments will be analyzed separately. Evaluation of the December 3, 2024 martial law declaration will be measured on the same 0-to-10 scale before treatment and near the end of the survey, after the main substantive outcome modules. Higher values indicate a more positive evaluation. The primary analysis will use the post-treatment evaluation as the outcome and control for the corresponding pretreatment evaluation. The within-respondent change in evaluation will also be reported. For each multi-item index, component outcomes will be oriented so that higher values have a common interpretation, standardized using the control-group mean and standard deviation, and averaged with equal weights. Individual component outcomes will be reported alongside the indices.
primary_outcomes: The primary endpoints are: (1) economic behavior and intentions, including the likelihood of purchasing durable goods, expected changes in savings and financial assets, desired financial-portfolio shares, intentions to shift assets abroad, and intentions to seek information or prepare for overseas migration; (2) risk and intertemporal preferences; (3) personal economic expectations, including expected labor-income growth and subjective job-loss probability; (4) preferences regarding income redistribution, social safety nets, fiscal stabilization, and government intervention in the economy; (5) macroeconomic expectations regarding changes in South Korea’s consumer prices, unemployment rate, and real GDP over the next 12 months; (6) trust in political and social institutions and evaluations of government performance; and (7) respondents’ evaluation of the December 3, 2024 martial law declaration.
randomization_method: Randomization will be implemented electronically by the survey software after respondents complete all pretreatment questions. Eligible respondents will be assigned with equal probability to one of the three experimental arms: the no-information control group, the crisis/accountability framing group, or the legitimizing/order-restoration framing group. Neither respondents nor researchers will select the assigned condition.
randomization_unit: The unit of randomization is the individual survey respondent.
secondary_outcome_explanation: The subjective well-being index will combine measures of current happiness, meaning in life, and overall quality of life. The stress and uncertainty index will combine economic stress, stress arising from the political and social situation, uncertainty about the future, expected personal instability, relationship-related stress, perceived lack of control over stress, and lack of peace of mind. Items will be oriented so that higher values have a common interpretation before standardization and averaging. Individual components will also be reported. Interpersonal trust will be measured using ratings of trust in neighbors and in people encountered in public. The perceived importance of institutional independence and checks and balances will be analyzed as a separate outcome. For time allocation, respondents report actual hours spent during the previous 24 hours on 14 activities before treatment and their ideal daily allocation across the same activities after treatment. Each activity will be analyzed separately. The post-treatment ideal allocation will be examined both in levels, controlling for the corresponding pretreatment actual allocation, and as the difference between ideal and actual hours. Expectations about the future child-rearing environment and intentions to have a child or an additional child will be analyzed separately using their original response categories. Non-substantive responses such as “not applicable” and “prefer not to answer” will be treated as missing in scalar analyses. Stress attributed to reported problems during the recent local-election voting process will be analyzed on its original five-point scale. Information-source outcomes will be constructed from respondents' ranked selections of up to three sources. For each source, we will construct indicators for being selected and for being ranked first, and compare post-treatment preferred sources with pretreatment sources normally used. Presidential-election voting intention will be analyzed as a categorical post-treatment outcome. We will also construct indicators for movement toward or away from the major parties by comparing current voting intention with the respondent's reported vote in the 2025 presidential election. Attitudes toward a potential special pardon of former President Yoon Suk Yeol will be measured on a five-point scale ranging from strong opposition to strong support and analyzed as a separate outcome.
secondary_outcomes: The secondary endpoints are: (1) subjective well-being, including happiness, meaning in life, and overall quality of life; (2) economic stress, political and social stress, uncertainty about the future, expected personal stability, relationship-related stress, perceived control over stress, and peace of mind; (3) interpersonal trust; (4) the perceived importance of institutional independence and checks and balances; (5) ideal daily time allocation across work, job search, household production, caregiving, education, leisure, civic participation, religious activity, and social interaction; (6) expectations about South Korea's future child-rearing environment and fertility intentions; (7) stress attributed to reported problems during the recent local-election voting process; (8) preferred sources for obtaining additional political, social, and economic information; and (9) current presidential-election voting intention; and (10) attitudes toward a potential special pardon of former President Yoon Suk Yeol.
title: Political Narratives and Economic Behavior: A Survey Experiment on South Korea’s 2024 Martial Law

abstract: We study strategic transmission decisions in networks using a laboratory experiment. Participants interact in a network in which they observe their own position and the states of other players. In each decision situation, active participants hold a token and choose which eligible neighbor receives it. This choice changes the state of the recipient and may affect subsequent opportunities and outcomes for the decision-maker. By experimentally varying the network structure and the states of players within the network, we examine how the characteristics and network positions of potential recipients shape transmission decisions. The experiment is primarily conducted using a neutral framing based on colors and tokens, with additional sessions designed to examine the role of employment framing.
experimental_design: Participants take part in laboratory sessions consisting of a sequence of network games. The experimental design systematically varies network structure, participants' positions within the network, and the initial distribution of states across participants. The design includes both short-run networks, in which participants interact for two periods, and longer-run networks, in which interaction extends over a larger number of periods. Different types of sessions combine different sets of networks and interaction horizons.
experimental_design_details: In each session, participants interact simultaneously in a series of networks. In each network, participants make decisions over a predetermined number of periods. The dynamics within each network are as follows. Period t=1. 1) Each network starts with a predetermined distribution of states across participants. Both the network structure and the initial distribution of states are part of the experimental design and vary systematically across networks to identify the mechanisms of interest. Participants observe the entire network structure, their own position, and the states of all other participants. Each participant can be in one of three states: green with a token, green without a token, or red. 2) Participants who are green and hold a token simultaneously decide which of their red neighbors (direct contacts) to transmit their token to. Participants in all other states make no decision. A red participant who receives at least one token becomes green. 3) Once all decisions have been implemented, the resulting outcomes of the decisions and the corresponding states are observed by the participants. These are the states that matter for payment. 4) Each green participant becomes red with probability (b). Second, each participant independently experiences an event with probability (a). If the participant is red when this event occurs, they become green; if the participant is green, they receive a token that they can transmit to one of their red neighbors in the next period. Period t=2. The second period starts with the distribution of states resulting from the previous period. The different processes from the previous period are then repeated. We consider short-run networks, in which participants interact for two periods, and long-run networks, in which interactions extend over a larger number of periods. In short-run networks, the interaction ends after (t=2), and participants proceed to the next network. In longer-run networks, the procedure described for (t=2) is repeated in each subsequent period until the predetermined number of periods is reached. Payments. Participants receive a fixed participation payment and an additional positive payment that depends on their state in the game across the different periods and networks. If a period is selected for payment, the participant receives the additional payment if his/her state after the decisions is green. Monetary incentives therefore depend on the participant's state in the network. Sessions. The experimental design comprises several types of sessions, which differ in the networks implemented and the mechanisms they are designed to study. A common set of “core” networks is designed to separately identify the role of three mechanisms: the degree of a participant's neighbors, local clustering, and the initial state or wealth of their neighbors. We will run three networks devoted to each mechanism. The core of the experiment therefore consists of nine networks, in each of which participants interact for two periods. Part of the sessions will combine these nine core networks with additional networks in which these mechanisms operate jointly, either in the same direction or by generating conflicting incentives. Other sessions combine core networks with persistence networks. The latter are played for approximately 15 periods and are designed to examine whether the effects identified in short-run interactions persist when interaction extends over a longer time horizon. Additional sessions examine long-run predictions related to individuals' positions and network topology, including the role of bridge positions and average path length. In each of these sessions, participants interact in networks for approximately 15 periods per network. Another type of session is devoted exclusively to a single larger network whose structure has characteristics closer to those observed in real-world networks. Unlike the other networks, participants interact in this same network throughout the entire session, with the dynamics described above repeated until the end of the session. Finally, the last type of session examines the robustness of the results to framing. These sessions reproduce the core-plus-conflicting-effects session and the core-plus-persistence session, while explicitly introducing a labor-market context, in which the green and red states represent employment and unemployment respectively, and the tokens are job offers. Experimental Design Details Transmission decisions are made simultaneously. Participants therefore do not observe other participants' current transmission decisions before making their own. As a result, a participant may receive tokens from multiple neighbors in the same period; receiving more than one token has no additional effect. The order of networks varies randomly with the following exceptions. Core networks are always presented as a block before conflict or persistence networks because they test the main hypotheses, and they are simpler and facilitate participants' understanding of the task, Also, we make sure that the networks that represent the simplest and the strongest examples of the mechanisms are presented in the first position (the only totally independent observations). The rest is randomized. In the persistence sessions, the order of the two persistence networks is alternated across sessions. In the sessions designed to study long-run network properties, the order of the four networks is randomized. The framing sessions exactly reproduce the network order of two corresponding neutral sessions to facilitate comparability across framing conditions.
intervention: The experiment will consist of more than 10 in-person laboratory sessions conducted in the experimental economics laboratory of the University Jaume I. Each session will last approximately 90 minutes. Before the experimental task begins, participants will receive detailed instructions explaining the rules of the experiment. Participants will then be presented with a sequence of networks. In each network, participants will observe the network structure, their assigned position, and the states of the other players. Assignment of positions will be assigned randomly and anonymously in every network. Players can have three states, red, green or green with token. Their state can change during a period. If they are green right after the decisions, they will receive a monetary compensation if that period gets selected for payment at the end. In every period, each green with token player will pass the token to a connected player that is red, if possible. If there is several connected red players, she will choose which one to pass the token to. A red player turns green when passed a token. Afterwards, players’ states may also change with given probabilities: red players may turn green, green players may turn red, and green players may receive a token. The experimental conditions will vary the structure of the network and the distribution of players' states, allowing us to study how the characteristics and network positions of potential recipients affect transmission decisions. Additional sessions will use an employment framing to examine whether transmission decisions depend on the framing of the experimental environment. Participants will receive monetary compensation for their participation by random selection of one or two periods for payment.

We will also obtain basic participants' demographic characteristics and information like gender and risk preferences. Finally, participants will complete a post-experimental questionnaire about the considerations and strategies underlying their transmission decisions.
title: Strategic Information Transmission in Networks: A Laboratory Experiment.

abstract: Existing research has largely explained variation in climate policy attitudes through environmental preferences, political ideology, and partisan identification. While these measures are widely used, their interpretation may depend on the socio-economic and institutional contexts in which respondents are embedded. Less attention has been paid to how citizens interpret climate policy in political contexts where climate issues remain weakly politicized and partisan signals are ambiguous. In many developing countries, climate policy is not represented by a distinct political party or stable partisan coalition comparable to those found in many Western democracies. As a result, climate policy may be less deeply embedded in established political identities, and citizens may have fewer partisan cues through which to interpret its costs and benefits. We argue that, in such contexts, the structure of economic insecurity becomes particularly important for shaping how citizens respond to political signals and evaluate climate policy. Where employment and income are insecure, the anticipated material consequences of climate regulation may provide a more immediate basis for evaluating policy than partisan endorsements. Individuals who face greater economic insecurity are therefore expected to perceive higher personal costs from regulatory change. Consequently, when climate policy is presented, political cues are expected to exert weaker effects among economically vulnerable respondents, who are likely to perceive the policy through the lens of their immediate material consequences. By contrast, economically secure individuals experience lower perceived adjustment costs and are therefore more likely to rely on political and ideological cues when evaluating the same policy proposal. The influence of political cues should therefore depend not only on the content of the cue but also on the economic position of the individuals receiving it. We further argue that an explicit partisan endorsement can change how citizens process otherwise identical policy information, but that the extent to which such a cue matters depends on the economic risks associated with policy change. We test these arguments using a randomized survey experiment conducted among private-sector employees in Türkiye, where climate policy has historically occupied a relatively limited place in partisan competition despite increasing policy salience. Respondents are randomly assigned to one of two versions of an identical climate policy proposal that differs only in whether the policy is explicitly associated with the incumbent government. The policy content, objectives, and expected consequences remain constant across conditions, allowing us to isolate the causal effect of political cueing. We estimate both the average treatment effect of the political cue and heterogeneous treatment effects across individuals with different levels of economic vulnerability. Our findings show that an explicit political cue increases average policy support, but that this effect is systematically conditioned by respondents’ economic circumstances. Economically vulnerable respondents are less responsive to the political cue and show greater sensitivity to the underlying material costs of regulation. We contribute to the political economy of climate policy by showing how the relationship between political cues and climate policy support depends on the broader political and economic context. In settings where climate policy lacks strong partisan representation, labor market insecurity can become an important basis through which citizens evaluate the potential consequences of climate regulation. Methodologically, the paper advances an experimental framework for disentangling expressed policy support from context-dependent interpretation in survey responses, demonstrating that part of observed variation in climate policy attitudes reflects differences in interpretive processes rather than substantive differences in environmental preferences, and highlighting the importance of accounting for structural economic circumstances when evaluating the comparability of survey-based measures across populations.
experimental_design: The study employs a between-subjects randomized survey experiment to identify the causal effect of an incumbent political cue on support for a proposed climate policy. In both conditions, respondents will read an identical vignette describing a proposed climate-related environmental regulation affecting large industrial firms. The treatment condition explicitly attributes the proposed policy to the AK Party government, whereas the control condition presents the same policy without a partisan attribution. All other elements of the vignette are held constant across conditions. Randomization occurs at the individual respondent level using simple random assignment with equal allocation to treatment and control (1:1). Following exposure to the vignette, respondents will report their level of support for the proposed policy and answer additional questions measuring their interpretation of the policy and perceived consequences. The study is designed to estimate the causal effect of an incumbent political cue on climate policy support and to examine whether this effect varies according to respondents' pre-treatment economic vulnerability.
experimental_design_details: This study employs a between-subjects randomized survey experiment designed to estimate the causal effect of an incumbent political cue on support for a proposed climate policy in Türkiye and to examine whether this effect is moderated by respondents' pre-treatment economic vulnerability. The unit of randomization is the individual respondent. Eligible respondents who enter and complete the survey will be randomly assigned by the survey platform to one of two experimental conditions using simple random assignment with equal allocation probabilities: Pr(Treatment) = 0.50 and Pr(Control) = 0.50. The target sample size is 2,000 completed interviews, yielding approximately 1,000 respondents in each experimental condition. In both conditions, respondents receive the same vignette describing a proposed environmental regulation affecting large industrial enterprises in Türkiye. The vignette provides the same background information concerning climate change and recent environmental developments in the European Union, describes the same proposed policy, and presents the same anticipated environmental benefits and potential economic consequences. The sole experimental difference between the two conditions is the attribution of the proposed policy to the incumbent government. In the treatment condition, the vignette explicitly states that the proposed policy is being prepared by the AK Party government. In the control condition, the identical policy is presented without explicit partisan attribution. No other substantive elements of the vignette—including the policy description, rationale, environmental objective, or anticipated economic consequences—will differ between conditions. Following exposure to the vignette, respondents will complete questions measuring their level of support for the proposed policy, their interpretation of the policy, perceived economic consequences, and other post-treatment measures specified in the preregistered analysis plan. The primary outcome is respondents' expressed support for the proposed policy, measured on a five-point scale ranging from strongly oppose to strongly support. The primary confirmatory moderator is perceived job insecurity, measured before treatment assignment. Respondents are asked how concerned they are about losing their current job, with responses ranging from "not at all concerned" to "very concerned." This measure is used as the preregistered primary operationalization of economic vulnerability. For the primary heterogeneous-treatment-effect analysis, the effect of treatment assignment is estimated as a function of respondents' pre-treatment level of perceived job insecurity. The primary confirmatory analyses estimate: (1) the average treatment effect of the incumbent political cue on expressed climate policy support; (2) the interaction between treatment assignment and perceived job insecurity; and (3) differences in respondents' reported interpretive frames across treatment conditions and levels of economic vulnerability. Randomization occurs independently at the individual level. To improve precision, the primary regression models will adjust for pre-treatment baseline environmental attitudes, age, gender, and education. Their inclusion is intended to improve estimation precision rather than to identify the causal effect of treatment. The principal causal estimand is the difference in policy support attributable to randomized exposure to the incumbent political cue, including heterogeneous effects according to pre-treatment perceived job insecurity. The survey questionnaire and all treatment materials will be finalized before the start of data collection.

abstract: STEM access and persistence remain highly unequal for academically talented students, especially those from low-income households, where safe, affordable after-school instruction and mentoring are often infeasible. We evaluate two scalable models of STEM support for high-achieving, low-income adolescents (ages 14–16) in rural Karnataka, India. Eligible students — identified through a state merit exam and an in-person screening assessment — are individually randomized into one of three groups: (1) a full intervention combining tablets, synchronous online instruction and annual residential STEM-preparation retreats; (2) a residential-retreat-only arm, receiving the same annual retreats but no tablets or academic instruction; or (3) a control group receiving no program component. We use program registration and screening records for baseline balance checks, a phone-based tracking survey, and a Grade 9 midline assessment (after roughly eight months of treatment) to measure learning, engagement, STEM identity and self-efficacy, educational and career aspirations, and parental expectations and support. Longer-run outcomes including Class 10 board exam scores and Class 11 science-stream choice are tracked in endline. The study will generate evidence on whether a lower-cost residential STEM-preparation model is sufficient to shift STEM persistence or whether sustained academic instruction and technology access are needed, with implications for reducing STEM talent misallocation in low-resource settings.
experimental_design: The goal of this study is to examine the effect of two scalable STEM-support models — a full intervention combining tablets, synchronous online instruction, and residential retreats (T1), versus a residential-retreat-only model (T2) — on the academic and STEM-related outcomes of high-achieving, low-income Grade 9 students in rural Karnataka, India. To estimate these effects, we conduct a stratified randomized controlled trial at the individual student level. We randomize 1,350 eligible students entering Class 9 (ages 14–16), drawn from 13 districts in Karnataka (Belagavi, Chikkodi, Dharwad, Dadag, Haveri, Bagalkot, Vijayapura, Uttar Kannada, Sirsi, Davangere, Bengaluru, Yadgir, and Raichur). Students were identified through the implementing partner's (Rajalakshmi Children Foundation) selection process, using National Means-cum-Merit Scholarship (NMMS) results, Pratibha Poshak program registration records, and partner screening data. Eligibility required scoring at least 55% in Class 8, passing the NMMS exam, and belonging to a household earning less than USD 250/month. This sample of 1,350 students was stratified by district and gender, and students within each stratum were individually randomized to one of three arms: 1. Control arm (449) 2. Full Intervention arm, T1 (449) 3. Residential STEM-Preparation arm, T2 (452) We use Pratibha Poshak program registration records and partner screening data — covering pre-treatment academic performance, demographic, household, and school information — to confirm balance across arms.
intervention: Eligible students (Class 9, ages 14–16) from low-income households in rural Karnataka are individually randomized, stratified by district and gender, into one of three groups. Students in the full intervention arm (T1) receive tablets, participate in approximately 12 hours per week of synchronous online instruction in English, Physics, Mathematics, and Analytical Reasoning, access asynchronous content through a learning management system, and attend annual three-day residential STEM-preparation retreats. Students in the residential-only arm (T2) attend the same annual retreats — covering STEM career-pathway information, analytical reasoning, peer-network formation, and role-model exposure — but receive no tablets, LMS access, or academic instruction. Students in the control group receive no program component during the study period.

abstract: Our study examines how Russian citizens evaluate political candidates under conditions of war and political repression. The full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 substantially transformed Russia’s domestic political environment, raising concerns that conventional surveys may overstate support for government and wartime policies because respondents face social and legal risks when expressing dissent. To address these challenges, the study employs a forced-choice conjoint experiment in which respondents evaluate pairs of hypothetical State Duma candidates whose profiles vary randomly across eight demographic and policy attributes. These include age, gender, occupation, positions on the war and its termination, internet and social-media restrictions, migration, budget priorities, and mobilization. The experiment estimates the relative importance of competing wartime and domestic policy preferences while reducing the salience of sensitive political questions. The study also investigates drivers of electoral turnout in Russia, distinguishing between abstention arising from candidate similarity (indifference) and dissatisfaction with the available candidates (alienation). Pre-registered hypotheses focus on preferences toward mobilization, war termination, veteran candidates, migration restrictions, social spending, and information controls, as well as differences across media consumption, age, gender, and education.
experimental_design: Forced-choice conjoint experiment.
intervention: Each respondent is shown six tasks asking to choose between two State Duma candidates with given characteristics, and asked which of them they would choose if the elections to be held. After that they are asked if they would turn out at all if these two candidates were the only ones on the ballot.

abstract: Universal health coverage has expanded across low- and middle-income countries, yet coverage has not widened access for all groups in practice. School-age children are one such group, often falling outside programmes designed for the under-fives, but carrying a substantial burden of malaria, anaemia and other treatable illness. This study evaluates a comprehensive school health programme delivered in rural Zambia, which aims to overcome this access barrier. The programme constructs dedicated health rooms in primary schools and trains and deploys school-based health workers who provide preventive care, screening, treatment and health education, supported by a clinical decision support tool and a priority referral arrangement with local clinics. School-age children in Zambia face a high burden of malaria, anaemia and other treatable illness, but are poorly served by facility-based care; the programme aims to bring timely, appropriate care to the place where children already are. We evaluate the programme through parallel-arm cluster-randomised trials in which the school is the unit of randomisation. We randomised 120 schools across four districts of Northern Province in June 2025 to the school health programme or pure control using stratified randomisation, with strata defined by district and by distance to the nearest health facility. Data come from repeated unannounced attendance spot checks and prospective household health diaries with an accompanying biomarker survey. Co-primary outcomes are use of healthcare — unconditional, and conditional on illness requiring care — and school attendance. Secondary outcomes cover malaria and anaemia prevalence, illness burden, and menstrual health. Analysis is intention-to-treat.
experimental_design: Randomisation: A school census identified 139 eligible schools in programme expansion regions. We randomly selected 120 from this list and these were randomised in June 2025 using a stratified procedure, with strata defined by district and by distance to the nearest health facility (above or below 1.5 km) and the school as the unit of randomisation. Treatment arms: The trial has two arms - full school health programme (60 schools) and a pure control arm (60 schools), split evenly within every stratum. Intervention was delivered in Term 3 2025 (September-November) Data collection activities: We collect data using two field instruments: the unannounced attendance spot checks (yielding register-based, cross-sectional attendance) and the health diaries and biomarker survey. Spot checks are repeated across terms 1, 2 and 3 in 2026, and terms 1 and 2 in 2027. Diaries are conducted in terms 1 and 2 2027, splitting the sample of schools randomly in half (preserving treatment allocation) which provides seasonal variation. Diaries follow a randomly selected sample of up to 24 learners per school, split evenly across gender and age groups, for 8 weeks with symptoms recorded daily; biomarkers are collected at the end of the diary periods so that any illness detected and treated does not affect the diary records. We do not collect a baseline survey.
intervention: The school health programme, delivered by the Zambian Government in partnership with Healthy Learners (HL), seeks to make schools an entry point into the healthcare system by training and supporting teachers as community health workers, tasked to engage with local communities, promote health behaviours, and refer sick learners to health facilities. The main components of the programme are described in detail below. 1) School Health Workers: In each school, teachers are selected to become school health workers (SHWs). Following a two-week training, SHWs perform two main roles: 1) they deliver health talks in all classes and coordinate the delivery of preventative care with local clinics (e.g. deworming campaigns); 2) they take turns to be on duty in the ‘school health room’, a purposefully constructed building where sick students can receive care and rest if needed. With the help of a tablet-based clinical decision support system (CDSS) which does not follow a branching logic to minimize input errors and uses Bayesian logic to weigh reported symptoms (Finette, McLaughlin et al. 2019), SHWs follow a suggested course of action which builds upon recommended WHO guidelines. At the end of each screening, a SHW follows one of three courses of action: - They provide reassurance that the symptoms are self-limiting and that no specific treatment is required beyond possible symptomatic relief medicines that they can dispense (e.g. paracetamol); - They provide treatment for a limited number of conditions (malaria, diarrhoea, schistosomiasis, pneumonia, conjunctivitis), - They refer the child to the public clinic associated to the school to be further assessed by a healthcare professional. The referral can be normal, in which case the guardian of the child is contacted and asked to take their child to the clinic, or urgent for severe conditions (in which case the SHW may accompany the child to the clinic themselves). This system ensures efficient health-seeking behaviours by school-age children, limiting unnecessary visits to the clinic (overuse) and lack of or delays in required referral (underuse). 2) Priority referral system: With the support from the Ministry of Health and engagement with the local clinics, children referred by SHWs are given priority by health care workers who see them within 30 minutes of arriving at the facility. This “fast-track” referral system is facilitated by the referral form containing information about symptoms and suggested diagnosis by the CDSS. The system ensures that parents do not have to waste precious time taking their children to facilities. 3) Monitoring of children’s illness. A proactive system is set up to actively monitor the absenteeism of children due to illness. A ‘buddy system’ is introduced in each class, whereby children are allocated to a small group and encouraged to signal to SHWs when one of the members of their buddy group is absent due to illness. SHWs follow-up with parents of signalled children to discuss health-seeking options. After a sick child is referred to a facility, SHWs receive a feedback form filled by the clinic which help them follow up with the parents to discuss adherence to treatment and return to school. 4) Preventive programs: SHWs coordinate with local health authorities and clinics to ensure the timely and smooth delivery of deworming drugs, which in theory should be provided routinely by health authorities.

secondary_outcome_explanation: Malaria prevalence (health-diary biomarker survey): a binary indicator equal to 1 if the RDT is positive for P. falciparum, non-falciparum species, or a mixed infection. Moderate-to-severe anaemia (health-diary biomarker survey): a binary indicator equal to 1 when measured hemoglobin (HemoCue, g/dL) falls below WHO thresholds. Haemoglobin is first adjusted for elevation using the WHO (2024) continuous adjustment, defined in g/L as 0.0056384 times elevation in metres plus 0.0000003 times elevation squared, evaluated at each school's recorded GPS elevation and subtracted from the measured value. Moderate-to-severe anaemia is considered when adjusted haemoglobin is below 11.0 g/dL, a threshold common to all age bands represented in our sample. Illness burden and recovery (health diaries): We will construct two measures from the daily roster's symptom records. The first is the share of diary days on which the child reported any symptom, defined for every child in the diary sub-sample including those who are never ill, and so requiring no conditioning on illness status. The second is episode duration, the number of consecutive symptom days in an illness episode, estimated as a discrete-time hazard of symptom resolution so that episodes still ongoing at the end of the observation window contribute their observed days rather than being dropped; episodes beginning on day 1 are excluded as truncated, as elsewhere. We report both overall and separately for serious episodes. Because duration is defined only among children who fall ill, and illness is itself a potential programme outcome, we read the episode-level estimates as characterising the mechanism behind the child-level share rather than as a causal contrast in their own right. Illness-related absence (health-diary): the diary's daily records flag whether the child attended school each day and record the reason for each absent day. The reasons are: illness (1), was menstruating (2), farming (3), school closure or school event (4), bad weather (5), religious reasons (6), market day (7), public holiday (8), fishing (9), mining (10), working with parents (11), no uniform/shoes/books (12), and other (-97). We treat a day as a health-related absence when the reason is illness (1) or menstruation (2). We restrict the sample to school days by dropping weekends and public holidays. Our measure is the share of the child's school days in the diary window lost to health-related absence: health-related absence days divided by total school days observed.

abstract: We conduct a survey experiment on household demand for new digital financial products in Japan and the United States. Despite the rapid growth of these products, little is known about which product characteristics households actually value, or how beliefs about risk shape those valuations. We field an online survey to approximately 22,000 respondents aged 20-79 (16,000 in Japan, 6,000 in the United States), oversampling current holders of new digital financial products in Japan. The survey elicits awareness, investment experience, holdings and portfolio shares for both conventional and new digital financial products, together with financial literacy, risk preferences, time preferences, and measures of budgeting and financial planning. Embedded in the survey is a randomized information-provision experiment: respondents are randomly assigned either to a control condition or to one of two conditions in which they receive brief factual information before completing a repeated stated-preference choice task over hypothetical products whose characteristics are randomly varied. We estimate how product characteristics map into stated demand, how randomly assigned information shifts those valuations, and how both vary with respondent characteristics and across the two countries.
experimental_design: Cross-sectional online survey experiment fielded simultaneously in Japan and the United States. Respondents aged 20-79 are drawn from online panels with sex and age quotas matching population proportions; in Japan, 6,000 of the 16,000 respondents are separately screened on current holdings of new digital financial products. After background modules on holdings, financial literacy and preferences, respondents read a standardised product explanation, are randomly assigned to one of three information conditions, and complete 14 binary choice tasks between two hypothetical products whose characteristics are randomly drawn, with levels randomised independently across tasks.
intervention: Within an online survey, respondents are randomly assigned to one of three conditions immediately before a repeated stated-preference choice task over hypothetical new digital financial products. The control group receives no additional information. Each of the two treatment groups receives a short, factually accurate statement about a different source of risk relevant to holding such products, displayed once, immediately before the choice task and repeated in the task instructions. All other survey content, including the choice task itself, is identical across the three conditions. The intervention is delivered on screen by the survey firm as part of the questionnaire; there is no follow-up contact with respondents.

abstract: Women hold just 18.5 percent of seats in the Brazilian Federal Senate. This project tests whether making that gap salient through a short digital ad, "Did you know women are more than 50 percent of the population but only 16 percent of Congress? Think about that when you vote," changes vote share for female Senate candidates in a live, competitive election. Prior evidence that this message shifts votes comes from the 2024 Brazilian municipal elections (De Albuquerque, Finan, Jha, Karpuska and Trebbi 2025, NBER Working Paper 33859); this project provides the first test of the same treatment in a federal, higher stakes race. In 200 municipalities in the state of Minas Gerais, municipalities are matched into pairs on the first principal component of local covariates and randomly assigned within pair, 100 to treatment and 100 to control. Treated municipalities receive a geo-targeted Instagram ad for one week, ending before the electoral silence period. The primary outcome is municipal-level vote share for female Senate candidates in the 2026 election.
experimental_design: The sample frame comprises 200 municipalities in Minas Gerais. Municipalities were matched into pairs by nearest neighbor on the first principal component of municipal covariates, then randomly assigned within pair, 100 to treatment and 100 to control. Treated municipalities receive the ad described above. Control municipalities receive no advertising.
experimental_design_details: The first principal component was estimated in Stata from population, 2010 HDI, urbanization rate, internet coverage, 2024 progressive vote share, and 2022 right-wing presidential vote share, all measured before randomization. Municipalities were ranked by this component within Minas Gerais and matched into 100 nearest-neighbor pairs. Within each pair, one municipality was randomly assigned to treatment and one to control using a fixed random seed. The 200-municipality frame itself was constructed by comparing, for each of the 853 municipalities in Minas Gerais, the combined vote share of candidates from left-leaning parties against the combined vote share of candidates from far-right parties in the 2024 mayoral election, keeping municipalities where the left-leaning total exceeded the far-right total.
intervention: Treated municipalities receive a single digital ad on Instagram, delivered through Meta Ads Manager, informing residents that women hold only 18.5 percent of seats in the Brazilian Federal Senate. The ad text reads "Did you know women are more than 50 percent of the population but only 16 percent of Congress? Think about that when you vote." The ad targets adult Instagram users residing in the treated municipality, with no further segmentation by sex or age. It runs for one week, from September 25 to October 1, 2026, ending before the electoral silence period ahead of the October 4 general election. Control municipalities receive no advertising from this campaign.

abstract: Women hold just 18.5 percent of seats in the Brazilian Federal Senate. This project tests whether a short digital ad naming that gap, "Did you know women are more than 50 percent of the population but only 16 percent of Congress? Think about that when you vote," changes vote share for female Senate candidates, and whether the effect depends on which audience receives the message. In 398 municipalities across the states of Maranhão and Ceará, matched by nearest neighbor on local covariates within state, municipalities are randomly assigned to one of four arms, an ad targeted to women, an ad targeted to men, an ad shown to all adults regardless of sex, or no advertising. Prior evidence that this message shifts votes comes from the 2024 Brazilian municipal elections (De Albuquerque, Finan, Jha, Karpuska and Trebbi 2025, NBER Working Paper 33859); this project tests whether targeting the message by gender changes who it moves. The primary outcome is municipal-level vote share for female Senate candidates in the 2026 election, compared across arms.
experimental_design: The sample frame comprises 398 municipalities in the states of Maranhão and Ceará. Within each state, municipalities were grouped into nearest-neighbor blocks on the first principal component of municipal covariates and randomly assigned to one of four arms, a women-targeted ad, a men-targeted ad, an all-adults ad, or no advertising (control), in an approximate ratio of 100 women-targeted, 100 men-targeted, 50 all-adults, and 148 control. Two municipalities, the state capitals of Maranhão and Ceará, were assigned to the all-adults arm by design rather than by random draw. Treated municipalities receive the ad described above, targeted according to their assigned arm. Control municipalities receive no advertising.
experimental_design_details: The first principal component was estimated in Stata from population, 2010 HDI, urbanization rate, internet coverage, and 2022 right-wing presidential vote share, all measured before randomization, excluding the two forced capitals from the estimation sample. Within each state, municipalities were sorted by this component with a random tie-break and grouped into blocks of 8, assigned in a 3 control, 2 women-targeted, 2 men-targeted, 1 all-adults ratio within each full block, using a fixed random seed. Municipalities left over after full blocks were assigned to hit exact per-state targets of 148 control, 100 women-targeted, 100 men-targeted, and 50 all-adults nationally. Fortaleza (Ceará) and São Luís (Maranhão) were removed from the randomizable pool and assigned directly to the all-adults arm before the random draw, for programmatic visibility reasons. Because these two municipalities are far larger and more urban than the rest of the sample, analyses of the all-adults arm should be reported both including and excluding them.
intervention: Treated municipalities receive a digital ad on Instagram, delivered through Meta Ads Manager, informing residents that women hold only 18.5 percent of seats in the Brazilian Federal Senate. The ad text reads "Did you know women are more than 50 percent of the population but only 16 percent of Congress? Think about that when you vote." Depending on the treatment arm a municipality is assigned to, the ad targets Instagram users who self-identify as women, users who self-identify as men, or all adult users regardless of sex, always restricted to residents of the treated municipality and over 18 years. It runs for one week, from September 25 to October 1, 2026, ending before the electoral silence period ahead of the October 4 general election. Control municipalities receive no advertising from this campaign.

abstract: This experiment is part of a broader study examining how large language models provide financial advice and whether their efforts to interpret user preferences and protect users distort their recommendations. The broader project combines administrative insurance choices, Reddit requests for advice, and controlled experiments involving insurance and retirement decisions. This study will compare retirement allocation recommendations from 350 adults recruited through Prolific with previously collected model recommendations. Participants will advise two hypothetical investors whose ages differ by ten years and whose other financial circumstances are identical, recommending how to divide retirement savings between diversified stock and bond funds. We will examine how human and model recommendations vary with investor circumstances and compare them with an institutional retirement glide path.
experimental_design: We will conduct an approximately five-minute online survey of 350 adults recruited through Prolific and administered through Qualtrics. Participants will be randomly assigned to a pair of hypothetical investor profiles, presented one at a time. The investors’ ages will differ by ten years, while their other financial circumstances will be identical within each pair. Across pairs, scenarios will vary investor age and household income. Each profile will describe retirement savings, planned contributions, retirement age, and liquidity needs. Participants will recommend the percentage of each investor’s current retirement savings to invest in a diversified stock fund, with the remainder invested in a diversified bond fund. Recommendations will be entered as whole numbers from 0 to 100, and the investor will be permitted to revise the allocation in future years. The design will allow comparisons of retirement recommendations across investor circumstances, within participants, and between human participants and language models.
