abstract: We aim to elicit judgments of various scenarios that describe the interaction of two people and vary in how much exploitation there is. Those judgments are on those people's wellbeing, the wrongfulness of the behavior in the scenario, and norms around that wrongfulness. We will recruit two samples: a professional academic philosopher sample, and an online sample through Prolific.
experimental_design: *Overview* This is a vignette experiment in which participants – in this case, professional philosophers and Prolific participants – see a subset of three scenarios, with philosopher participants able to choose three additional scenarios, drawn from a pool of 12 scenarios in the way described in the Randomization Unit section below. All the scenarios concern the hypothetical purchase, sale and production of mugs. They differ along various dimensions: the explicit exercise of power, the existence of inequality, background luck, the satisfaction of basic needs, an unjust source of power and disrespect. We introduced these scenarios in Ferguson et al. (2026), where participants reported how much exploitation they saw in them on a 0-100 scale. Based on the data in that study, we selected 12 vignettes for the current study to form three categories in terms of the level of exploitation participants saw in them: four low-exploitation, four medium-exploitation, and four high-exploitation scenarios. Using the coding in the Supplementary Materials of that paper (Section B available here: https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/action/downloadSupplement?doi=10.1111%2Fajps.70058&file=ajps70058-supp-0001-Appendices.pdf), those are: Low = {R3B, R3L, R1D, R3D} Medium = {R3N, R2L, R4B, R3U} High = {R2N, R4D, R4N, R4U} We will provide summary statistics on the response data from the earlier study for these scenarios in the paper or its appendix. For each scenario: (i) Participants assess how the well-being of the two people changes as a result of the scenario for each of three categories of subjective well-being (Satisfaction, Happiness, Flourishing, which appear in a random order) on a five-point Likert scale (falls significantly, falls somewhat, no impact, rises somewhat, rises significantly). (ii) They next assess how morally wrong they find A's behavior on a five-point Likert scale (not at all, a little, moderately, significantly, extremely). (iii) They next report what they think the most frequent response to the wrongfulness question (of point ii) is. The full transcripts (of the initial email confirmation page for the professional philosopher sample and the main survey for each sample) are attached to this registry entry. An outline of our analysis plan is attached to this registry entry. *Payments to participants* Individual choices on subjective well-being and wrongfulness judgments are not incentivized. The norm-elicitation question is incentivized for both samples. The philosopher draw awards ten Amazon vouchers worth USD 100 (or the local-currency equivalent) each to eligible participants so long as they have not opted out; the Prolific draw awards ten bonuses worth USD 100 each. These are two independent draws. Participation is compensated by a fixed payment of 4 GBP for the Prolific sample via the platform. For the professional philosopher sample, participation is compensated via a prize draw for Amazon vouchers worth 100 USD which will be sent to ten randomly selected participants from the set of respondents who complete the survey (so long as they have not opted out of the prize draw). This third draw is also independent from the others. *Participants: philosophers* We will recruit philosophers (academic philosophers and philosophy graduate students) online, through two well-known philosophy blogs (detailed just below); the Philos-L listserv (hosted by the University of Liverpool); and a direct email campaign. Participants responding via the blogs and the Philos-L listserv are required first to enter their institutional email address in an initial one-page form, which then emails them a personalized link to the main survey. This helps us verify their association with a recognized academic institution. The blogs are Leiter Reports: A Philosophy Blog (https://leiterreports.com) and Crooked Timber (https://crookedtimber.org). Leiter Reports is the preeminent blog in professional philosophy, reporting “news and views about philosophy, the academic profession, academic freedom, intellectual culture, and other topics.” It is edited by Prof. Brian Leiter (Chicago), receives over 300,000 monthly visits, and is ranked 233,978 on SimilarWeb.com (as of 12 September 2026). Crooked Timber is a popular blog focusing on moral and political issues, with significant contributions from 15 core editors, many of whom are philosophers. It receives around 100,000 monthly visits and is ranked 580,800 on SimilarWeb.com (as of 12 September 2026). A database of ~2100 professional philosophers’ emails was compiled from the addresses available on the websites of the world’s top-rated philosophy departments, as ranked by the Philosophical Gourmet Report (https://www.philosophicalgourmet.com). After the scenarios, we ask professional philosophers about their areas of specialization, broad philosophical and political views, and demographic characteristics. Professional philosophers may of course be from anywhere in the world. The locations we selected in the Trial Information section of this entry reflect the location of our Prolific sample, which we detail next. We expect to receive approximately 550 responses after exclusions, as in Ferguson et al. (2026), but we will include all responses passing our exclusion criteria received in the specified time frame (see the Planned Number of Observations section). *Participants: public* We will recruit participants from the public via the online subject-pool operated by Prolific. We will restrict participation using Prolific's filters such that they are resident in one of the countries listed in the Trial Information (US or UK) and that English is their Primary Language, First Language, Fluent Language, and Earliest Language in Life. We will recruit 300 participants from each location (with the expectation that up to 50 are excluded by the criteria below in total over the two locations). This follows the roughly 50/50 composition of the public sample across these two locations in Ferguson et al. (2026). Following the primary questions, Prolific participants answer basic demographic questions (and are not asked opinion and professional questions relevant to philosophers). *Exclusion criteria* From either sample, we will exclude a participant's data if: (a) their response time on any of the main question pages (covering points (i)-(iii) above) is less than 2 seconds; (b) their response is flagged by Qualtrics' or Prolific's built-in bot detector; (c) their IP address falls within a listed subnet of known VPNs and data centers (available here: https://github.com/X4BNet/lists_vpn, we will add an amendment to this registry with a permalink to the version that we apply); (d) their response is incomplete. For participants on Prolific, we exclude their data if: (e) they fail the CAPTCHA (in which they are unable to complete the study); (f) they fail two attention checks (in which case they are returned to Prolific). From the philosopher sample, we will exclude a participant's data if: (g) they provide a non-institutional email domain (we intend to collect data from academic philosophers and philosophy graduate students only); (h) they declare themselves to be undergraduate students. Data from participants meeting any of the criteria (a)-(h) will not be analyzed or presented. We will report how many exclusions there are, and of what type. *References* Ferguson, B., Matthews, P. H., Ronayne, D., & Veneziani, R. (2026). What exploitation is. American Journal of Political Science. https://doi.org/10.1111/ajps.70058

abstract: Administrative sludge in sexual violence reporting systems, including narrative requirements in intake forms and procedural barriers to accessing those forms, may shape entry into the reporting process and progression to a formal complaint. We conduct an online survey experiment with Title IX coordinators and officers at U.S. colleges and universities to study their reporting-system preferences and their responses to empirical evidence about administrative burden. We plan to survey 500 eligible administrators through collaboration with the Association of Title IX Administrators (ATIXA). Before the information intervention, respondents report their professional roles, office constraints, and beliefs about false-reporting rates and the share of sexual assaults reported to their institution. Respondents are randomly assigned at the individual level to a workload and capacity module or a discrete-choice module eliciting preferences over intake-form attributes. Within each module, respondents are subsequently randomly assigned to an evidence summary about Title IX reporting systems or an active-control summary about knowledge retention in professional training. Computerized randomization in Qualtrics targets equal allocation between the two modules and between the two information conditions within each module, yielding four experimental cells. Following the information intervention, respondents recommend one of three intake-form designs and one of three landing-page designs. The co-primary outcomes are indicators for recommending the lowest-burden intake form and the lowest-burden landing page. Additional measures include expected consequences of the recommended designs, reasons for recommendations, and stated willingness to contribute part of the participation payment toward an institutional consultation. The primary analysis estimates the effect of assignment to the evidence summary relative to the active control, averaged across the two elicitation modules. Outcomes are measured during the survey and concern administrators’ recommendations and expectations.
experimental_design: This is an individually randomized online survey experiment with a two-by-two design. The target population is Title IX coordinators and officers currently working at U.S. colleges and universities. We plan to survey 500 eligible administrators through the ATIXA ListServ. Eligibility requires a current role in a U.S. college or university Title IX office and informed consent. Participants’ eligibility to participate in the survey will be confirmed through our partner organization and at the beginning of the survey. All respondents first complete common questions about their professional background, office constraints, and baseline reporting beliefs. They are then randomly assigned to one of two elicitation modules. The workload and capacity module elicits the importance of workload, a workload trade-off threshold, predictions about peers’ responses, and willingness to pay for a workload toolkit instead of an access toolkit. The discrete-choice module presents four paired choices between intake forms whose attributes vary, followed by questions about confidence and design priorities. Within each module, respondents are subsequently randomly assigned to either an evidence summary about the relationship between burden in Title IX reporting systems and reporting outcomes, or an active-control summary about knowledge checks and spaced review in professional training. Thus, the four cells are workload/control, workload/evidence, discrete choice/control, and discrete choice/evidence. The target allocation is approximately one quarter of participants to each cell. All respondents then recommend an intake-form design and a landing-page design, report their reasons and expected consequences, and state willingness to contribute part of their participation payment toward an institutional consultation. The principal comparison is assignment to evidence versus active control, averaged across the two elicitation modules. All survey outcomes are collected during the same session. Recruitment will run until 500 participants have completed the survey. If we have not achieved our targeted number of surveys by the intervention end date, we will run the analysis on the sample available to us.
intervention: The information intervention presents administrators responsible for Title IX reporting systems with a summary of empirical research concerning the relationship between administrative burden in reporting systems and reporting outcomes. The active-control condition presents a summary of unrelated research concerning professional training and does not provide information about Title IX reporting processes. Before the information assignment, respondents complete one of two randomized elicitation modules concerning workload and capacity trade-offs or intake-form preferences.

primary_outcome_explanation: The intake-form outcome uses question Q56 (internal identifier QID56), and the landing-page outcome uses Q88 (QID88). For each outcome, Design A is coded 1 and either Design B or Design C is coded 0. Coding follows design identity, not screen position. An unanswered item is missing and is not coded 0. Design A in the intake task allows optional contact information and a short optional narrative, requires no supporting documents, and requests only basic incident information. Design A in the landing-page task provides a prominent reporting button and direct access to the form without login or intermediate steps. The primary estimand is the effect of information assignment on the probability of recommending Design A, averaged equally across the two elicitation modules. We estimate the evidence-minus-control difference within each module and average those two differences with equal weights. We will report effect estimates and confidence intervals for both co-primary outcomes and apply Holm’s procedure to their two-sided p-values to control the family-wise error rate at 5%.
primary_outcomes: Two co-primary outcomes, measured immediately after the information intervention in the same survey: An indicator for recommending the lowest-burden intake-form design (Design A). An indicator for recommending the lowest-burden reporting landing-page design (Design A).
randomization_method: Computerized randomization within Qualtrics. A first Survey Flow randomizer presents one of the two elicitation modules, using the “Evenly Present Elements” setting. A separate randomizer within each module then assigns one of the two information conditions using the same setting. The target allocation is 1:1 between modules and 1:1 between evidence and active control within each module. Final completed-response counts may differ because of attrition. Within the discrete-choice module, respondent-specific form profiles are generated by computer across five attributes: narrative requirements; contact-information requirements; date, time, and location requirements; requirements to name the accused; and supporting-document requirements. The generator redraws identical pairs and pairs ordered in the same direction on every coded attribute, subject to its programmed retry limit. These within-respondent profile draws are distinct from assignment to the four experimental cells.
randomization_unit: The individual survey respondent (Title IX administrator) for both module assignment and information assignment. Within the discrete-choice module, attributes of the two form profiles vary across four tasks for each respondent. These repeated tasks do not constitute additional participants.
secondary_outcome_explanation: The full design-choice distributions use Q56 and Q88. Expected consequences use the individual 1–7 responses in Q61 and Q92. Perceived characteristics of the chosen intake form use Q62 (internal identifier QID113), with each item retained separately. Confidence uses Q68 and Q93. Alternative-objective choices use Q110–Q112 and Q114–Q116. Closed-ended reasons use Q124 and Q91, and open-ended explanations use Q87 and Q109. Consultation willingness to pay uses Q119, measured from $0 to $25. Free-text explanations will be exploratory unless a coding protocol is specified before analysis. The reporting-rate and false-reporting beliefs in Q21–Q24, workload measures and toolkit willingness to pay in the workload module, and the four discrete-choice tasks are collected before information assignment. They describe baseline beliefs and preferences relative to the information intervention and will not be interpreted as outcomes of that intervention. Perceived consequences of a chosen design combine possible changes in the chosen design and changes in its evaluation; comparisons do not identify belief updating about a fixed design alone.
secondary_outcomes: The full distribution of intake-form and landing-page recommendations across Designs A, B, and C; expected consequences of the recommended designs; perceived deterrence of truthful and false reports and legal defensibility of the chosen intake form; confidence in recommendations; designs preferred under alternative stated objectives; reported reasons for recommendations; and willingness to contribute to an institutional consultation.

abstract: This study examines whether and how proactive information about student financial aid affects young people’s beliefs about such aid and, subsequently, their educational aspirations. Pupils in their final year of school before high school graduation are given access to the same general AI-based career advisor, while the treatment group is randomly granted additional access to an expert module on Germany’s federal student aid program (i.e., BAföG).
experimental_design: Two-arm individual randomized online experiment with a common active-control chatbot. Eligible participants complete the same baseline questionnaire before treatment-specific content is activated. Participants are assigned approximately equally to control or proactive study-finance treatment (pure randomization). The primary follow-up is administered 14 days after baseline, with up to seven days to respond. We have a rolling sign-up in the treatment window, i.e. after the summer break, such that the exact date might vary. As we will randomize on the individual levels to ensure power, we will report diagnostics regarding spillovers.
experimental_design_details: Incentives will be used to keep attrition low. This incentives have a group and individual sphere and target both sign-up and the 14-outcome questionnaire. For recruitment and due to legal restrictions, we are left to individually recruit students. We will use established stakeholder channels we used for a pre-setup (Lohre, Fynn et al. 2026. "Level-Up: Understanding Parental Roles in the Career Choices of High-School Graduates." AEA RCT Registry. June 03. https://doi.org/10.1257/rct.18742-1.0) as well as recruit through our instagram/tiktok. All recruitment efforts will transparently be reported. As we are aware there might be selection to be in our sample, we will provide balance tests and further diagnostics how our sample differs from the general population. Already in place is the German SOEP as one data source to do this. We will open the sign-up until end of October. However, if we, for whatever reasons, are close to our sample size target at the end of this timeline, we reserve the right to open sign-up for 14 more days and will report this. In this case, we will report our main outcomes for everyone within the initially planned group in the appendix.
intervention: We study a two-arm, individually randomized online experiment. All participants receive access to the same general AI career chatbot and see a common, persistent reminder (i.e., nudge) at the top of the bot window emphasizing the importance of informing oneself about educational pathways to promote general usage. The treatment arm additionally receives proactive, salient information about BAfoeG (i.e., student aid) and a route to a BAfoeG calculation module. The control arm receives no proactive finance messages or treatment-specific call to action.

mde_text: With 2,000 analyzed individuals, equal assignment, a two-sided alpha of 0.05, and 80 percent power, the approximate unadjusted minimum detectable effect is 0.125 standard deviations for a continuous outcome and 6.3 percentage points for a binary outcome with a control mean of 0.50. If 80 percent of baseline completers provide the day-14 outcome, analyzed N is approximately 1,600 and the corresponding unadjusted continuous-outcome MDE is approximately 0.140 standard deviations. abstract: Companion survey to a study of Brazilian housing-credit (consórcio) lotteries and fertility. An online panel of 1,500 Brazilian adults, sampled by housing-purchase status, judges hypothetical scenarios in which a young couple’s housing differs in one attribute or in the timing of housing access, and then reports its own housing and fertility history.
experimental_design: Online survey (Qualtrics, Brazilian Portuguese) with quota sampling on housing-purchase status. After screening and basic demographics, 15 percent of respondents read a note that research finds housing important for family decisions, 15 percent that it is a minor factor, and 70 percent read nothing. All respondents then see five of ten pairwise scenarios, drawn with even presentation, in which a childless couple aged 30 faces two housing options that differ in exactly one attribute, everything else equal: space, neighborhood, tenure stability (a guaranteed lease of 5 or 10 years), ownership or monthly income (a food voucher of R$500, R$1,000 or R$2,000); one slot shows ownership versus a permanent protected lease with probability one third. The side of each option, the voucher amount and the lease length are randomized at the respondent level; half of the respondents answer an early comprehension check in each scenario; half of those who see ownership versus income also answer a cash version. Respondents are then assigned with equal probability to one of three modules: (1) housing timing, in which a recently married, childless couple aged 25 or 35 receives a paid-off program apartment now or, in a second scenario shown in random order, only at age 45; (2) the same timing scenarios with the couple’s ideal number of children fixed at three; (3) a couple aged 30 wins R$300,000 that either must buy a home or is invested and locked for ten years, with a cash follow-up. Half of the sample also answers a stated ranking of the attributes. The survey ends with the respondent’s own housing and fertility history and demographics; other blocks are exploratory.

abstract: This study evaluates a career-guidance intervention designed to reduce gender-stereotypical educational and occupational choices among secondary-school students in Armenia. Armenia provides a distinctive setting: despite relatively high female educational attainment and no gender gap in actual mathematics performance, substantial gender segregation persists in STEM fields. To our knowledge, this is the first role-model RCT in a post-Soviet, lower-middle-income setting, where these gender gaps coexist with a nascent but growing AI industry. The intervention combines modules on career interests, gender stereotypes and values, and exposure to female role models working in AI-related occupations. In contrast to existing role-model interventions centered on traditional STEM fields, the study focuses specifically on women in AI-adjacent careers, reflecting an increasingly important segment of Armenia’s technology sector. Using randomization both across schools and across classes within treated schools, the design identifies the impact of the overall program as well as the AI-module component. Outcomes include gender stereotypes, interest in engineering and ICT, and knowledge of and interest in AI-related careers, with particular attention to gender differences. The findings are intended to inform career-orientation programs in Armenia at a time of substantial investment in STEM education.
experimental_design: The intervention is a four-module classroom-based career-guidance program ("Career Guidance Program Promoting Gender Balance, STEM-Oriented"), developed to be consistent with the Ministry of ESCS’s pilot standard for the "Career Guidance" course (grades 8–11) and delivered by professional career-orientation trainers. Total program duration is 180 minutes, split across four modules: • Module 1 — Self-Awareness and Discovery of Interests (introductory). A neutral module in which students complete a validated vocational-interest inventory (Holland/RIASEC) and reflect on their own interests and strengths. Delivered to all three arms (Control, Treat 1, Treat 2). • Module 2 — My Values and Stereotypes. Students work through exercises eliciting and critically examining gender stereotypes in career and profession choice. • Module 3 — Meeting with a STEM Specialist (role-model module). A woman working in a technical/AI role at a Yerevan AI or technology company (e.g., Krisp, Podcastle, Diagnocat, SuperAnnotate, Cognaize, YerevaNN, NVIDIA Yerevan, PicsArt) visits the classroom to describe her career path and current work, using a structured role-model protocol. Role models are recruited through the research team’s professional networks, LinkedIn outreach, and referrals from AI companies operating in Yerevan. • Module 4 — Action Planning (closing session, not evaluated). Students complete an individual career-planning exercise. Delivered to Treat 1 and Treat 2 only, after both content modules; not designed to be separately evaluated and excluded from the primary and secondary outcome analysis. The two active treatment arms receive the identical set of modules but in reversed order, which is the key design feature enabling separate identification of the role-model module from the values-and-stereotypes module: • Treat 1: Baseline survey → Module 1 → Module 2 (Values and Stereotypes) → [Survey 2] → Module 3 (Role model) → Module 4 • Treat 2: Baseline survey → Module 1 → Module 3 (Role model) → [Survey 2] → Module 2 (Values and Stereotypes) → Module 4 • Control: Baseline survey → Module 1 only → [Survey, timed to match Survey 2] Module 1 is delivered approximately 5 days after the baseline survey; the first content module (Module 2 for Treat 1, Module 3 for Treat 2) follows approximately 3–5 days later. Survey 2 (the main evaluation, see Section 3.4) is administered immediately after this first content module and before the crossover module is delivered, so that at the time of Survey 2, Treat 1 has received Module 1 + Module 2 only and Treat 2 has received Module 1 + Module 3 only — allowing the T1-vs-Control and T2-vs-Control contrasts to isolate the effect of Module 2 and Module 3, respectively. The crossover module is delivered immediately after Survey 2, and the closing Module 4 follows approximately 8 days later, both for Treat 1 and Treat 2. The intervention is evaluated in a difference-in-differences design, comparing students in treated and control classes at endpoint vs baseline survey.

abstract: We test whether partisan negativity increases the reach and engagement of political social media posts. Using a randomised field experiment across major social media platforms, we compare substantively equivalent positive and partisan-negative versions of political posts to estimate the causal effect of negative partisan framing on social media post performance.
experimental_design: We test whether partisan negativity increases the reach and engagement of political social media posts. Using a randomised field experiment across major social media platforms, we compare substantively equivalent positive and partisan-negative versions of political posts to estimate the causal effect of negative partisan framing on social media post performance.
experimental_design_details: Primary estimand The primary estimand is the intention-to-treat effect of assignment to partisan-negative framing on the log of the preregistered platform-specific outcome. For X, Facebook and LinkedIn, this principally represents an effect on post exposure. For Bluesky, it represents an effect on observable engagement. The pooled four-platform coefficient should therefore be interpreted as the average proportional effect on the preregistered platform-specific post-performance measure, rather than literally as an effect on an identical "views" metric across all four platforms. All observations will be analysed according to their random assignment irrespective of accidental deviations in the wording ultimately published. Primary analysis Let iindex content events and pindex platforms. The primary model will be: log⁡(Outcome_ip )=α_i+γ_p+βTreatment_ip+ϵ_ip where: Outcome_ipis the preregistered platform-specific primary outcome; Treatment_ipequals one for posts assigned partisan-negative framing and zero for posts assigned positive framing; α_idenotes content-event fixed effects; and γ_pdenotes platform fixed effects. The coefficient of interest is β. Content-event fixed effects compare treatment and control platform-posts concerning exactly the same underlying announcement. They also account for factors common to that content event, including topic and the length of time that the posts have been live when outcomes are collected. Platform fixed effects account for persistent differences in audience size, platform scale and outcome measurement across X, Facebook, Bluesky and LinkedIn. The treatment coefficient will be converted into an approximate percentage difference in the relevant platform-specific outcome for ease of interpretation. Statistical inference The primary hypothesis test will use two-sided randomisation inference based on the preregistered assignment procedure. Treatment assignments will be repeatedly re-randomised in a manner that preserves: two treated and two control platforms within every content-event block; exactly 200 treatment and 200 control observations overall; and exactly 50 treatment and 50 control observations within each platform. The randomisation-inference p-value will be calculated using at least 100,000 valid random assignments. For conventional confidence intervals, the study will additionally report estimates using standard errors clustered by content event. Wild cluster bootstrap confidence intervals will also be reported. Statistical significance for the primary outcome will be assessed at the 5 per cent two-sided level. No multiple-testing adjustment is required for the single pooled primary treatment test. Secondary outcomes and platform-specific treatment estimates will be identified as secondary. Platform-specific estimates In addition to the pooled primary estimate, treatment effects will be estimated separately for X, Facebook, Bluesky and LinkedIn. These estimates are particularly useful because the primary outcome metric differs across platforms. The platform-specific estimates are secondary. The pooled estimate is the principal confirmatory treatment estimate. Robustness analyses The following analyses will be reported as robustness checks rather than alternative primary specifications: the untransformed platform-specific outcome; Poisson pseudo-maximum-likelihood estimation with content-event and platform fixed effects; exclusion of each platform in turn; and a pooled analysis restricted to X, Facebook and LinkedIn, where a direct measure of views, impressions or reach is available. The fourth specification will provide an estimate based solely on measures of post exposure and will therefore avoid reliance on Bluesky engagement as an exposure proxy. No post will be winsorised or removed because it has unusually high engagement or exposure. Viral posts are part of the outcome the experiment is designed to measure. Other heterogeneity No topic-specific or other subgroup heterogeneity analysis is designated as confirmatory. Exploratory analyses may examine whether effects differ by broad subject matter, post characteristics or other predetermined characteristics, provided that these analyses are clearly identified as exploratory.

mde_text: With 400 platform-post observations, divided equally between treatment and control, the approximate minimum detectable treatment effect is 0.28 residual standard deviations at 80 per cent power and a two-sided 5 per cent significance level. This is an approximate calculation. Actual precision will depend on the amount of variation explained by the content-event and platform fixed effects and on the distribution of the platform-specific outcome measures.

primary_outcomes: Primary outcome The primary outcome is the platform-specific measure of the number of times a post was viewed or displayed, measured at the end of the experiment. Because social media platforms differ in the metrics they make available, the following measurement rules will be specified in advance. X The primary measure will be the post's impressions. X reports the total number of times a post has been viewed on a screen. This measure is not a count of unique users and can include multiple views by the same user. If the standard X impression count is unavailable for a particular experimental post because of a change in platform functionality, the closest available exposure measure supplied by X or its analytics interface will be used. As a secondary measure, engagement rate will be calculated by dividing total observable engagements (likes, comments, bookmarks and retweets/quote tweets) by post impressions. Facebook The preferred measure will be the post-level views measure available through Facebook or Meta Business Suite. Views can be used consistently across text, image, link and video posts. If a directly comparable post-level views measure is unavailable, post reach will be used. Reach measures displays of the content and is therefore conceptually closer to the X impression measure. Reach measures the number of unique accounts or users exposed to the post and will be used only where a display-based measure is unavailable. The metric used will be recorded consistently for all Facebook experimental posts wherever platform data availability permits. As a secondary measure, engagement rate will be calculated by dividing total observable engagements (reactions, comments, and shares) by post views. LinkedIn The primary measure will be post impressions. LinkedIn defines impressions as the estimated number of times a post was displayed on the platform. This is the closest available analogue to the X view count and will be used for all content formats. If post impressions become unavailable, members reached, which measures distinct members or Pages that saw the post, will be used as the fallback measure. For video posts, format-specific video-view counts will not replace impressions where impressions remain available, since impressions provide a measure that can be used consistently across text, image, link and video posts. As a secondary measure, engagement rate will be calculated by dividing total observable engagements (reactions, reposts, saves and comments) by post impressions. Bluesky At the time of preregistration, Bluesky does not provide post-level views, impressions or reach. The primary Bluesky outcome will therefore be total observable engagement, defined as: likes + replies + reposts + quote-posts. This is an engagement measure rather than a direct exposure measure. It is preregistered as the closest consistently observable post-level indicator of performance available on Bluesky. If Bluesky introduces a native post-level views or impressions measure during the experiment, the measure available at the commencement of the experiment will remain the preregistered primary outcome for Bluesky. Any analysis using a subsequently introduced exposure measure will be reported separately as a supplementary analysis.
randomization_method: Randomisation will be conducted by computer before the first experimental post. The underlying content event will be the randomisation block. For every content event, exactly two of the four platforms will receive the partisan-negative treatment and two will receive the positive control. The experiment will contain 100 complete content-event blocks. Randomisation will be constrained so that: • every content event contains exactly two treatment platform-posts and two control platform-posts; • each platform receives exactly 50 treatment assignments and 50 control assignments; and • the experiment overall contains exactly 200 treatment platform-posts and 200 control platform-posts. A random allocation schedule satisfying these constraints will be generated before the experiment begins. Its order will be randomly determined using a recorded random seed. The randomisation code, seed and resulting allocation schedule will be stored before the intervention begins. For each content event, the two versions of the post will be finalised before the relevant treatment allocation is revealed.
randomization_unit: The unit of randomisation is the platform-post. Randomisation is blocked by content event.
secondary_outcomes: Where available, secondary outcomes measured at the end of the experiment will include: • likes or reactions; • comments or replies; • shares, reposts or quote-posts; and • total observable interactions. For X, Facebook and LinkedIn, an engagement rate may also be calculated by dividing observable interactions by the relevant exposure measure. Because Bluesky does not provide an exposure denominator, a directly comparable engagement rate will not be calculated for Bluesky. These outcomes will be clearly identified as secondary. The preregistered platform-specific exposure or fallback measure remains the sole confirmatory primary outcome.

abstract: This study examines how peer network exposure shapes farmers' decisions to adopt plant food production, and whether spillover effects emerge among untreated farmers. Despite growing policy interest in diversification away from livestock, the role of social network exposure in such transitions remains empirically underre-searched. The study is embedded in a multi-wave randomized controlled trial (2026–2028) with three arms in the Canton of Lucerne (advisory only, advisory plus a CHF 10,000 experimental budget, internal control) and an external control group in Cantons Aargau, Thurgau, and St. Gallen. Farm-level outcomes are measured through both stated survey-based change figures and revealed behavioural out-comes from farm census data.
experimental_design: The study follows all four arms across three data-collection waves over approximately three years (baseline September–October 2026, Year 1 November 2027, Year 2 November 2028), with an optional Year 3 wave in November 2029 pending a decision on study extension. Farm-level survey data are linked to farm census data via farm identification number across all waves, allowing comparison of stated (survey) and revealed (census) preferences. We recruit from Canton Lucerne as the treatment region and from Cantons Aargau, Thurgau, and St. Gallen as an external control region with comparable farm structural characteristics. Within both regions, farms are eligible if they are located in the respective recruitment region, are eligible for Swiss direct payments, and operate animal production at the time of recruitment (standard livestock unit > 0). Contact data for outreach is provided by the Federal Office for Agriculture (BLW); farms already at the BLW's cap on survey invitations in the current calendar year cannot be proactively invited but remain eligible and may register by contacting the project team directly; eligible farms are then granted access to the survey. Eligible farms with available contact data are invited near-exhaustively within each region. The study deliberately targets farms that have not already fully committed to plant food production; subject to sufficient overall sample size, the analysis may exclude farms for which plant food production already constitutes 91–100% of agricultural income at baseline, and farms that indicate at baseline they would not accept either treatment if assigned, with such restrictions pre-registered and applied only if they do not compromise statistical power. Eligible farms receive a written invitation letter and follow-up email, with a reminder letter and email sent to non-respondents two weeks later, and two information events (in-person and hybrid) before registration closes at the end of October 2026. Farms are informed of their arm assignment by letter post and email in early December 2026; farms assigned to Arms 1 and 2 must actively confirm participation via a confirmation link. Replacement farms are recruited from the pool of registered control farms with similar characteristics on pre-specified balancing variables where withdrawals or non-confirmations occur.
intervention: Farms within Canton Lucerne are randomly assigned to one of three arms — two treatment arms (advisory services (Arm 1); advisory services plus an experimental budget (Arm 2)) and an internal control (Arm 3); farms in the external control can-tons (Aargau, Thurgau, and St. Gallen) are assigned directly to the external control (Arm 4), without random assignment among themselves. • Arm 1 — Advisory services (n≈75): Farms first receive an initial advisory session: a three-hour on-site consultation conducting a location and poten-tial analysis with the farm operator, enabling an informed choice of a subse-quent tailored advisory track: (1) specialty crops or specialty arable farming, (2) Agri-PV combined with specialty crops, (3) regenerative plant food pro-duction, (4) agroforestry, or (5) a voucher for an equivalent advisory service of the farm's own choice. Tailored advisory is delivered by regional public advisory services and specialised consultancies. • Arm 2 — Advisory services plus experimental budget (n≈50): Farms re-ceive the same initial and tailored advisory as Arm 1, plus a one-time un-conditional cash payment of CHF 10,000, disbursed in July 2027 via the cantonal agricultural authority, conditional on completion of the initial adviso-ry session. The same fixed sum is paid to every Arm 2 farm irrespective of farm size. Prior to disbursement, Arm 2 farms submit a non-binding intention document describing their planned use of the budget; no repayment obliga-tion applies if a farm subsequently withdraws or uses the funds differently than stated. • Arm 3 — Internal control (n≈300–600): Located within the treatment region (Canton Lucerne); receives no treatment; participates in all three survey waves and provides farm census data access. • Arm 4 — External control (n≈300–600): Located in Cantons Aargau, Thur-gau, and St. Gallen; receives no treatment; same survey and census partici-pation as Arm 3. Both control groups (Arms 3 and 4) are jointly eligible for a prize draw after each survey wave (20 farms, CHF 500 each, drawn from both groups combined), as compensation for survey participation rather than a treatment component.

randomization_method: Following completion of survey registration, eligible farms in Canton Lucerne will be randomly assigned to the three study arms: 75 farms to Arm 1, 50 to Arm 2, and the re-maining eligible farms to Arm 3. Farms in the external control cantons (Aargau, Thurgau, and St. Gallen) will be assigned directly to Arm 4 and will not enter this randomization procedure. We will use rerandomization to improve covariate balance. Candidate allocations will be generated by computer and evaluated using Mahalanobis distance across a set of co-variates grouped into priority tiers, including baseline outcomes, geographic character-istics, and other farm-level characteristics. Balance thresholds for each tier will be cali-brated beforehand using simulated allocations and fixed prior to the final randomiza-tion. For the final randomization, a new and independent set of allocations will be generated by computer, and the allocation ultimately used will be drawn uniformly at random from those satisfying all balance criteria. Randomization will take place after survey registra-tion closes but before treatment delivery and before any post-treatment outcomes are observed.
secondary_outcome_explanation: • Network Exposure weighted by raw adopter count: As an alternative to the primary exposure ratio, we test a specification that additionally weights exposure by the absolute number of contacts who expanded their plant food production (Bi). Under the ratio alone, a farmer with one contact who adopted (NE=1.0) scores higher than a farmer with ten contacts, four of whom adopted (NE=0.4), despite the latter having more farmers in absolute terms in their network who expanded their plant food production. The alternative specification accounts for this by scaling the ratio by the raw adopter count. • Network Exposure (pre-treatment baseline) weighted by intensity of interaction: As a second alternative to the primary exposure ratio, we test a speci-fication that weights exposure by the intensity of interaction with adopting contacts, on the grounds that not all exchange relationships carry equal informational or normative weight. A high exposure ratio driven by superficial contact plausibly has less influence on the farmer's own decision-making than the same ratio sustained through frequent, in-depth exchange.

abstract: Rice straw burning is widely used to clear fields after harvest but contributes to local air pollution and greenhouse gas emissions. This study evaluates approaches to increasing farmers’ use of a microbial product that helps rice straw decompose in the field, providing an alternative to burning. In rice-growing villages in Vietnam, we use a cross-randomization design to evaluate two dimensions of the roll-out of a new technology. More specifically, we test: (i) whether farmers or local agricultural shops help to better spread awareness of and adoption of the product; and (ii) whether top-down (recommendation by village leaders) or bottom-up (peer nominations) invitation procedures for training farmers leads to greater adoption of the product. The study will assess whether these approaches increase use of the product and ultimately reduce rice straw burning.
experimental_design: In treated villages, we organize trainings and fields demonstrations for farmers on the use of microbial as an alternative way to manage rice straw instead of burning. Following the training, participants receive free bags of microbial product and vouchers to obtain these products at a discounted price. We cluster-randomize our interventions at the village level. We randomly assign villages to a combination of different recruitment and marketing approaches to increase widespread adoption. Using a cross-randomization design, we experimentally vary: (i) how training participants are recruited (either recommended by the village leader or peer nominations by farmers); and (ii) the type of participants (farmers or local agricultural retailers) who will further the adoption of the microbial.

abstract: Best management practices (BMPs) in agriculture play an important role in reducing nutrient losses, greenhouse gas emissions, and improving nitrogen use efficiency. Despite the agronomic and environmental benefits associated with improved nitrogen management practices, Canadian agricultural producers differ in their adoption of bio-stimulants and nitrogen stabilizers (Daly et al., 2025). This variation could be related to how producers process and interpret scientific information, particularly when evidence about product performance is presented with varying levels of detail (Mastenbroek et al., 2021; Wuepper et al., 2023). This study aims to investigate whether the complexity of scientific information provided to producers affects their willingness-to-pay (WTP) for nitrogen management technologies and whether this effect differs between bio-stimulants and nitrogen stabilizers. We will conduct a lab-in-the-field experiment with agricultural producers at the 2026 Canada’s Outdoor Farm Show (COFS) in Woodstock, Ontario (September 15 - 17). Participants will be randomly assigned to one of three information treatments: a control, a concise scientific information treatment, or a detailed scientific information treatment. Participants will subsequently bid on two nitrogen management products using an incentive-compatible cost-share Becker-DeGroot-Marschak (BDM) mechanism (Becker et al., 1964). The primary outcome of interest is producers’ bids, measured as the percentage of the market price that participants are willing to pay for each product under different information treatments.
experimental_design: The experiment will investigate the causal effect of scientific information complexity on producers’ willingness-to-pay for nitrogen management technologies. Participants will be recruited at Canada’s Outdoor Farm Show, where, after providing informed consent, participants will receive instructions explaining the experimental auction and the BDM mechanism. Participants will also complete comprehension questions to assess their understanding of the bidding mechanism. Each participant is then randomly assigned to one of the three information treatments. Participants subsequently submit bids between 0 and 100% on both products, with product order randomized with equal probability between the two possible orders. After the bidding tasks, participants will complete a post-experiment questionnaire covering farm characteristics, prior experience with the products, information level preferences, fertilizer management practices, 4R Nutrient Stewardship knowledge, and demographic characteristics. Each participant will receive $20 CAD as compensation and will have the opportunity (1 in 100) to purchase one of the randomly selected products using the BDM mechanism. The experiment is programmed in Python and HTML and administered on iPads.

intervention: Control (T0) Participants assigned to the control receive general product information in the form of an infographic, describing the product and its intended purpose. No scientific evidence, yield estimates, or environmental performance data are presented. Treatment 1 (T1): Concise Scientific Information Participants assigned to Treatment 1 receive the same general product information in the form of an infographic, followed by a concise scientific message summarizing relevant evidence on product performance. For both the bio-stimulant and the nitrogen stabilizer, the message presents scientific evidence regarding potential yield improvements and reductions in synthetic fertilizer use. The quantitative evidence is presented as a single estimate for each performance measure, providing participants with a concise summary of the reported effects. References to the scientific evidence presented are provided at the end of the message. Treatment 2 (T2): Detailed Scientific Information Participants assigned to Treatment 2 receive the same general product information in the form of an infographic, followed by a detailed scientific message summarizing relevant evidence on product performance. For both the bio-stimulant and the nitrogen stabilizers, the message presents scientific evidence with quantitative ranges for potential yield improvements and reductions in synthetic fertilizer use. Unlike T1, the quantitative evidence is presented as ranges of potential effects rather than single estimates, providing information on the variation in reported yield and fertilizer-use outcomes. Additionally, the message also provides information on factors that may affect product performance. This includes environmental effects, application requirements, management conditions, and implementation considerations. References to the scientific evidence presented are provided at the end of the message.

abstract: Livestock production is a major driver of greenhouse gas emissions, nutrient imbalances, and land-use pressure, and a shift toward more plant food production is needed but remains slow. The effectiveness of policy instruments to support this shift has not been tested experimentally. This study evaluates whether tailored agricultural advisory services and a one-time financial experimental budget increase plant food production and value creation among livestock and mixed farms in Switzerland. The study uses a multi-wave randomised controlled trial with three arms in the Canton of Lucerne (advisory only, advisory plus a CHF 10,000 experimental budget, internal control) and an external control group. Farm-level outcomes are measured through both stated survey-based change figures and revealed behavioural outcomes from farm census data, allowing comparison of intention-to-treat and treated-to-treat effects on plant food production and value creation over a two-year horizon.
experimental_design: The study follows all four arms across three data-collection waves over approximately three years (baseline September–October 2026, Year 1 November 2027, Year 2 November 2028), with an optional Year 3 wave in November 2029 pending a decision on study extension. Experimental Design Details Farm-level survey data are linked to farm census data via farm identification number across all waves, allowing comparison of stated (survey) and revealed (census) preferences. We recruit from Canton Lucerne as the treatment region and from Cantons Aargau, Thurgau, and St. Gallen as an external control region with comparable farm structural characteristics. Within both regions, farms are eligible if they are located in the respective recruitment region, are eligible for Swiss direct payments, and operate animal production at the time of recruitment (standard livestock unit > 0). Contact data for outreach is provided by the Federal Office for Agriculture (BLW); farms already at the BLW's cap on survey invitations in the current calendar year cannot be proactively invited but remain eligible and may register by contacting the project team directly; eligible farms are then granted access to the survey. Eligible farms with available contact data are invited near-exhaustively within each region. The study deliberately targets farms that have not already fully committed to plant food production; subject to sufficient overall sample size, the analysis may exclude farms for which plant food production already constitutes 91–100% of agricultural income at baseline, and farms that indicate at baseline they would not accept either treatment if assigned, with such restrictions pre-registered and applied only if they do not compromise statistical power. Eligible farms receive a written invitation letter and follow-up email, with a reminder letter and email sent to non-respondents two weeks later, and two information events (in-person and hybrid) before registration closes at the end of October 2026. Farms are informed of their arm assignment by letter post and email in early December 2026; farms assigned to Arms 1 and 2 must actively confirm participation via a confirmation link. Replacement farms are recruited from the pool of registered control farms with similar characteristics on pre-specified balancing variables where withdrawals or non-confirmations occur.
intervention: In Switzerland, Farms within Canton Lucerne are randomly assigned to one of three arms — two treatment arms (advisory services (Arm 1); advisory services plus an experimental budget (Arm 2)) and an internal control (Arm 3); farms in the external control cantons (Aargau, Thurgau, and St. Gallen) are assigned directly to the external control (Arm 4), without random assignment among themselves. Arm 1 — Advisory services (n≈75): Farms first receive an initial advisory session: a three-hour on-site consultation conducting a location and potential analysis with the farm operator, enabling an informed choice of a subsequent tailored advisory track: (1) speciality crops or speciality arable farming, (2) Agri-photovoltaic (Agri-PV) combined with speciality crops, (3) regenerative plant production, (4) agroforestry, or (5) a voucher for an equivalent advisory service of the farm's own choice. Tailored advisory is delivered by regional public advisory services and specialised consultancies. Arm 2 — Advisory services plus experimental budget (n≈50): Farms receive the same initial and tailored advisory as Arm 1, plus a one-time unconditional cash payment of CHF 10,000, disbursed in July 2027 via the cantonal agricultural authority, conditional on completion of the initial advisory session. The same fixed sum is paid to every Arm 2 farm irrespective of farm size. Prior to disbursement, Arm 2 farms submit a non-binding intention document describing their planned use of the budget; no repayment obligation applies if a farm subsequently withdraws or uses the funds differently than stated. Arm 3 — Internal control (n≈300–600): Located within the treatment region (Canton Lucerne); receives no treatment; participates in all three survey waves and provides farm census data access. Arm 4 — External control (n≈300–600): Located in Cantons Aargau, Thurgau, and St. Gallen; receives no treatment; same survey and census participation as Arm 3. Both control groups (Arms 3 and 4) are jointly eligible for a prize draw after each survey wave (20 farms, CHF 500 each, drawn from both groups combined), as compensation for survey participation rather than a treatment component.

abstract: Policy feedback theory holds that policies are not only outputs of politics but also inputs into future politics, reshaping the material incentives and interpretive beliefs of those who experience them. This study tests whether Swiss farmers who receive agricultural advisory services and/or a one-time experimental budget shift their support for agri-food policy instruments as a result, and through which channel: material or interpretive belief change. The study uses a multi-wave randomised controlled trial as to assess these questions, with three arms in the Canton of Lucerne (advisory only, advisory plus a CHF 10,000 experimental budget, internal control) and an external control group in three other Swiss cantons. Policy support is measured via a survey battery covering both plant-production-promoting and animal-production-reducing policy instruments; whether treatment effects vary by instrument type (incentive vs. disincentive; financial, regulatory, or information-based) is examined exploratively.
experimental_design: The study follows all four arms across three data-collection waves over approximately three years (baseline September–October 2026, Year 1 November 2027, Year 2 November 2028), with an optional Year 3 wave in November 2029 pending a decision on study extension. Experimental Design Details Farm-level survey data are linked to farm census data via farm identification number across all waves, allowing comparison of stated (survey) and revealed (census) preferences. We recruit from Canton Lucerne as the treatment region and from Cantons Aargau, Thurgau, and St. Gallen as an external control region with comparable farm structural characteristics. Within both regions, farms are eligible if they are located in the respective recruitment region, are eligible for Swiss direct payments, and operate animal production at the time of recruitment (Standard Livestock Unit > 0). Contact data for outreach is provided by the Federal Office for Agriculture (BLW); farms already at the BLW's cap on survey invitations in the current calendar year cannot be proactively invited but remain eligible and may register by contacting the project team directly; eligible farms are then granted access to the survey. Eligible farms with available contact data are invited near-exhaustively within each region. The study deliberately targets farms that have not already fully committed to plant food production; subject to sufficient overall sample size, the analysis may exclude farms for which plant food production already constitutes 91–100% of agricultural income at baseline, and farms that indicate at baseline they would not accept either treatment if assigned, with such restrictions pre-registered and applied only if they do not compromise statistical power. Eligible farms receive a written invitation letter and follow-up email, with a reminder letter and email sent to non-respondents two weeks later, and two information events (in-person and hybrid) before registration closes at the end of October 2026. Farms are informed of their arm assignment by letter-post and email in early December 2026; farms assigned to Arms 1 and 2 must actively confirm participation via a confirmation link. Replacement farms are recruited from the pool of registered control farms with similar characteristics on pre-specified balancing variables where withdrawals or non-confirmations occur.
intervention: In Switzerland, Farms within Canton Lucerne are randomly assigned to one of three arms — two treatment arms (advisory services (Arm 1); advisory services plus an experimental budget (Arm 2)) and an internal control (Arm 3); farms in the external control cantons (Aargau, Thurgau, and St. Gallen) are assigned directly to the external control (Arm 4), without random assignment among themselves. Arm 1 — Advisory services (n≈75): Farms first receive an initial advisory session: a three-hour on-site consultation conducting a location and potential analysis with the farm operator, enabling an informed choice of a subsequent tailored advisory track: (1) speciality crops or speciality arable farming, (2) Agri-PV combined with speciality crops, (3) regenerative plant production, (4) agroforestry, or (5) a voucher for an equivalent advisory service of the farm's own choice. Tailored advisory is delivered by regional public advisory services and specialised consultancies. Arm 2 — Advisory services plus experimental budget (n≈50): Farms receive the same initial and tailored advisory as Arm 1, plus a one-time unconditional cash payment of CHF 10,000, disbursed in July 2027 via the cantonal agricultural authority, conditional on completion of the initial advisory session. The same fixed sum is paid to every Arm 2 farm irrespective of farm size. Prior to disbursement, Arm 2 farms submit a non-binding intention document describing their planned use of the budget; no repayment obligation applies if a farm subsequently withdraws or uses the funds differently than stated. Arm 3 — Internal control (n≈300–600): Located within the treatment region (Canton Lucerne); receives no treatment; participates in all three survey waves and provides farm census data access. Arm 4 — External control (n≈300–600): Located in Cantons Aargau, Thurgau, and St. Gallen; receives no treatment; same survey and census participation as Arm 3. Both control groups (Arms 3 and 4) are jointly eligible for a prize draw after each survey wave (20 farms, CHF 500 each, drawn from both groups combined), as compensation for survey participation rather than a treatment component.

randomization_method: Following completion of survey registration, eligible farms in Canton Lucerne will be randomly assigned to the three study arms: 75 farms to Arm 1, 50 to Arm 2, and the remaining eligible farms to Arm 3. abstract: This study evaluates whether educational interventions designed to (1) improve academic performance and (2) promote rational-emotive behavioral thinking can prevent or remediate student burnout. We conduct a randomized controlled trial among University of Arizona students. Participants are randomly assigned in approximately equal numbers to one of four conditions in a 2 x 2 between-subjects factorial design: (1) control, (2) Academic-Performance Treatment (APT), (3) Rational-Emotive Behavioral-Thinking Treatment (REBT), or (4) a combined APT+REBT treatment. The interventions consist of online educational and informational modules delivered through the University of Arizona Brightspace platform. The primary outcome is student burnout. Secondary outcomes include academic performance and overall well-being. Four survey waves will allow us to examine changes in burnout and well-being over the semester, as well as potential mechanisms through which the interventions operate. Academic performance during the Fall 2026 semester will also be assessed. The study will estimate intention-to-treat effects of assignment to each intervention condition.
experimental_design: The experiment is a four-arm randomized controlled trial employing a 2 x 2 between-subjects factorial design. The two intervention factors are: (1) access to the Academic-Performance Treatment (APT) and (2) access to the Rational-Emotive Behavioral-Thinking Treatment (REBT). Participants will therefore be assigned to one of four conditions: 1. Control: no APT, no REBT 2. APT: APT only 3. REBT: REBT only 4. Combined: both APT and REBT Participants will complete a baseline survey prior to treatment assignment and three follow-up surveys during the Fall 2026 semester. Treatment materials will be delivered through University of Arizona Brightspace. The control group will not receive the intervention materials during the study.
experimental_design_details: Participants will be recruited from University of Arizona students employed by University Recreation Centers. Recruitment and informed consent will occur through an in-person meeting. Following informed consent and completion of the baseline survey, participants will be stratified according to academic major (STEM versus non-STEM), class standing (freshman, sophomore, junior, or senior), and gender. Within these strata, participants will be randomly assigned in approximately equal numbers to the four experimental groups. Four survey waves will be administered during the Fall 2026 semester. The baseline survey is scheduled for September 12, followed by survey waves on October 22-25, December 2-7, and December 18-20. Academic performance in Fall 2026 courses will also be measured.
intervention: Participants will be randomly assigned to one of four study groups in a 2 x 2 factorial design involving two intervention components: an Academic-Performance Treatment (APT) and a Rational-Emotive Behavioral-Thinking Treatment (REBT).

abstract: This study examines how employees aged 45 and above value different job attributes in a sample of workers employed by medium-to-large firms in Italy. Respondents complete a conjoint experiment in which they repeatedly compare two otherwise equivalent hypothetical job offers that differ in monthly net salary and selected non-wage job characteristics. The attributes include employer-provided Long-Term Care insurance, the possibility of working remotely, and the composition of the immediate work team. For each pair, respondents indicate which job they prefer and rate each profile on a 0–10 scale. Attribute levels are randomly assigned to profiles within choice tasks. The primary analysis estimates Average Marginal Component Effects (AMCEs) on forced job choice. Secondary analyses examine profile ratings, marginal means, monetary valuations relative to salary, and heterogeneity by worker demographic characteristics.
experimental_design: Respondents complete a conjoint experiment concerning hypothetical job offers. They are asked to imagine that they are looking for a new job and have received two offers from firms and positions that are equivalent in all respects except for the characteristics shown in the experiment. In each task, respondents compare Job A and Job B, select the job they prefer overall, and assign a 0–10 rating to each option. The job profiles vary along four dimensions: - Net monthly salary: EUR 1,700; EUR 1,900; EUR 2,100; EUR 2,300. - Employer-provided Long-Term Care insurance: an individual policy paying EUR 500, EUR 1,000, or EUR 1,500 per month if the employee becomes unable to perform at least two of six Activities of Daily Living because of illness, injury, or cognitive deterioration. - Work-location flexibility: always on-site; one day of smart working per week; two days of smart working per week. - Office team composition: one of three pre-specified visual team profiles. The three images are fixed in the survey instrument and vary the apparent age and gender composition of a four-person office/operational team. (i) 1 Young; 2 Mid-Age; 1 Old; (2) 1 Young; 1 Mid-Age; 2 Old; (3) 1 Young; 3 Old. The scenario is explicitly hypothetical. Respondents are instructed to compare the two offers with one another rather than with their current job. Each respondent repeat the stated-choice five times.

abstract: Mindfulness-based programs (MBPs), rooted in contemplative practices, have emerged as promising interventions for promoting psychological well-being and positive functioning. Increasingly, MBPs are being delivered via digital platforms (i.e., mobile apps) to expand reach (Mrazek et al., 2019). However, no large-scale study has evaluated the effectiveness of a digitally delivered, weekly module-based MBP with pre-recorded guided mindfulness practices for university students in China, a population with a high prevalence of mental health challenges. Building off an evaluation study of an in-person MBP implemented in fall 2025, this study aims to evaluate the impact of a digital MBP specifically tailored for university students. We will investigate the effects on the primary outcomes of anxiety symptoms, depression symptoms, and perceived stress, alongside potential mediators (state mindfulness, emotion regulation skills, self-compassion, gratitude), and secondary well-being indicators (including sleep quality and perceived online social support). The study design will be a two-arm randomized controlled trial (RCT) with undergraduate students enrolled at three universities in China.
experimental_design: The experimental design will be a randomized study with undergraduate students recruited from three universities in China. Using the RCT method of impact evaluation, we will be able to ensure that the intervention and control groups have similar characteristics at baseline, which is vital for drawing a causal connection between the intervention and any changes in student. By assuring the similarity of characteristics (such as sex, baseline mental health, etc.) between the treatment and control groups at baseline, we can confidently attribute any significant differences in outcomes between the control and intervention group to the program. All study participants will receive adequate financial compensation for participating in the study.

Students will learn core mindful awareness practices such as sitting meditation, body scans, and mindful movement. For the duration of the eight weeks, will be asked to conduct at least 15-20 minutes of mindfulness practice, six days per week.

abstract: We conduct a field experiment in China to estimate the value of shorter workweeks and to examine whether these valuations vary nonlinearly with workweek length. We further examine whether these valuations vary systematically with how participants expect to use the additional nonwork time. Finally, we explore heterogeneity in these valuations across individual characteristics.

We further examine whether these valuations vary systematically with how participants expect to use the additional nonwork time. Finally, we explore heterogeneity in these valuations across individual characteristics.
experimental_design_details: We recruit participants via a large Chinese online survey platform. Eligible participants are aged 22–28 and are either currently employed or considering entering the labor market, representing an early-career population. Participation is voluntary and compensated. • Incentives To encourage participation, participants are offered both informational and material incentives. Specifically, the job preferences elicited through the experiment are used to generate personalized job recommendations drawn from real recruitment postings that align with participants expressed preferences. In addition, participants receive 5 RMB as a participation reward. • Profile generation and randomization The experimental profiles are constructed to capture the salient characteristics of the job search process. Each profile presents two categories of information: the job seeker's characteristics at the time of job offer and job attributes. Participants are instructed to assume that all non-displayed characteristics are held constant across profiles and that all job offers are located in the same city as the respondent. The job seeker's characteristics at the time of offer receipt vary along age, educational attainment, and work experience. The job offer’s attributes vary along monthly after-tax salary, employer type, layoff risk, and weekly working days. The attributes and their corresponding levels are as follows. - Age ranges from 22 to 28 years old, spanning seven discrete levels. Both alternatives within a task have the same age. - Educational attainment is related with age: bachelor’s degree at ages 22–24; bachelor’s or master’s degree at ages 25–28. - Work experience has three levels: 0, 1, 2 and 3 years. - Monthly after-tax salary takes five levels: RMB 3,000, RMB 5,000, RMB 7,000, RMB 9,000, and RMB 11,000. - Employer type includes four categories: public-sector institutions, state-owned enterprises, foreign-invested enterprises, and private enterprises. - Layoff risk is assigned conditional on employer type. Public institutions have low risk; state-owned enterprises have low or medium risk; foreign-owned and privately owned enterprises may have all three levels-low, median or high. This conditional assignment reflects the institutional reality of employment security in the Chinese labor market. - Weekly working days takes three levels: 4 days, 5 days, and 6 days. We employ D-efficient design to optimize covariate balance and statistical efficiency, with attribute levels exogenously varied to ensure sufficient variation across profiles. • Choice Following the approach of Andrew and Adams (2025), Mas and Pallais (2017) and Nagler et al. (2024), participants are presented with two profiles per choice set and are asked to indicate their preference. Participants are instructed to treat the personal characteristics displayed in each profile as their own and to choose the employment situation they would prefer. A practice task precedes the formal choice module and is excluded from the analysis. In each subsequent choice set, participants answer the question, “Which employment situation would you choose?” Each respondent completes 20 binary choice tasks. References Andrew, A., & Adams, A. (2025). Revealed Beliefs and the Marriage Market Return to Education. The Quarterly Journal of Economics, 140(3), 2107～2162. https://doi.org/10.1093/qje/qjaf020 Mas, A., & Pallais, A. (2017). Valuing alternative work arrangements. American Economic Review, 107(12), 3722～3759. https://doi.org/10.1257/aer.20161500 Nagler, M., Rincke, J., & Winkler, E. (2024). Working from home, commuting, and gender. Journal of Population Economics, 37(3), 58. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00148-024-01035-6

abstract: We conduct a field experiment in China to estimate the value individuals place on public-sector employment. We further examine potential sources of this value, focusing on marriage-market returns, employment security and benefits, career prospects, social and family recognition, and earnings expectations. Finally, we explore heterogeneity in the valuation of public-sector employment across individual characteristics.
