abstract: This study was conducted to evaluate the effectiveness of the Hold Me Tight® (HMT) program in addressing relationship difficulties associated with gaslighting and triangulation among Pakistani families. The intervention was based on Emotionally Focused Therapy (EFT; Johnson, 2019). It was culturally adapted through the integration of Islamic teachings and Shariah compliant mediation principles. This was done to enhance its relevance, acceptability, and applicability within the Pakistani sociocultural context. Two parallel randomized controlled evaluations were conducted using independent samples. Study 1 examined married couples (N = 100 individuals, 50 dyads). Study 2 examined triangulation among adolescents (N = 300). In both studies, participants were randomly assigned to an experimental or control condition. The experimental condition received two 2 hour workshops delivering the Islamically integrated HMT Seven Conversations protocol for couples, or its adolescent and family adaptation, Hold Me Tight–Let Me Go® (HMT LMG). The control condition received two 2 hour general psychoeducational workshops, matched in contact time but without the HMT protocol or Islamic integration content. Equating the two conditions on session number and duration helped isolate the active therapeutic components of the HMT protocol from the non specific benefits of therapeutic attention and social contact (Kazdin, 2017; Shadish, Cook, & Campbell, 2002). In the couples sample, a cross sectional dyadic Actor Partner Interdependence Mediation Model (APIMeM; N = 50 dyads) showed that both husbands' and wives' couple satisfaction significantly and positively predicted their own emotional intimacy (husbands, β = .75, p < .001; wives, β = .72, p < .001). Gaslighting did not significantly mediate this relationship for either partner. After the intervention, the experimental group (n = 50) showed significant improvements across all variables: couple satisfaction (M = 59.60 to 66.84, t(49) = 5.55, p < .001), emotional intimacy (M = 53.92 to 60.74, t(49) = 6.36, p < .001), and gaslighting (M = 66.74 to 23.04, t(49) = 10.07, p < .001). The control group (n = 50) showed no significant change on any variable (all p > .15). At post test, the experimental group scored significantly higher than the control group on all variables (all p < .001). In the adolescent sample, triangulation was significantly and negatively associated with parental bonding, r(298) = .13, p = .026, and self esteem, r(298) = .15, p = .007. Parental bonding did not significantly mediate the relationship between triangulation and self esteem (indirect effect = .012, 95% CI [.026, .001]). After the intervention, the experimental group (n = 150) showed significant reductions in triangulation (M = 77.05 to 66.91, t(149) = 19.68, p < .001), and significant increases in parental bonding (M = 77.72 to 82.56, t(149) = 16.15, p < .001) and self esteem (M = 21.70 to 26.69, t(149) = 20.12, p < .001), with large effect sizes throughout (d = 1.32 to 1.64). The control group (n = 150) showed no meaningful change on any variable (all absolute d values ≤ 0.29). Groups were statistically equivalent at baseline (all p ≥ .125). At post test, the experimental group scored significantly better than the control group on triangulation and self esteem (both p < .001). Parental bonding did not differ significantly between groups at that time point. Together, these findings provide controlled, Pakistan specific evidence that a culturally and Islamically integrated Hold Me Tight® program improves relational and psychological outcomes for both married couples and adolescents beyond the effect of general psychoeducation alone. These results support the central premise that Islamic integrated, EFT based psychoeducation is both an effective and a culturally acceptable intervention for Pakistani families. Keywords: Hold Me Tight, Emotionally Focused Therapy, Islamic-integrated intervention, randomized controlled evaluation, couple satisfaction, gaslighting, emotional intimacy, triangulation, parental bonding, self-esteem, actor–partner interdependence model
experimental_design: Design Both studies used a randomized, controlled pretest posttest design. Participants in each study were randomly assigned to an experimental condition or a control condition. The experimental condition received workshops based on the culturally and Islamically integrated Hold Me Tight® protocol (Study 1, couples) or its adolescent and family adaptation, Hold Me Tight–Let Me Go® (Study 2, adolescents). The control condition received general psychoeducational workshops on family relationships that did not include the HMT protocol or the Islamic integration content. All participants completed the study measures immediately before and immediately after the sessions (posttest). 5.2 Study-1 Married Couples Married couples (N = 50 dyads, 100 individuals) were recruited through purposive sampling and randomly assigned to the experimental (n = 50 individuals, 25 couples) or control (n = 50 individuals, 25 couples) condition. All participants completed the Couple Satisfaction Index (16 items; Funk & Rogge, 2007), the Gaslighting Scale (20 items; Stern, 2007), and the Emotional Intimacy Scale (14 items; Eukie, 2022) at both time points. Since both members of each couple were sampled, husbands' and wives' scores are statistically non independent. The cross sectional relationships among these variables were therefore modeled dyadically (Section 5.4). The pre post intervention evaluation, however, treated individuals as the unit of analysis, consistent with the paired and independent samples comparisons 5.3 Study-2 Adolescents Adolescents (N = 300; 150 boys, 150 girls; aged 13 to 19 years) were recruited from public and private educational institutions and randomly assigned to the experimental (n = 150) or control (n = 150) condition. All participants completed the Triangulation Scale (27 items; Riaz & Iqbal, 2023), the Parental Bonding Instrument (25 items; Parker et al., 1979), and the Rosenberg Self Esteem Scale (10 items; Rosenberg, 1965) at both time points 5.4 Intervention The experimental condition in both studies delivered EFT based Hold Me Tight® (couples) or Hold Me Tight–Let Me Go® (adolescents) content integrated with Islamic teachings. This included Quranic guidance on marital and family relationships (Surah Ar Rum 30:21; Surah An Nisa 4:19), Hadith on marital harmony (Sunan Abi Dawood 3544), and the Shariah compliant mediation principles of Tahkim, Wasatah, and Maslaha. The content was delivered through interactive lectures, guided discussion, reflective exercises drawn from the Hold Me Tight® Participant Workbook, and experiential activities. The control condition delivered general psychoeducational content on family relationships and communication. This was matched to the experimental condition in terms of structure, but it omitted the HMT protocol and the Islamic integration content. As a result, any between group difference in outcomes can be attributed to the specific content of the HMT protocols rather than to the non specific benefits of participating in a structured group activity (Kazdin, 2017).

abstract: We evaluate Feelings Detectives, a teacher-delivered programme designed to support emotional self-regulation among primary-school children in Kyiv, Ukraine. The programme teaches children to recognise feelings and body cues, select and use regulation strategies, return to goal-directed activity, seek appropriate help and manage peer interactions. It comprises ten weekly classroom lessons with supporting routines and materials. The study uses a classroom-randomised waitlist-control design within seven schools. The confirmatory sample comprises 52 classrooms in Grades 2-4, with 26 assigned to immediate programme delivery and 26 to waitlist control. Four Grade 1 classrooms are randomised separately and will be analysed only as exploratory. Outcomes are measured using tablet-based behavioural tasks, child reports, teacher ratings and peer nominations. Data are collected from both groups at three points: baseline; a first endline after the initial treatment group completes the programme, and a second endline, moths after the treatment group has finished. The first endline identifies the effect of programme assignment relative to the not-yet-treated control group. The second endline assesses whether outcomes persist several months after programme completion. The study examines whether assignment to Feelings Detectives improves children’s emotional understanding, inhibitory control and stability of incentivised choices. Four primary endpoints capture these domains: taught-cue and transfer-item emotion-recognition accuracy, Hearts and Flowers mixed-block accuracy, and switching across identical time and risk choices administered before and after a standardised classroom activity. Secondary outcomes assess teacher-reported regulation, social behaviour and peer relationships, while exploratory outcomes include wellbeing and academic task performance. Classroom randomisation identifies the effects of programme assignment relative to waitlist control. Changes in choice stability will be interpreted alongside the other outcomes, without assuming that every switch reflects a failure of self-regulation or that the within-session contrast isolates the effect of emotional activation.
experimental_design: The study is a classroom-randomised controlled trial in seven Kyiv schools. The confirmatory sample consists of 52 classrooms in Grades 2–4, with 26 assigned to the programme and 26 to waitlist control. Four Grade 1 classrooms are randomised separately and analysed as an exploratory sample. Measurements include tablet-based child assessments, teacher reports and peer nominations. The main endline is scheduled before waitlist programme delivery. Effects will be estimated by original classroom assignment, regardless of programme attendance.
experimental_design_details: Confirmatory assignment occurred on 31 July 2026. A computer-generated restricted randomisation assigned exactly 26 classrooms to each arm while keeping treatment and control classroom counts within one classroom of each other in every school. Of 100,000 unique eligible allocations, the best-balanced 25 percent were retained using Mahalanobis distance based on grade composition and school-demeaned classroom size. One allocation was selected uniformly from this retained set. Grade 1 assignment was conducted separately, with one treatment and one control classroom in each of two schools. For each primary endpoint, the proposed main analysis estimates endline intention-to-treat effects using OLS with school and grade fixed effects and classroom-clustered standard errors. Baseline outcomes will not enter as regressors. Randomisation-inference sensitivity analyses will respect the actual assignment restrictions. Randomisation and some baseline data collection preceded registration. Baseline data from 10–11 September 2026 were inspected descriptively for performance, comprehension, missingness and timing; live progress was inspected on 14 September. The registration will disclose the complete investigator data-access history. Missing outcomes will not be coded as zero, and low task performance alone will not justify excluding children.
intervention: Feelings Detectives is a teacher-delivered programme supporting emotional understanding and self-regulation among primary-school children in Kyiv, Ukraine. It comprises ten approximately weekly, 40-minute classroom lessons, supported by teacher training, teaching materials and short classroom routines. Activities address recognising emotions and bodily cues, understanding emotional intensity, using regulation strategies, responding to frustration, returning to activities, seeking help and managing peer interactions. Treatment classrooms receive the programme during the evaluation period. Waitlist classrooms continue their usual schooling and are scheduled to receive the programme after the main endline assessment.

mde_text: Preliminary normal-approximation calculations use 52 confirmatory classrooms, 1,078 pupils, equal classroom sizes, no attrition and no baseline-outcome adjustment. With 80 percent power and a conservative two-sided significance threshold of 0.0125 for four primary endpoints, the approximate MDE is 0.29 outcome standard deviations at an ICC of 0.05, 0.35 at an ICC of 0.10, and 0.45 at an ICC of 0.20. These are illustrative sensitivities, not final outcome-specific calculations; they do not incorporate unequal classroom sizes, finite-cluster inference or the exact restricted randomisation. Percentage-point equivalents require outcome-specific variances

primary_outcome_explanation: Emotion recognition produces two separate scores: the number of correct responses to four taught-cue items, ranging from 0–4, and two transfer items, ranging from 0–2. Higher scores indicate greater accuracy. The items and scoring remain unchanged across assessment waves. Hearts and Flowers accuracy is the proportion of correct responses across 33 scored mixed-block trials. Practice trials are excluded. Incorrect responses and recorded response-window timeouts count as incorrect; trials missing because an assessment was interrupted are not automatically coded as errors. Choice switching is the number of decisions that differ between two administrations of identical choice lists: four time choices and four risk choices, separated by a researcher-led Simon Says activity. The score ranges from 0–8; lower scores indicate greater stability, not necessarily better preferences or definitive evidence of emotional regulation. All eight matched choice pairs are required to construct this endpoint. These are four separate primary endpoints, not a combined index. We will apply Holm correction across the four primary tests, controlling the family-wise error rate at 5 percent, and report all estimates.
primary_outcomes: The primary outcomes, measured at the first post-programme endline before waitlist delivery, cover three domains: 1. Emotional understanding: taught-cue emotion-recognition accuracy and transfer-item emotion-recognition accuracy. 2. Inhibitory control: Hearts and Flowers mixed-block accuracy. 3. Choice stability: total item-level switching across repeated incentivised time and risk choices administered before and after a standardised classroom activity.
randomization_method: Computer-generated restricted randomisation in Stata. The confirmatory draw used seed 13082026 and selected uniformly from a retained pool of balanced eligible allocations. The separate Grade 1 draw used seed 13082027.
randomization_unit: Classroom. Grades 2–4 form the confirmatory sample; Grade 1 classrooms are randomised separately for exploratory analysis.
secondary_outcome_explanation: Teacher outcomes are eight separate ratings of stopping when calm, stopping when emotionally activated, awareness of emotional intensity, independent strategy use, recovery, persistence, regulation during conflict and helping peers. We also examine the activated-minus-calm stopping contrast. Ratings use a five-category scale; insufficient opportunity to observe is treated as missing. No overall eight-item score is assumed. Social outcomes include stars sent in the trust game, the mean fraction returned across four contingent receipt amounts, stars allocated in the giving game, and isolation in friendship and help networks. The return measure is a descriptive task summary, not a validated scale. Network isolation means receiving no nomination of the relevant type among participating nominators; unavailable nomination data are not coded as isolation. Choice outcomes include time and risk switching separately and the numbers of delayed-reward and risky choices in the first administration. Greater patience, risk-taking or giving will not automatically be interpreted as improvement. The exploratory distress measure sums four study-specific seven-day items, ranging from 0–12 when all responses are observed. It is not a validated PHQ-4 administration and will not use clinical cutoffs. Secondary tests will use Holm correction within each of the three named families; exploratory analyses will be identified separately.

abstract: Participatory budgeting gives citizens a direct role in deciding how public resources are spent. Existing studies show that such participation can improve citizens’ evaluations of government. Yet my previous survey experiment in Uzbekistan finds close to zero average effects of participatory budgeting on state legitimacy. I argue that this puzzle can be explained, in part, by attribution. Participatory institutions can increase state legitimacy only when citizens directly credit the state for public goods that these institutions bring. Citizens may instead credit their communities or view the state and community as jointly responsible. I test this argument with a five arm survey experiment in Uzbekistan. Respondents receive different information about who is responsible for the same successful participatory budgeting project: the government, the community, both actors, or no actor in particular. I examine how these different attribution frames affect state legitimacy, evaluations of government, horizontal trust and collective efficacy, and support for participatory budgeting. I also test whether knowledge of social rights shape how citizens respond to state credit. The study shows how attribution can help explain when participatory institutions strengthen state legitimacy and when their effects remain at the community level.
experimental_design: The study will recruit adult participants from Uzbekistan via online advertisements on the Telegram messaging platform, leveraging large Telegram channels/groups. Using an online survey allows broad reach and an approximately nationally diverse sample of citizens active on social media. My target sample size is approximately 2500 respondents, which (accounting for some attrition) should provide around 1500-2000 analyzable cases. Participants will be randomly assigned with equal probability into one of five treatment groups. A simple random assignment will be implemented through the survey platform Qualtrics to ensure true randomization. A small caveat: if a respondent begins but does not complete the survey, it may slightly affect the distribution of random assignment, potentially resulting in minor imbalances across treatment groups. Each participant will thus have a somewhat equal chance of being in any one condition:
experimental_design_details: All treatment vignettes will be presented in the Uzbek language and will be of similar length (~2-3 short paragraphs) to ensure a comparable reading load. The survey will instruct participants to read the text carefully, as one factual question will follow to serve as a manipulation check. After the treatment (or nothing, for control), respondents will answer the main outcome questions on legitimacy perceptions and related attitudes. Manipulation Checks To verify that participants received and understood the treatments, we include manipulation check questions immediately after the treatment vignettes for many respondents, and for a portion of respondents after the key outcome measures. These checks are simple factual or recall questions about the content of the vignette or task: • What did the project improve in the neighborhood? The water supply, The roads, The schools, or I do not remember. • In your view, who was mainly responsible for making this project happen? Mostly the community and residents, Mostly the government, Both about equally, or Not sure. This item is not asked in T2. • If government or both is selected: Which government do you have in mind mainly? The national government, The regional or district authorities, The mahalla leadership, or Not sure. I use the manipulation check to see whether the treatments change who respondents credit for the project. I expect respondents in the government credit condition to give more credit to the government, those in the community credit condition to give more credit to the community, and those in the combined condition to credit both. I use these results to assess how well the treatments worked. I do not exclude respondents based on their answers to the manipulation check. The primary analysis includes all respondents according to their assigned treatment.
intervention: I use an original online survey with a target of 2,500 adults who are permanent residents of Uzbekistan. I randomly assign eligible respondents with equal probability to one of five unlabeled conditions in a between-subjects design. T1 is a pure control. T2 through T5 receive the same common description of Initiatives Budgeting and the same successful clean-water project. The four treated arms differ only in the attribution language that follows the common description.

abstract: Microbusinesses face severe constraints in access to formal credit, even when they exhibit adequate repayment capacity. These constraints arise from both supply-side factors—such as difficulties in assessing credit risk—and demand-side factors, including self-exclusion driven by fear of rejection or misaligned financial products. Given that a large share of microbusinesses are led by women, gender-based barriers further exacerbate credit access gaps. This study evaluates the impact of credit allocation using an artificial intelligence (AI)–based credit scoring model on microbusiness outcomes in Colombia. The intervention leverages alternative data and debiasing techniques that explicitly exclude gender and race from credit decisions. Using a randomized controlled trial with delayed access to credit, the study examines the effects of credit access on formal financial inclusion, repayment behavior, and proxies of economic activity. The analysis further explores heterogeneous impacts by credit score and by gender, assessing whether AI-based models can both expand access to credit and mitigate gender disparities without increasing credit risk.
experimental_design: The study population consists of individuals who apply for a loan through Quipu, a fintech platform that provides credit to microbusinesses with limited or no formal credit history. Quipu has issued credit to approximately 7,000 microbusinesses since 2022 and operates nationwide in Colombia. Credit applications are submitted via WhatsApp, and approved applicants typically receive funds within a few days. Eligible participants are applicants who obtain an approved credit score according to Quipu’s AI-based credit model. The target sample size is approximately 1,500 applicants, with 750 assigned to the treatment group and 750 to the control group.
experimental_design_details: The study population consists of individuals who apply for a loan through Quipu, a fintech platform that provides credit to microbusinesses with limited or no formal credit history. Quipu has issued credit to approximately 7,000 microbusinesses since 2022 and operates nationwide in Colombia. Credit applications are submitted via WhatsApp, and approved applicants typically receive funds within a few days. Eligible participants are applicants who obtain an approved credit score according to Quipu’s AI-based credit model. Certain populations are excluded from the study for ethical and operational reasons, including migrants and applicants using specific application channels that Quipu prioritizes for business reasons. The target sample size is approximately 1,500 applicants, with 750 assigned to the treatment group and 750 to the control group. Once the target sample is reached, Quipu resumes its standard credit allocation procedures.
intervention: The intervention evaluates access to credit granted through an AI-based credit scoring model that relies on alternative data sources and incorporates debiasing techniques to eliminate gender and race as decision variables. Among eligible applicants, individuals are randomly assigned to one of two groups: Treatment group: receives a credit offer following Quipu’s standard approval timeline. Control group: receives a notification indicating that credit cannot be approved at that time but is invited to reapply after a specified period. Applicants who score above the minimum AI-based scoring model are not eligible for credit and thus comprise a second control group for the study. After follow-up data collection is completed (between 6 and 18 months after application), individuals in the control groups are proactively contacted and offered access to credit. The intervention therefore delays—but does not deny—access to the financial product.

abstract: Firms compete along multiple dimensions, yet investments that reduce externalities may go unrewarded when too few consumers value them. We ask whether the \emph{presentation} of quality information can change this, focusing on whether information about different product dimensions is reported separately or bundled into a single score or rating. In a multi-round monopoly setting with binary quality choices, de Haan and Knutsen (2025, Management Science) show that bundling information can induce reputation-conscious monopolists to invest more in attributes that consumers otherwise ignore. We test whether this result extends to a competitive environment and to continuous rather than binary investment choices. In our laboratory Bertrand duopoly, sellers choose a price and quality levels in two attributes. We vary whether consumers observe separate ratings for the two attributes or a single rating combining them. Theory predicts that separate ratings drive investment in the externality-reducing attribute to zero, whereas a combined rating sustains strictly positive investment even when no consumer directly values that attribute. We test this prediction, together with the associated predictions for prices and investment in quality attribute A. In this initial two-treatment design, attribute B receives a 25 percent weight in the bundled rating, rather than the 50 percent used by de Haan and Knutsen. We hold this weight fixed to isolate the effect of separate versus combined ratings. In subsequent sessions, intended for the full paper, we plan to vary the weight placed on attribute B and to compare the linear rating rule used here with a threshold rule, under which investment in attribute B contributes to the combined rating only if a minimum investment level is reached.
experimental_design: Subjects are randomly assigned to fixed matching groups of three: two sellers and one buyer. Roles and group membership are fixed for the whole session, so each matching group is a single independent observation. Each round has three stages. The two sellers simultaneously choose quality in attribute A, quality in attribute B, and a price. The buyer then sees both offers, displayed in randomised order, and chooses one of them or neither. Finally all group members receive feedback. Groups play up to 15 rounds with fixed matching and no rematching. A session ends after round 15 or after one hour of play, whichever comes first. The stopping rule is announced in the instructions and the number of rounds each group completes is recorded. Sessions begin with six instruction screens, a practice screen on which subjects can enter hypothetical combinations of the two quality levels and a price and see the resulting seller profit, consumer payoff and rating, and five incentivised comprehension questions with answers displayed afterwards. Subjects receive a starting capital of 50 points and cumulative earnings are floored at zero, so no subject can finish with negative earnings. Points are converted to cash at a rate announced in advance. The two treatments differ only in whether the buyer sees two separate attribute ratings or one combined rating. All other features are identical.
experimental_design_details: Feedback. At the end of each round all members of a matching group see whether a purchase occurred and, for the traded offer, attribute A, attribute B and the price separately, together with their own earnings. Note that this reveals the decomposition of the rating to buyers in the combined-rating treatment after the fact. We retain this feature because it is the natural learning environment and because it makes the combined-rating prediction harder to obtain rather than easier. Analysis. The unit of analysis is the matching group mean over rounds 4 to the last completed round. The main hypothesis is tested by comparing these group means across treatments using both a Mann-Whitney rank-sum test and a t-test. Secondary outcomes are analysed the same way. We will not conduct interim analyses or stop early on the basis of results. A pilot session was run on 31 August 2026 with 15 subjects in 5 matching groups over 10 rounds. It is not part of the confirmatory sample and is used only to calibrate the between-group variance for the power calculation and to fix the analysis window.
intervention: We vary how information about two product attributes is displayed to consumers in a laboratory Bertrand duopoly. In each matching group, two sellers simultaneously choose quality in attribute A, quality in attribute B, and a price. A single consumer observes both offers and buys at most one unit, or abstains. The consumer's payoff depends only on attribute A and the price, so attribute B has no consumption value. Attribute B stands for an investment, such as reducing an externality, that is costly to the seller and not directly valued by the buyer. The two treatments differ only in what the consumer sees: Separate ratings: the consumer observes attribute A and attribute B for both sellers, each displayed as its own rating, together with both prices. Combined rating: the consumer observes a single rating for each seller, equal to 0.75 times attribute A plus 0.25 times attribute B, together with both prices. The question is whether bundling attribute B into the displayed rating induces sellers to invest in it even though the consumer places no value on it.

mde_text: The outcome is mean attribute B investment per matching group, measured in points on a 0 to 100 scale. The matching group is both the unit of randomisation and the unit of analysis, so clustering is fully accounted for by aggregating to the group level before testing. A pilot session gives a pooled between-group standard deviation of attribute B of 4.0 points, but estimated on only 3 degrees of freedom, so the 95 percent interval for the standard deviation runs from 2.3 to 15.1. We therefore report minimum detectable effects across a range of standard deviations rather than relying on the pilot point estimate. Because the primary test is nonparametric and the outcome is bounded below at zero, power was simulated rather than taken from a normal-theory formula. The simulation draws the group-level outcome as a normal censored at zero, to reproduce the mass of groups that settle on zero investment, and applies the Mann-Whitney rank-sum test at the 5 percent two-sided level. With 18 groups per arm, the minimum detectable difference at 80 percent power is 4.08 points if the standard deviation is 4, 5.04 points if it is 5, 6.09 points if it is 6, 8.07 points if it is 8, and 10.12 points if it is 10. The predicted treatment effect is 15 to 16.67 points, and the pilot difference over the analysis window was 14.06 points. Expressed relative to the predicted effect, the design detects effects of roughly 25 to 40 percent of the predicted size for standard deviations between 4 and 6. At the pilot effect size, simulated power exceeds 0.99 for any standard deviation up to 8, and is 0.97 even at a standard deviation of 10. A t-test applied to the same simulated data gives minimum detectable effects within about 1 percent of the rank test, so the choice between the two does not drive the sample size. A normal-theory t formula would give figures about 5 percent smaller, but that formula assumes an uncensored normal outcome and therefore understates the minimum detectable effect for this design. Simulated size of the rank test is approximately 0.05 under equal variances.

abstract: Food systems in Sub-Saharan Africa are increasingly exposed to shocks and stressors, including climate variability, global price shocks, social conflict, and the lingering effects of the COVID-19 pandemic. These disturbances threaten agricultural production and food security, disproportionately affecting smallholder farmers who depend on rain-fed agriculture and often lack the resources to absorb or adapt to shocks. Strengthening food system resilience - defined as the capacity of food systems and their actors to provide sufficient, appropriate, and accessible food in the face of disturbances - is therefore an urgent policy priority. This study examines whether targeted agricultural and gender-transformative interventions can strengthen the resilience of smallholder farmers in rural Tanzania. Specifically, it evaluates the causal impact of Farmer Field Business Schools (FFBS), implemented through Village Savings and Loan Associations (VSLAs), on household resilience and livelihoods. FFBS aim to improve access to agronomic and market information, strengthen financial inclusion, and enhance production and investment decisions. The analysis is based on a stratified cluster randomized controlled trial conducted in 120 villages across three districts in Tanzania. Villages were randomly assigned to one of three arms: (i) FFBS only, (ii) FFBS enhanced with a gender-transformative Social Analysis and Action (SAA) approach, or (iii) a control group. The baseline sample comprises 1,680 smallholder households, with at least one respondent per household a member of a VSLA (14 per village). Primary outcomes include the use of agricultural advisory services, productive use of financial resources, adoption of climate-resilient agricultural practices, agricultural productivity and the value of crop production, loss of planted area due to weather shocks, food security, and women's empowerment and attitudes toward gender norms. The findings provide policy-relevant insights into how information, financial mechanisms, and gender-transformative approaches can enhance households’ ability not only to improve outcomes in normal times, but also to withstand and recover from adverse shocks.
experimental_design: This study employs a stratified cluster randomized controlled trial (RCT) to evaluate the impacts of Farmer Field Business Schools (FFBS), implemented either alone or in combination with a gender-transformative Social Analysis and Action (SAA) approach, on small-scale farming households in rural Tanzania. Villages are the unit of randomization because the interventions are delivered at the community level. The study is conducted in the districts of Iringa, Kilolo, and Wanging'ombe. A total of 139 villages met the program eligibility criteria, including the presence of an active savings group (VICOBA or VSLA) meeting minimum membership requirements, sufficient participation by women and crop farmers, and no prior exposure to FFBS or gender-transformative interventions. From these, 120 villages were selected and stratified into six strata defined by the combination of district (Iringa, Kilolo, and Wanging'ombe) and agroecological zone (hot/mild and cold/very cold) before being randomly assigned to one of three study arms: (1) FFBS only (40 villages); (2) FFBS combined with SAA (40 villages); and (3) a control group receiving no project intervention during the evaluation period (40 villages). Within each study village, fourteen households were randomly selected from savings group membership lists, yielding a baseline sample of 1,680 households (560 per study arm). Baseline data were collected in March 2024, and endline data will be collected from the same households between October and November 2026. The study is designed to estimate both the impact of FFBS relative to the control group and the additional impact of integrating SAA with FFBS.
intervention: The SADIFU project evaluates the impact of Farmer Field Business Schools (FFBS), implemented alone or in combination with a gender-transformative Social Analysis and Action (SAA) approach, among small-scale farming communities in rural Tanzania. The study focuses on smallholder farmers who are members of existing Village Savings and Loan Associations (VSLAs), and therefore operate under relatively less binding liquidity constraints compared to non-members. The evaluation is designed to compare the effects of FFBS alone with those of FFBS combined with SAA, thereby identifying the additional contribution of the gender-transformative component to agricultural, economic, and intra-household outcomes. The intervention has two active treatment arms. In the first arm (FFBS), farmers participate in group-based Farmer Field Business Schools built on existing Savings and Loan Associations (SLAs). The objective of FFBS is to enhance farmers’ knowledge, improve adoption of CRA practices, increase agricultural productivity and market participation, and ultimately strengthen household income, food security, and resilience against weather shocks. FFBS is a learning-by-doing model that provides training in climate-resilient agricultural (CRA) practices (e.g. minimum tillage, crop rotation, intercropping), post-harvest handling, nutrition, financial literacy, and farm business management. The program also strengthens access to savings and credit within SLAs, promotes improved record-keeping, and facilitates linkages to input suppliers, buyers, and market actors. The FFBS intervention operates through several mechanisms. Training and experiential learning increase farmers’ knowledge and skills, which are expected to translate into greater adoption of CRA practices. Improved access to savings and credit relaxes liquidity constraints, and, when combined with increased knowledge and skills, enables farmers to invest in agricultural inputs and technologies. Market linkages and business training improve commercialization and price realization. Together, these channels are expected to increase crop productivity, farm income, and food security. The second treatment arm (FFBS+SAA) includes all FFBS components and adds a gender-transformative Social Analysis and Action (SAA) approach. The addition of SAA is expected to influence outcomes through changes in intra-household dynamics and social norms. SAA consists of structured community dialogues, household-level engagement, and village-level activities aimed at challenging restrictive gender norms and strengthening women’s agency in agricultural and household decision-making. The approach promotes reflection on gender roles, joint planning within households, and community-level norm change, supported by trained facilitators and gender champions. By promoting critical reflection and dialogue on gender roles, SAA aims to increase women’s decision-making power, control over resources, and confidence. These changes are expected to improve the allocation of labor and inputs, enhance cooperation within households, and facilitate the adoption of agricultural and economic practices promoted through FFBS. By addressing gender-based constraints that limit women’s access to resources, information, and decision-making, the SAA component is expected to amplify the impacts of FFBS on agricultural productivity, income generation, and household welfare. The target population consists of small-scale farming households in villages with active Savings and Loan Associations in a region highly exposed to weather shocks, like droughts. The intervention particularly targets female SLA members and female-headed households, while also engaging men and broader community members to promote inclusive and sustained change. The intervention is implemented through community-based facilitators, including paraprofessionals and community trainers, each responsible for supporting multiple FFBS groups within their villages. The interventions rely on several key assumptions. First, farmers are willing to participate in group-based learning and adopt new practices. Second, VSLAs function effectively and provide reliable access to finance. Third, market actors engage with farmers and provide viable market opportunities. Fourth, both men and women participate in SAA activities and are receptive to changes in gender norms. These assumptions are critical for the intervention to achieve the intended outcomes and will be explored empirically through complementary qualitative methods and targeted survey modules. Overall, the intervention aims to improve smallholder farmers' resilience to weather shocks, agricultural performance, food security, and women's empowerment in vulnerable rural communities.

mde_text: We conduct power calculations using baseline data and the planned cluster-randomized design. The calculations assume 40 villages per study arm, 14 households per village, a two-sided significance level of 5%, and 80% statistical power. We base the calculations on pairwise comparisons between two study arms and estimate minimum detectable effects (MDEs) separately for each outcome using its baseline mean, standard deviation, and intracluster correlation coefficient (ICC). We also account for expected precision gains from stratified randomization and the planned ANCOVA specification. To capture the gains from stratification, we estimate the share of between-village variation explained by the randomization strata, which ranges from 3% to 43% across outcomes. For the ANCOVA adjustment, we consider baseline-endline correlations of 0.4 and 0.7, representing conservative and optimistic scenarios, respectively. The accompanying table reports the baseline mean, standard deviation, ICC, and MDE for each outcome. We express MDEs in the original outcome units, as a percentage of the baseline mean, and in standard deviation units. Under the unadjusted design, MDEs range from 0.22 to 0.39 standard deviations. Accounting for stratification and ANCOVA improves precision, reducing this range to 0.19-0.35 standard deviations under the conservative scenario and 0.15-0.27 under the optimistic scenario. For most outcomes, the adjusted MDEs lie between 0.15 and 0.25 standard deviations. For example, the MDE for maize yield decreases from 23% of the baseline mean under the unadjusted design to 19.8% under the conservative scenario and 15% under the optimistic scenario. Overall, these results suggest that the study is sufficiently powered to detect moderate and policy-relevant changes in the main outcomes included in the program's theory of change, although smaller effects may remain below the minimum detectable threshold.

abstract: This study examines whether the grammatical gender of occupational titles affects perceived earnings. We conducted two representative online surveys of adults and adolescents in Germany. The adult sample consists of 1,575 respondents aged 18–75, and the adolescent sample consists of 1,629 respondents aged 14–17. Respondents were randomly assigned at the individual level to a masculine-title or feminine-title condition and subsequently estimated the earnings associated with five occupations. The occupations comprise a physician, the head of a large company, a supermarket salesperson, an unskilled factory worker, and a member of the German Bundestag. Treatment assignment was approximately balanced between the two conditions. The primary outcome is respondents' reported earnings estimates. The experiment tests whether otherwise equivalent occupations are assigned different earnings depending solely on whether they are presented using a masculine or feminine occupational title.
experimental_design: The experiment was embedded in two standardised online surveys of adults and adolescents in Germany. Respondents were randomly assigned at the individual level, with approximately equal probability, to one of two conditions. In the masculine-title condition, all five occupations were presented using masculine German occupational titles; in the feminine-title condition, the same occupations were presented using feminine titles. The five occupations were physician, head of a large company, supermarket salesperson, unskilled factory worker, and member of the German Bundestag. Apart from the grammatical gender of the occupational title, question wording was held constant across conditions. Respondents estimated the typical monthly gross earnings associated with each occupation. Each respondent remained in the same title condition across all five occupations. Randomisation was not clustered.

In one condition, five occupations were presented using masculine German occupational titles; in the other condition, the same occupations were presented using feminine occupational titles. All other wording and the earnings questions were held constant. Respondents were asked to estimate the typical monthly gross earnings associated with each occupation.

abstract: The study of Economics at university heavily relies on quantitative (mathematical) skills.Often students differ substantially in their pre-existing knowledge of mathematical concepts used in economics, depending e.g. on their choice of A levels or whether their secondary education was in the UK or overseas. Differences in pre-existing knowledge are likely to impact students’ learning experience in their Economics degree programme. Moreover, students’ knowledge endowment from secondary education is likely to differ systematically with demographic characteristics (SES included) thus raising issues of ensuring equal opportunity for all our students. Existing research indiates the presence of differences in academic outcomes by student background, which can partially be explained by individal preparedness and pre-existing knowledge of quantitative skills. This study will investigate whether targeted support in the form of adaptive learning help to close any gaps in academic performance. To do so this study will use experimental methods to investigate whether the introduction of an adaptive learning method into the module Statistics for Economics has an effect on student outcomes, in the form of exam grades, and on behaviour, in the form of enagement. The results can inform educational policy at the host institution and elsewhere, for instance if a positive effect is identified that is large enough to be economically relevant.

abstract: This study proposes a randomised controlled trial to evaluate interventions designed to increase the supply, quality, and market value of bamboo produced by smallholder farmers in India. The study uses a sampling frame of 6,349 bamboo-growing households across Ajara, Sawantwadi, and Hukkeri taluks. A sample of 3,300 households is selected through a stratified, multi-stage design in which villages are first classified by bamboo cultivation system and geography, and are then assigned to five village-level arms: production/action-plan, quality-market access, bundle, near-control, and far pure-control. Within treatment villages, households are randomly assigned to direct treatment without the behavioural overlay, direct treatment with the behavioural overlay, or spillover status. The behavioural overlay is cross-randomized among directly treated households and combines future-profit salience, loss framing, implementation intentions, soft commitment, reminders, and technical-support cues. The design enables estimation of direct treatment effects, within-village spillovers, cross-village spillovers, and behavioural mechanisms. The empirical strategy will use ANCOVA specifications with far pure-control households as the omitted reference category and standard errors clustered at the village level.
experimental_design: The study uses a randomized controlled trial to evaluate interventions designed to improve bamboo production, quality upgrading, and market participation among bamboo-growing farm households in India. The experiment is implemented among listed bamboo-growing households across selected villages in Maharashtra and Karnataka. The study follows a multi-stage randomized design. Villages are first stratified by bamboo cultivation system, distinguishing villages where bamboo is primarily grown as monocrop, mixed crop, or border crop. Within these strata, villages are assigned to different experimental arms. The main treatment arms are a production/action-plan intervention, a quality-market-access intervention, and a bundled intervention that combines both components. The comparison group includes control villages, with some control villages classified as geographically or economically closer to treatment areas and others as far pure-control villages. Within treatment villages, only a randomly selected subset of sampled households receives the intervention directly. Other sampled households in the same treatment villages do not receive direct treatment and are included to measure possible spillovers within villages. This structure allows the study to distinguish direct effects of the intervention from indirect effects that may arise through neighbours, relatives, farmer groups, traders, or local market interactions. The production/action-plan intervention provides practical information on bamboo clump management, thinning, cleaning, rejuvenation, mature culm identification, and harvesting practices. The quality-market-access intervention provides information on bamboo grading, quality requirements, buyer options, price comparison, and market channels, including possible links to processors, industries, farmer collectives, or organized buyers. The bundled intervention combines the production and market components. A behavioural support component is cross-randomized among directly treated households. This component includes future-profit salience, loss framing, an individualized bamboo action plan, soft commitment, reminders, and technical-support cues. It is designed to test whether behavioural support improves follow-through on bamboo management and marketing decisions. The primary comparisons will estimate the effect of each treatment arm relative to the far pure-control group. Additional comparisons will examine within-village spillovers, differences between near-control and far pure-control villages, and the added effect of the behavioural support component among directly treated households. Outcomes will be measured through household surveys, field verification, and, where available, buyer or transaction records. The main outcomes include bamboo management practices, number of clumps managed, harvestable culms, bamboo quality, buyer search, sale channel, price received, and bamboo income.
intervention: This study will test practical ways to help bamboo-growing farmers increase the quantity and quality of bamboo they produce and sell. The interventions are designed to address three common barriers: limited technical knowledge about bamboo management, weak links to better-paying markets, and difficulty turning good intentions into action. The first intervention is a production and action-plan training. Farmers will receive simple, practical advice on how to manage bamboo clumps better. This will include guidance on cleaning clumps, removing old or dead culms, thinning overcrowded clumps, identifying mature culms, avoiding premature harvesting, and planning when key bamboo-management activities should be carried out. The second intervention is a quality and market-access intervention. Farmers will receive information on how bamboo quality affects price, how to sort and grade bamboo, how to compare buyers, and how to calculate the net price after transport, labour, commissions, and other deductions. Where possible, the intervention will also connect farmers with processors, industries, Farmer Producer Organizations, or other organized buyers who may be willing to pay more for better-quality bamboo. The third intervention is a bundled intervention that combines the production training with the quality and market-access support. This will test whether farmers benefit most when technical advice is linked to a credible market opportunity. In addition, some directly treated farmers will receive a behavioural support component. This will include a simple future-profit calculation, a discussion of avoidable losses from poor harvesting or selling decisions, a written bamboo action plan, a soft commitment to follow the plan, reminder messages or calls, and information on whom to contact for technical support. This component is designed to help farmers follow through on actions that may bring benefits later but require effort today. Some households in treatment villages will not receive the intervention directly. These households will allow the study to understand whether information spreads naturally through neighbours, relatives, traders, or farmer groups. Control villages will not receive the intervention during the study period and will provide a comparison group for measuring impact.
mde_text: The power calculations are based on a planned baseline sample of 3,300 bamboo-growing farm households across approximately 149 village clusters, allowing for around 10% attrition, which gives an expected endline sample of about 3,000 households. The calculations assume 80% power, a 5% two-sided significance level, and adjustment for village-level clustering. For the main supply-side outcome, log(1 + bamboo area in acres), the standard deviation of the log outcome is 0.321. The minimum detectable effect is approximately 0.093 log points, equivalent to about 0.29 standard deviations, or a 9.7% increase in bamboo area. For the second main production-stock outcome, log(1 + number of bamboo clumps), the standard deviation of the log outcome is 1.477. The minimum detectable effect is approximately 0.278 log points, equivalent to about 0.19 standard deviations, or a 32% increase in the number of clumps. Summary: Accounting for village-level clustering, 80% power, and a 5% two-sided significance level, the study is powered to detect an effect of approximately 0.093 log points, or 9.7%, for log(1 + bamboo area in acres), where the standard deviation is 0.321. For log(1 + number of bamboo clumps), where the standard deviation is 1.477, the study is powered to detect an effect of approximately 0.278 log points, or 32%. The calculations are based on a planned baseline sample of 3,300 households and an expected endline sample of about 3,000 households after attrition.

primary_outcomes: The effectiveness of the interventions will be assessed through outcomes at four levels: behavioural mechanisms, adoption and management behaviour, market behaviour, and final production and income. This follows the structure of agricultural extension evaluations that first examine knowledge, then adoption, then production, market participation, and welfare outcomes. In this study, the main production outcomes are bamboo area, number of clumps, clumps managed, mature culms per clump, total harvestable mature culms, culms harvested, and culms sold. The main market outcomes are buyer search, sale channel, quality grade, price per culm, marketing costs, net price, and bamboo income. To reflect multidimensional learning, the outcome framework will distinguish awareness, technical know-how, subtle know-how, adoption, and correct combinations of practices. Simple awareness will capture whether a farmer has heard about clump cleaning, quality grading, buyer premia, or delayed harvest. Technical know-how will capture whether the farmer knows how to perform specific tasks. Subtle know-how will capture whether the farmer understands complementarities, for example that quality premia require mature harvesting, sorting, and credible buyer access, or that clump cleaning must be timed with labour availability and future harvest planning. Mistakes in combinations, such as harvesting immature culms after receiving a quality-premium message or grading culms without comparing net prices, will be measured as a separate outcome category. The universal behavioural mechanism index will combine future-profit salience, loss awareness, action-plan existence and quality, plan implementation, self-efficacy, buyer trust, and willingness to wait for a premium. This index will be measured for all households and used as a mechanism outcome. A separate treatment-fidelity index will be created only for psychology-overlay households to verify whether the behavioural intervention was delivered as intended. The treatment-fidelity index will not be used as a main impact outcome because it is mechanically related to treatment assignment.
randomization_method: Randomization will be conducted in office by computer using a reproducible random-number generator. A fixed random seed will be used so that the village and household allocations can be replicated and audited. The randomization will be implemented in stages. First, villages will be stratified by bamboo cultivation system and location. Within each stratum, villages will be randomly assigned by computer to one of the experimental village arms: production/action-plan, quality-market access, bundle, near-control, or far pure-control. Second, within treatment villages, sampled households will be randomly assigned by computer to direct treatment without behavioural support, direct treatment with behavioural support, or spillover status. Households in control villages will be sampled from villages assigned to near-control or far pure-control status. The randomization will not be conducted by field enumerators. Field teams will receive the final assignment list after randomization is completed. The randomization file will record the random seed, strata, village IDs, household IDs, and assigned treatment status.
randomization_unit: The study uses more than one level of randomization. The first unit of randomization is the village. Villages will be randomly assigned to one of the main experimental environments: production/action-plan treatment, quality-market access treatment, bundled treatment, near-control, or far pure-control. Village-level randomization is used because information, learning, buyer contacts, and market behaviour may spill over across households within the same village. The second unit of randomization is the household within treatment villages. Within villages assigned to one of the active treatment arms, sampled households will be randomly assigned to receive the intervention directly, to receive the intervention directly with the behavioural support component, or to remain untreated within the village as spillover households. Thus, the design is a two-stage randomized design: village-level randomization determines the treatment environment, and household-level randomization within treatment villages determines direct exposure to the intervention and the behavioural support component.

abstract: This study has a large number of teams attempt the same research task (in applied microeconomics and causal inference) with a goal of seeing how research choices and outputs vary between those researchers. experimental_design: The main outline of the study is repeated-measures. At six different opportunities, participants will submit their results and take a survey. Analysis will compare these results across the six opportunities. 1. Initial research task 2. Optional revision following peer review 3. Research task with more precisely-defined research question 4. Optional revision following peer review 5. Research task with more precisely-defined research question and pre-cleaned data 6. Optional revision following peer review Within this structure, the peer review stages (2, 4, 6) are randomized and there are two-group comparisons, where 2/3 of the participants will be assigned to treatment (performing a peer review and having peer review performed on their work), and the rest to control. Among those assigned to treatment, they will be assigned to random pairs, and those pairs will review each others' work. There will then be between-group comparisons, evaluating the work of those who did peer review against those who did not, and also comparing the different randomly-assigned pairs of peer reviewers against each other.

abstract: How does the distribution of consumer value differences affect price competition between horizontally differentiated products? We separately vary the average absolute value difference and the concentration of the distribution near zero. Human participants act only as sellers; a computer implements the buyer's purchase. The experiment tests strategic pricing responses to these demand environments.
experimental_design: The study uses a 2 × 2 between-subject laboratory design with four treatments. Participants remain sellers for 60 paid games and are randomly rematched after every game within fixed six-seller matching groups. In each market, two sellers simultaneously set prices and an automated buyer purchases one product based on treatment-specific consumer values.
experimental_design_details: Participants take part in one treatment and remain in fixed six-seller matching groups. In each game, sellers are randomly paired within their group and simultaneously choose prices from 0 to 150; marginal cost is zero. The computer draws the absolute consumer-value difference from the treatment-specific distribution and randomly determines which product has the higher value. Product values are 155 + D/2 and 155 − D/2, and the buyer purchases the product with the highest value minus price. Sellers then observe both prices, the realized value difference, the purchase decision, and their own profit.
intervention: Participants act as sellers in repeated two-seller markets with an automated buyer. The four treatments vary (i) the mean absolute difference in consumer values and (ii) whether these differences follow a uniform distribution or are concentrated near zero. Sellers observe the treatment-specific distribution before setting prices but do not observe the realized consumer values.

abstract: This study examines how employers value individual soft skills and combinations of soft skills when evaluating entry-level candidates. We recruit 600 U.S.-based professionals with hiring experience to complete 12 discrete-choice tasks, each presenting two hypothetical candidates and a no-hire option. Candidate profiles experimentally vary academic performance, experience, gender, expected wage, and soft skills. The two confirmatory hypotheses are that employers treat reliability and teamwork as complements and initiative and planning as substitutes. We also estimate descriptive willingness to pay for improvements in each of eight soft skills and conduct secondary analyses of trade-offs across skills, preference heterogeneity, and the association between employers' beliefs about skill co-occurrence and their valuations of skill combinations.
experimental_design: We recruit 600 U.S.-based professionals with hiring experience through Prolific. Each employer completes 12 choice tasks, each presenting two hypothetical candidates and a no-hire option. Candidate profiles experimentally vary academic performance, experience, gender, expected wage, and three displayed soft skills. Every task includes either reliability and teamwork or initiative and planning as a focal pair. The two confirmatory hypotheses are that reliability and teamwork are complements and that initiative and planning are substitutes.

The two confirmatory tests are adjusted jointly using a Romano–Wolf step-down procedure with employer-level resampling. Further specifications and reporting rules are provided in the attached pre-analysis plan.

It is associational, not a causal mechanism decomposition. Other secondary outcomes are defined in the attached pre-analysis plan.
secondary_outcomes: - Marginal rates of substitution across soft skills. - Model-implied preference heterogeneity. - Belief moderation of focal-skill interaction valuations. - Exploratory interactions and state-dependent willingness to pay for other design-identified skill pairs. - Stated-versus-revealed skill valuations. - Heterogeneity by sector and firm characteristics.
title: Skill Complementarities in Hiring: Experimental Evidence on Employer Preferences over Soft-Skill Bundles

abstract: This individually randomized feasibility pilot tests the implementation of assigned access to a university-provided generative artificial intelligence (AI) tool during formal assessments in one undergraduate course. After the consent deadline, students who have provided informed consent are included in the fixed randomization roster and assigned in approximately equal numbers to two sequences. Sequence G1 receives AI access for the Part A assessment and no AI access for the Part B assessment; G2 receives the reverse sequence. Both groups then complete a common cumulative assessment without AI. Students who do not consent are not randomized, complete all assessments without AI under the examination pathways available in the course, and are excluded from the research dataset. Primary outcomes concern consent, assessment completion, technical implementation, and research-data completeness. Academic-performance contrasts are exploratory. The pilot will inform the protocol and preregistration of a separate, larger main experiment.
experimental_design: The pilot is conducted in one undergraduate course at Bocconi University. All students on the eligible course roster receive the participant information and decide whether to consent before randomization. After the consent deadline, the fixed roster of consenting students is randomized individually and in approximately equal numbers to G1 or G2. Only these students enter the experimental assessment procedure. Students who do not consent are not randomized; they may choose among the examination pathways available in the course, complete all assessments without AI, and are excluded from the research dataset. Randomized students following the partial-assessment pathway receive their assigned sequence. Graders are blinded to sequence assignment when grading the three assessment components. Research analyses include randomized participants with the outcome required for the relevant analysis.
intervention: The intervention is assigned access to a university-provided generative artificial intelligence (AI) tool during one part-specific course assessment. G1 has AI access for the Part A assessment and no AI access for the Part B assessment. G2 has no AI access for Part A and AI access for Part B. Immediately after the Part B assessment, both groups complete a cumulative assessment on Parts A and B without AI and without receiving feedback or solutions between the two assessments. Students assigned AI access may choose not to use the tool. The main comparisons follow assignment rather than actual use.

abstract: Ghana's Public Procurement Authority (PPA) carries out a national assessment of how public entities, such as ministries, district assemblies, hospitals and universities, manage their procurement. After each assessment, PPA sends every entity a report with its results and recommendations. Ghana has also introduced an electronic procurement system (GHANEPS), but many entities still carry out much of their procurement outside it. This study tests whether changes to how assessment results are communicated to procuring entities can improve their procurement practices.
experimental_design: Procuring entities covered by PPA's national procurement assessment are randomly assigned in equal proportions to three groups: a control group that receives the standard assessment report, a first treatment group that also receives a one-page performance snapshot addressed to the head of the procurement unit, and a second treatment group in which that snapshot is also sent to the head of entity. Random assignment is at the entity level, stratified by entity type and by baseline procurement performance. The three groups are compared over the 12 months after delivery using administrative data.
experimental_design_details: Materials. The one-page snapshot is designed with PPA and built from the entity's own assessment results and GHANEPS records. It shows: (a) the entity's GHANEPS usage rate and its share of contract value awarded through open competitive tendering; (b) how each has changed since the previous cycle; and (c) two or three concrete next steps. It reports entity-level results only and does not name or rate individual officials. Delivery. PPA delivers all reports through its normal channel for assessment results. In Treatment 1, the snapshot is addressed to the head of the procurement unit. In Treatment 2, the same snapshot is sent both to the head of the procurement unit and directly to the head of entity, and the cover message to the procurement unit states that the head of entity has received a copy. Delivery and receipt are recorded for every entity. Comparisons. Treatment 1 versus control identifies the effect of the snapshot itself. Treatment 2 versus Treatment 1 identifies the effect of the head of entity also receiving it, following Celhay, Gertler, Olivares and Undurraga (2024), who find that performance reports to procurement officers in Chile reduced overspending only when managers could also see them. Treatment 2 versus control identifies the combined effect. Strata. Entity type (ministries, departments and agencies; metropolitan, municipal and district assemblies; hospitals; universities and colleges; other) crossed with whether baseline competitive share is above or below the median. Estimation. OLS with strata fixed effects and the baseline outcome as a control, with robust standard errors. Comparisons are made pairwise between arms.
intervention: PPA sends every procuring entity a report with its results and recommendations after the national procurement assessment. This study varies the format of that communication and who receives it. Control group: the entity receives PPA's standard assessment report, delivered as it is today. Treatment 1: the entity receives the standard report plus a one-page performance snapshot, sent to the head of the procurement unit. The snapshot highlights a small number of priority indicators, including the entity's use of the national e-procurement system (GHANEPS) and its use of competitive procurement methods, and suggests next steps. Treatment 2: the same as Treatment 1, and the one-page snapshot is also sent directly to the head of the entity. The procurement unit is informed that the head of entity has received a copy.

abstract: This online randomized controlled trial examines the external validity of prior evidence that linguistic framing can influence intertemporal decision-making. Specifically, the study tests whether the relationship generalizes to a different language, participant population, and online research setting. Participants recruited through Prolific will complete a series of incentivized choices between rewards available at different times. The study experimentally varies linguistic framing while holding the underlying economic information and incentives constant, and examines participants’ choices, decision times, and perceptions of the choice scenarios. Additional questionnaire measures will be collected to support the interpretation of participants’ decisions. One randomly selected decision will determine each participant’s bonus payment.
experimental_design: This study is a two-arm, individually randomized online conceptual replication and extension of prior research on linguistic framing and intertemporal decision-making. The planned sample is 400 participants recruited through Prolific. Allocation to the two conditions is determined by individual randomization with equal probability, so the realized numbers in each condition may differ. The study examines whether previously documented effects of linguistic framing generalize to a different language, participant population, and online implementation. After providing consent and completing an audio check, participants receive instructions and complete 24 incentivized choices between rewards available at different times. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two linguistic framing conditions, while the underlying economic content and incentives are held constant. One decision is randomly selected for bonus payment. The study records participants’ choices and decision times, followed by measures concerning their perceptions, reasoning, and demographic characteristics.
experimental_design_details: The study is designed as a conceptual replication and external-validity extension of Chen and He (2021). The original study was conducted in Mandarin Chinese with 135 student participants recruited at National Taiwan University. Its main randomized comparison involved 95 participants assigned to the ‘I’ or ‘No Pronoun’ condition; a separate Direct Address condition included another 40 participants recruited later. The present study focuses on the two principal linguistic framing conditions and tests whether the result generalizes to Russian-language materials, a broader online Prolific sample, and remote individual participation. The planned sample is 400 Prolific participants, individually assigned with equal probability to either the first-person linguistic framing condition or the impersonal infinitive framing condition. Randomization is implemented in the Qualtrics survey flow. After consent, an audio check, task instructions, and payment instructions, each participant completes 24 binary intertemporal-choice rounds. In every round, the participant chooses between 100 tokens today and a larger delayed amount. The delayed amounts are 105, 110, 115, 120, 125, 130, 135, and 140 tokens, crossed with delays of 1, 4, and 12 weeks. The order of the three delay-horizon blocks is randomized, while delayed amounts are presented in ascending order within each block. Each statement is displayed as text and played as audio using the participant’s assigned linguistic frame. The choice options, amounts, delays, recordings’ substantive content, and incentive structure are otherwise identical between conditions. Response time is measured from the appearance of the choice options until a response is recorded. After the 24 decisions, participants describe the reasoning behind their final choice, rate the perceived psychological distance of the final choice scenario, and answer demographic questions. One of the 24 rounds is selected at random for payment through Prolific, using the participant’s choice in that round. The primary outcome is selection of the delayed reward in each round. Secondary outcomes include response time, switching patterns across delayed amounts, perceived psychological distance, and the written reasoning response. For each delay horizon, the eight delayed amounts are ordered from lowest to highest. A participant is classified as a multiple-switch participant if, within at least one delay horizon, their choices change between the immediate and delayed options more than once as the delayed amount increases. In the descriptive calculation of the proportion of delayed-reward choices within each randomized condition, all recorded choices from eligible participants are included, including those of multiple-switch participants. For every other analysis, including treatment-effect estimation, regression analyses, switch-point comparisons, and analyses of secondary outcomes, a multiple-switch participant is excluded in full: none of that participant’s decisions at any delay horizon or other outcome observations enter those analyses. Exclusion is at the participant level, not at the single-round or single-horizon level. For retained participants, the switch point is coded on a 10-category ordered scale: Line 1 for always choosing the delayed option; Lines 2 through 9 for switching to the delayed option at 105, 110, 115, 120, 125, 130, 135, or 140 tokens, respectively; and Line 10 for always choosing the immediate option. Always-delayed and always-immediate patterns are not classified as multiple-switch patterns.
intervention: Participants are randomly assigned to one of two linguistic framing conditions adapted from prior research on intertemporal decision-making. The conditions differ only in how otherwise equivalent reward information is linguistically presented. The precise wording of the conditions is withheld until completion of the study. Monetary amounts, delay periods, task structure, and financial incentives are held constant across conditions.
