abstract: This study is embedded within a cluster-Randomized Controlled Trial (cRCT) of an integrated, multi-component, school- and community-based mental health care program, Pamoja Tunaweza (henceforth Pamoja), targeting adolescents in refugee settlements in Western Uganda. The primary cRCT analysis, led by War Child Alliance (WCA), evaluates the program’s impact on mental health outcomes of adolescents and their caregivers. Our study complements the primary analysis by providing evidence on the effects of the intervention on adolescents’ other life domains beyond mental health, as well as on underlying mechanisms. In particular, it evaluates the impact of the intervention on (i) education and, relatedly, child labor, (ii) peer-to-peer violence, (iii) parent-to-child violence, and (iv) health behaviors.
experimental_design: We refer to the primary Statistical Analysis Plan (SAP) of the Pamoja cRCT for full details on the experimental design, study population, sampling, timeline and data collection (https://www.isrctn.com/ISRCTN34179105). Here, we provide a summary of the main aspects. The cRCT uses a two-stage random sampling design. First, 18 zones (clusters) were selected within three refugee settlements in South-Western Uganda, based on (i) refugee presence from the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) (target is more than 70% in overall sample); (ii) operational capacity of WCA or partners; (iii) absence of WCA evidence-based mental health interventions (e.g. TeamUp, BeThere, EASE) or comparable interventions by other organizations implemented in the 6 months prior to baseline; and (iv) local authority approvals. The study included one eligible school per zone. Schools qualified if they (i) served ages 11-16 (at least 300); (ii) were willing to participate; (iii) could provide enrolment lists; (iv) were located more than 5 kilometers from a school in an adjoining cluster that had been enrolled in the study; and (v) were run by the government. In case of multiple eligible schools per zone, one school that met eligibility criteria was randomly selected. The 18 schools were matched by number of students to form 9 pairs. Within each pair, one school was randomly assigned to the Pamoja intervention (treatment arm) and the waitlist control arm. Schools and families from zones in the control arm did not receive any of the Pamoja intervention components during the first year after the baseline assessment. They received the program upon completion of the endline assessments, one year after baseline. Treatment assignment of schools and classes was masked to the investigators, except the scientific coordinator, until endline data collection and data cleaning was completed. The target population includes 11-to-16-year-old adolescents (at the time of baseline), living in one of three refugee settlements in South-Western Uganda – Kyangwali, Kyaka, and Nakivale. These settlements primarily host refugees from the DRC; 27-29% of their populations are below age 18. For the Pamoja cRCT, a random sample of 252 adolescents, aged 11-16, was drawn from each school. Adolescents were randomly sampled from enrolment lists, stratified by gender (1:1). Eligibility criteria for adolescent participation included (i) living in the study zone; (ii) being aged 11 to 16 years old at the time of baseline; and (iii) speaking one of the four local languages (Kinyabwisha, Congolese Kiswahili, Runyankole or Runyoro/Rutooro). The Pamoja cRCT study sample hence comprises 4,536 adolescents across 18 clusters (9 per arm), with 252 respondents per cluster, and their primary caregivers. Our study will be conducted using the same sampling frame and experimental design as the primary Pamoja cRCT.
intervention: This study evaluates a multi-level mental health program for adolescents residing in refugee settlements. The program is described in detail in the main cRCT protocol. It combines five components delivered over one school year: (1) TeamUp, movement-based activities to enhance children’s well-being through sports and play in school; (2) ReachNow, training facilitators and community leaders to identify internalizing and externalizing symptoms in adolescents, and encourage help-seeking behavior; (3) EASE, WHO group-based therapy sessions targeting psychological distress in adolescents; (4) BeThere, group-based caregiver support to reduce stress and strengthen positive parenting; (5) Community Tales, to reduce mental health stigma among school staff. The components are conceptually linked through a shared theory of change. We anticipate: (i) improved adolescent mental health through TeamUp, with ReachNow enabling identification and referral of high-need adolescents to EASE; (ii) enhanced family functioning via BeThere, further improving adolescents’ mental health; and (iii) improved school and community climate through BeThere, Community Tales and TeamUp. The individual components are evidence-based, and locally adapted. Their feasibility and effectiveness have been tested in multiple conflict-affected settings. The cRCT is the first study to evaluate their impact as an integrated package.

abstract: The cost of living underpins modern welfare measurement but assumes fully rational consumers. In this study, I embed bounded rationality into classical index-number concepts, yielding a behavioural cost-of-living index that is identified with traditional data via revealed preference and which reduces to the classical measure under full attention. Part of this project involves a simple survey experiment studying how accurately consumers perceive prices and inflation that is the subject of this registry entry. Specifically, an online survey of 750 UK adults will estimate prices for a range of everyday goods and services, with half of the sample randomly assigned to receive an informational intervention in the form of feedback comparing their estimates with benchmark prices. The experiment will compare the groups’ post-treatment perceptions of UK price growth over the past 12 months (the primary outcome) and the percentage income adjustment respondents believe their household would need today to be as well off as 12 months ago considering only changes in the prices faced (a secondary outcome).
experimental_design: This is a two-arm, individually randomized online survey experiment involving a representative sample of UK adults recruited through Prolific. Before treatment, all participants report purchase recency and contemporary price estimates for 12 goods and services: milk, bread, eggs, and petrol are common to all participants, with eight other goods or services selected from a balanced rotating set of 20 items. Questions about household energy are administered separately to everyone. The survey instrument records item-level confidence and elicits the basis of partipants' estimates before the treatment occurs. Participants are randomly assigned to either a control or treatment arm in a 1:1 ratio. Participants in the treatment arm, receive, on an in-survey screen, information about current benchmark prices for the goods and services they estimated prices for their alongside their own estimates and information about the accuracy of these. Individuals in the control arm do not receive this information. Both arms then answer the same questions about inflation in the past year and their cost of living.
intervention: Before treatment, all participants estimate the current price and the price a year earlier for 12 assigned ordinary goods and services comprising four common objects and eight objects from a rotating set. Participants assigned to the feedback arm will receive an informational intervention comprising an in-survey feedback page showing their (current) price estimates beside a corresponding benchmark price for each good or service. Participants assigned to the control arm do not receive this feedback.

abstract: This study uses a representative telephone survey of adult women living in urban areas of Burkina Faso to document experiences and perceptions of sexual corruption in interactions with public officials and to examine whether information about the prevalence of sexual corruption affects women’s economic and migration-related intentions. The study has two components. First, we estimate the prevalence of sexual corruption and examine how prevalence varies across public services and related dimensions of respondents’ experiences and perceptions. Second, we implement a randomized information experiment in which respondents are randomly assigned to receive either objective information about the prevalence of sexual corruption among women in Burkina Faso or neutral demographic information. We examine the causal effects of this information on entrepreneurial motivation and intentions to migrate internationally.
experimental_design: The phone survey opens with a module on demographic and economic characteristics, followed by a module including questions concerning experiences and perceptions of sexual corruption. Thereafter, respondents are randomly assigned with equal probability to one of two information conditions. Randomization is at the individual respondent level, with approximately 50% of respondents assigned to each condition. The estimand is therefore the causal effect of receiving information about the prevalence of sexual corruption relative to receiving neutral demographic information. We do not interpret the experiment as identifying the effect of information relative to no information. An open comprehension question is administered following the information statement. Respondents who do not understand the information are given the information again. Comprehension will not be used to define the primary analysis sample. The primary analysis will therefore be a treatment effect analysis based on randomized assignment. To assess the sensitivity of the responses to question eliciting the prevalence of sexual corruption experiences to privacy concerns, we also apply a garbling technique for 50% of all respondents (randomly assigned) who are also informed about this privacy procedure. For a randomly selected 50% of respondents, responses are garbled as follows: • if the true response indicates an experience of sexual corruption — Rarely, Sometimes, Often or Very Often — it is recorded as “Never” with probability 0.10; • if the true response is “Never”, it is recorded as one of the four non-Never categories with probability 0.10, with the particular category selected at random. We will retrieve the true estimate from this distribution and compare it to the prevalence estimate in the subsample without garbling, and to the prevalence to the questions about peers' experiences with sexual corruption and broader perceptions of the incidence of sexual corruption.
intervention: Respondents are randomly assigned with equal probability to one of two information conditions. Treatment condition: Treatment respondents receive an information about the objective prevalence of sexual corruption amongst women in Burkina Faso, as estimated in Borcan et al (2025). abstract: This study examines how response ranges and elicitation formats affect the reporting of a continuous variable: time use. We plan to recruit 900 students and randomly assign them to six conditions. Five use identical sliders with upper bounds of 24, 12, 8, 6, or 4 hours, while the sixth uses numerical entry. We estimate effects on total reported time and its distribution, and compare within-condition standardized distributions to assess whether differences reflect shifts in location and scale or changes in distributional shape. We also compare slider and numerical-entry responses in terms of dispersion, heaping, and internally inconsistent reports. Finally, we characterize how reports under one elicitation method map into those under another using distributional comparisons and quantile-based transformations. The study provides experimental evidence on how survey response design shapes continuous self-reported outcomes.
experimental_design: Randomization is conducted within class. Larger allocation shares increase precision for comparisons among the wider slider ranges. 60 % of students are assigned equally to slider conditions with upper bounds of 24, 12, and 8 hours, Remaining 40 % are assigned equally to the 6-hour, 4-hour, and numerical-entry conditions.
intervention: The intervention varies the response format used to report time use. In five conditions, students report time using the same slider interface, with the slider upper bound set to 24, 12, 8, 6, or 4 hours. In the sixth condition, students report time using an numerical-entry field.

abstract: There is almost no causal evidence on whether shelters reduce intimate partner violence. This 16-month pilot randomized controlled trial tests the feasibility, safety and acceptability of integrated shelter-based support for women experiencing severe intimate partner violence in rural Mara Region, Tanzania, in preparation for a full-scale trial. Forty women are randomized 1:1:1:1 to four arms: delayed-shelter control; shelter for up to six months; shelter plus an economic empowerment program; and shelter plus a non-violent conflict management program for husbands. Women are interviewed at baseline and at 2, 7 and 12 months. The pilot is not powered to detect treatment effects. It is judged against pre-specified feasibility thresholds and estimates outcome variance for the full trial.
experimental_design: A 16-month individually randomized pilot feasibility trial: four arms, 1:1:1:1, 40 women in one rural district of Mara Region, 10 per arm. Eligible women are 18 or older, married, cohabiting or recently separated, not pregnant, have experienced intimate partner violence in the past year and need shelter for safety, and can be interviewed privately. Danger level is not a ground for exclusion. The baseline survey comes before randomization. Women are interviewed privately by trained female enumerators, never at home. Husbands in Arm 4 are interviewed separately.
intervention: All arms receive safety planning and referrals. Arm 1 (control): shelter offered after the final follow-up. Arm 2: shelter for up to six months. Arm 3: shelter plus an economic empowerment program (vocational and business skills, coaching). Arm 4: shelter plus a non-violent conflict management program for the husband, using cognitive behavioral methods, offered only with the woman's permission and after a safety review.

abstract: Gender norms and stereotypes consolidate in early adolescence and shape aspirations, human capital investment and behavior for years. Socio-emotional and affective education programs for early adolescents are increasingly offered by municipalities and associations, in or outside school hours, but rigorous evidence on what these programs change is scarce. This multi-site study evaluates such programs among Italian lower secondary school students (ages 11 to 14) with one standardized, paper-based instrument administered in class before and after each program. The study has two components. The first is a survey experiment embedded in the baseline questionnaire: each student is randomly assigned, within the classroom, to a version in which the protagonists of two hypothetical peer scenarios are girls or boys. We measure students’ own judgments (first-order beliefs), their predictions of the modal judgment of male and of female classmates (second-order beliefs, incentivized), and the resulting misperception of peer norms, and we test whether these differ by the gender of the protagonists and by the gender of the peer group referenced, and whether students misperceive the norms of the other gender more than those of their own. The second component is a non-randomized evaluation of the program. At each site, a school unit that hosts the program is compared with a similar unit of the same school that does not, before and after the program (difference-in-differences). Within the treated unit, students enroll individually, which lets us separate the effect on participants from spillovers on their non-participating classmates, using sociometric network data collected at baseline. Sites are added under a pre-specified inclusion rule and analyzed jointly with site fixed effects. Site 1 is Fuori Bordo, a program of extracurricular laboratories (theatre, photography, mindfulness) promoted by the Municipality of Collepasso (Lecce, Italy) with two local associations, in collaboration with the comprehensive school Collepasso-Tuglie; the comparison unit is the Tuglie (Lecce, Italy) unit of the same school, where the program is not offered.
experimental_design: The study is a multi-site, two-wave, paper-based survey in lower secondary school classrooms. Each site consists of a treated school unit, where the program is offered, and a comparison unit of the same school or a closely matched school where it is not. All students of both units are surveyed before and after the program with the same instrument. Component 1 (randomized). Within each classroom, questionnaires alternate between two versions that differ only in the gender of the protagonists of two group-chat scenarios: in scenario 1 a group mocks a classmate for a gender-atypical reaction (a boy crying at the cinema; a girl shouting at the referee) while one member defends the classmate and another stays silent; in scenario 2 a jealous partner controls the other (a boy checking his girlfriend’s messages; a girl told by her boyfriend not to go out with a male friend) while the chat members justify or challenge it. The version is assigned at the individual level by alternating the pre-sorted pile of questionnaires along the seating order, independently of student gender and of program enrollment. The version is recorded on the class roster and each student receives the same version in wave 2. For each scenario and for the seven common statements, students first predict the modal answer of male and of female classmates (second-order beliefs, incentivized), then report their own answer (first-order beliefs). Classmates are identified by roster numbers read aloud, so that network items can be collected without names. Component 2 (non-randomized). The program is not randomly assigned. At site 1 the treated unit was determined by the promoters (the Municipality of Collepasso and the associations) before the study; within the treated unit enrollment is voluntary and individual. Participation is defined as enrollment in at least one laboratory; the number of sessions attended (self-reported in wave 2) is used as a dosage measure. Identification relies on a difference-in-differences comparison between units, on parallel trends supported by baseline balance, and on the within-unit contrast between participants and non-participants for spillovers. We state this limitation explicitly and pre-specify the analyses below.
experimental_design_details: Estimating equations. Component 1, wave 1 data. For first-order beliefs and vignette judgments: Y_ic = a_c + b1 Female_version_i + b2 Girl_i + b3 Female_version_i x Girl_i + e_ic, with classroom fixed effects a_c and heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors (the version is randomized at the individual level). b1 tests H1. For second-order beliefs and misperception, each student contributes two observations, one per target group (male classmates, female classmates): Y_ict = a_c + d1 Girl_i + d2 FemaleTarget_t + d3 Girl_i x FemaleTarget_t + e_ict, with standard errors clustered at the student level. d2 tests H2 (norms attributed to male versus female peers); d3 tests H4, the in-group versus out-group asymmetry, since the four respondent-by-target cells (boys about boys, boys about girls, girls about boys, girls about girls) are identified by Girl_i and FemaleTarget_t. The randomized vignette version enters as a further interaction to test whether the gender of the protagonists shifts beliefs about male and female peers differently. Misperception (H3) is the difference between the second-order belief and the actual modal (and mean) first-order belief of classmates of the target gender, computed within classroom excluding the respondent; it is tested against zero overall and in each of the four cells. Cells with fewer than five classmates of the target gender are excluded from the misperception measure. Component 2, panel data. Intention to treat at the unit level (H5 to H7): Y_it = a_i + l_t + g Post_t x TreatedUnit_i + e_it. Participants and spillover (H8): Y_it = a_i + l_t + g1 Post_t x Participant_i + g2 Post_t x NonParticipantTreatedUnit_i + e_it, where g2 is the spillover on non-participating students of the treated unit relative to the comparison unit; among non-participants we also estimate Post_t x ShareFriendsParticipating_i, with the share computed on baseline friendship nominations. For misperception outcomes the same models are estimated on student-by-target data, adding the interaction with FemaleTarget_t and with the respondent-by-target cell, to test whether the program reduces out-group misperception more than in-group misperception (H6b). Standard errors are clustered at the classroom level with the wild cluster bootstrap (Webb weights) given the small number of clusters. Baseline balance between units is tested on all primary outcomes and covariates; results are also reported with entropy balancing on baseline outcomes. Multi-site analysis. Sites are pooled with site fixed effects and site-by-wave effects. We report site-specific estimates and a random-effects meta-analytic summary as robustness. Inclusion rule: a site enters the pooled analysis if (i) it uses the standard instrument without changes to the primary-outcome items, (ii) it has a baseline and a follow-up wave, (iii) it has a comparison unit or comparison classrooms not exposed to the program, and (iv) its site sheet was filed as an amendment to this registration before its baseline. Sites that fail (ii) or (iii) may contribute to component 1 only and are analyzed separately. Heterogeneity, pre-specified: respondent gender; target-group gender (in-group versus out-group); version of the questionnaire; baseline misperception (above or below the median); baseline network centrality. Attrition. Students absent in one wave are kept in the cross-sectional analyses of that wave and dropped from panel models; we report attrition by unit and test whether it correlates with baseline outcomes. Codes that do not match across waves (expected 5 to 10 percent) are matched by classroom, sex and month of birth as a secondary key; unmatched cases are dropped.
intervention: At each site, an external organization (a municipality, an association or a foundation) delivers a program on emotional and socio-relational competencies to lower secondary school students, in or outside school hours. Programs differ across sites in content, format, setting and dosage, and each is documented in a standardized site sheet (provider, content, number and length of sessions, calendar, enrollment rule) filed with the site amendment before its baseline. The common feature is the aim: promoting socio-emotional competencies, positive relationships between girls and boys, and critical reflection on gender norms and stereotypes. Site 1 (Collepasso and Tuglie, Lecce). The program “Fuori Bordo. Laboratori per scoprirsi liber*” is promoted by the Municipality of Collepasso with the associations L’Albero delle Parole and Donato Metallo APS, in collaboration with the Istituto Comprensivo Collepasso-Tuglie. It is extracurricular: three laboratories (theatre, photography, mindfulness) held outside school hours in September and October 2026, [number] sessions in total, ending with a public exhibition and performance. The program is presented in the Collepasso unit of the school and students enroll individually and voluntarily, independently of their class. The comparison unit is the Tuglie unit of the same comprehensive school (same head teacher, neighboring town), where the program is not offered during the study period; the program will be proposed to that unit in the following school year. Program period: [first session date] to [last session date]. At every site, all students of both units complete the same printed questionnaire in class, before and after the program, whether or not they enroll. Questionnaires are administered by a research assistant, never by program staff, and are linked across waves by a self-generated anonymous code. Half of the students in each classroom receive the version of the questionnaire with female protagonists and half the version with male protagonists (see Experimental design). To encourage accurate reporting of second-order beliefs, one prediction item is drawn at random after data collection and the four students of each classroom with the most accurate predictions receive a 5 euro voucher.

primary_outcome_explanation: Items are standardized within outcome family using the control group and baseline mean and standard deviation, and combined into family indices (equally weighted average of standardized items, following Kling, Liebman and Katz, 2007). Families: (a) vignette judgments, (b) acceptability of controlling and aggressive behaviors, (c) gender stereotype scale, (d) second-order beliefs, (e) misperception. Hypotheses are tested on the family index first and on single items second, with correction for multiple testing within family (Romano and Wolf step-down). Hypotheses for component 1. H1: judgments of the same behavior differ by the randomly assigned gender of the protagonists; we expect mocking of a boy who cries and control of a girlfriend to be judged more acceptable than the female-protagonist counterparts. H2: second-order beliefs differ by the gender of the peer group referenced, with norms attributed to male peers more permissive of control and aggression. H3: students overestimate the acceptability of controlling and aggressive behaviors among their peers (positive misperception), more so for male peers. H4: out-group misperception is larger than in-group misperception; in particular, girls overestimate the acceptability of controlling and aggressive behaviors among boys more than boys overestimate it among their own group. H4b: within group, misperception is larger among boys than among girls. Hypotheses for component 2. H5: exposure to the program reduces agreement with stereotype and violence-justifying statements (P4). H6b: the reduction in misperception is larger for out-group beliefs (beliefs about the other gender) than for in-group beliefs, consistent with the mixed-gender setting of the laboratories. H7: exposure increases the intention to challenge mocking or controlling behavior (P6). H8: effects on non-participating students of the treated unit are positive and increase with the share of their baseline friends who participate (spillover).
primary_outcomes: Component 1, baseline survey experiment (all sites, wave 1). • P1. First-order beliefs: the student’s own agreement (1 to 5) with each character’s action in the two scenarios and with seven statements on control, jealousy, image sharing and physical aggression among peers. • P2. Second-order beliefs: the student’s prediction of the modal answer of male classmates and, separately, of female classmates, for the same items. • P3. Misperception: the gap between the student’s second-order belief for a given peer group and the actual modal (and mean) first-order belief of classmates of that gender, computed within classroom excluding the respondent. Component 2, program evaluation (all sites, wave 2 minus wave 1). • P3b. In-group and out-group misperception: P3 computed separately for the four respondent-by-target cells (boys about boys, boys about girls, girls about boys, girls about girls). In-group misperception is the diagonal (pluralistic ignorance); out-group misperception is the off-diagonal (beliefs about the other gender). • P4. Change in first-order beliefs (P1) and in the Gender Stereotypical Traits and Roles scale (Global Early Adolescent Study, 11 items). • P5. Change in misperception (P3). • P6. Change in behavioral intentions: agreement with the defending character versus the mocking or controlling characters, and the coded content of the message the student would send in the group chat (coded blind to treatment as challenging, joining, neutral or silent).
randomization_method: Questionnaire version: assigned in the classroom by alternating a pre-sorted pile of the two versions along the seating order; no computer randomization. Program: not randomized. The treated and comparison units are pre-existing units of the same comprehensive school; the treated unit was chosen by the program promoters.
randomization_unit: Individual student, for the questionnaire version. The program is offered at the school-unit level with individual enrollment. Questionnaire version: no. Program: yes, at the school-unit level, with individual take-up within the treated unit.
secondary_ids: This study does not extend or rely on any prior registered trial. Sites added after site 1 will reference this registration.
secondary_outcome_explanation: S1 to S5 are analyzed with the same models as the primary outcomes. S6 is used to define exposure and to test the integrity of the comparison unit; if more than 20 percent of comparison students report friends who participated, results are reported with and without this subgroup. Family background (parental education and occupation, division of domestic and care work) is used for covariate adjustment and heterogeneity.

Gender identity and self-perception: felt femininity and masculinity, importance of conforming, free associations with “feminine” and “masculine”. • S3. Appearance-based self-evaluation and beliefs about the role of appearance for women and for men. • S4. Peer networks: friendship, collaboration, personal-disclosure, participation and admiration nominations; network density, gender homophily and cross-gender ties; change in the position of participants. • S5. Educational aspirations: desired level of education, ranking of upper secondary tracks, reasons for the choice including same-gender peers. • S6. Program exposure and awareness in wave 2: participation and number of sessions attended; for all students, having heard of the program, friends who participated, conversations about it (used to measure contamination in the comparison unit). • S7. abstract: Forced displacement is a profound economic, social, and psychological shock. Newly arrived refugees must learn how to generate income, access services, and navigate an unfamiliar environment. Many struggle because they lack information, local connections, and confidence. At the same time, more established refugees have accumulated settlement-specific knowledge, skills, and social networks, and may have time and a willingness to help. Search and matching frictions, lack of trust, geographic distance, and uncertainty about others' needs and abilities can nevertheless prevent mutually beneficial relationships from forming. We design and evaluate the Buddy Program, a matching intervention that pairs recently arrived refugee households with more established refugee households in Kyangwali refugee settlement, Uganda. Pairs are formed based on a shared language, gender preferences, and geographic proximity. We form 600 pairs (1,200 households) and randomly assign them either to the Buddy Program or to a control group. In treated pairs, the two households are introduced through a facilitated meeting and agree on how they will interact and how the established household may support the newcomer. Control pairs are not introduced. Support is non-financial and may include practical assistance, information, accompaniment, and connections to services or economic opportunities. We study effects on both sides of the match. We combine baseline data with follow-up surveys. The midline, conducted shortly after the Buddy Program ends, focuses on psychological well-being, time use, and social outcomes, including social cohesion, belonging, social capital, and community engagement. Secondary outcomes include physical health, food security, employment and labor supply, land access, financial resilience, responses to shocks, and access to humanitarian assistance. An endline approximately six months later will examine whether effects persist and whether more downstream economic outcomes, particularly employment and financial outcomes, emerge over time.
experimental_design: The sample consists of 1,200 refugee households in the Bukinda area of Kyangwali refugee settlement, western Uganda, an area with mixed villages in which both newly arrived and established refugees reside. Using OPM/UNHCR administrative data, we identified and listed 714 newly arrived households (settled within the last 18 months) and 789 established households (resident for at least 2 years). The listing recorded household demographics, GPS coordinates, willingness to take part, the preferred gender of the counterpart, and the interview language. Each newly arrived household is paired one-to-one with an established household by an exact assignment algorithm subject to three hard constraints: (1) each household's stated gender preference for its counterpart (female, male, or any) is satisfied; (2) both households were interviewed in the same language, which must be Swahili or Alur; and (3) the distance between them lies between 150 and 2,000 meters. Subject to these, the algorithm maximizes the number of pairs and then minimizes the sum of squared distances. The final pairing is drawn by lot from 500 near-optimal candidate matchings. This yielded 631 pairs; 600 are selected for the RCT and 31 are replacements. After a baseline survey with all 1,200 household heads (September 2026), pairs are randomized into Buddy Program - treatment (300 pairs) and control (300 pairs). The Buddy Program runs for three months, until mid-December 2026, with two follow-up surveys of all pairs during the intervention, a midline survey at the end of the intervention (January 2027), and an endline survey six months post-midline (July 2027).
intervention: The intervention, the Buddy Program, pairs a recently arrived refugee household (settled in Kyangwali refugee settlement, Uganda, within the last 18 months) with a more established refugee household (resident for at least 2 years). Pairs are formed one-to-one by an optimal matching algorithm that requires the two households to share a language and to satisfy each other's stated gender and household composition preference for the counterpart, and that minimizes the walking distance between them (see Experimental Design for details). Treatment (Buddy Program): The two households of a pair are introduced to each other in a structured introductory meeting facilitated by a staff member of our partner NGO (AVSI Foundation), following an agreed-upon script. Both households are introduced to the volunteering project and informed that they have been matched. During the meeting, the households agree upon how the established household will support the newcomer (the assistance is non-financial and may include practical help such as fixing the house or fetching water, information, accompaniment, talking, and connections to services or income-generating opportunities) and the frequency of interaction, and exchange contact details. The intervention runs for three months. Over the course of three months, our partner NGO monitors time-use activities of the paired newly arrived and established households using three short follow-up surveys. Control: Status quo. The paired newly arrived and established households are not introduced to each other. Over the course of three months, our partner NGO monitors time-use activities of the paired newly arrived and established households using three short follow-up surveys.

Analyzing volunteer households and recipient households separately (n = 600 each, 300 treatment and 300 control), the study has 80% power to detect an effect size of 0.23 standard deviations (power of 0.45, 0.69, 0.86, and 0.96 for effect sizes of 0.15, 0.20, 0.25, and 0.30 s.d., respectively). abstract: We investigate how single-parent family (SPF) backgrounds shape individuals’ opportunities in the marriage market via two field experiments in a large online dating market. In the first experiment, we create fictitious dater profiles with varying family backgrounds and send dating invitations to real online daters to examine whether SPF backgrounds affect initial matching opportunities. We further examine whether these effects vary with the gender of the custodial parent and the profile owner. To investigate the mechanisms underlying these differences, we conduct a second field experiment in which we exogenously manipulate the disclosure of positive and negative non-material personal characteristics and examine whether the effects of such disclosure differ by profile gender.

experimental_design: Fictitious profiles were constructed so that displayed characteristics other than the experimentally varied attributes were statistically comparable across conditions. Eligible decision-makers were active platform users residing in an experimental city, aged 24–37 years and with a profile photograph. Fictitious profiles sent a standardized invitation to randomly selected eligible decision-makers. Experiment I was conducted in Beijing, Guangzhou, Chengdu, Wuhan, Harbin, and Nanning. It crossed two profile genders with three family-background conditions. In addition, income, age, and education were varied across profile configurations. Experiment II was conducted in Shanghai, Shenzhen, Changsha, Chongqing, Shenyang, and Jinan. It crossed two profile genders, three family-background conditions, and three information-disclosure conditions. Income was varied across profile configurations, while age and education were held fixed.
intervention: The study used fictitious profiles on a large Chinese online dating-for-marriage platform to send standardized, gender-neutral dating invitations to eligible users. Experiment I employs a 2 × 3 between-subjects factorial design in which two profile characteristics – family background and gender – are experimentally manipulated. Family background was signaled through the self-assessment text and the platform’s family-status field. Income, age, and education were additionally varied across profile configurations. Experiment II retained the profile-gender and family-background manipulations and added three non-material information disclosure conditions: no additional information, negative personality information, and positive marriage-attitude information. Income was also varied across profile configurations, while age and education were held fixed. Other displayed profile characteristics were kept statistically comparable across experimental conditions.

abstract: This randomized controlled trial examines whether generative artificial intelligence (AI) access during learning improves academic performance and changes achievement gaps by prior preparation. Conducted in an Introductory Econometrics course at City University of Macau with approximately 120 third-year undergraduates, it includes consenting enrolled students. After a supervised diagnostic test and collection of pre-treatment GPA, participants are individually randomized in roughly equal proportions through blocked randomization to fixed AI-access or control groups. Both groups complete identical supervised weekly tasks with equal time allowances and non-AI materials; only the treatment group may use AI. Common closed-book midterm and final examinations prohibit AI. Primary analyses estimate the average assignment effect on standardized final-examination scores and its interaction with baseline diagnostic achievement. Secondary analyses examine midterm scores, weekly performance, and examination-score dispersion. The study distinguishes AI-assisted performance from unaided learning and assesses whether initially lower- or higher-achieving students benefit more.
experimental_design: This individually randomized trial recruits approximately 120 consenting third-year students from an undergraduate Econometrics course at City University of Macau. Students are assigned in approximately equal proportions to unrestricted generative artificial intelligence (AI) access or no AI during 12 weeks of lecturer-monitored in-class practice. Primary outcomes are practice, midterm and final-examination scores; both examinations prohibit AI. The secondary outcome is AI-use behavior measured from submitted dialogues.
experimental_design_details: The study examines whether access to generative artificial intelligence (AI) improves academic performance and whether its effects vary with students’ initial achievement. It distinguishes performance during AI access from learning demonstrated in examinations without AI. The planned sample comprises approximately 120 consenting third-year students enrolled in Introductory Econometrics at City University of Macau. Before assignment, students complete a supervised diagnostic test without AI, internet access, notes or other digital assistance. The test assesses basic statistics, probability, quantitative reasoning, interpretation of tables and graphs, elementary mathematics and introductory regression intuition. Pre-treatment grade point average (GPA) provides a complementary measure of prior achievement. The baseline survey records demographic and socioeconomic characteristics, prior AI use and digital skills. Diagnostic scores and GPA are standardized across participants using pre-treatment observations. Randomization occurs at the individual-student level after baseline measurement and before the first treatment session. Computer-generated assignment allocates approximately half of the students in each randomization block to AI access and half to control. When a block contains an odd number of students, the additional allocation is determined randomly. The blocks follow the saved allocation procedure specified in the Randomization Method field. The allocation file is retained, and assignment remains fixed across all 12 practice weeks. Treated students may use AI without restrictions during practice, including requesting explanations, generating complete answers, checking calculations or reasoning, and asking follow-up questions. No prompting strategy or limit on assistance is imposed. For each session, they must submit their practice answers and the entire AI dialogue, including all prompts and responses used for the task. Control students submit their practice answers and may not use AI. Both groups receive the same questions, time allowance and non-AI course materials. The entire answering process takes place in class under the lecturer’s monitoring to enforce the no-AI condition for controls. The primary outcomes are scores from the 12 weeks of practice, the midterm examination and the final examination. Practice answers are marked using the reference answers and rubric for that week, applying common criteria to both groups. Both examinations are closed-book and prohibit AI for all students. The midterm measures learning after intermediate exposure and the final measures learning after full-course exposure. Raw scores and maximum possible marks are retained. For analysis, each assessment is standardized separately using the pooled mean and standard deviation across both arms among students with an observed score. This accommodates differences in maximum marks and difficulty across weeks. The analysis follows intention to treat. Separate analysis-of-covariance regressions for the midterm and final include randomized assignment, standardized baseline diagnostic score, standardized pre-treatment GPA and fixed effects for the actual randomization blocks. The assignment coefficient estimates the effect of access under the treatment protocol. A pooled student-by-week regression for practice scores includes the same covariates and block fixed effects, together with week fixed effects. This estimates the average practice-performance effect across the 12 weeks. Assignment-by-week interactions describe changes in that effect over time. Examination regressions use heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors with a small-sample correction; weekly-panel standard errors are clustered by student. To examine achievement gaps, each performance model adds the interaction between assignment and the continuous standardized baseline diagnostic score, retaining both main effects. A negative interaction indicates larger effects for students with lower initial achievement; a positive interaction indicates larger effects for higher-achieving students. Twice the interaction coefficient gives the treatment-induced change in the signed predicted score difference between students one baseline standard deviation above and below the mean, holding other regressors fixed. GPA is used as an alternative measure of baseline achievement. These are heterogeneity analyses of the primary performance outcomes. The secondary outcome is AI-use behavior among treated students. Complete submitted dialogues are coded at the student-session level for the number of student prompts, requests for answer generation or explanations, checking and error correction, and follow-up engagement. Purpose categories may overlap. Follow-up measures identify requests for clarification, challenges to AI responses and further questions after the first exchange. Measures are summarized by student and week. The coding protocol is documented, and incomplete or missing dialogues are flagged. Associations between usage patterns and performance are descriptive because students’ usage choices are not randomized.
intervention: The treatment is access to generative artificial intelligence (AI) during 12 weeks of in-class econometrics practice.

abstract: This study examines whether perceived government corruption and national identity causally affect political trust and related political attitudes among Canadians. We use an experimental design that induces exogenous variation in these two constructs to identify their downstream effects on trust, attitudes toward political institutions, and related policy views.
experimental_design: After completing a pre-treatment block of background questions and passing an initial attention check, respondents are randomly assigned to one of four conditions in a 2×2 factorial design: a corruption treatment, a national-identity treatment, both treatments together, or a control condition receiving neither. All respondents then answer the same set of outcome questions described above.
experimental_design_details: One quarter of respondents are assigned to the corruption-only condition, which presents eight real Canadian news stories about official misconduct, most concerning police, bureaucrats, municipal officials, or other public employees rather than party politicians, so as to raise the salience of official misconduct without attributing it to a specific political party. One quarter of respondents are assigned to the identity-only condition, which presents a well-known 2000 Molson beer commercial widely regarded as an ode to Canadian patriotism, intended to make a shared, nonpartisan national identity salient. One quarter of respondents are assigned to the combined condition, in which they see both the corruption headlines and the identity video described above, with the order in which the two are presented independently randomized. The remaining quarter of respondents constitute the control group and receive neither treatment.

abstract: This study examines how professionals’ use of artificial intelligence affects clients’ choices relative to gender, experience, and practice size. An online conjoint experiment administered by SWG will involve 2,600 adults across legal, economic, technical, and medical services. Each respondent will complete four choices between hypothetical professional profiles with randomized characteristics, before answering other AI-related survey questions. After each choice, respondents will report the minimum discount required to switch to the rejected professional. We will estimate Average Marginal Component Effects separately by professional category and pooled across categories, comparing the magnitude of the AI effect with those of the other attributes. Discount responses will provide a complementary measure of preference intensity conditional on the initial choice.
experimental_design: An online conjoint experiment with 2,600 adults, comprising 650 respondents in each of four professional categories. Each respondent completes four choices between two hypothetical professionals. Profile characteristics are randomized, and the experiment precedes the survey’s AI-related questions.
experimental_design_details: Each professional category uses a fixed service scenario, with equal specialization and similar fees across profiles. Randomized dimensions are AI use, gender conveyed through names and applicable titles, experience (about 5 versus 20 years), and practice size (small versus large). Each choice is followed by a discount question. Attribute effects are estimated separately by category and pooled, using linear probability models with respondent-clustered standard errors.
intervention: A survey-based conjoint experiment examining how clients choose legal, economic, technical, and medical professionals. Respondents choose between hypothetical professional profiles with randomly varied characteristics, including the use of artificial intelligence.

abstract: This completed randomized controlled trial examined the effects of technology-enhanced multisensory instruction on biology learning and delayed retention among lower secondary school students in Morocco. A total of 152 students aged 13 to 16 years were matched according to baseline biology knowledge and randomized within 76 matched pairs to either an experimental condition or an active control condition. The intervention consisted of three biology lessons combining, depending on the topic, three-dimensional digital models, animations, physical models, gestures, and hands-on activities. The active control group studied the same biology content with the same teacher and comparable instructional time using conventional classroom materials. Primary outcomes assessed delayed retention approximately one month after the relevant lessons, while secondary outcomes assessed immediate learning after each lesson. Analyses adjusted for baseline knowledge and students’ original class.
experimental_design: This was a two-arm individually randomized controlled trial conducted in a public lower secondary school in Morocco. A total of 152 students were matched into 76 pairs according to baseline biology knowledge and similarity of pretest scores. Within each pair, one student was randomly assigned to the experimental condition and the other to the active control condition, resulting in 76 students per condition. Both conditions covered the same biology topics, were taught by the same teacher, and received comparable instructional time. The study included a baseline pretest, three instructional sessions, three immediate post-session assessments, and two delayed retention assessments.
experimental_design_details: After individual randomization, four instructional groups of 38 students were formed for practical organization, with two groups per study condition. This grouping did not alter the original randomized assignments. The experimental condition used technology-enhanced multisensory instruction, while the active control condition used the usual classroom approach. All students were analyzed according to their original randomized condition.

abstract: TThis study examines how neighboring regions can reduce pollution when they compete to attract industry and pollution crosses regional borders. Participants act as regional decision-makers and choose how strictly to regulate pollution, balancing economic benefits, environmental harm, and regulatory costs. We compare five settings: no additional policy, compensation for environmental protection, joint assessment of regional pollution, and minimum regulatory standards with either low or high penalties. The study will recruit 240 participants across 30 sessions, with each participant completing 30 decision rounds. We examine how these policies affect regulatory choices, the location of polluting industry, pollution levels, and participants’ earnings.
experimental_design: We conduct a 30-round laboratory experiment in which participants represent one of two neighboring regions and choose an environmental regulation intensity from 0 to 100. Participants are randomly assigned to fixed regional roles and one of five treatments: baseline, ecological compensation, joint environmental assessment, a minimum standard with a low penalty, or a minimum standard with a high penalty. Choices jointly determine industrial location, pollution, regulatory costs, and payoffs. We compare regulatory choices, pollution outcomes, compliance, and payoffs across treatments. Experimental hypothesis: We test four hypotheses: (1) In the baseline, Region B chooses less stringent regulation than Region A and attracts a larger share of polluting industries. (2) Ecological compensation increases regulatory stringency more strongly in Region B than in Region A, narrowing the regulatory gap and reducing Region B’s share of polluting industries. (3) Joint assessment increases average regulatory stringency and reduces total regional pollution relative to the baseline. (4) High penalties increase compliance with minimum standards and concentrate choices near the prescribed thresholds, whereas low penalties yield lower compliance and outcomes closer to the baseline.
intervention: This laboratory experiment examines how environmental governance institutions affect regulatory choices and pollution across two neighboring regions. Participants represent regional governments and simultaneously choose regulatory stringency on a 0–100 scale over 30 rounds, with fixed regional roles and anonymous random rematching each round. Five treatments are compared: a baseline without policy intervention; ecological compensation paid by Region A to Region B in proportion to B’s regulatory effort; joint assessment that deducts earnings from both regions according to their combined pollution burden; and minimum regulatory standards of 63 for Region A and 43 for Region B, enforced with either high or low fixed penalties for noncompliance. Participants receive monetary payments based on their accumulated experimental earnings.

abstract: Pakistan has one of the lowest rates of female labor force participation in the world, and its garment industry is mostly male even though the same industry employs large numbers of women in comparable neighbors like Bangladesh, Vietnam, and Cambodia. We test whether this is held in place by what people on each side of the labor market believe and know. Factory managers may be wrong about how women perform on a production line, and about what other factories in their district already do. Households may weigh the costs of a woman working against a situation they have never examined, and may not know which nearby factories are hiring. We work with 200 garment firms in Sialkot, Faisalabad, and Lahore, each paired with the residential census block closest to it, and with 20 households in each block that contain a woman aged 16 to 45. We randomly assign these 200 firm and block pairs to one of four groups: a documentary-style short film shown to hiring managers about two comparable local firms that grew by hiring women (demand-side treatment); a package delivered to households that helps them think the decision through and gives them the contact details of nearby factories (supply-side treatment); both; or neither. Within the household treatment, half the blocks also see a documentary-style short film about what factory work is actually like. We follow firms and households 3-4 months and 8-9 months later, and ask whether firms hire more women, whether women look for and find work outside the home, and what changes in between.
experimental_design: The study is a 2x2 factorial experiment at the level of the firm and its neighboring census block. We recruited 200 garment manufacturers with at least 50 employees across three districts of Punjab: Sialkot, Faisalabad, and Lahore. Using census blocks list from the Punjab Bureau of Statistics, we matched each firm to a census block within a 30-minute commute, connected by road, and not a high-income neighborhood. A census block is the smallest unit used in the national census and holds 200 to 250 households. This gives 200 firm and block pairs, which we call dyads. Within each block we selected 20 households containing at least one woman aged 16 to 45, using systematic random sampling with a fixed skip interval. In each household we interview the household head, the target woman, and, where the head is not himself an adult male, a secondary adult male. Within each firm, we sample at least one manager, giving priority to those with hiring authority. After the baseline, the 200 dyads were randomly assigned in equal numbers to four groups of 50: no intervention (control); the demand-side treatment (film) only; the supply-side treatment (household package) only; and both. Within the two groups receiving the household package, half the blocks were randomly assigned to also receive the household film. Assignment was stratified by district. We follow firms and households roughly three months after the intervention and again roughly eight months after. At the second follow-up, funding covers half the households in each block, so we will survey a random 50% of households per block and all 200 firms, keeping all 200 dyads intact.
intervention: There are two interventions, one on each side of the labor market. The firm intervention is a ten-minute documentary-style film shown to hiring managers. Two mid-sized garment firms from Punjab describe how they began hiring women onto their production lines, what it cost them, and what happened afterwards to defect rates, productivity, the range of products they make, and the markets they sell to. The film ends with practical advice on how to start, beginning with one line of women on the same contracts as men. The household intervention has three parts, delivered together by an enumerator in a single visit. First, a structured exercise, called decisional balance sheet (DBS), in which the household head and the target woman lay out the decision as a ledger. For two situations, the woman working in a garment factory and the woman staying home, they name up to three benefits and three costs, both for the household and for the woman herself, and rate how much each one matters. The enumerator reads the balance back to them, asks what would make the costs that matter tolerable, and records where the household stands. Note that the DBS exercise argues for nothing and contains no persuasive material. Second, every household receives a printed sheet with the names, addresses, and phone numbers of up to three nearby garment factories. Third, in random half the treated blocks, households also watch a five-minute docuentary-style short film covering the things the exercise tends to raise as worries (or costs), such as the work environment, mixed-gender workplaces, commuting safety and employer transport, pay, hours, maternity and sick leave, and testimony from women already doing this work, and from husbands who support their wives working.

abstract: This study examines whether facilitated municipal titling produces durable changes in property investment, political support, collective action, and fiscal cooperation in Quelimane, Mozambique. The original experiment included 792 eligible properties in Bazar and Murropue, identified through mapping and a baseline survey. Eligible properties lacked qualifying formal documentation and were considered suitable for regularization. Within 192 matched strata based on geography and baseline housing quality, 397 properties were assigned to an offer of municipal documentation and assistance obtaining a Tombo, while 395 were assigned to control. The longer-term follow-up combines a household survey, an incentivized public-goods game, political and institutional measures, and observation of whether households display a commonly offered municipal sticker. Direct and indirect questions measure reports of historical voting and savings. Following the survey, planned municipal activities include tax-awareness sessions, assessment and bill delivery, and administrative tracking of property-tax payments. The intended protocol provides comparable information and payment opportunities across the original treatment and control groups. Assessment, liability, bill delivery, and collection activity will be documented to distinguish fiscal cooperation from changes in administrative access and tax obligations. Primary analyses estimate intention-to-treat effects of the original assignment on four outcomes: property-tax payment, municipal-sticker display, public-goods contribution, and construction or expansion. Analysis will retain the original matched strata, address multiple testing and missing outcomes, and distinguish property-level effects from outcomes of current owners and original respondents. Findings from an immediate compliance survey, conducted shortly after the treatment, inform the hypotheses; access to new follow-up outcomes will be disclosed at registration.
experimental_design: This is a longer-term follow-up of a two-arm randomized experiment involving 792 properties in Bazar and Murropue, Quelimane. Mapping and baseline data identified properties lacking qualifying formal documentation that could be regularized through the municipal programme. Original treatment allocation is retained; the titling treatment will not be rerandomized. Properties were assigned within 192 matched strata constructed using geography and baseline housing quality. The allocation comprises 397 treatment and 395 control properties. All original properties will be targeted for follow-up, retaining assignment after sale, migration, demolition, subdivision or other ownership changes. Administrative and physical-property outcomes will be linked to the original plot through documented crosswalks. Principal person-level outcomes use one designated current owner per original plot. Joint-owner selection follows a stable pre-interview rule. Original respondents, including movers where feasible, form a separately identified secondary panel. Current-owner estimates may include treatment-induced ownership composition changes and are not necessarily within-person effects on the original residents. The main estimand is the intention-to-treat effect of original assignment. Each primary endpoint will be regressed on assignment, original stratum fixed effects and six baseline covariates: secondary-school completion, sex, literacy, age, residential property use and being born in Quelimane. All covariates come from the archived baseline; the endline field named female will not substitute for baseline sex. Missing baseline covariates receive pooled-mean imputation and accompanying missingness indicators. A stratum-only specification will also be reported. Binary outcomes use linear probability models. One-observation-per-property analyses use HC2 heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors. Repeated observations will be aggregated to the endpoint or analysed with appropriate property-level clustering. A sensitivity will account for a shared owner representing multiple plots. Actual title receipt, bill delivery, tax liability, construction and other post-treatment variables will not be controlled for in the primary total-effect regressions. Comparisons concern own assignment under the experiment's treatment saturation and subsequent common municipal programme; the study does not independently identify every spillover or the effect of titling an entire city.
intervention: The randomized intervention offered eligible property holders assistance obtaining municipal property documentation. It combined a municipal despacho, facilitation of administrative requirements, and support for obtaining a free of charge Tombo (property right). Assignment to treatment constituted an offer of this package; actual receipt and the different administrative stages are recorded separately. Control properties did not receive the original experimental offer, although subsequent acquisition of documentation outside the programme is possible. The follow-up retains this original randomized comparison. Planned activities comprise an independent survey, behavioural measurements, a standardized municipal-sticker offer followed by an observation visit, and subsequent municipal tax-awareness and billing activities. The municipal protocol aims to provide comparable assessment attempts, information, bill-delivery procedures, payment access, and reminder intensity across the original assignment groups. Tax amounts may differ according to applicable valuation and exemption rules. Implementation differences will be documented.

abstract: We conduct an incentivized field experiment in China to study how young adults perceive the labor-market returns to graduate education and how these perceptions shape early-career choices. Participants complete a series of hypothetical choices involving employment and graduate education decisions. We use these data to estimate perceived returns to graduate education and further compare choice-based revealed beliefs with directly elicited beliefs and examine heterogeneity across career stages and individual characteristics.
experimental_design: We conduct two choice experiments to students and early-career employers in China. The first measures preferences over job characteristics; the second presents choices among accepting a job, continuing to search, and entering graduate school. We study the belief of graduate education returns in China by combining these two experiments.
experimental_design_details: 1. Recruitment We collaborate with Credamo, a Chinese online survey and research platform, to recruit participants. Eligible participants are aged 22–28 and are entering or actively participating in the labor market. Student respondents are restricted to relevant final-year undergraduate or master’s cohorts according to the final screening questionnaire. Participation is voluntary and incentivized. 2. Incentives Participants receive a fixed monetary reward for completing the study. In addition, preferences elicited through the experiment are used to generate personalized job recommendations drawn from real recruitment postings. Respondents are informed about these incentives before making their choices. 3. Module order and practice tasks All respondents complete both modules. Respondents are randomly assigned to complete either the ex-post or ex-ante module first. Each module begins with a practice task that is excluded from the analysis. The formal modules contain 20 choice tasks each. 4. Ex-post profile generation Each ex-post task presents two employment profiles. Participants are instructed to treat the displayed personal characteristics as their own at the time of receiving the offer, to assume that both jobs are located in the same city as the respondent, and to hold all undisclosed characteristics constant. Displayed job-seeker characteristics include age, educational attainment, and full-time work experience. Job attributes include monthly after-tax salary, employer type, layoff risk, and weekly working days. Age ranges from 22 to 28. Educational attainment and work experience are assigned subject to feasible age–education–experience combinations. Monthly after-tax salary takes five levels: RMB 3,000, RMB 5,000, RMB 7,000, RMB 9,000, and RMB 11,000. Employer type includes public-sector institutions, state-owned enterprises, foreign-invested enterprises, and private enterprises. Weekly working days take three levels: four, five, and six days, with daily hours fixed at eight. Layoff risk varies across low, medium, and high levels, subject to restrictions reflecting the support observed for different employer types in the Chinese labor market. We use a D-efficient design to improve balance and statistical efficiency. Respondents are assigned to one of ten blocks. Alternative placement and attribute order are randomized subject to the design restrictions. 5. Ex-ante profile generation and choice Each ex-ante task contains three components: the job seeker’s characteristics, a current job offer, and a graduate-school offer. The first two components largely follow the same conceptual attributes as the ex-post profiles, with some minor modifications, while the type of graduate school is added as an additional attribute. The third component introduces the type of graduate-school offer. Participants report the probability of choosing each of three options: accepting the displayed job offer, rejecting it and continuing to search for another job, or rejecting it and accepting the graduate-school offer. The profiles use a Latin-square design to vary states and offers systematically. Respondents are assigned to one of ten ex-ante blocks.

abstract: This study examines whether generative artificial intelligence (AI) affects gender differences in employers’ performance beliefs and hiring decisions. The experiment uses applicant profiles generated from a previously conducted job-seeker experiment in which participants completed mathematics and logic tasks either with or without access to generative AI. Participants acting as employers will be randomly assigned to an AI or no-AI applicant environment and will make ten incentivized hiring decisions between pairs of applicants. They will observe applicant characteristics, including gender, age, high-school arts/science track, intermediate-task performance, and AI-use condition, and will predict each applicant’s subsequent advanced-task performance before making hiring decisions. The experiment tests whether generative AI changes employers’ perceived gender differences in task performance and whether such changes are reflected in hiring decisions.
experimental_design: This study uses a between-subject experimental design. Participants acting as employers will be randomly assigned to one of two applicant environments: an AI environment, in which all applicant profiles are drawn from job seekers who completed the relevant tasks with access to generative AI, or a no-AI environment, in which all applicant profiles are drawn from job seekers who completed the tasks without access to generative AI. Each participant will make 10 independent and incentivized hiring decisions. In each round, the participant will observe a pair of applicant profiles drawn from a previously conducted job-seeker experiment. The profiles contain information on applicants’ gender, age, high-school academic track, intermediate-task performance, and AI-use condition. Participants will predict the advanced-task performance of both applicants and select one applicant to hire. To construct employers’ beliefs and hiring decisions, applicant profiles may differ along one or more observable characteristics. The order of the 10 hiring rounds will be randomized, and applicant pairs will not be repeated for the same participant. Hiring decisions are incentivized. One of the 10 rounds will be randomly selected for payment, and the participant’s bonus will depend on the advanced-task performance of the applicant selected in that round. After completing the hiring decisions, participants will answer a post-experiment questionnaire measuring their beliefs about the performance of male and female applicants under AI and no-AI conditions, as well as their knowledge of and attitudes toward generative AI.

abstract: We study how to explain economic mechanisms to lay participants.
experimental_design: Subjects will read an explanation, participate in a mechanism, and answer comprehension questions.
experimental_design_details: All sessions follow the same internal structure; what varies between sessions is the explanation read aloud and the stakes level. A session proceeds as follows: 1. Explanation. The session’s randomly assigned explanation is read aloud to participants. There are nine explanation conditions: one null (uninformative) explanation; one explanation produced by a large language model; and seven explanations produced by individual economist experts. 2. Auctions. Participants then complete four incentivized VCG auctions against two computerized opponents. Each auction sells two goods; participants’ values and computerized opponents’ values are drawn independently from the same distribution. 3. Comprehension questions. Participants answer a battery of incentivized multiple-choice questions about the mechanism. Questions are pre-organized into topic / difficulty sub-groups. The order of questions within each sub-group is randomized at the participant level; the order of sub-groups across the questionnaire is fixed. 4. Exit questionnaire. Participants complete an unincentivized exit questionnaire with attitude items (organized by topic) and demographic / self-report measures. All sessions use the auctions-first ordering described above. Cross-cutting the nine explanation conditions, sessions are randomly assigned to one of two stakes levels: · Normal stakes: $0.30 per correct comprehension answer (up to a $10.50 maximum); expected auction earnings of approximately $2 per round. · Double stakes: Both comprehension and auction payments doubled, so perfect comprehension plus expected auction earnings yield approximately $37 in expected bonus payments (in addition to a show-up fee). The double-stakes condition targets approximately ⅙ of participants, but actual proportions will vary with session-day attendance and are not committed to exactly ⅙. Sessions will be run at Cornell University and Ohio State University, with additional sites under discussion (potentially the University of Pittsburgh and the University of California, San Diego).

abstract: Access to high-quality AI systems often improves performance in difficult problem-solving tasks. Yet their use remains contested in environments such as professional interviews where evaluators aim to assess test-takers' inherent ability rather than assistive performance. Often, evaluators explicitly express a preference against the use of AI as an external source of help. Test-takers therefore face a trade-off between enjoying the performance gain from AI assistance while compromising on the evaluator’s preference for independent work. This is alarmingly important in light of unreliable AI-use detection. We examine whether individuals are willing to depart from an evaluator's stated preference for independent work when external AI assistance is abundantly available. More specifically, we ask whether such a departure is specific to available AI assistance or instead reflects a broader tendency to rely on any sufficiently capable external source, such as an equally capable human. In this experiment, we evaluate whether individuals seek external help from an AI more than an equally capable human to complete a moderately difficult task, in cases when they choose to seek external help because of their lower intrinsic perceived accuracy in solving the task.
experimental_design: We conduct an online experiment in which participants complete a text-based judgment task using transcripts from the television game show To Tell the Truth. For each transcript, participants first identify which of the three contestants is the genuine individual described in an accompanying affidavit and report their confidence and perceived task difficulty. The study varies the source of external assistance available to participants. Using a within-subjects design, each participant encounters two transcripts: in one, the available external help comes from an AI system; in the other, it comes from a human source. The assignment of the help source to the transcript and the order of transcript presentation are randomized. Participants are informed that the two sources of assistance are equally capable. After completing their initial judgments for both transcripts, participants revisit each decision and choose whether to submit their own initial answer or the answer provided by the external resource. The primary outcome is participants’ uptake of external assistance. Across experimental treatments, we additionally vary whether participants are explicitly told that independent work is preferred and that they should not use external help (Baseline vs Nudge treatments). This allows us to examine how the source of assistance and an expressed preference for independent work affect decisions to rely on external help. Following each decision, participants answer questions about how they perceive the external resource and about their beliefs regarding the prevalence and social appropriateness of using such assistance. Participants also complete a brief demographic and prior-AI-use questionnaire at the end of the study.
