abstract: This experiment will test the effect of subscription-based pricing for electric vehicle (EV) charging on driver charging behavior. Subscription pricing charges an upfront flat monthly fee in return for a lower marginal cost (dollar per kWh) price for charging. The setting is a university campus, comprised mostly of workplace charging, and includes staff, faculty, students, and community members. Drivers are randomized to receive one offer of a subscription pricing plan and invited to enroll. Pricing plans differ in monthly fee and volumetric discount.
experimental_design: This study is an RCT field trial with a total sample size of 2,261 EV drivers. The randomization is at the individual driver level. To account for differences in driving and charging behavior, the sample is stratified (blocked) into two distinct groups by vehicle type: battery EV (BEV) drivers (n=1,832) and plug-in hybrid EV (PHEV) drivers (n=429). BEV drivers are randomly allocated to 5 parallel arms, one of four treatment arms or control. Because the treatment is an offer of new pricing and drivers may either accept or decline the offer, we balance the size of each group assuming an opt-in rate of 35 percent. Balancing is done, moreover, on the subset of drivers that have recently charged on the university network. We thus have treatment arms of approx. 421 drivers per arm and a control group with 148 drivers. PHEV drivers are assigned to 3 parallel arms, one of two treatment arms or control, following the same logic. Each treatment arm has approx. 183 drivers and the control group has 64 drivers. The intervention tests subscription-based pricing for workplace EV charging. Each treatment arm is a unique offer of subscription-based pricing, which charges an upfront flat monthly fee in exchange for lower marginal (dollar per kWh) prices at the charger. For PHEVs, only the lower-cost subscription price will be tested. Randomization was conducted with computer-generated random assignment. Outcomes will be tracked using charging station data, which provides the plug-in time, plug-out time, and energy consumption of every session tied to the individual driver. The intervention period is roughly 3 months.
intervention: The intervention is the subscription pricing plan offered to drivers. Drivers are assigned to one of four treatment arms (or control) and invited to enroll: 1. Control: the base rate marginal price offered today, with no monthly fee 2. $5/month for 16% off the base rate 3. $5/month for 31% off 4. $10/month for 16% off 5. $10/month for 31% off Because battery EVs (BEVs) are greater in number at our university, BEV drivers will be assigned to one of groups 1–5. Because there are fewer plug-in hybrid EVs (PHEVs) and they demand less electricity, PHEV drivers will be assigned to one of groups 1–3 (i.e., we will test only the smaller monthly fee).

abstract: This study examines whether financial incentives change the behavior of landlords who exclude families with children from rental housing. We conduct a correspondence study on the largest online real estate platform in Russia, targeting listings in Moscow that state children are not accepted. We send messages expressing interest in the property and stating that the applicant household includes a two-year-old child. Acknowledging the listing's restriction, the applicant asks the landlord to make an exception. Landlords are randomly assigned to receive one of several versions of this message, which differ only in the financial incentive offered. The applicant is otherwise described identically in all versions. Our primary outcome is whether the landlord responds within seven days. We also record how quickly the landlord responds and whether the response is positive. This is Phase 2 of a two-phase study. Phase 1 (AEARCTR-0017892) studied landlords who state that they welcome children.
experimental_design: We conduct a correspondence study on an online real estate platform. The target population is listings that explicitly state that children are not accepted. We randomly assign listings to one of four arms: a control arm in which the applicant asks for an exception with no financial incentive, and three treatment arms in which the applicant offers a different financial incentive alongside the exception request. The specific incentive amounts are specified in the pre-analysis plan and will be made public when data collection closes. Randomization is at the listing level. Listings are stratified by asking price and divided into blocks of four, with one listing per arm per block. Because new listings appear continuously on the platform, sampling proceeds in rounds; a round whose length is not a multiple of four may leave leftover listings, which are assigned to arms uniformly at random without replacement and pooled with the blocked listings for analysis. All messages follow a common template and differ only in the incentive clause. The applicant is a married woman with a generic Russian name, seeking housing for herself, her husband, and their two-year-old son. All applicants are described as Russian citizens, and all landlords are contacted through the platform's messaging system. The target sample is 2,750 contacted listings. Data collection is expected to take between 16 and 18 weeks.
experimental_design_details: We conduct a correspondence study on cian.ru, the largest online real estate platform in Russia. Phase~1 (AEARCTR-0017892) tested truth-telling among landlords who signal that they welcome children. In each treatment arm, the applicant acknowledges the restriction and offers the corresponding incentive if it would help arrange a viewing. The applicant is a married woman with a generic Russian name, seeking housing for herself, her husband, and their two-year-old son. All applicants are described as citizens of the Russian Federation, which holds nationality fixed and avoids confounding the estimated effect of incentives with differential treatment on nationality grounds. All landlords are contacted through cian.ru's messaging system. Randomization is at the listing level. Listings are stratified by asking price and divided into blocks of four, with one listing assigned to each arm per block. Because new listings appear continuously on the platform, sampling proceeds in rounds. A round whose length is not a multiple of four may leave leftover listings; these are assigned to arms uniformly at random without replacement and pooled with the blocked listings for analysis. Listings are randomly assigned to one of four versions of this message. The first arm offers no financial incentive (control). The remaining three offer alternative financial incentives. The specific incentives are described in the pre-analysis plan and will be made public when data collection closes.

abstract: This document presents the pre-analysis plan for the research project “Impact Evaluation of an Online Counseling Program Providing Neighborhood Information to Rental Voucher Recipients in Chile.” The Chilean Ministry of Housing and Urbanism (MINVU) introduced the first rental voucher program in Latin America in 2013. Yet take-up remains limited: each year, approximately six out of ten awarded vouchers are not used, and many households that do use their vouchers relocate to neighborhoods with relatively poor characteristics. This project evaluates strategies to improve the performance of public agents who assist beneficiaries of the Chilean Rental Voucher Program. Public workers are randomly assigned to a control group or one of five treatment groups. All groups use Aprendo y Arriendo (AyA), an online platform that provides standardized counseling tools and neighborhood-level information to support interactions with beneficiaries. The control group receives basic training on the platform and standard lists of beneficiaries. The treatments vary along two experimental dimensions. First, agents may receive performance feedback in addition to the basic platform training. Second, beneficiary lists may be prioritized according to the expected cost of successfully completing a rental placement, distinguishing between relatively high- and low-cost cases. Some treatment groups receive performance feedback only, others receive prioritized beneficiary lists only, and two groups receive both interventions. This design allows us to separately and jointly estimate the effects of performance feedback and case prioritization on agent behavior and performance. We study whether these interventions increase voucher utilization, improve the efficiency of agents’ efforts, and affect the characteristics of the neighborhoods into which beneficiary households relocate.
experimental_design: Public agents and rental voucher beneficiaries are randomly assigned to experimental groups. The design varies two dimensions: whether agencies receive performance information in addition to basic training, and whether beneficiaries are assigned to agent lists prioritized toward relatively high-cost or low-cost cases. This generates five treatment groups and one control group. The design allows us to estimate the separate and joint effects of performance feedback and case prioritization on agent performance and voucher utilization.
intervention: The intervention is implemented through Aprendo y Arriendo (AyA), an online platform used by public agents who support beneficiaries of Chile’s Rental Voucher Program. The platform provides standardized counseling tools, beneficiary information, and neighborhood-level information to assist agents in helping households use their vouchers and search for rental housing. All study groups receive access to the AyA platform and basic training on its use. The experimental interventions vary along two dimensions. First, some agents receive performance feedback based on metrics related to their work with beneficiaries. Second, some agents receive prioritized beneficiary lists that rank cases according to their expected difficulty or cost of achieving a successful rental placement. The prioritization can emphasize either relatively high-cost or relatively low-cost cases. The five treatment arms combine these interventions in different ways: performance feedback only, high-cost prioritization only, low-cost prioritization only, performance feedback plus high-cost prioritization, and performance feedback plus low-cost prioritization. The control group receives basic platform training and standard, non-prioritized beneficiary lists without performance feedback.

abstract: Why does freely available information go unused? Two answers dominate the literature and are hard to tell apart. Attending to information is costly, or people would rather not know. They imply the same purchases and opposite policies: if attention is the constraint, simplifying the signal or making it more prominent helps; if people are turning away from it, those same interventions do nothing, and the case for acting on the product rather than on the label is stronger. Purchase data alone cannot distinguish them, because both produce the same basket. Food is the sharpest case. Whether a packaged product is healthy depends on its nutritional content, its additives and how processed it is. All of it is printed on the package, and none of it is easy to put together at the moment of choice. Online, it sits behind a click, on a page most shoppers never open. This study runs a randomised experiment inside real online grocery shopping. Adults in the United States who already order from Walmart.com at least weekly install a browser extension built for the study and complete one ordinary order, in their own account and with their own money. The extension varies at random, between participants, both how much nutritional information about each product is available to them and what it takes to see it. Two contrasts follow. Holding the effort fixed and varying the content asks what the detail behind a summary signal is worth. Holding the content fixed and varying the effort asks what it costs to look at information that is identical and one click away. Because the study observes not only what was bought but whether the participant engaged with the information at all, the two explanations come apart. If attending is what is costly, shoppers consult the score when the stakes are high, whatever they expect it to say. If they are avoiding it, they turn away precisely when they expect bad news about something they meant to buy. Engagement is observed on two margins: as an absence, where information offered is left unopened, and as an act, where information already on screen is closed and the number that was on screen is known. The primary outcome is the nutritional quality of the completed basket, measured as the average score of the items purchased, weighted by what was spent on each. A closing question with real money attached measures what continued access to the information is worth to participants. The extension runs only on Walmart.com. It records which products were displayed and which were purchased, under a randomly generated study code, never collects names, addresses or payment details, and stops collecting when the shopping session ends. Approved by the Cornell University Institutional Review Board, protocol IRB0151136.
experimental_design: Individually randomised four-arm experiment, conducted in participants' own browsers during a single real grocery purchase on Walmart.com. Equal allocation. Randomisation occurs at the end of the enrollment questionnaire, after all baseline characteristics have been recorded and before any study content is shown.
experimental_design_details: Recruitment runs through Prolific, a message in Yuka's standard welcome email to newly registered US users, and Cornell SONA. Eligibility is screened before randomisation: 18 or older, US resident, Chrome as primary browser, an existing Walmart.com account used regularly, primary grocery shopper for the household, and at least weekly grocery ordering on Walmart.com. Order of operations: consent and eligibility screen, background questionnaire, randomisation, extension install, shopping session, checkout. A return code generated at checkout brings the participant back to the closing survey; entering that code also stops all data collection on Walmart.com. Removal instructions follow. The extension fails closed: with no assigned condition it renders nothing and records nothing, so a failure of assignment produces a missing participant rather than a mislabelled one. Pre-specified exclusions from the primary analysis, applied identically across arms and reported by arm: no completed checkout; no item present in the reference table; failure of the attention check in the closing survey; and sessions with no recorded page impressions, which indicate an installation failure rather than a choice. Intention to treat is the estimate of record.
intervention: Participants install a browser extension built for this study and complete one ordinary grocery order on Walmart.com, in their own account and with their own money. The extension changes how nutritional information about each grocery product is made available to them while they shop. Which version they receive varies between participants and is assigned at random. Participants are told in advance that the display varies and that it is decided by chance; they are not told which version they received until the study is over. The extension runs only on Walmart.com, records data under a randomly generated study code, never collects names, addresses or payment details, stops collecting when the shopping session ends, and is removed at the end of the study.

primary_outcome_explanation: For participant i the outcome is Y_i = sum_j (s_j × e_ij) / sum_j e_ij, where e_ij is the dollars participant i spent on product j in the completed order and s_j is product j's nutritional score on a 0-100 scale, taken from the study's fixed reference table. Weighting by expenditure rather than by item count means the measure reflects what was actually bought rather than how many distinct products were tried. The reference table is fixed and versioned before the first participant enters and is identical across arms and participants; scores are never recomputed at runtime. Items with no entry in the table are excluded from both numerator and denominator, and the share of basket expenditure so excluded is reported and tested for differences across arms. Baskets containing no scorable grocery item are excluded from the primary analysis and counted in the attrition table. Three contrasts are pre-specified. Control versus T1 is the effect of the bare signal. T1 versus T2 is what the detail behind the signal is worth. randomization_method: Computer-generated, by the randomiser built into the Qualtrics survey software, at the end of the enrollment questionnaire. Equal allocation across the four arms, no stratification. The assignment is written to the participant's survey record as an embedded field and read from there by the browser extension, so the arm recorded in the survey and the arm delivered on Walmart.com cannot diverge.
randomization_unit: Individual participant. There is a single level of randomisation; no group or session-level assignment.
secondary_outcome_explanation: 1. The threshold of 60 is fixed in advance at the boundary between the two middle bands of the score, computed on the same expenditure weights as the primary outcome. Robustness to thresholds of 50 and 70 is reported. 2. This is the mechanism test and the reason the study is run as an experiment rather than on purchase data. Two explanations for unused information predict the same baskets: that attending to it is costly, and that people prefer not to know. They separate in engagement rather than in outcomes, and the study observes engagement on two margins. Where the information is offered but not shown, disengagement is an absence: the placeholder is left unopened. Where it is shown without being asked for, disengagement is an act: it is closed, and the score that was on screen when it was closed is known. If attending is what is costly, engagement rises with the stakes attached to the product and does not depend on what the participant expects the score to say, which cannot be known before opening. If the information is being avoided, disengagement concentrates on products the participant intends to buy and whose score is unfavourable. 3. The participant states the minimum amount v they would accept to keep the extension installed until their next grocery checkout. A price p is drawn from an announced distribution, independent of v. If p is at least v the participant keeps the extension and is paid p; otherwise the study ends there. Payment is conditional on the extension still being installed at the next purchase, and participants are told this before stating v. Keeping the extension bundles continuing to receive the information and continuing to be observed. In the control arm no information is shown, so v measures the cost of being observed alone; in the treated arms it measures that cost net of the value of the information. The difference between arms is the revealed dollar value of the disclosure, and the ordering across T1, T2 and T3 prices the detail separately from the bare signal. The control arm is not an ordinary comparison group here: it is what makes the other three interpretable.
secondary_outcomes: 1. Share of basket expenditure on products scoring 60 or above. 2. Total basket expenditure, and number of distinct grocery items purchased. 3. Participant engagement with the nutritional information shown: whether it was opened or removed, how long it was on screen, and how that varies with the score and with whether the product was purchased. 4. Willingness to accept, elicited with real money, for keeping the extension installed until the next grocery purchase. 5. Products displayed with a score, considered, and not purchased.

abstract: We conduct a nationwide audit correspondence field experiment of over 90,000 US K-12 public, charter, and private schools to quantify discrimination in admissions by race, ethnicity, disability, SES, and sexual orientation or gender identity (SOGI). Private schools can legally discriminate on most dimensions, and we will be the first to quantify whether they discriminate differently from public or charter schools. We will email school administrators (SAs) as mothers seeking to enroll their children and inquiring about the application process and fit, mimicking the crucial information-gathering phase when accessing schools of choice. These emails will be on average identical except signals of race or ethnicity (Black, Hispanic, Arab, White), SOGI, SES, and disability. We quantify discrimination by comparing response rates and quality by group and school type. We inform how to reduce discrimination by investigating the mechanisms of discrimination, such as how numerous policies (e.g., anti-DEI, anti(pro)-LGBTQIA+ policies, vouchers) associate with discrimination.
experimental_design: Our general experimental design follows those of similar email-correspondence studies (e.g., Gaddis et al., 2024; Giulietti, Tonin, and Vlassopoulos, 2019). We conduct a nationwide audit correspondence field experiment of approximately 88,000 US K-12 traditional public, charter, and private schools. Each school's point of contact (usually the school secretary or administrative assistant) receives two emails from fictitious mothers inquiring about enrollment and the application process, sent at least 21 days apart. Within each pair, we randomly assign signals of race or ethnicity, SOGI or disability, gender, SES, and academic achievement, so that the two emails differ only in these signals and minor phrasing. We quantify discrimination by comparing response rates across groups and by school type (private and charter relative to traditional public).
intervention: We send emails to school administrators (SAs) at K-12 traditional public, charter, and private schools nationwide, posing as mothers inquiring whether their child could enroll and how to apply. Each school receives two emails from two fictitious families, sent at least 21 days apart. The emails are on average identical except for randomly assigned signals of the family's race or ethnicity (White, Black, Hispanic, Arab), the child's sexual orientation or gender identity (SOGI) or disability, the child's gender, the family's socio-economic status (SES), and the child's academic achievement.

abstract: This laboratory experiment examines whether holding an existing financial position affects the willingness to acquire optional information about the environmental consequences of an investment decision and subsequent investment choice. Participants make an incentivised investment decision under different information and position conditions. The primary outcomes capture information acquisition and investment choice. Eye-tracking data provide exploratory evidence on information processing. The planned sample is 300 participants.
experimental_design: A three-condition between-subjects laboratory experiment conducted at the Mainz Behavioral and Experimental Laboratory (MABELLA). Participants make one incentivised choice between two investments that differ in private payoff and an associated carbon-offset contribution. Across conditions, we manipulate the availability of information about the environmental consequences and whether one option constitutes an existing position. Random assignment occurs at the individual level within experimental sessions.
experimental_design_details: Design. Own payoffs are 60 Taler for Investment A and 50 Taler for Investment B, with 1 Taler equal to 0.10 EUR, and each option carries a carbon-offset payment of either 10 or 50 Taler. In Treatments B and C these offset amounts are concealed behind a costless reveal button on the decision screen, and in Treatment C Investment A is additionally assigned as the participant's current position. Procedure. All treatments follow the same sequence. Consent, general instructions and carbon-offset information open the session. Two practice examples and four comprehension questions follow, with the rules restated after each error. A 20-second holding screen and treatment-specific decision instructions precede the decision screen. The manipulation check, mechanism items, reason ratings in the hidden-information treatments and belief items for non-revealers follow the choice. A questionnaire covers investment preferences, climate attitudes, individual responsibility, subjective financial knowledge and investment experience. A final item records awareness of the gaze recording, followed by demographics. A closing screen states the study purpose, the implementation of the offset contributions and a contact address. Treatments A and B show a neutral holding screen of identical duration, so that Treatment C differs only in the assigned position and in the elements that implement it. Rating blocks use discrete seven-point sliders with the handle initially unset, a required response, and item order randomised within blocks. No time limit applies to the decision screen. Exclusions and flags. Excluded from all analyses are participants who do not consent or who abort before submitting the investment choice, and observations lost to documented technical failure. Participants have up to three attempts per comprehension question and are flagged rather than excluded after a third failed attempt. Participants answering at least three of the four questions incorrectly within a single attempt are also flagged. One instructed-response attention-check item is embedded in a post-decision rating block, and failing responses are retained but flagged. All confirmatory tests are re-estimated without flagged participants as a robustness check. Gaze quality is reported as a measure and never removes anyone from the behavioural analyses. Because calibration is completed before the treatment is assigned, calibration quality cannot depend on treatment. Pilot. A pretest was completed in three sessions on 24, 25 and 27 August 2026, with 54 recordings, after the ethics approval and before this registration. Its pre-specified purposes were technical feasibility of the gaze recording and the data pipeline, comprehension of the instructions, whether the position manipulation reaches the participant, and orders of magnitude for sample-size planning. The pretest was descriptive and not a hypothesis test, and its data are not pooled with main-study data. No changes to the incentivised design resulted from it, and the payoff parameters, the situation probabilities and the treatment procedures are all retained.
intervention: Participants make an incentivised choice between two investments that differ in their private payoff and environmental consequences. Three between-subjects conditions, labelled Treatments A, B and C, vary whether information about the environmental consequences is initially available and whether one investment is established as the participant's existing position. The design therefore allows us to examine whether an existing position affects optional information acquisition and subsequent choice. Eye-tracking data are collected as an exploratory process measure.

secondary_outcome_explanation: The gaze layer is specified in advance and is exploratory throughout. It carries no confirmatory hypothesis and does not affect the behavioural hypotheses. Its focus is whether an existing position changes how participants allocate attention on the decision screen before the decision is submitted, in particular between the two payoff dimensions. Gaze later in the decision screen is examined as well. Gaze is recorded over the full screen, so further process measures may be added, and all gaze results are labelled exploratory. The position manipulation check comprises six seven-point items on how participants experienced the position and is reported descriptively. The mechanism items and all further gaze analyses are exploratory.
secondary_outcomes: Visual attention to the two payoff dimensions on the decision screen, measured by eye tracking and analysed exploratorily; the position manipulation check; post-decision mechanism items; and a control item on awareness of the gaze recording.

abstract: This study aims to examine how human oversight and explainability affect banking professionals' acceptance of artificial-intelligence-assisted credit decisions. We will embed a 2 x 2 between-subject factorial randomized experiment in an online survey of approximately 1,000 employees of Spanish banks. All respondents will read the same vignette describing a personal-loan application for which an artificial intelligence (AI) system recommends declining credit. We will independently randomize whether a qualified professional reviews the AI recommendation before the final decision and may confirm or modify it (human oversight: yes/no), and whether the AI provides a short explanation of the factors driving its recommendation and their direction (explanation: yes/no). The primary outcomes are trust in a final decision reached through the described procedure (0-10) and the maximum weight respondents would allow the AI recommendation to carry in the final decision (0-100%). A secondary outcome measures the perceived appropriateness of using the described procedure for credit decisions (0-10). The design aims to identify the main causal effects of human oversight and explanation, as well as their interaction. The experiment will focus on banking professionals, who are directly familiar with the institutional setting in which AI-assisted credit decisions may be implemented.
experimental_design: We conduct a between-subject 2 x 2 factorial survey experiment embedded in an online questionnaire administered to employees of the Spanish banking sector. Two binary factors are randomized independently at the individual level. The first factor is Human Oversight: before the final decision is adopted, a qualified professional either reviews the AI recommendation and the information used by the system and may confirm or modify the recommendation, or no such professional review occurs. The second factor is Explanation: the AI either provides a concise explanation identifying the factors that most influenced its recommendation and the direction of those influences, or provides no information about which factors influenced the recommendation. All respondents read the same underlying loan-application vignette and receive the same AI recommendation to decline the application. The four experimental conditions differ only in the two randomized procedural features. Outcomes are elicited immediately after treatment exposure, followed by manipulation checks. - Common scenario A person applies to the respondent's institution for a EUR 20,000 personal loan with a five-year maturity. The bank uses an AI system that analyzes the economic and financial information normally used in this type of decision. The applicant has stable employment, net monthly income of EUR 2,400, no payment defaults during the previous three years, existing financial obligations of EUR 850 per month, and approximately 70% utilization of available credit-card limits. After analyzing this information, the AI system recommends declining the credit application. Treatment manipulations - Human oversight - no: the AI recommendation is not reviewed by a qualified professional before the final decision is adopted. - Human oversight - yes: before the final decision is adopted, a qualified professional reviews the AI recommendation and the information used by the system and may confirm or modify the recommendation. - Explanation - no: the system communicates its recommendation but provides no information on which factors influenced it or in which direction. - Explanation - yes: together with its recommendation, the system states that employment stability and the absence of recent defaults influenced the recommendation positively, while current indebtedness and high utilization of available credit influenced it negatively, with the negative factors receiving greater overall weight.
intervention: The intervention consists of a 2×2 between-subject randomized survey experiment embedded in the questionnaire. All respondents are presented with the same hypothetical scenario in which a customer applies for a €20,000 five-year personal loan and an artificial intelligence system, after assessing standard financial information, recommends rejecting the application. Respondents are then randomly assigned to one of four experimental conditions that vary independently along two dimensions: human oversight and explainability. In the human-oversight condition, a qualified professional reviews the AI recommendation and the underlying information before the final decision and may confirm or modify it; in the no-oversight condition, no such review takes place. In the explanation condition, the AI system provides information on the factors that contributed positively or negatively to its recommendation, whereas in the no-explanation condition no information is provided about the factors underlying the recommendation. The four treatment arms therefore allow us to estimate the separate and joint effects of human oversight and explainability on respondents’ reactions to AI-assisted credit decisions.
mde_text: The planned sample is approximately N = 1,000, with equal allocation across the four treatment cells (approximately 250 respondents per cell). abstract: Digital credit scoring can expand access to finance for smallholder farmers, but its benefits depend on whether borrowers understand how scores are generated and how their actions affect future credit access. Transparency may help farmers respond to digital credit scoring with clear information that push them toward productive practices that are genuinely relevant for creditworthiness. On the other hand, by making the scoring logic more visible, transparency may also encourage farmers to focus strategically on practices they believe are rewarded by the score. Whether the transparency provided to farmers improves investment decisions, induces score-targeting behavior, or has limited behavioral effects is therefore an underexplored area. This paper examines whether making a digital agricultural credit score more transparent improves farmers’ understanding and changes investment behavior. We study Dvara E-Registry (DER)’s KhetScore, a digital credit-scoring system that uses remote sensing and machine learning approaches to assess farmers’ creditworthiness. Using a lab-in-field experiment with 1,210 smallholder farmers, we compare a control group with two information treatments: a basic KhetScore information intervention (Treatment 1) and an enhanced treatment that adds repayment salience (Treatment 2). We hypothesize that KhetScore information will improve farmers’ understanding of the scoring system and may change input choices toward practices they learn as score-relevant by the intervention. We also hypothesize that repayment salience provided in Treatment 2, may affect behavior beyond information alone by making farmers more attentive to repayment risk, future credit access, and the consequences of investment choices under uncertain production conditions. Findings will have immediate relevance for our implementing partner and policymakers.
experimental_design: The experimental design takes the form of a cluster-randomized trial. The study sample consists of 122 eligible villages in Jajpur district in Odisha, where DER’s KhetScore-based operations are active. Villages were assigned to different arms, stratified by block and village-size category. Randomization resulted in approximately equal allocation of villages across three arms: Control, Treatment 1, and Treatment 2, and a final sample size of 1,210 farmers. Randomization was conducted at the village level to minimize spillovers arising from information sharing within villages.
intervention: The intervention tested whether transparency about KhetScore, a digital agricultural credit score for agricultural lending, improves farmers’ understanding and affects investment behavior. Treatment 1 is provided with the information on how KhetScore is generated and how farm-management practices can affect the score. Treatment 2 received the same information, plus a repayment-salience message linking timely repayment to future access to KhetScore-based loans. The control group received a placebo video without information on KhetScore or credit access.

abstract: Theories of limited attention suggest that decision-makers selectively focus on relevant information and update expectations accordingly. In this paper, we conduct multiple surveys to empirically investigate the impact of perceived information relevance on household expectation formation. We begin by developing innovative measures to assess the perceived relevance of various macroeconomic data to household decision-making processes. We show that individuals are more attentive to information deemed relevant to their decisions and respond more strongly to news on relevant information. Perceived relevance makes an individual's subjective macroeconomic models more consistent with macroeconomic theories, such as the consumption Euler equation. These observations offer significant insights for policy-making geared towards household expectation management.
experimental_design: Two-part online survey on consecutive days with US respondents recruited on Prolific. Part 1 elicits unprimed relevance and attention (open-ended), primed relevance and news attention, prior one-year-ahead expectations and forecast uncertainty for inflation, the unemployment rate, and the federal funds rate, and demographics. Respondents are then randomized at the individual level into an information arm or a no-information control arm. Part 2, on the following day, elicits posterior expectations and uncertainty, (an incentivized recall of the information in the treatment arm for treatment group participants,) and expected household financial outcomes. Analysis is intention-to-treat on all respondents who complete both parts.
intervention: This trial is a robustness wave for "Focusing on What Matters: Perceived Relevance and Macroeconomic Expectations." It replicates the two-day design of Study 1 with US respondents on Prolific and adds a pure control arm. On Day 1, respondents answer open-ended questions about which economic factors they consider in household financial decisions and which economic news they recall, and report one-year-ahead expectations for inflation, the unemployment rate, and the federal funds rate. They are then randomly assigned to an information arm, which shows published professional forecasts for the three variables, or to a control arm, which shows no forecasts. On Day 2, all respondents report their expectations again.

abstract: This project investigates how generative AI can support—or disrupt—personalized learning, depending on students’ academic skills and perceptions of their own skills. Although AI-generated guidance has the potential to improve learning and performance, students may differ in their capacity to evaluate and use it critically; some may engage thoughtfully with AI suggestions, while others may rely on them uncritically. Using field-based randomized controlled trials, the study compares students completing assessment tasks with and without AI support. It examines how AI assistance affects both actual performance and students’ perceptions of their performance, and whether these effects vary with academic ability, self-perceived ability, and perceived AI literacy. The project seeks to identify the cognitive and behavioural barriers that prevent students from benefiting fully from generative AI. It will also explore whether these barriers differ across levels of academic ability, degrees of self-confidence, and subject areas. The findings will inform the design of educational practices and AI-based learning tools that help a broader range of students engage with AI critically and effectively. The topic of this project is linked to an earlier pre-registered trial (https://www.socialscienceregistry.org/trials/15659). No data of that trial is used for the current project.
experimental_design: This randomized controlled trial involves undergraduate students who are assigned different versions of an assignment. Some versions include AI-generated answer suggestions. Assignment data will be matched with administrative records on student prior academic performance to analyze heterogeneity in outcomes.
intervention: Undergraduate students are randomly assigned to different versions of an summative assignment. Some versions include GenAI-generated answer suggestions below questions. The intervention is the provision of these AI-generated suggestions, enabling a comparison between students who receive this support and those who do not.

abstract: This study exploits a rare opportunity to validate survey measures of job search behavior by benchmarking self-reported responses against administrative records from an online job platform, using data from a follow-up survey of technical diploma students in Bangladesh. We embed three randomized survey design experiments in this survey, each targeting a distinct source of measurement error: the length of the recall window; the presence of filter questions and the level of detail in prompts; and whether being surveyed itself influences job search behavior on the platform. A distinctive feature of the setting is that individual-level administrative records of login events, job search, and application submissions provide a behavioral benchmark that is rarely available in these settings.
experimental_design: Accurate measurement of job search behavior in surveys is challenging. Respondents may misremember the frequency or timing of activities, question design may prompt or suppress recall, and awareness of being observed may itself alter behavior. This study exploits a rare opportunity to validate survey measures of job search by benchmarking self-reported job search behavior against administrative records from an online job platform. We embed a set of randomized survey design experiments within a follow-up survey of technical diploma students in Bangladesh, two thirds of whom were introduced and trained to use an online job search platform. We investigate three distinct measurement questions. First, we investigate how varying the recall period affects self-reported measures of job search activity and the accuracy of those measures relative to administrative records. Respondents are randomly assigned to report their job search behavior over either the past 14 or past 30 days. While it is well established that recall length changes how individuals respond, direct evidence on whether shorter periods produce more accurate responses is limited because true benchmarks are often not available. Administrative data from an online job platform — logins, job post views, and application submissions at the individual level — allow us to evaluate accuracy directly for each recall window. Second, we examine how question structure affects reported job search activity, varying two design features across randomly assigned groups. One group receives a simplified question sequence with no filter question (e.g., respondents are asked directly “how many times did you log in to the platform?” without first being asked whether they logged in at all). A second group receives the question sequence with the addition of filter questions before quantity questions, with those who answer “no” to the filter skipped past the follow-up. A third group receives the same question sequence as the first group, except that the initial question regarding search on the platform is accompanied by a detailed probe that further clarifies the activities that qualify as “search” behavior (e.g., that “search” on the platform includes logging in, viewing job adverts, updating their CV, in addition to submitting applications). This design allows us to separately identify the role of filtering from the role of aided recall, and again to benchmark responses against administrative records. Third, we test for Hawthorne effects – changes in job search behavior arising from awareness of being surveyed – by randomly assigning 10% of the study sample to be administered an abbreviated survey that doesn’t include questions about job search. A distinctive feature of this setting is that the survey and the job search activity being measured occur through separate mediums, avoiding the interaction fatigue that can generate negative Hawthorne effects when the survey and the activity of interest share the same platform. Together, these experiments contribute methodological evidence to survey design and measurement of job search, particularly in low- and middle-income country contexts where administrative benchmarks are rarely available.
intervention: The measurement design experiments are embedded in a follow up phone survey with technical diploma students who are enrolled in a cluster-randomized controlled trial evaluating the impacts of an online job platform on job search and employment (for more details please refer to AEA RCT registry ID: AEARCTR-0019605). The follow up survey, in which the measurement design experiments are implemented, is conducted approximately four months after the baseline was conducted. Hawthorne: Among the 3,571 students who participated in the workshops and baseline survey, 10% are randomly selected to receive an abbreviated version of the follow up survey, which only verifies contact information and captures work experience prior to the workshops. The remaining 90% will receive the full survey, which, in addition to contact verification and work experience, includes measures of online and offline job search and perceptions of online search methods. Randomization is stratified by base treatment assignment (whether the half-day workshop included the session of training on an online job platform) and gender. Recall period: Among the 90% of students assigned to receive the full follow up survey, half of students are given a recall length of 14 days in the job search questions while the other half are given a recall length of 30 days. Randomization is stratified by base treatment assignment and gender. Probing and filter questions: Within the base treatment group (who received training on an online job platform at baseline) and are assigned to the full survey, 1/3 are assigned to each of the following, and randomization is stratified by gender: 1. Simple: A sequence of job search questions without filter questions (for example, “how many applications did you send through the online job platform?”). 2. Simple with filter: The same sequence of job search questions as (1) with the addition of filter questions (for example: “did you send any applications through the online job platform?”, then if ‘yes’, “how many applications did you send through the online job platform?”). 3. Simple with detail probe: The same sequence of job search questions as (1), with an additional probe accompanying the question “In the last [14/30] days, did you use the online job platform to search for jobs?”, which states, “This includes sending job applications through the platform, but also includes logging into the platform, updating your CV, viewing job adverts (even if you didn't apply to any jobs), using the learning videos. Did you do any of those things?” to clarify activities on the platform that qualify as search. Within the base treatment arm, the Recall Period and Probing and Filter Questions assignments are cross-randomized. Administrative data provided by the online job platform serves as the benchmark with which to compare measures of job search behavior.

abstract: We survey economists (have or pursuing a PhD in economics or finance) to elicit ratings of the validity and relevance of robustness checks for a key empirical finding in each of several papers published in the American Economic Review. Each participant is randomly assigned four papers and, for each paper, evaluates six robustness checks drawn without replacement from a larger fixed pool of candidate checks for that paper's key result. Check order and paper order are randomized. For each check, participants rate its validity and relevance on a 0–10 scale and separately predict the average rating other participants will give the same check (their second-order belief), with a financial incentive tied to forecast accuracy. Participants also answer incentivized comprehension questions about each paper's main result, rate the paper's credibility and their own familiarity with its methods, and answer background questions on seniority, sub-field, region, and gender. We test whether ratings and second-order beliefs differ by type of the check, and whether raters agree with each other more for checks from one source than the other — separately for two sets of papers — along with exploratory associations with rater seniority, sub-field match, familiarity, and engagement with the source paper. Recruitment is by invitation to faculty and PhD students at economics departments, participants in the Institute for Replication games, and professional networks, targeting 300 participants who complete the survey (up to 300 × 24 = 7,200 check-level rating and forecast observations). Compensation includes a show-up fee, payment for correct comprehension answers, and a forecast-accuracy bonus, for a maximum of $62 per participant.
experimental_design: Within-subject design with no between-participant treatment arms. Each participant is randomly assigned four of 23 eligible papers (two from each of two paper sets) and, for each paper, six robustness checks drawn from a larger fixed per-paper pool, split across two comparator sources without disclosing what differentiates them. Paper order and check order are randomized; assignment balances how many times each check and each paper is shown across participants. Recruitment is by invitation to faculty and PhD students at economics departments, Institute for Replication replication-game participants, professional networks, and the authors' personal networks, targeting 300 participants who complete the full survey (four papers each).
experimental_design_details: Paper set 1 (11 papers) is derived from Campbell et al. (2026); paper set 2 (12 papers) comprises 2024–2026 AER publications meeting four eligibility criteria (available data, working code, a causal claim, not an experiment). For each paper, an AI-check pool of 20 highest-ranked, feasibility-screened checks was frozen in advance, alongside an eligible human-comparator pool (expert-approved checks with verified descriptions for set 1; the original authors' own published checks for set 2). Using seed 20260917, six-check shortlists were drawn without replacement from each pool for each paper (fewer where a paper's comparator pool held fewer than six). One AI check for Pop-Eleches & Urquiola (2013) was excluded pre-launch for an undefined measure and replaced via seed 20260919, drawing uniformly from the 14 remaining checks in that paper's original top-20 pool. Across both sets, shortlists total 138 AI checks and 129 comparator checks. Each participant's six checks per paper (three AI, three comparator) are drawn from that paper's shortlist, balancing presentation counts across checks and papers within each set. Primary hypotheses test whether mean robustness ratings and second-order beliefs differ by source, separately for the two paper sets ("AI robustness test I" for set 1, "AI robustness test II" for set 2). Secondary hypotheses test whether rating disagreement differs by source, and whether a blinded AI quality score (the same scoring procedure used to rank AI proposals, applied post hoc to every survey check regardless of source, without revealing source) predicts participant ratings and second-order beliefs. Full hypothesis wording, variable definitions, and estimation specifications are in the confidential Pre-Analysis Plan upload.
intervention: Participants are shown, for each of four randomly assigned papers published in the American Economic Review, a description of the paper's key empirical result (hypothesis, coefficient, standard error, t/z-value, p-value) and a link to the published article. After answering incentivized comprehension questions and rating the paper's credibility and their own familiarity with its methods, participants are shown six candidate robustness checks for that paper's key result, drawn without replacement from a larger, fixed pool of candidate checks assembled in advance for that paper. For each check, participants (i) rate its validity and relevance on a 0–10 scale and (ii) predict, also on a 0–10 scale, the average rating other participants will give the same check, excluding their own rating; the second task carries a monetary accuracy incentive. Checks are presented in random order. The target population is economists and economics/finance PhD students, recruited by invitation, targeting 300 participants who complete all four assigned papers.

abstract: This study examines how the level of detail in mandatory pay transparency affects employers’ wage-setting and position-assignment decisions. Employers are randomly assigned to one of three conditions: no transparency, mandatory disclosure of the aggregate firm-level gender pay gap, or mandatory disclosure of gender pay gaps separately by position. Employers assign male and female employees to manager and clerk positions and set their wages, while employees complete incentivized real-effort tasks. The study measures how transparency affects the overall gender wage gap and whether employers respond by changing wages, position assignments, or both.
experimental_design: We conduct a three-wave, asynchronous online experiment with UK-based participants recruited through Prolific. Employers are randomly assigned, with equal probability and stratified by employer gender, to one of three pay-transparency regimes: no transparency, mandatory aggregate firm-level gender pay-gap disclosure, or mandatory position-level gender pay-gap disclosure. Employers assign six employee profiles to manager and clerk positions and set their wages subject to a fixed wage budget. Employees complete incentivized real-effort tasks and are matched to employer-assigned profiles based on gender and performance group. A randomly selected subset of employer decisions is implemented, determining employees’ positions, wages, and the pay information they receive.
intervention: The intervention consists of varying the pay-transparency regime that employers know will apply to the wage and position decisions they make for employees. Employers are randomly assigned to one of three conditions: no transparency, mandatory aggregate firm-level gender pay-gap disclosure, or mandatory position-level gender pay-gap disclosure. In the no-transparency condition, employees receive information only about their own position and wage. In the aggregate-transparency condition, employees additionally receive information on the firm’s gender composition and overall gender pay gap. In the position-level transparency condition, employees instead receive gender pay-gap information separately for manager and clerk positions, together with the gender composition of each position. All disclosed information is calculated directly from the employer’s actual wage and position assignments.

abstract: Generative AI tools such as ChatGPT are changing how students learn and the work they will do after graduating. We study whether a structured course can help engineering students build strong programming skills while learning to use these tools well. Third-year students at four engineering colleges in India are randomly assigned either to the course or to a series of online seminars on other topics. We compare the two groups on programming and problem-solving skills, how they work with AI tools, and early employment outcomes.In a smaller experiment within the first assessment, we also test whether asking students to plan how they will use an AI tool before a task changes how they work.
experimental_design: Individual-level randomized trial. Students who took part in a baseline survey and assessment are assigned by lottery to the course or the comparison group, and outcomes are compared between the two groups.
experimental_design_details: Consenting students who completed the baseline session enter the lottery. Within each campus, 300 seats (1,200 in total) are allocated across strata in proportion to stratum size. Strata are campus × department group, plus gender at the two co-educational campuses, with a minimum stratum size of 40. Offer probabilities are 0.33 to 0.50 across campuses and equal within a campus. There is one draw, on a frozen extract taken after the survey closes, with a seed fixed in advance from **[a public source announced before the draw]**. Students who decline or drop out are not replaced. The main analysis is intention-to-treat with stratum fixed effects and a control for baseline assessment performance.
intervention: Students in the course group take a programming course over one academic year, combining in-person and online sessions. The course teaches programming alongside how to use AI tools and how to check their work. Students in the comparison group attend a small number of online seminars on unrelated topics. Both groups continue their regular college classes.

abstract: This study aims to understand how smallholder farmers in Telangana respond to monsoon-onset forecasts delivered through WhatsApp and whether their responses vary by message format: text only, text with an image, or text with a video (image + voice-over bundle). It will examine how farmers interpret these forecasts across the different formats and whether the information influences key agricultural decisions, including the timing and method of sowing, irrigation, and input use, during the 2026 Kharif season. Additionally, it will also test the impacts of the WhatsApp dissemination on populations without access to WhatsApp in order to track spillover effects from peer message sharing. The study evaluates a monsoon-onset forecast dissemination pilot implemented by the Department of Agriculture, Government of Telangana, which provides AI-based, probabilistic forecasts to farmers registered under the Rythu Bharosa scheme.
experimental_design: Study Design This study examines how farmers interpret and use monsoon-onset forecasts disseminated through WhatsApp during the 2026 Kharif season in Telangana, India. The study will evaluate whether access to these forecast messages influences farmers' early-season agricultural decisions. Forecast messages are disseminated through the Department of Agriculture’s WhatsApp channels to farmers registered under the Rythu Bharosa scheme. Treatment and Comparison Groups The 524 study clusters were randomly assigned to a control arm or one of three treatment arms. The treatment group comprises 333 clusters, with 111 clusters assigned to each of the following formats: WhatsApp Text Only, WhatsApp Text + Image and WhatsApp Text + Video (image and voice bundle). The remaining 191 clusters were assigned to the control group. Farmers in control clusters do not receive forecast messages through the pilot. They receive only a one-time benign, non-forecast WhatsApp message used to assess message reachability via WhatsApp. The study will compare outcomes between farmers in the control and treatment clusters (pooled as well as broken down by the three treatment formats). It will also examine potential information spillovers by comparing farmers for whom messages were not delivered in treatment clusters with comparable farmers in control clusters. Study Sample The anticipated survey sample includes up to 7,860 farmers per survey round, selected from administrative databases. Respondents will be drawn from the 524 study clusters, 333 treatment clusters and 191 control clusters. Within each cluster-by-message-delivery stratum, respondents will be selected using simple random sampling.
intervention: The intervention, implemented by the Department of Agriculture, Government of Telangana, consists of WhatsApp messages containing AI-based monsoon-onset forecasts tailored to each farmer’s mandal. Depending on the treatment assignment of the farmer’s agricultural extension cluster, forecasts are delivered as text only, text with an image, or text with a video (image + voice bundle).

abstract: Enteric fermentation accounts for roughly 50 percent of dairy cattle methane emissions, making it a primary mitigation target (Dijkstra et al., 2018; Hristov et al., 2022). Among the inter- ventions available, feed additives, especially 3-nitrooxypropanol (3-NOP), have the most robust emission reduction potential across studies (de Oliveira et al., 2025; Kebreab et al., 2023; Pupo et al., 2025; Van De Gucht et al., 2025; Maigaard et al., 2024; Islam et al., 2025; Maigaard et al., 2025). Yet adoption ultimately depends on many factors such as net revenue, feed intake, milk yield, management time that determine producers’ assessment of the technology. We extend earlier work about the effectiveness of 3-NOP and the willingness to accept (WTA) 3-NOP among Swedish dairy farmers by further aspects related to technology adoption Gottlieb and Rommel (2025). First, how domestic positive peer information compares to foreign negative peer information in shaping adoption decisions, a distinction motivated by real-world reporting on 3-NOP that ranges from optimistic domestic coverage of carbon-credit earnings (The Bul- lvine, 2025) to mixed foreign accounts of Bovaer-linked feed intake and milk yield declines on 426 out of 642 Danish dairy farms (Nielsen et al., 2025; SEGES Innovation, 2025; The Bullvine, 2026). Second, how such information shape the beliefs about 3-NOP (Kumar et al., 2023; Dietrich et al., 2024). To address these gaps, this study examines the market potential of 3-NOP in the U.S. dairy industry by eliciting producer atti- tudes toward the technology and the compensation they would require to adopt it, particularly after exposure to positive domestic versus negative foreign peer information.
experimental_design: We use a between-subject design, splitting the sample into groups that each receive a different information treatment prior to the contingent valuation questions. Information treatments are designed upon consultation with the project partners from the Clean Air Task Force (Fernanda Ferreira), The Nature Conservancy (Partha Ray, Alisha Staggs), and the Environmental Defense Fund (Joe Rudek). Every respondent will see the same information: “Dairy farmers continually face decisions about feed management, including choices about feed ingredients, ration formulation, and feeding strategies. These decisions can affect milk produc- tion, cow health, and farm profitability.One feed additive that has received recent attention is 3- Nitrooxypropanol (3-NOP). It is designed to reduce enteric methane emissions from dairy cows.” Followed by one out of the three information treatments are nothing in case of the control group explained in Table 2. Additionally, we randomize the starting net revenue level presented in the contingent valuation question across eight values, ranging from $30 to $149 per cow per year in equal sized increments of approximately $17. In combination with the three information treatments plus control, we have a total of 32 survey versions. abstract: This cluster-randomized controlled trial examined whether teacher professional development support can translate access to a digital learning platform into improved mathematics achievement. We randomly assigned 108 Uruguayan public primary schools to a control group or to an intervention of the High Touch High Tech (HTHT) program, which integrates workshops, instructional materials, and mentoring on integrating the platform into the standard curriculum. Randomization took place at the school level. Of the 108 schools, 28 were assigned to control and 80 to HTHT, which was delivered at two levels of support intensity (51 "Soft" and 29 "Hard" schools). The study sample comprised 155 fifth-grade teachers and 2,709 fifth-grade students. Students in all schools, including control schools, had the same access to Ceibal's digital mathematics platform, so the trial isolates the effect of teacher support, not of access to technology. The intervention ran for one academic semester in 2022, with baseline and endline assessments in April and October. The primary outcome was mathematics achievement on Uruguay's national adaptive assessment (SEA+). Secondary outcomes were platform engagement from administrative log data (learning episodes completed and weeks of sustained classroom-wide use) and students' reported attitudes toward mathematics and digital learning. Analyses estimated intention-to-treat effects adjusting for baseline achievement and randomization strata, with standard errors clustered at the school level. Heterogeneity by platform engagement and implementation fidelity was examined.

primary_outcome_explanation: Uruguay's national adaptive assessment, administered by the National Administration of Public Education (ANEP) in collaboration with the Technical Inspection of Primary and Secondary Education. SEA+ is administered nationwide from the third year of primary school through the third year of secondary school. The assessment is designed to provide a common reference framework for student learning and to support teacher reflection on the content it assesses. Assessments are delivered online using the devices and connectivity provided through Ceibal, which allows system-wide administration and immediate reporting of results to teachers. SEA+ is computer-adaptive: item difficulty adjusts to each student's responses, and ability is estimated by item response theory (IRT). Scores are reported on a scale metric that is a linear transformation of the estimated ability parameter, with mean 1,000 and standard deviation 100 in the norming population. We report all estimates on two scales: the IRT scale metric, which preserves the assessment's own units, and a standardized score constructed using the baseline mean and standard deviation of the analytical sample in the current study. Standardizing on the baseline control distribution ensures the denominator is unaffected by any treatment-induced change in score dispersion. SEA+ was administered at baseline in April 2022 and at endline in October 2022.

randomization_method: Stratified cluster randomization. Schools were grouped into blocks by crossing school type (regular urban, APRENDER, and full-time schools) with the quintile of the school's sociocultural context index, giving up to 15 strata (3 × 5). Within each stratum, schools were randomly assigned to the treatment or control group by Stata. This ensured that treatment and control groups were balanced on school type and socioeconomic context.

abstract: We study the effect of reserve prices on clicks, bids, prices, and revenue in a digital auction platform. Search queries on a digital platform are randomly assigned to one of eight reserve price policies. The status quo reserve price policy receives 93\% of queries; each of seven alternatives receives 1\%. These alternatives vary around the status quo and a reserve price policy estimated from historical data. The experiment lasts for four weeks. The study will examine whether the alternative reserve price policies increase revenue, and how consumer activity, bidding behavior, and quoted prices respond to the reserve price.
experimental_design: 7% of queries are assigned independently to one of seven alternative reserve price policies, and 93% of queries are assigned to the status quo reserve price policy. The experiment lasts for four weeks. All reserve prices on this platform are secret. Bidders are informed of how many queries they miss due to a bid below the reserve price.
intervention: Each query contains several auctions. The auction has a secret reserve price, which may depend on query and item characteristics. The intervention sets the reserve price policy mapping query and item characteristics to the reserve price used for all auctions in the query.

abstract: This study examines how prospective workers value environmental characteristics in job offers and the extent to which they are willing to trade salary for such characteristics. The experiment is embedded in the CRAFT project, which studies environmental knowledge, values, representations, and forms of environmental engagement among university students. Participants are students enrolled in business and management, engineering, economics, and architecture programmes at the University of Lille and the Lille National School of Architecture and Landscape Architecture. They complete a discrete choice experiment in which they choose between pairs of fictitious but realistic job offers. Respondents are randomly assigned to one of three experimental blocks, each containing six binary choice tasks. Job offers vary experimentally along six dimensions: environmental mission content, ISO 14001 environmental certification, green employer discourse, public versus private organisation, telework availability, and monthly gross salary. The occupational framing and reference salary are adapted to respondents’ field of study, while the experimental attributes retain the same conceptual meaning across occupational versions. The primary outcomes are respondents’ choices between job offers. The main estimands are the effects of environmental mission content, environmental certification, and green employer discourse on job choice. Because salary is experimentally varied, the study also estimates the monthly salary-equivalent value of each environmental job attribute. Secondary analyses examine differences in preferences according to environmental worldviews, value orientations, socio-demographic characteristics, and programme of study.
experimental_design: The study uses a discrete choice experiment embedded at the beginning of a questionnaire administered to university students. Each respondent completes six binary choice tasks involving pairs of fictitious but realistic job offers. The offers vary in environmental mission content, ISO 14001 environmental certification, green employer discourse, public versus private organisation, telework availability, and monthly gross salary. Respondents are randomly assigned to one of three blocks, each containing six prespecified choice tasks. The experiment includes 18 choice sets in total. Occupational framing is adapted to respondents' programme of study using plausible entry-level occupations, while the experimental job attributes retain the same conceptual meaning across programmes. The primary analysis estimates the relationship between experimentally varied job characteristics and offer choice using conditional logit models, with standard errors clustered at the respondent level. Because salary varies across offers, the design also permits estimation of salary-equivalent valuations for non-wage job characteristics.
experimental_design_details: The experiment contains 18 binary choice sets divided into three blocks of six. The choice sets were constructed before data collection in R from an orthogonal main-effects array, with five two-level attributes and one six-level salary attribute. For each of the five binary attributes, the rotation procedure assigns complementary levels to the two alternatives within each task. Salary varies across six prespecified levels generated by applying fixed multipliers to an occupation-specific reference monthly gross salary. The analysis uses the actual salary displayed to each respondent. The primary analytical sample contains respondents from prespecified participating programmes who provide valid consent and complete at least one valid DCE choice task. No respondent is excluded on the basis of their substantive pattern of choices. The primary specification is a conditional logit containing all six experimentally varied attributes jointly. Standard errors are clustered at the respondent level. A linear probability model with respondent-task fixed effects is used as a complementary specification. The three primary environmental coefficients are tested using two-sided tests and 95% confidence intervals. Holm-adjusted p-values are reported across these three primary tests. Three secondary pairwise contrasts between the environmental coefficients constitute a separate family of tests and are also Holm-adjusted within that family.
intervention: Participants complete a discrete choice experiment designed to measure preferences for environmental and other characteristics of prospective jobs. In six successive tasks, respondents choose between two fictitious but realistic job offers. The offers vary experimentally along six dimensions: environmental mission content, ISO 14001 environmental certification, green employer discourse, public versus private recruiting organisation, telework availability, and monthly gross salary. The occupational title and salary scale are adapted to respondents' programme of study to make the choices relevant to plausible post-graduation employment. Respondents are randomly assigned to one of three prespecified blocks of six choice tasks. The choices generated by the experiment are used to estimate the value respondents place on the different job characteristics and their willingness to trade salary for environmental job attributes.

primary_outcome_explanation: For every completed choice task, each of the two alternatives is represented by a binary choice indicator equal to one for the selected offer and zero for the alternative not selected. Unanswered choice tasks are treated as missing. The effects of environmental mission content, environmental certification, and green employer discourse are estimated jointly with telework availability, public-sector status, and displayed monthly gross salary using a conditional logit model in which the respondent-task constitutes the choice set. The primary monetary outcomes are salary-equivalent valuations calculated from the ratio of each environmental-attribute coefficient to the salary coefficient. Salary is expressed in hundreds of euros, so the monthly gross salary-equivalent valuation for environmental attribute k is: WTP_k = 100 × beta_k / beta_salary. These valuations will be interpreted as willingness to forgo monthly gross salary when the estimated salary coefficient is positive. Average changes in predicted choice probabilities will also be reported for the three environmental attributes.
primary_outcomes: The primary outcome is the respondent's choice between the two job offers presented in each completed discrete-choice task. The primary preference estimands are the effects on job choice of three experimentally varied environmental job attributes: environmental mission content; ISO 14001 environmental certification; and green employer discourse. The study also estimates salary-equivalent valuations for each of these three environmental attributes, representing the amount of monthly gross salary respondents would be willing to forgo to obtain the corresponding job characteristic.
randomization_method: Respondents are randomly assigned by computer within the survey to one of three prespecified discrete-choice blocks. Each block contains six fixed binary choice tasks drawn from the 18 prespecified experimental choice sets. The experimental profiles and attribute combinations within each block are constructed prior to data collection and are therefore not independently re-randomized for each respondent.
secondary_outcome_explanation: A secondary environmental-attribute index is constructed as the sum of environmental mission content, ISO 14001 certification, and green employer discourse. It ranges from zero to three and measures the number of environmental characteristics associated with an offer. Pairwise contrasts compare the coefficients on environmental mission content, environmental certification, and green employer discourse without imposing a prespecified ordering. Heterogeneity analyses interact experimentally varied job attributes with respondent-level characteristics. These analyses are secondary and exploratory and are not interpreted as causal effects of the respondent characteristics. Post-DCE assessments are collected after the experimental choices and therefore do not determine inclusion in the primary analytical sample and are not used as confirmatory moderators.
secondary_outcomes: pairwise differences in the valuation of the three environmental attributes; the effect of the total number of environmental characteristics attached to an offer; preferences for telework availability and public versus private recruiting organisations; average changes in predicted choice probabilities associated with experimentally varied job attributes; and heterogeneity in preferences according to respondent characteristics, including environmental worldviews, value orientations, declared pro-environmental behaviours, environmental-policy support, gender, scholarship status, parental occupational categories, urban residence, French-language proficiency, programme of enrolment, and study level. Post-experiment measures of application intentions, perceived realism of the job offers, recognition of the study purpose, and stated rankings of job characteristics will be analysed descriptively and exploratorily.
