abstract: The Special Supplemental Nutrition Program for Women, Infants and Children (WIC) is an important part of the safety net for pregnant women, infants, and young children, yet the program is significantly under-enrolled. WIC includes a provision where categorically eligible individuals—pregnant, post-partum, or breast-feeding women and children under five—who themselves are participating in Medicaid or who live in households where someone is participating in SNAP are automatically eligible (“adjunctively eligible”) for WIC. These adjunctively eligible individuals can enroll in WIC simply by confirming participation in Medicaid or SNAP. We have partnered with the state of Utah to provide a unique linkage between administrative WIC, Medicaid, and SNAP databases which allows us to identify households that are adjunctively eligible for WIC, but are not actively participating in the program. We randomized these adjunctively eligible, non-participating households to receive one of three experimental text messages communicating potential eligibility for WIC sent from our state partner or to a control group that did not receive a communication. We will experimentally test the effectiveness of these communications at increasing both short- and long-term WIC take-up and targeting. Importantly, we will test the relative effectiveness of messages conveying general information on income eligibility for the program versus messages that explicitly highlight the household’s adjunctive eligibility and the ease of applying for adjunctively eligible households.
experimental_design: Our intervention identifies adjunctively eligible, non-participating households in the state of Utah and randomly assigns them to receive text communications sent from WIC administrators informing households of the WIC program along with details on program eligibility. We will assess how these communications affect take-up and targeting of the program.
experimental_design_details: Summary. Our intervention identifies adjunctively eligible, non-participating households in the state of Utah and randomly assigns them to receive text communications sent from WIC administrators informing households of the WIC program along with details on program eligibility. We will assess how these communications affect take-up and targeting of the program. Sample. Our sample includes households containing pregnant, post-partum, or breast-feeding women and/or children under five who are enrolled in either Medicaid or SNAP at the time of random assignment, but are not currently enrolled in WIC. Communications. Sample households were assigned to one of three text messages or to a control group that received no communications from state WIC administrators. Households selected to receive text communications received an initial communication followed up with two reminder communications, each roughly one month apart. Each treatment message included the following information: (i) a greeting from the program administrator (ii) basic program details and average benefit amounts (iii) how to apply. Each message also included information on eligibility for the program, but varied in content. Half of households assigned to receive communications received general information on WIC eligibility. The other half received information on adjunctive eligibility and, specifically that the household itself was likely adjunctively eligible. Finally, half of the messages providing adjunctive eligibility information included an additional line on ease of application. Sample period. The intervention was rolled out in five monthly waves from March to July 2026, beginning with pregnant women in a subset of counties, then expanding to other eligibility categories and locations. Households that became newly adjunctively eligible during the study period were added to the randomization pool each month. Randomization: Randomization was conducted at the household level. Households were block-randomized based on randomization month, county of residence (with small counties pooled), whether the household had previously participated in WIC, program source (Medicaid only versus any SNAP participation), and whether more than one household member was eligible. 20 percent were assigned to the control group, 40 percent were assigned to the basic information message, 20 percent were assigned to the adjunctive eligibility message, and 20 percent were assigned to the adjunctive eligibility plus ease-of-application message. Model. Primary estimates are intent-to-treat specifications. Utah WIC records households screened out at each send (do-not-call flags, appointments already scheduled, undeliverable numbers) and the texting vendor records delivery status; these allow us to produce treatment-on-the-treated estimates instrumenting receipt with assignment. Analyses will compare the overall effectiveness of the messages relative to the control group, as well as the relative effectiveness of each message, with a particular focus on the importance of information on adjunctive eligibility.
intervention: The Special Supplemental Nutrition Program for Women, Infants and Children (WIC) is an important part of the safety net for pregnant women, infants, and young children, yet the program is significantly under-enrolled. WIC includes a provision where categorically eligible individuals—pregnant, post-partum, or breast-feeding women and children under five—who themselves are participating in Medicaid or who live in households where someone is participating in SNAP are automatically eligible (“adjunctively eligible”) for WIC. These adjunctively eligible individuals can enroll in WIC simply by confirming participation in Medicaid or SNAP. We have partnered with the state of Utah to provide a unique linkage between administrative WIC, Medicaid, and SNAP databases which allows us to identify households that are adjunctively eligible for WIC, but are not actively participating in the program. We randomized these adjunctively eligible, non-participating households to receive one of three experimental text messages communicating potential eligibility for WIC sent from our state partner or to a control group that did not receive a communication. We will experimentally test the effectiveness of these communications at increasing both short- and long-term WIC take-up and targeting. Importantly, we will test the relative effectiveness of messages conveying general information on income eligibility for the program versus messages that explicitly highlight the household’s adjunctive eligibility and the ease of applying for adjunctively eligible households.

abstract: We study how exposure to urban public goods affects university students’ beliefs and choices in Bogotá, Colombia. We randomly assigned Universidad de los Andes students to paid research-assistant fieldwork involving public transport, parks, and other public spaces in southern Bogotá, or to an active control involving shopping malls in northern Bogotá. The two primary outcome indices measure safety and exploration; and public provision, state capacity, and taxation. They combine non-incentivized survey responses, actual choices, and incentivized belief elicitations. Exploratory secondary analyses examine matched narrow versions that exclude only non-incentivized survey questions, component outcomes, mechanisms, and heterogeneity. The comparison captures the combined differences in destinations, activities, and experiences between the assignments.
experimental_design: RECRUITMENT AND ELIGIBILITY The university advertised a paid research-assistant opportunity to Universidad de los Andes undergraduates on Aug 12, 2026. Applicants completed screening and a baseline survey before randomization. Screening verified basic student information and collected socioeconomic characteristics used to construct the recruitment sample. We received 1,838 valid screening responses and randomized 1,211 students. To fit the recruitment target, the team randomly subsampled applicants in the (middle class) socioeconomic strata 3 and 4, where applications were most numerous, and included all applicants from the highest socioeconomic strata 5 and 6. After random assignment, the team withdrew invitations from minors and prior-pilot participants (who were erroneously not screened out pre-randomization). Updated exclusions imply 1,161 eligible students: 584 treatment and 577 control. ASSIGNMENT AND COMPARISON We assigned 606 students to public-goods fieldwork and 605 to mall fieldwork on Sep 8, 2026. The main comparison is the effect of assignment to public-goods fieldwork relative to the active mall control, regardless of task completion. MAIN ANALYSIS Our target is the intention-to-treat effect of assignment among eligible students. We will estimate regressions using available outcomes, accounting for randomization strata and baseline controls selected by double LASSO. We project approximately 800 completed endlines; the observed count will depend on endline and behavioral-measure completion and may differ across outcomes. We plan paid endline follow-up for eligible students who do not complete their field tasks. We will report standard p-values and p-values adjusted across the two primary outcome tests. For exploratory component analyses, we will report standard and adjusted p-values across the two immediate safety/exploration components, and separately across the three immediate public-provision components. SPILLOVERS We may explore spillovers from friends or associates in the experimental sample, using the number assigned to treatment while controlling for the number of named peers in the randomized sample and the total number named. Whether we include peer-assignment terms in the main specification will depend on network coverage, exposure variation, the implemented randomization, and opportunities for interaction. We will make that choice using network and assignment information, without examining outcome associations. The network is still being cleaned and constructed, and its suitability for this analysis remains uncertain. PILOT DEVELOPMENT A pilot experiment in the first half of 2026 informed the experimental design and major measurement decisions. It ran with 182 students assigned to public-goods treatment (100) or an active mall control (82). Controls visited Parque La Colina and El Retiro shopping malls; the main study replaces El Retiro with Titán Plaza. This pilot sample is entirely separate from the full experimental sample. REGISTRATION TIMING This registration follows random assignment and the start of intervention and endline collection. Randomization occurred on Sep 8, 2026. The team is submitting the plan after confirming launch and correct implementation of randomization. Some students completed their tasks and endlines quickly. As of September 24, 2026, 27 students (2.23% of the 1,211 randomized students) had completed endline. Researchers prepared this registration blinded to endline data.
intervention: Eligible students are invited to paid research-assistant work observing urban spaces and infrastructure. The treatment assignment involves experiencing public goods, including travel by public transport and visits to parks and other public spaces in southern Bogotá. These spaces and neighborhoods are intended to be less familiar to the participants and are often perceived as unsafe. The active control involves fieldwork in private shopping malls in northern Bogotá. The routes span poorer and wealthier areas of the city. Both assignments require the same types of fieldwork deliverables: 1. Visit the assigned locations during daylight, following the route and safety instructions and completing the required check-ins and photo verifications. 2. Complete a structured observation log, recording arrival and departure times and how the spaces function and are used. 3. Submit the observation log and two short texts: a reflection on the visit and a recommendation describing the places to a friend or relative. 4. Complete the endline survey.

abstract: Climate variability makes agricultural decision-making increasingly difficult for smallholder farmers in Côte d’Ivoire. SMS-based agricultural advisory services can provide farmers with timely information, but the way this information is presented may also affect whether farmers engage with the advice and act on it. This study examines whether framing the same agricultural advice in terms of potential gains or potential losses leads to different responses from farmers. The study will use a randomized controlled trial with smallholder farmers in northern Côte d’Ivoire. Participating farmers will be randomly assigned to one of two groups. Farmers in the first group will receive SMS advisories that emphasize the benefits of adopting recommended climate-smart agricultural practices. Farmers in the second group will receive advisories that emphasize the potential losses associated with not adopting the same practices. Both groups will receive the same underlying agricultural information; only the framing of the messages will differ. Farmer responses will be measured using baseline and endline surveys, SMS engagement data, and verification of selected agricultural practices. The main analysis will compare engagement and adoption outcomes between the two groups. The study will also examine whether responses to the two types of framing differ according to farmer characteristics and exposure to production risk. The study is intended to determine whether a relatively simple change in the wording of SMS advisories can affect farmer engagement and the adoption of recommended agricultural practices. The results will contribute to research on behavioral framing in agricultural extension and provide practical evidence for organizations using digital advisory services to reach smallholder farmers.
experimental_design: This study is an individually randomized, two-arm field experiment involving smallholder farmers in Côte d’Ivoire. The experiment is designed to test whether the behavioral framing of agricultural advisory messages affects farmer engagement with an SMS-based advisory service and the adoption of recommended agricultural practices. Eligible participants will complete a baseline survey before random assignment. Participants will then be randomly assigned in equal proportions to one of two experimental conditions: a gain-framed SMS condition or a loss-framed SMS condition. Participants assigned to the gain-framed condition will receive agricultural advisory messages that emphasize the benefits or positive outcomes associated with implementing recommended practices. Participants assigned to the loss-framed condition will receive substantively equivalent messages that emphasize the risks, costs, losses, or forgone benefits associated with not implementing the same practices. All participants will receive agricultural advisory messages; there is no no-message control group. For each agricultural recommendation, the underlying technical advice will be the same across the two experimental conditions. The messages will differ only in their behavioral framing. Other features of message delivery, including language, timing, frequency, sender identity, and available response options, will be kept equivalent across the two conditions to the extent operationally possible. The intervention will run for eight weeks, with participants expected to receive approximately three SMS advisory messages per week. Message timing will consider the agricultural calendar and the relevance of individual recommendations to participants’ crops and farming conditions. Randomization will occur at the individual-participant level using reproducible statistical code, with a 1:1 allocation ratio between the two framing conditions. Randomization will be stratified by geographic study area and gender. Principal crop may be included as an additional stratification variable if the final recruited sample contains sufficiently large numbers within crop categories to avoid sparsely populated strata. All stratification variables and their definitions will be finalized before random assignment. Random assignment will take place only after recruitment, eligibility verification, completion of the baseline survey, resolution of duplicate or household records, and finalization of the randomization dataset. Recruitment personnel and baseline enumerators will not know participants’ framing assignments during recruitment and baseline data collection. Outcomes will be measured using endline survey data and records of participant engagement with the advisory service. Where prespecified and operationally feasible, reported adoption of promoted agricultural practices will also be independently verified for the full sample or a prespecified randomly selected validation subsample. The primary analysis will estimate intention-to-treat effects by comparing participants according to their original randomized framing assignment.

primary_outcome_explanation: The Farmer Engagement Index will be constructed from five prespecified domains: (1) message recall, (2) message comprehension, (3) active interaction with the advisory service, (4) information-seeking behavior, and (5) message discussion and continued use. Message recall will be measured as the proportion of a prespecified subset of relevant agricultural recommendations that the participant correctly recalls at endline. Message comprehension will be measured as the proportion of prespecified questions correctly answered regarding the recommended practice, the agricultural problem addressed, and the expected consequences of implementing or not implementing the recommendation. Active interaction with the advisory service will be constructed from applicable binary indicators capturing whether the participant responded to an SMS prompt, contacted a designated project or extension representative in response to a study message, or requested clarification or additional agricultural information through an approved study channel. Information-seeking behavior will be constructed from indicators capturing whether the participant consulted an extension agent or project representative, requested additional technical information, consulted another knowledgeable farmer, or attended a relevant agricultural training or field demonstration after receiving related SMS advice. Message discussion and continued use will be constructed from indicators capturing whether the participant discussed at least one study message with another farmer or household member, reported reading most or all study messages, saved or revisited at least one message, and correctly identified the approximate timing or agricultural context in which at least one promoted recommendation should be implemented. All component variables will be coded so that higher values indicate greater engagement. Applicable components within each domain will first be averaged to obtain a domain score. Each of the five domain scores will then be standardized using the mean and standard deviation of that domain among participants assigned to the loss-framed condition. The five standardized domain scores will receive equal weight and will be averaged to construct the Farmer Engagement Index. Higher values of the resulting index indicate greater engagement with the SMS-based agricultural advisory service. A domain score will be calculated when valid data are available for at least half of the component items assigned to that domain. The overall Farmer Engagement Index will be calculated when valid scores are available for at least four of the five domains. If four domains are available, the index will equal the average of those four standardized domain scores. Participants with fewer than four valid domain scores will be treated as missing for the complete-case confirmatory analysis.
primary_outcomes: Primary outcomes 1. Farmer Engagement Index (FEI). The first primary outcome is a composite measure of participants’ engagement with the SMS-based agricultural advisory service during the intervention. The index will capture five dimensions of engagement: (i) recall of agricultural recommendations received through the SMS service; (ii) comprehension of the recommendations; (iii) active interaction with the advisory service, including responses, requests for clarification, or contact with designated project or extension personnel where applicable; (iv) information-seeking behavior related to the recommendations; and (v) discussion and continued use of the information received. The five domain scores will be standardized and equally weighted to construct the Farmer Engagement Index. Higher values will indicate greater engagement with the advisory service. 2. Adoption of at least one promoted agricultural practice. The second primary outcome is a binary indicator equal to one if a participant adopts at least one eligible agricultural practice promoted through the SMS intervention during the prespecified outcome measurement period, and zero otherwise. A practice will count toward this outcome only if it was included in the finalized experimental message library, was relevant to the participant’s farming context, had not already been fully adopted by the participant at baseline, and was implemented during the study period. Adoption will be measured primarily through the endline survey. Where operationally feasible and prespecified before random assignment, reported adoption will also be independently verified for the full sample or a randomly selected validation subsample.
randomization_method: Randomization will be conducted by computer using reproducible statistical code in Stata. Eligible participants will be randomly assigned in a 1:1 ratio to either the gain-framed or loss-framed SMS messaging condition. Randomization will be stratified by geographic study area and gender. Principal crop will be included as an additional stratification variable only if the final sample contains sufficiently large numbers of participants within each crop category. A fixed random-number seed will be selected and archived before randomization, together with the randomization script and treatment-assignment file.
randomization_unit: The unit of randomization is the individual participant. Eligible farmers will be individually randomized in a 1:1 ratio to either the gain-framed or loss-framed SMS messaging condition. There is no additional level of randomization.
secondary_outcomes: Secondary outcomes will include: (i) message recall and comprehension; (ii) intention to adopt recommended agricultural practices; (iii) perceived relevance and usefulness of the SMS advisories; (iv) agricultural self-efficacy; (v) agricultural risk perception, including perceived probability and severity of adverse agricultural outcomes and perceived ability to prevent or control them; (vi) information-seeking behavior; and (vii) willingness to continue receiving the SMS advisory service and willingness to pay for continued access.
title: The Impact of Behavioral Framing on Farmer Engagement: A Randomized SMS Extension Experiment in Côte d’Ivoire

abstract: This pre-analysis plan (PAP) describes the empirical strategy for a multi-country laboratory experiment investigating the determinants of community investment in public goods aimed at enhancing local resilience under natural disaster risk. The experiment simulates a community of four homogeneous members who generate income through electricity consumption. The decision environment focuses on how community members collectively determine the scale of investment in an Electrical Energy Storage (EES) system as a local public good that preserves the community's capacity for economic activity through mitigating the risk of disaster-induced outages. The experiment is conducted across four countries: South Korea; the United States; China; and Germany, with a minimum total of 960 student participants. Two institutional treatments govern the EES investment decision: in the first treatment (TR1), a standard voluntary contribution mechanism (VCM) is implemented, replicating a pure public goods game. In the second treatment (TR2), each of the four community members independently proposes their preferred EES scale; the community's EES level is then determined by the average of these proposals, with costs shared equally among members. Primary outcome variables include EES contribution levels, in-experiment disaster realizations, individual subjective disaster probability assessments, social norm measures, community-level income and inequality indicators. This PAP specifies directional hypotheses and pre-registers the causal identification strategy for examining how disaster experience, institutional coordination mechanisms, intra- and inter-community comparison, economic inequality, and cross-national cultural factors shape cooperative investment behavior.

experimental_design: We conduct a multi-country computerized laboratory experiment in South Korea, the United States, China, and Germany. Participants are assigned to fixed communities of four members and interact anonymously throughout the experiment. The experiment consists of a sequence of electricity purchase and community EES investment games. Participants make repeated decisions under natural disaster risk and under one of two institutional mechanisms governing community EES investment. The design allows us to examine how institutional arrangements, disaster experience, risk perceptions, social norms, and economic conditions affect cooperative investment in community resilience.
experimental_design_details: The experiment is conducted in computerized laboratory settings using the same experimental design and standardized procedures across four countries. Following a practice session, participants are randomly assigned to fixed groups of four, referred to as communities. Participants remain anonymous to one another and communication is prohibited. The experiment consists of seven sequential parts: four Electricity Purchase Games (EPGs) and three EES Investment Games. Each EPG contains five rounds. Participants initially receive 200 tokens, and each EPG begins with a balance of 100 tokens. In the disaster-risk EPGs, a disaster occurs independently with probability 0.20 per round for communities assigned to the stochastic-disaster condition. Communities assigned to the no-disaster condition experience no disasters. Before each disaster-risk EPG, participants make an EES investment decision. The EES system provides backup electricity during the immediately following EPG. Each EES unit costs 5 tokens. The experiment has a two-dimensional treatment structure: (1) institutional mechanism, TR1 versus TR2; and (2) disaster exposure, stochastic disaster risk versus no-disaster condition. Participants also receive information about the earnings and EES investment outcomes of neighboring communities, allowing analysis of informational benchmark effects.
intervention: This study examines community investment in Electric Energy Storage (EES) as a local public good under natural disaster risk. Participants are assigned to one of two institutional mechanisms governing community EES investment. In the first treatment (TR1), participants make decentralized voluntary contributions to the EES project. In the second treatment (TR2), participants propose their preferred level of EES investment, and the community-level investment is determined collectively with equal cost sharing. The experiment also varies communities' exposure to natural disaster risk.

Power calculations account for clustering at the four-person community level, an assumed intra-class correlation of 0.05–0.10, three repeated EES decision stages per participant, and attrition of up to 20%. The calculations are based on Monte Carlo simulations with 10,000 iterations.

primary_outcome_explanation: Individual EES contribution decisions are measured three times for each participant (EES1, EES2, and EES3). Under TR1, the individual outcome is the participant's voluntary contribution to the EES project. Under TR2, the corresponding individual outcome is the participant's proposed EES level. To facilitate comparisons across participants and institutional settings, we also construct a normalized contribution rate by dividing the individual contribution by the participant's available account balance at the time of the EES decision. The extensive-margin outcome equals one when the participant makes a positive contribution or proposal and zero otherwise. At the community level, installed EES capacity is calculated from aggregate contributions under TR1 and from the community-level EES quantity determined by the average of individual proposals under TR2.
